GERD and Esophagitis

Pathophysiology

Pills, caustics, allergens, infection, or refluxed HCl injure the esophageal mucosa and inflame it, and reflux, the most common route, follows a weak antireflux barrier, increased gastric pressure, or poor clearance.

  1. Barrier fails or an irritant arrivesReflux, pill, caustic, allergen, or microbe
  2. Epithelium injuredGaps between cells open
  3. InflammationPartly cytokines, not only acid
  4. Erosion and ulcerPain and bleeding
  5. HealingStricture, or Barrett esophagus

What the injury does

  • AMucosal inflammationOdynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain
  • BUlcersBleeding, with hematemesis and melena
  • CStricturesScar narrows the lumen: dysphagia
  • DPerforationPneumomediastinum and mediastinitis; the wall has no serosa to contain it
  • EBarrett esophagusIntestinal metaplasia, on its own page

What the reflux does

  • FFailed barrierTLESRs, a low LES pressure, or a hiatal hernia lets HCl pass
  • GIncreased pressurePushes HCl upward
  • HMucosal injuryErosive in some; in most, only microscopic (nonerosive)
  • IMetaplasiaBarrett esophagus after years
  • JAspirationCough, laryngitis, and pneumonia

What normally protects

  • BarrierLES, crural diaphragm, and the angle of entry
  • ClearancePeristalsis, gravity, and swallowed saliva (HCO3−)
  • ResistanceMucus, tight junctions, and blood flow
  • Why after mealsAn acid pocket floats on food, beneath a relaxing LES
  • Why at nightNo gravity, less saliva, and few swallows

How EoE develops

  1. Food allergenIn an atopic person
  2. AlarminsTSLP from a leaky epithelium
  3. Th2 responseIL-4, IL-5, and IL-13
  4. EosinophilsDrawn in by eotaxin 3
  5. RemodelingFibrosis: rings and strictures

Note: EoE is not mediated by IgE, so skin and blood allergy tests do not find the trigger foods.

Etiology

Esophagitis

  • Swallowed
  • 1Pill-inducedNSAIDs, KCl, doxycycline, and bisphosphonates, lodging where the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium narrows the esophagus
  • 2CausticAlkali liquefies deeply; acid coagulates more superficially
  • 3Eosinophilic (EoE)Food antigens, in people with asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis; men more than women
  • Infection
  • 4InfectiousImpaired cell-mediated immunity, or inhaled corticosteroids: Candida in most, then HSV and CMV
  • From the stomach
  • 5Reflux-associatedGERD, by 6–9

GERD

  • 6Weak LESTLESRs are the main mechanism; fat, alcohol, smoking, nitrates, CCB, anticholinergics, and morphine lower the pressure; scleroderma
  • 7Hiatal herniaSliding (type I) in over 95%: separates LES from diaphragm; paraesophageal (types II–IV) can twist
  • 8Increased HCl productionZollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • 9Increased intragastric pressureObesity, pregnancy, and gastroparesis

Note: Symptoms and injury match poorly: severe heartburn may have a normal lining, and Barrett esophagus may be painless.

Symptoms and complications

  1. HeartburnAfter meals, lying, or bending
  2. RegurgitationSour fluid in the throat
  3. Alarm featuresDysphagia, bleeding, or weight loss
  4. ComplicationsStricture, Barrett, and cancer

The pattern

CauseClue
Reflux (5)Heartburn and regurgitation
Pill (1)Sudden odynophagia, hours to days after a pill taken lying down
Caustic (2)Drooling, stridor, and oral burns; the mouth can be clear
EoE (3)Young atopic adult with solid dysphagia and food impaction; child with vomiting or food refusal
Infectious (4)Odynophagia, in immunosuppression; oral thrush may be absent

Extraesophageal

  • Chronic cough
  • Asthma
  • Laryngitis and hoarseness
  • Sore throat
  • Dental erosions

These are weakly linked to reflux, so look for another cause first.

Complications

  • Peptic strictureProgressive dysphagia, as heartburn eases
  • BleedingHematemesis, melena, or iron deficiency
  • Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinomaAfter years of reflux
  • PerforationCaustic, EoE (with vomiting), or dilation
  • Food impactionEoE or stricture
  • Aspiration pneumoniaAbove all at night
  • Caustic stricture and cancerSquamous cell carcinoma, decades later
  • Gastric volvulusParaesophageal hernia

Diagnosis

Typical GERD without alarm features is diagnosed by a response to a PPI, and everything else needs EGD, with biopsies that name the cause.

  1. Chest pain?ECG and cardiac causes first
  2. Alarm features?EGD first
  3. PPI trial8 weeks, once daily before a meal
  4. No response, or relapseEGD, off PPI for 2–4 weeks
  5. EGD normalpH monitoring, off PPI

Red flags

  • Dysphagia
  • Odynophagia
  • Bleeding or anemia
  • Weight loss
  • Persistent vomiting
  • Several Barrett risk factors

Grading erosive esophagitis

  • KGrade A5 mm or less: not proof of GERD
  • LGrade BOver 5 mm, not joining folds: proof
  • MGrade CJoins folds, under 75% of the circumference
  • NGrade D75% or more

What proves GERD (Lyon 2.0)

TestProvenExcluded
EGDLA grade B, C, or D; Barrett esophagus on biopsy; peptic stricture—
pH monitoring off PPIAET above 6%AET below 4% every day, without symptom association
Reflux episodesOver 80 a day supportsUnder 40 a day opposes
Normal AET, but symptoms follow refluxReflux hypersensitivity—

Other tests

  • BiopsyAt least 6, from two levels, for EoE, even if the lining looks normal
  • ManometryBefore antireflux surgery, to exclude achalasia and absent contractility
  • Impedance-pH on PPIProven GERD that still hurts
  • Barium swallowHernia and strictures; not for diagnosing reflux
  • CTPerforation, and caustic injury when EGD is unsafe

Find the cause

  • 1Pill-inducedDrug history; ulcer in the middle third
  • 2CausticEGD within 24 hours (96 at most) grades it; avoid days 5–15, when the wall is weakest
  • 3Eosinophilic (EoE)Rings, furrows, exudates, edema, and strictures; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field
  • 4InfectiousCandida: plaques. HSV: small deep ulcers, multinucleated cells, Cowdry A. CMV: large shallow ulcers, inclusions. HIV test
  • 5Reflux-associatedLA grade; erosions at the junction
  • 6Weak LESDrug list; antibodies if scleroderma
  • 7Hiatal herniaEGD, barium, or manometry
  • 8Increased HCl productionFasting gastrin off PPI
  • 9Increased intragastric pressureBMI, pregnancy test, gastric emptying

Treatment

Reflux is treated with weight loss and a PPI, stepped down once healed unless the disease is severe, and the other causes each have their own treatment.

  1. LifestyleWeight, meals, and bed head
  2. PPI8 weeks, 30–60 minutes before a meal
  3. RespondsStop, or lowest dose that works
  4. Does notCheck use, then test
  5. Proven and refractorySurgery

Lifestyle

  • Weight loss
  • Raise the head of the bed
  • No meals 2–3 hours before bed
  • Lie on the left side
  • Stop smoking
  • Avoid personal trigger foods

Drugs

PPIIrreversibly blocks H+/K+ ATPase that is active, so before foodFirst-line

Is a long-term PPI safe?

  • LikelyMore intestinal infection
  • Possible, unprovenFractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, low B12 and Mg2+
  • SoGive when indicated, at the lowest dose; do not stop it in severe disease out of fear

Surgery

  • ForProven GERD with severe esophagitis, large hernia, or persistent regurgitation
  • ChoicesFundoplication; magnetic sphincter; gastric bypass if obese
  • BeforeManometry: a full wrap is avoided with absent contractility
  • Paraesophageal herniaRepair if symptomatic; emergency if twisted or strangulated

EoE

PPIHistological response in about 4 in 10

DietRemove milk first, or 6 foods (milk, wheat, egg, soy, nuts, seafood)

Treat the cause

  • 1Pill-inducedStop the drug; a full glass of water, upright 30 minutes
  • 2CausticAirway, NPO, no vomiting or neutralizing; surgery if perforated; dilate strictures later
  • 3Eosinophilic (EoE)PPI, swallowed corticosteroid, diet, or dupilumab
  • 4InfectiousFluconazole 14–21 days; acyclovir; ganciclovir; treat HIV
  • 5Reflux-associatedAs above
  • 6Weak LESChange the drug; PPI
  • 7Hiatal herniaRepair if large or refractory
  • 8Increased HCl productionHigh-dose PPI; find the gastrinoma
  • 9Increased intragastric pressureWeight loss; treat gastroparesis

Note: A PPI is not a treatment for infection or caustic injury, where its role is unproven.

Review article

GERD and esophagitis: routes of mucosal injury, failure of the antireflux barrier, and Barrett esophagus

Esophagitis is inflammation of the esophagus that follows mucosal damage from pills, caustics, allergens, infection, or reflux, and GERD, in which HCl enters the esophagus through a weak antireflux barrier or under increased gastric pressure, is its most common cause. The route of injury determines management: endoscopy with biopsy identifies most causes by pattern and histology, whereas uncomplicated reflux is treated empirically with a PPI and investigated only when alarm features are present or treatment fails. The principal threats are bleeding, perforation, strictures, aspiration, and progression through Barrett esophagus to adenocarcinoma. Here, we review the causes, diagnosis, complications, and management of esophagitis and GERD, and consider how they relate to motility disorders, gastritis and PUD, and cardiac disease.

Key points

  • Pills lodge in the mid-esophagus, alkali penetrates deeper than acid, eosinophilic esophagitis is allergic, and infection follows impaired cell-mediated immunity.
  • Four mechanisms drive reflux: decreased LES tone, hiatal hernia, increased HCl production, and increased intragastric pressure.
  • EGD with biopsy separates the causes of esophagitis: white plaques in Candida, small deep ulcers in HSV, large shallow ulcers in CMV, and 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field in eosinophilic esophagitis.
  • In suspected GERD, chest pain needs an ECG and alarm features need EGD; otherwise an 8-week PPI trial comes first, with EGD and ambulatory pH monitoring if it fails.
  • Barrett esophagus is salmon-colored mucosa 1 cm or more above the gastroesophageal junction with goblet cells, surveyed every 3–5 years without dysplasia.
  • Odynophagia favors esophagitis and dyspepsia favors GERD; caustic ingestion needs EGD within 24 hours and no induced vomiting.

Pathophysiology

Pills, caustics, allergens, infection, and reflux all injure the esophageal mucosa, and the resulting inflammation causes odynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain. Deeper injury forms ulcers that bleed, with hematemesis and melena, and healing can narrow the lumen, causing strictures with dysphagia and obstruction. Full-thickness injury perforates, causing pneumomediastinum and mediastinitis, and chronic injury can progress through intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

In GERD, decreased LES tone or a hiatal hernia lets HCl pass into the esophagus, and increased intragastric pressure pushes it upward, more so when HCl production is increased. The HCl damages the esophagus, causing heartburn, dyspepsia, and chest pain. Chronic injury can progress through intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma, and refluxed HCl that reaches the airway causes aspiration pneumonia.

Etiology and mechanisms

Causes are best grouped by how injury reaches the mucosa. Pills, including NSAIDs, KCl, doxycycline, and bisphosphonates, lodge in the mid-esophagus, where the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium narrows it, especially when taken lying down with little water. Strong alkali causes liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply, whereas strong acid causes coagulative necrosis that is more superficial, with skip lesions. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergic reaction to food and air antigens, in patients with asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis. Infection follows impaired cell-mediated immunity, as with HIV, chemotherapy, or corticosteroids, and is due to Candida in 88%, HSV in 10%, and CMV in 2%. Reflux-associated disease arises from GERD, including conditions nonresponsive to PPIs.

LES tone is decreased by transient LES relaxations or a low resting pressure, by smoking, alcohol, and caffeine, and by drugs (nitrates, CCB, anticholinergics, theophylline, and morphine). Hiatal hernias promote reflux; sliding hernias (type I) make up over 95%, and paraesophageal hernias (types II–IV) can also cause volvulus and strangulation. HCl production is increased by smoking, alcohol, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and aspirin and other NSAIDs are also risk factors. Intragastric pressure is increased by obesity, gastroparesis, and pregnancy.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients present with dysphagia, odynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain, and eosinophilic esophagitis often presents with food impaction. Complications include bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis), strictures and ulcers, obstruction, and aspiration pneumonia. Barrett esophagus may also develop, in which intestinal metaplasia progresses through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Patients present with heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, dyspepsia, and chest pain, and extraesophageal symptoms include chronic cough, asthma, laryngitis and hoarseness, sore throat, and dental erosions. Complications are bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis), strictures with progressive dysphagia, obstruction, aspiration pneumonia, and Barrett esophagus, in which intestinal metaplasia progresses through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Barrett esophagus is salmon-colored mucosa 1 cm or more above the gastroesophageal junction with goblet cells; its risk factors are male sex, White race, age over 50, central obesity, smoking, and a family history, screening is advised when chronic reflux comes with 3 or more, and fewer than 5% develop adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis

EGD with biopsies of the proximal, mid, and distal esophagus identifies the cause by its endoscopic pattern, and histology confirms it. Pill injury produces an ulcer in the middle third, at the aortic arch or left atrium, with symptoms within hours to 10 days of the pill. In caustic ingestion, EGD within 24 hours grades the injury and predicts strictures, whereas after 96 hours friable tissue risks perforation. Eosinophilic esophagitis shows rings, longitudinal furrows, white exudates, and strictures, with 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, and biopsy after an 8-week PPI trial separates it from GERD; endoscopy is normal in up to 10%, so biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal.

Candida produces white plaques that do not wash off, HSV small, deep ulcers with multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry type A inclusions, and CMV large, shallow ulcers with intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. Reflux-associated disease is worked up as GERD. Bleeding is evaluated by EGD with biopsy, and perforation by contrast esophagram and CXR, followed by surgery.

In suspected GERD, chest pain is first evaluated with an ECG. Alarm features, namely dysphagia, odynophagia, anemia, weight loss, and hematemesis or melena, call for EGD first; otherwise a PPI trial of 8 weeks, taken before the first meal, is initiated, and EGD with pH monitoring follows if there is no improvement. Ambulatory pH monitoring is the only test of abnormal acid exposure, by a wireless capsule for 48–96 hours or 24-hour pH-impedance. Manometry is performed before antireflux surgery to exclude achalasia or a scleroderma-like esophagus, and barium swallow shows strictures, hiatal hernia, and tumors but has little role in uncomplicated reflux.

Management

PPIs are given in all cases to prevent further mucosal damage, followed by treatment of the cause. Offending pills are stopped, and pills are taken with at least 6 oz of water, staying upright for 30 minutes. Caustic ingestion requires securing the airway, NPO, EGD within 24 hours to grade the injury, avoidance of induced vomiting, and surgery for perforation, and strictures are the main late complication. Eosinophilic esophagitis is treated first with a PPI, then with elimination of trigger foods (cow's milk, wheat, peanuts and tree nuts, egg, soy, and seafood) or swallowed topical fluticasone or budesonide for 8 weeks, and strictures are dilated once it is treated. Candida esophagitis is treated with oral fluconazole for 14–21 days, always systemic rather than topical, and HSV and CMV with antivirals.

PPIs or H2R antagonists are always prescribed. Lifestyle measures are weight loss, raising the head of the bed, no meals 2–3 hours before bed, avoiding chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, and spicy food, and stopping smoking. A PPI is given at standard dose before the first meal for 8 weeks, and a bedtime H2RA is added for nighttime symptoms. Patients on NSAIDs stop the offending drug, refractory disease is treated with Nissen fundoplication after manometry, avoided in scleroderma, and a paraesophageal hernia is repaired surgically, as an emergency for volvulus or incarceration. In Barrett esophagus, EGD is repeated every 5 years without dysplasia if the segment is under 3 cm and every 3 years if 3 cm or more, in 6 months on twice-daily PPI for indefinite dysplasia, and low- or high-grade dysplasia is treated by endoscopic eradication, such as radiofrequency ablation.

Relationships to other conditions

. These share dysphagia and aspiration but are neuromuscular rather than mucosal. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset favors a motility disorder, for which manometry is the gold standard. Scleroderma produces reflux through low LES tone, whereas achalasia has high LES tone and is often mistreated as GERD, and manometry confirms normal peristalsis before Nissen fundoplication, which is avoided in scleroderma.

. NSAIDs cause all three by different mechanisms: a lodged pill injures the esophagus directly, whereas COX inhibition injures the stomach. Pain on swallowing favors esophagitis, and epigastric pain that changes with meals favors PUD. Perforation produces pneumomediastinum in esophagitis, assessed by contrast esophagram and CXR, and pneumoperitoneum in PUD, assessed by upright CXR. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome also links reflux to PUD through increased HCl production, and PPIs treat both. Intestinal metaplasia is common to both, but Barrett esophagus leads to esophageal adenocarcinoma, whereas chronic H. pylori infection leads to gastric cancer.

Cardiac disease. As chest pain overlaps with cardiac causes, an ECG should be obtained first, and chest pain is presumed cardiac until proven otherwise, particularly with cardiovascular risk factors.

Viral hepatitis. CMV and HSV also cause hepatitis in immunocompromised patients.

Esophageal Motility Disorders

Pathophysiology

When the nerves or smooth muscle of the esophagus fail, the LES does not open, or the body contracts too early, too hard, or too weakly, and food and liquid both stick.

  1. SwallowVagus starts inhibition, then contraction
  2. LES opens, body relaxesNO and VIP
  3. PeristalsisACh, in a timed wave
  4. Nerve or muscle failsTight, spastic, or weak
  5. DysphagiaSolids and liquids alike

Why the LES will not open

  • NormalNO and VIP open the LES, and time the wave
  • AchalasiaT cells destroy these inhibitory neurons, so ACh is unopposed: a tight LES and no peristalsis

What the dysfunction does

  • AFailed LES relaxationAchalasia and outflow obstruction
  • BDisorganized contractionPremature or too strong: spasm and chest pain
  • CAtrophy and fibrosisWeak body and LES: scleroderma, with reflux
  • DRetained foodRegurgitation, aspiration, and, after years, cancer

What manometry measures

  • IRPDoes the LES relax? High means it does not
  • DLIs the wave on time? Below 4.5 seconds is premature
  • DCIHow strong? Below 100 failed, 100–450 weak, over 8000 too strong

Note: Striated muscle (upper third, mixed in the middle) and smooth muscle (lower third and LES) fail in different diseases: myasthenia and myositis above, scleroderma and achalasia below.

Etiology

  • The LES does not open
  • 1AchalasiaIdiopathic, probably autoimmune; 1 in 100000 a year, at any age
  • 2EGJ outflow obstructionHigh IRP with some peristalsis: hernia, stricture, opioids, artifact, or early achalasia
  • The body contracts wrongly
  • 3Distal esophageal spasmPremature contractions in 20% or more of swallows; once called diffuse
  • 4Hypercontractile esophagusOver 8000 mmHg·s·cm in 20% or more of swallows; jackhammer when repetitive
  • 5Ineffective or absent contractilityOver 70% ineffective, or 50% failed; often with reflux
  • Part of another disease
  • 6SclerodermaSystemic sclerosis, often limited (CREST): smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis
  • 7Other secondaryChagas disease, opioids (spasm, type III), cancer at the EGJ, diabetes, and surgery

Note: Opioids alone can mimic spasm or achalasia, so manometry is best done off them.

Symptoms and complications

  1. DysphagiaTo solids and liquids
  2. RegurgitationUndigested, bland food
  3. AdaptationEats slowly, stretches, drinks to push it down
  4. LateWeight loss and aspiration

Diagnosis

EGD first excludes a blockage or cancer, and high-resolution manometry then names the disorder, with barium or FLIP when it is unclear.

  1. DysphagiaTo solids and liquids
  2. EGD with biopsiesCancer, stricture, and EoE
  3. ManometryIRP, then DL, then DCI
  4. UnclearTBE or FLIP
  5. CauseDrugs, skin, travel, and CT

  • JHypercontractileLES opens; DCI above 8000

Treatment

No treatment restores the nerves, so achalasia is treated by weakening the LES, spasm by relaxing muscle or removing its trigger, and weak motility by treating reflux.

  1. Type itManometry
  2. Fit for a procedure?Dilation, myotomy, or POEM
  3. Not fitBotulinum toxin
  4. FollowSymptoms, TBE, and reflux

  • 6SclerodermaPPI; rheumatology

Note: Reflux symptoms that persist on a PPI, with dysphagia to liquids, should raise suspicion of achalasia before anyone considers fundoplication.

Review article

Esophageal motility disorders: neuromuscular failure of the LES and esophageal body

Esophageal motility disorders are neuromuscular dysfunctions of the esophagus that cause dysphagia. Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, and esophageal scleroderma are separated by the state of the LES and the pattern of mid-distal motility, seen on barium swallow and defined by high-resolution manometry, the gold standard. Endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia, and structural causes of dysphagia, including Zenker diverticulum, Schatzki ring, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, and eosinophilic esophagitis, must be distinguished. Complications include aspiration pneumonia and cancer. Here, we review their mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how they relate to esophagitis and GERD.

Key points

  • LES tone separates the disorders: increased in achalasia and decreased in esophageal scleroderma.
  • Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, a bird's beak on barium swallow, and an IRP over 15 mmHg with absent peristalsis on manometry.
  • Diffuse esophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and a corkscrew esophagus.
  • EGD excludes pseudoachalasia from a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction.
  • Achalasia is treated by disrupting the LES, whereas scleroderma is treated with PPIs and Nissen fundoplication is avoided.

Pathophysiology

Neuromuscular dysfunction in the LES or mid-distal esophagus stops food passing normally, causing dysphagia. In achalasia, decreased NO and VIP raise LES tone; in diffuse esophageal spasm, mid-distal contractions become uncoordinated; and in scleroderma, atrophy and fibrosis weaken smooth muscle, decreasing LES tone and motility. Food that stays in the esophagus predisposes to aspiration pneumonia and cancer.

Etiology and mechanisms

Achalasia is idiopathic or due to Trypanosoma cruzi. Decreased myenteric plexus activity lowers NO and VIP neurotransmitter activity, which increases LES tone and decreases mid-distal esophageal motility. In diffuse esophageal spasm, a trigger, possibly increased ACh release, produces simultaneous, premature contractions and disorganized mid-distal motility. In esophageal scleroderma, systemic sclerosis, often the limited form (CREST), causes atrophy and fibrosis of the distal smooth muscle, decreasing LES tone and mid-distal motility while proximal motility is preserved.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, chest pain, weight loss, and heartburn. Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, and weight loss, with heartburn in 27–42% that is often mistreated as GERD, so reflux symptoms that persist despite PPIs should raise suspicion of achalasia. Diffuse esophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and intermittent dysphagia, set off by eating quickly or by hot or cold drinks, and the pain can mimic angina. Esophageal scleroderma causes severe reflux, within CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. Complications are aspiration pneumonia and cancer, squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma in achalasia.

Diagnosis

Barium swallow is the first test, EGD excludes pseudoachalasia from cancer, and high-resolution manometry, interpreted by the Chicago classification, is the gold standard. Achalasia shows a bird's beak with a dilated esophagus on barium, and an IRP over 15 mmHg with absent peristalsis on manometry: type I without pressurization, type II with panesophageal pressurization, and type III with premature, spastic contractions. Diffuse esophageal spasm shows a corkscrew or rosary-bead esophagus, with premature contractions in 20% or more of swallows, and esophageal scleroderma weak distal peristalsis and low LES pressure, with proximal motility preserved.

Other causes of dysphagia must be distinguished. Pseudoachalasia reflects a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction or fundus, found by EGD. Zenker diverticulum affects older men, with regurgitation of food, halitosis, aspiration, and food sticking in the throat, and is shown by barium swallow, as manometry is unhelpful; it is a false diverticulum herniating through the Killian triangle between the cricopharyngeus and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. Schatzki ring causes intermittent dysphagia to solids or food impaction, shown by barium swallow and EGD. Plummer-Vinson syndrome affects middle-aged women with iron-deficiency anemia and postcricoid dysphagia, investigated with iron studies and EGD for an upper esophageal web, and eosinophilic esophagitis presents with atopy and food impaction, diagnosed by EGD with biopsy.

Management

Achalasia is treated with pneumatic dilation, first-line for most types, or myotomy, Heller with a partial fundoplication or POEM, which is preferred for type III; CCB, nitrates, or botulinum injection are used if patients are unfit for these, and type II responds best and type III least. Diffuse esophageal spasm is treated with CCB or nitrates, with pneumatic dilation or botulinum injection as other options. Esophageal scleroderma is treated with PPIs, and Nissen fundoplication is avoided. Zenker diverticulum is treated with cricopharyngeal myotomy and diverticulectomy, open or endoscopic, Schatzki ring with dilation followed by a PPI to prevent recurrence, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome with iron replacement and dilation of the web if needed, with surveillance for squamous cell carcinoma.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause dysphagia and aspiration, but motility disorders are neuromuscular rather than mucosal. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset favors a motility disorder, whereas odynophagia favors esophagitis, and food impaction with atopy favors eosinophilic esophagitis.

. Achalasia and scleroderma are opposites at the LES, and scleroderma behaves like severe GERD because low LES tone permits reflux. Treatments are therefore opposed: Heller myotomy lowers LES pressure and Nissen fundoplication tightens it, so each would worsen the other condition, and achalasia should be suspected when reflux symptoms persist despite PPIs.

Autoimmune liver disease. Scleroderma (CREST) is associated with PBC.

Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease

Pathophysiology

When acid and pepsin outweigh the mucosal barrier, the stomach inflames as gastritis, with erosions that stop at the muscularis mucosae; injury that passes it is a peptic ulcer, which can bleed, perforate, or obstruct.

  1. Barrier weakens or acid risesInfection, drugs, ischemia, or gastrin
  2. GastritisInflamed mucosa
  3. ErosionStops at the muscularis mucosae
  4. UlcerPasses the muscularis mucosae
  5. Vessel, hole, or scarBleeding, perforation, or obstruction

What gastritis does

  • AWeakened mucus layerCOX inhibition → decreased PG → decreased mucus, HCO3−, and blood flow
  • BIncreased HClGastrin, less PG, or increased CN X activity → erosions
  • CMucosal ischemiaHypovolemia, as in severe burns → stress ulcers
  • DParietal cell lossAutoantibodies and T cells → decreased HCl and IF → atrophy

What an ulcer does

  • EWeakened barrierH. pylori, NSAIDs, and alcohol thin the mucus
  • FIncreased HClIncreased gastrin or decreased PG
  • GUlcer craterPast the muscularis mucosae → epigastric pain
  • HVessel erosionHematemesis and melena
  • IPerforationFull thickness → pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis

One infection, two diseases

  • KAntral gastritisFewer D cells → less somatostatin → more gastrin, acting on a healthy body → high acid → metaplasia and ulcer in the duodenal bulb
  • LGastritis of the bodyParietal cells lost → low acid, then atrophy and metaplasia → gastric ulcer and adenocarcinoma

Why symptoms appear

  • Pain with mealsAcid bathes a gastric ulcer as food arrives
  • Relief with mealsFood buffers acid at a duodenal ulcer, until it empties
  • Anemia firstAutoimmune gastritis: iron falls early, B12 years later
  • EdemaProtein lost from giant folds (7)

Note: many ulcers, especially with NSAIDs or in older adults, are silent until they bleed.

Etiology

  • Gastritis and ulcers
  • 1NSAIDs and alcoholThe second most common cause of ulcers; risk highest with piroxicam and ketorolac, lowest with ibuprofen and celecoxib; also aspirin
  • 2H. pyloriThe most common cause of ulcers; urease makes ammonia that shields it from acid
  • Ulcers
  • 3GastrinomaGastrin → high acid; 20–30% with MEN1
  • Stress
  • 4Curling ulcerSevere burns → hypovolemia → ischemia
  • 5Cushing ulcerIncreased ICP → increased CN X activity → high acid; more likely to be deep and perforate
  • Special types

  • 7Ménétrier diseaseExcess TGF-α activates EGFR → giant folds in the body and fundus
  • 8Bile refluxAfter gastric surgery or with a lax pylorus; few inflammatory cells
  • 9UncommonLymphocytic (celiac disease), eosinophilic, granulomatous (Crohn disease), CMV, radiation, ischemia

H. pylori: how it injures

  • SurvivesUrease, flagella, and adhesins
  • DamagesCagA and VacA, mucinases, phospholipases, and PAF

No cause found: idiopathic ulcers are rising as H. pylori falls, so recheck for hidden NSAIDs and a false negative test first.

EGD proves an ulcer and biopsies it; in a young patient without alarm features, a noninvasive H. pylori test comes first.

Review article

Gastritis and peptic ulcer disease: mucosal injury on either side of the muscularis mucosae

Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach's mucosa with shallow erosions that stop at the muscularis mucosae, whereas a peptic ulcer extends beyond it. They share their main causes, H. pylori and NSAIDs with alcohol, while gastrinomas cause ulcers, burns and increased ICP cause stress gastritis, and autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells, causing pernicious anemia rather than erosions. Bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction are the major complications of ulcers, and chronic H. pylori infection leads to gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, including H. pylori eradication, and consider their relationship to GERD, diarrhea, and malignancy.

Key points

  • Depth is the boundary: gastritis stays within the mucosa, whereas PUD extends beyond the muscularis mucosae; Curling and Cushing ulcers are not true ulcers.
  • H. pylori is the most common cause of PUD, and first-line eradication is triple therapy.
  • Gastric ulcer pain worsens with eating; duodenal ulcer pain improves with eating and worsens with fasting.
  • Stop PPIs 2 weeks before H. pylori testing, and ABX and bismuth 4 weeks before; if H. pylori is absent, check gastrin and then a secretin stimulation test.
  • Autoimmune gastritis decreases HCl and IF, causing body and fundus atrophy, pernicious anemia, and, through high gastrin, type 1 gastric carcinoid.
  • Chronic H. pylori gastritis leads to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, so it is always eradicated.

Pathophysiology

Damage to the stomach inflames the mucosa and forms shallow erosions that do not pass the muscularis mucosae. COX inhibition decreases PG and so decreases mucus production, while NSAIDs, alcohol, H. pylori, and increased CN X activity increase HCl. Hypovolemia from severe burns causes mucosal ischemia in Curling ulcers. In autoimmune gastritis, autoantibodies against parietal cells decrease HCl and IF, causing fundal atrophy rather than erosions.

In PUD, H. pylori, NSAIDs, and alcohol damage the mucosa and decrease mucus, and increased gastrin or decreased PG brings more acid to it. Once injury passes the muscularis mucosae, an ulcer forms, causing epigastric pain. An ulcer that reaches a vessel bleeds, with hematemesis and melena, and full-thickness injury perforates, causing pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

NSAIDs and alcohol cause COX inhibition, which decreases PG, increasing HCl production and decreasing mucus production. H. pylori infection increases gastrin production and therefore HCl production. In Curling ulcers, severe burns cause hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia. In Cushing ulcers, increased ICP increases CN X activity and submucosal activity, which increases HCl production. In autoimmune gastritis, autoantibodies attack parietal cells, decreasing HCl and IF production and causing fundal atrophy rather than inflammation or erosions. H. pylori survives gastric acid because its urease makes ammonia. Autoimmune gastritis affects the body and fundus and spares the antrum, and often accompanies autoimmune thyroid disease.

H. pylori is gram-negative and urease-positive, has multiple flagella, and lives in the gastric mucosa. Its virulence factors are ureases, cytotoxins (VacA, CagA), mucinases, phospholipases, and PAF. Chronic infection leads to gastritis, then atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, then dysplasia and gastric cancer, and to gastric MALT lymphoma. NSAIDs and alcohol, the second most common cause, act through COX inhibition, decreasing PG, increasing HCl production, and decreasing mucus production; the risk is highest with piroxicam and ketorolac and lowest with ibuprofen and celecoxib. Gastrinomas, as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, increase gastrin production and therefore HCl production. H. pylori causes 90% of duodenal and 70–90% of gastric ulcers, and its urease makes ammonia, which neutralizes acid around it. Gastrinomas occur with MEN1 in 20–30%, and cause refractory or multiple ulcers, including jejunal ulcers, with diarrhea.

Curling and Cushing ulcers are not true ulcers because they do not erode past the muscularis mucosae.

Clinical presentation and complications

Gastritis is often asymptomatic; otherwise it causes epigastric pain, bloating, nausea, and vomiting, and erosions can bleed with hematemesis or melena. Autoimmune gastritis is usually found through anemia: parietal cell loss decreases IF and HCl, B12 malabsorption develops over 2–5 years, and pernicious anemia follows, with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, then peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration. Low acid raises gastrin, which makes ECL cells grow and can cause a type 1 gastric carcinoid. Other complications of gastritis are gastric adenocarcinoma, as H. pylori leads to atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia; gastric MALT lymphoma from chronic H. pylori infection; iron and B12 deficiency from atrophic gastritis; and hemorrhage in stress gastritis without prophylaxis. Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, the most common, forms glands and is linked to H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, smoking, and salt-preserved, smoked, or N-nitroso foods. Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma lacks cell adhesion, often with CDH1 mutations, has signet ring cells, infiltrates the wall as linitis plastica, or leather bottle stomach, and is linked to blood group A. Metastatic signs are the Virchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Irish node (left axilla), Krukenberg tumor (ovary), and Blumer shelf (pelvic cul-de-sac); paraneoplastic signs are acanthosis nigricans, diffuse seborrheic keratoses, and Trousseau syndrome. In Ménétrier disease, excess TGF-α activates EGFR and causes giant folds in the body and fundus, sparing the antrum, with decreased acid and protein loss that leads to hypoalbuminemia and edema. It affects mostly men, at a median age of 55, is progressive and premalignant in adults, and has a self-limited form in children after CMV.

Pain is epigastric, dull, and burning in both types; gastric ulcer pain is worse with eating and better with fasting, and duodenal ulcer pain is the reverse. Other symptoms are nausea, vomiting, heartburn, bloating, fullness, belching, and fatigue. Complications are bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting, pain, malnutrition, succussion splash), intestinal metaplasia, gastric cancer, and gastric MALT lymphoma. Gastric ulcers are usually on the lesser curvature, with pain 15–30 minutes after meals, and duodenal ulcers in the duodenal bulb, with pain 2–3 hours after meals and at night. A bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery, and a lesser curvature ulcer the left gastric artery.

Diagnosis

Dyspepsia is evaluated with H. pylori testing, by urea breath test, the most accurate noninvasive test, or stool antigen. Alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, a mass, persistent vomiting, and family history of gastric cancer) or age 60 or older call for EGD with biopsies from 5 sites. Autoimmune gastritis shows anti-parietal cell antibodies, which are sensitive, and anti-IF antibodies, which are specific, with body and fundus atrophy and intestinal metaplasia on biopsy, and B12 and iron are checked. In pernicious anemia, the FBC shows macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, though one-third have no macrocytosis. Ménétrier disease shows giant folds on EGD, confirmed by biopsy, which may need to be deep, with low albumin. Eradication is confirmed by a noninvasive test 4–6 weeks after finishing ABX or PPI.

Perforation is evaluated with an upright CXR, and bleeding with EGD with biopsy. H. pylori is detected by urea breath test, stool antigen test, rapid urease test, or histology. PPIs are stopped 2 weeks before testing, and ABX and bismuth 4 weeks before testing. If no H. pylori is detected, gastrin levels are checked, followed by a secretin stimulation test for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. EGD is the gold standard, used for age 60 or older with new dyspepsia or for alarm features at any age. A fasting gastrin over 1000 pg/mL, 10 times normal, is diagnostic of gastrinoma, after stopping PPIs for 1 week; if it is equivocal, a paradoxical rise over 120 pg/mL after secretin confirms it, and MEN1 is screened with calcium, PTH, and prolactin.

Management

Perforation is treated with IV fluids, IV PPI, IV ABX, and surgery, and bleeding with IV fluids, IV PPI, EGD, and surgery. Acid is suppressed with antacids, H2R antagonists, and PPIs, and the mucosa is protected with misoprostol, sucralfate, and bismuth. First-line H. pylori eradication is triple therapy, bd for 7–14 days: PPI, amoxicillin (metronidazole if allergic), and clarithromycin. Alternative regimens are PPI, amoxicillin, and levofloxacin; PPI, metronidazole, tetracycline, and bismuth; and PPI, amoxicillin, and rifabutin. NSAID ulcers are treated by stopping the NSAID or lowering the dose, with misoprostol to prevent ulcers in those who must continue, and gastrinoma with a high-dose PPI and resection if localized. A refractory ulcer, over 5 mm and not healed after 8–12 weeks of PPI, prompts a search for persistent H. pylori, NSAIDs, gastrinoma, or cancer, then vagotomy or partial gastrectomy. Cure is confirmed by urea breath test 4–6 weeks after treatment.

H. pylori gastritis is eradicated with the same regimens, and cure is confirmed. Gastritis from NSAIDs or alcohol is treated by stopping the cause and giving a PPI. Critically ill patients receive stress prophylaxis with a PPI first-line or an H2R antagonist second line. H. pylori-negative dyspepsia under 60 is treated with an empiric PPI, then a prokinetic or tricyclic antidepressant. Autoimmune gastritis is treated with IM B12 1000 µg daily or on alternate days for 1–2 weeks, then IM or high-dose oral B12 for life, iron replacement, and EGD every 3 years if atrophy is advanced. Gastric MALT lymphoma is treated by H. pylori eradication if t(11;18) negative, with an 80% complete response, and otherwise by radiotherapy or systemic therapy. Ménétrier disease is treated with a high-protein diet, PPI, and albumin, treatment of CMV or H. pylori, and total gastrectomy if refractory.

Relationships to other conditions

. All are treated with PPIs and can bleed, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome links them through increased HCl production. Perforation produces pneumoperitoneum here, assessed by upright CXR, and pneumomediastinum in the esophagus, assessed by contrast esophagram and CXR.

. Gastrinomas also cause chronic secretory diarrhea, so ulcers with diarrhea suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Malignancy. Gastric ulcers can be malignant and are biopsied, whereas duodenal ulcers are rarely malignant. MEN1 links gastrinomas to .

Autoimmune versus H. pylori gastritis. Autoimmune gastritis targets the body and fundus, where parietal cells live, and causes low acid with high gastrin. H. pylori gastritis typically starts in the antrum. Autoimmune disease also leads to B12 deficiency and raises the risk of gastric carcinoid tumors.

. Autoimmune gastritis can accompany conditions such as Hashimoto thyroiditis and vitiligo.

Gastric Tumors

Pathophysiology

A chronic stimulus or a mutation, such as H. pylori, high gastrin, or a KIT mutation, drives growth in one layer of the wall, and the mass bleeds, obstructs, spreads, or secretes hormones.

  1. Stimulus or mutationH. pylori, gastrin, or KIT
  2. Growth in one layerEpithelium, muscle, or lymphoid tissue
  3. Mass or thick wallOr an ulcer
  4. Bleeding or obstructionOften late
  5. SpreadNodes, liver, or peritoneum

What the tumor does

  • ABleedingMelena, hematemesis, or iron deficiency anemia
  • BObstructionAntrum: early satiety and vomiting; cardia: dysphagia
  • CSpreadLymphatics, portal blood to the liver, and peritoneum
  • DHormonesType 2 NET comes with ZES; carcinoid syndrome is rare

Adenocarcinoma (4): the cascade

  1. H. pylori gastritisChronic inflammation
  2. AtrophyGlands lost, acid falls
  3. Intestinal metaplasiaIncomplete type is riskier
  4. DysplasiaPrecancerous
  5. Intestinal-type cancerTakes decades

Review article

Gastric tumors: from incidental polyps to adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, and tumors beneath the mucosa

Gastric tumors arise from every layer of the stomach wall: polyps, adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors, and lymphoma from the mucosa, lipomas from the submucosa, and leiomyomas, GISTs, and sarcomas from the muscularis propria. Most polyps and benign tumors beneath the mucosa are found incidentally, whereas adenocarcinoma, the main gastric cancer, usually presents late with weight loss, bleeding, or signs of spread. Chronic stimuli such as H. pylori and high gastrin, and mutations such as those of KIT and CDH1, link many of these tumors to their causes and treatments. Here, we review the pathophysiology, etiology, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of gastric tumors, with particular attention to adenocarcinoma, and consider how they relate to gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Key points

  • Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma follows H. pylori gastritis through atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia, whereas diffuse-type adenocarcinoma lacks cell adhesion from CDH1 loss, contains signet ring cells, and causes linitis plastica.
  • Adenocarcinoma spreads to the Virchow, Sister Mary Joseph, and Irish nodes, the ovaries as Krukenberg tumors, the rectal pouch as a Blumer shelf, the peritoneum, and the liver.
  • Adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by EGD with multiple biopsies and staged by EUS, CT, PET-CT, and staging laparoscopy; early tumors suit endoscopic resection, and deeper tumors need perioperative chemotherapy and gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.
  • MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori in over 90% and responds to its eradication in over 75%, except when t(11;18) is present.
  • GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal with KIT or PDGFRA mutations, stain for KIT and DOG1, and are resected, with imatinib for high-risk or metastatic disease.
  • Type 1 gastric NETs arise from ECL cells driven by the high gastrin of autoimmune gastritis, type 2 from ZES with MEN1, and type 3 sporadically with aggressive behavior.

Pathophysiology

A chronic stimulus or mutation, such as H. pylori, high gastrin, or a KIT mutation, drives uncontrolled growth in one layer of the stomach wall and forms a mass, whether in the mucosa or beneath it. The mass can then cause harm in four ways. An ulcerated tumor bleeds, causing melena, hematemesis, or occult loss with iron deficiency anemia. A tumor at the antrum or pylorus obstructs the outlet, causing early satiety and vomiting, whereas one at the cardia causes dysphagia. Malignant tumors spread through lymphatics to the Virchow node, across the peritoneum to cause ascites and Krukenberg tumors, and through portal blood to the liver. Finally, NETs release hormones such as gastrin or serotonin, and type 2 NETs arise with ZES and its peptic ulcers.

Etiology and mechanisms

Polyps are the most common gastric tumors, and over 90% are found incidentally. Fundic gland polyps are the most common type and are linked to PPI use and FAP; hyperplastic polyps arise from the chronic inflammation of H. pylori and atrophic gastritis; adenomas are precancerous; and hamartomas occur in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis. Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors of the muscularis propria that stain for desmin and smooth muscle actin but not for KIT or CD34, and lipomas are yellow, soft collections of submucosal fat that need no biopsy when their EUS appearance is typical.

Among malignant tumors, adenocarcinoma is the main gastric cancer. Gastric lymphomas are mostly MALT lymphoma, driven by H. pylori in over 90%, or DLBCL, which together make up nearly 90% and most often affect the antrum. Leiomyosarcoma is exceptionally rare, about 1% of malignant gastric tumors, and stains for smooth muscle actin but not for KIT or DOG1. Two tumors have variable malignant potential. GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal in the muscularis propria, occur in the stomach in 60%, carry KIT (CD117) mutations in 75–80% and PDGFRA mutations in 5–10%, stain most specifically for DOG1, and occur in NF1 and the Carney triad. NETs, or carcinoids, arise from ECL cells: type 1 with autoimmune gastritis and high gastrin, making up 70–80%; type 2 with ZES and MEN1; and type 3 sporadically, with aggressive behavior.

Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma develops in steps: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis, which progresses to atrophic gastritis with loss of glands, then to intestinal metaplasia, which raises the risk up to 10 times, then to dysplasia, and finally to a gland-forming mass or ulcer. It is the most common type, follows precursor lesions such as atrophic gastritis, metaplasia, and pernicious anemia, is more common in men, and is declining. Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma has no cell adhesion because of CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss, contains signet ring cells, and infiltrates the wall without a mass, producing linitis plastica, the leather bottle stomach; it has no precursor lesion, affects men and women equally, and is linked to blood type A.

Risk factors for adenocarcinoma include infection with H. pylori or, for the proximal stomach, EBV; diets high in salt, smoked and cured foods, and N-nitroso compounds and low in vitamins A and C, with no refrigeration; and smoking. Obesity, GERD, and bile reflux after gastric surgery raise the risk of proximal and GEJ tumors. Atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, and gastric ulcers predispose, as do inherited factors: CDH1 mutations in hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, FAP with a 10% risk, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with a 29% risk, and blood type A. Distal, intestinal-type cancer has fallen with better diet and treatment of H. pylori, while proximal and GEJ cancers are rising.

Clinical presentation and complications

Polyps, leiomyomas, lipomas, and small NETs often cause no symptoms. Otherwise, gastric tumors cause dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss, nausea and vomiting, dysphagia with proximal tumors, melena or hematemesis, iron deficiency anemia, and an epigastric mass, and lymphoma can cause B symptoms. Adenocarcinoma often reveals itself by its spread: a left supraclavicular Virchow node, reached through the thoracic duct; a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph node; a left axillary Irish node; Krukenberg tumors, signet ring cell metastases to the ovaries that are often bilateral; a Blumer shelf, a mass in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch; ascites and hepatomegaly from peritoneal carcinomatosis and liver metastases; and skin signs, the Leser-Trélat sign of sudden, multiple seborrheic keratoses and acanthosis nigricans.

Complications include bleeding from adenocarcinoma, GISTs, lymphoma, and hyperplastic polyps; gastric outlet obstruction from antral tumors and large polyps or lipomas; perforation and fistula in advanced adenocarcinoma, which are rare in lymphoma; transformation of adenomas to adenocarcinoma and of MALT lymphoma to DLBCL in 2–8%; rupture of a GIST, which raises recurrence; and, rarely, carcinoid syndrome from a NET with liver metastases.

Diagnosis

Any suspected gastric tumor is examined by EGD with biopsies, including biopsies of the surrounding mucosa for atrophy, metaplasia, and H. pylori. Polyps are biopsied or removed, including fundic gland polyps over 1 cm, hyperplastic polyps over 0.5 cm, and all adenomas. Lesions beneath the mucosa are characterized by EUS, on which GISTs and leiomyomas are hypoechoic and arise from the muscularis propria, whereas a lipoma is homogeneously hyperechoic, and EUS-guided FNA obtains tissue. GISTs are imaged first with contrast CT, which shows their size and spread to the liver and peritoneum, and are confirmed by KIT (CD117) and DOG1 staining. Lymphoma is confirmed by biopsy with immunohistochemistry: MALT lymphoma cells are CD19, CD20, and CD79a positive and CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1 negative, with lymphoepithelial lesions, and testing for H. pylori and t(11;18) and staging follow. NETs are typed by serum gastrin and gastric pH, with high gastrin and low acid in type 1, high gastrin and high acid in type 2, and normal gastrin in type 3; biopsies stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin and are graded by Ki-67, patients with type 2 tumors are screened for MEN1 with PTH, calcium, and prolactin, and urinary 5-HIAA is measured if carcinoid syndrome is suspected.

Adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by EGD with multiple biopsies, and every suspicious ulcer is biopsied, because cancer can present as a nonhealing ulcer; seven biopsies raise sensitivity to 98%. EUS then defines the depth, or T stage, and the nodes, since T1 tumors may suit endoscopic resection. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis looks for distant metastases, PET-CT follows if CT shows none, and staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings finds peritoneal disease in up to 40%. HER2 is amplified in 12–27% and guides targeted treatment, whereas tumor markers such as CEA and CA 19-9 add little to diagnosis.

Management

Fundic gland polyps are removed if over 1 cm. Hyperplastic polyps are treated by eradicating H. pylori, after which most regress within a year, and are removed if over 0.5 cm. Adenomas are resected endoscopically, with EGD at 1 year and every 3–5 years after. Leiomyomas and lipomas need no treatment when small and silent, but are excised or enucleated when symptomatic. MALT lymphoma is treated by eradicating H. pylori, even when testing is negative, with a response in over 75%; cure is confirmed at 6 weeks and EGD repeated in 3–6 months, and radiotherapy or rituximab is used when H. pylori is absent or t(11;18) is present. DLBCL grows independently of H. pylori and is treated with chemotherapy. Sarcomas are resected. GISTs are removed completely, without rupture, with adjuvant imatinib for high-risk tumors and imatinib as first-line treatment when unresectable or metastatic. NETs under 1 cm are watched, those of 1–2 cm are removed by EMR or ESD, type 1 tumors that are multiple or recurrent can be treated with somatostatin analogs, type 2 tumors need high-dose PPI and care of MEN1, and type 3 tumors need gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy.

Adenocarcinoma confined to the mucosa or superficial submucosa without high-risk features can be removed endoscopically by EMR or ESD. Deeper tumors and those with involved nodes are treated with perioperative chemotherapy and gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, which removes node stations 1–11. Distal tumors are treated by subtotal gastrectomy, whereas proximal, extensive, or diffuse tumors need total gastrectomy, which signet ring cell histology requires, and carriers of a germline CDH1 mutation may have a prophylactic total gastrectomy. Unresectable or metastatic disease is treated with palliative chemotherapy, HER2-directed treatment when HER2 is amplified, and radiotherapy for palliation. Over 50% of localized distal cancers are cured, but only 10–20% of cancers in the United States are found early and disseminated disease is almost never cured, whereas routine endoscopy in Japan and South Korea finds cancers early.

Relationships to other conditions

. Chronic gastritis is the soil for three gastric tumors. H. pylori gastritis leads to intestinal-type adenocarcinoma through atrophy and metaplasia and to MALT lymphoma through chronic lymphoid stimulation, whereas autoimmune gastritis leads to type 1 NETs through the high gastrin of achlorhydria. Eradicating H. pylori treats MALT lymphoma and hyperplastic polyps and lowers the risk of adenocarcinoma.

and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. A gastric adenocarcinoma can look like a benign ulcer, so suspicious gastric ulcers are biopsied and their healing confirmed. Both type 1 and type 2 NETs have high gastrin, but in type 1 acid is low from atrophic gastritis, whereas in type 2 a gastrinoma with ZES makes acid high and causes peptic ulcers; gastric pH separates them.

GIST and leiomyoma. Both arise from the muscularis propria and look alike on EUS as hypoechoic masses, so staining separates them: GISTs stain for KIT and DOG1, whereas leiomyomas stain for desmin and smooth muscle actin and leiomyosarcomas for smooth muscle actin, and neither stains for KIT. Many tumors once called leiomyosarcomas were GISTs, which is why gastric leiomyosarcoma is now so rare.

Malabsorption

Pathophysiology

Food must be digested in the lumen, taken up by a healthy lining, and carried away in blood or lymph, and malabsorption follows when any of these steps fails.

  1. DigestEnzymes and bile salts
  2. AbsorbBrush border and villi
  3. TransportBlood and lymph
  4. Step failsNutrients stay in the lumen
  5. Diarrhea, deficiencyDepends on the nutrient

What failed absorption does

  • AInjured villiLess surface, so every nutrient can suffer
  • BFailed digestionToo few enzymes or bile salts leave food too large to absorb
  • CUndigested carbohydrateDraws in water; bacteria make gas and acid → bloating, acidic stool
  • DUndigested fatGreasy stool, and colonic bacteria turn it into acids that cause secretion
  • ELost micronutrientsAnemia, bone disease, bleeding, neuropathy

Where each nutrient goes

  • FDuodenumIron, calcium, folate, zinc
  • GJejunumSugars, amino acids, fat, vitamins A, D, E, and K
  • HTerminal ileumB12 and bile salts; nothing else can take over for them

Two kinds

Mucosal or transportLuminal (maldigestion)
What failsVilli, enzymes of the brush border, or lymphPancreatic enzymes or bile salts
Fat in stoolPresentPresent, often more
D-xylose absorbedNoYes
TreatmentHeal the liningReplace what is missing

Note: The D-xylose test separates the two in theory, but serology, elastase, and biopsy have largely replaced it.

Etiology

The causes sit along the path that food takes: lining, lumen, or transport.

Causes

  • Mucosal
  • 1Celiac diseaseGluten; see its own page
  • 2Tropical sprueMonths in the tropics; bacteria and injury after infection
  • 3Whipple diseaseTropheryma whipplei inside macrophages; middle-aged men
  • 4GiardiasisWater, travel, children, CVID
  • 5Crohn disease and ileal lossInflammation or resection of the ileum
  • 6Short bowel syndromeLess than 200 cm of small bowel remains
  • 7Lactose intoleranceLactase falls after childhood, or is lost after infection
  • Luminal
  • 8Pancreatic insufficiencyChronic pancreatitis, cancer, cystic fibrosis, surgery
  • 9Bile salt deficiencyCirrhosis, cholestasis, ileal loss
  • 10SIBOStasis: diabetes, scleroderma, blind loop, opioids; low acid, adhesions
  • Transport
  • 11AbetalipoproteinemiaMTTP gene; no apo B lipoproteins
  • 12Lymphatic and protein lossLymphangiectasia, lymphoma, heart failure, Fontan circulation

Who to suspect

  • Chronic steatorrheaAny luminal or mucosal cause
  • SurgeryIleal resection, gastric bypass, Whipple procedure
  • TravelTropical sprue, giardiasis, Strongyloides
  • Immune deficiencyGiardiasis, CVID, SIBO

Symptoms and complications

  1. Bloating, gasCarbohydrate
  2. Greasy stoolFat
  3. Weight lossEnergy
  4. EdemaProtein
  5. Deficiency signsAnemia, bone, nerve

By nutrient

LostCauses
CarbohydrateWatery diarrhea, bloating, gas, acidic stool
ProteinEdema, muscle loss, poor wound healing
FatPale, greasy, foul stool that is hard to flush; weight loss
IronAnemia, spoon nails
B12Macrocytic anemia, neuropathy, glossitis
FolateMacrocytic anemia without neuropathy
Vitamin ANight blindness, dry eyes
Vitamin D and calciumOsteomalacia, tetany
Vitamin EAtaxia, neuropathy, hemolysis
Vitamin KBleeding, long prothrombin time
ZincRash around the mouth and groin, hair loss

Clues to the cause

  • Itchy vesiclesCeliac disease (1)
  • Joint pain for years, fever, then diarrheaWhipple disease (3)
  • Camping, foul greasy stoolGiardiasis (4)
  • Pain after eating, weight loss, diabetesPancreatic insufficiency (8)
  • Jaundice, itchBile salt deficiency (9)
  • Bloating, surgery, sclerodermaSIBO (10)
  • Ataxia and retinal disease in a childAbetalipoproteinemia (11)
  • Edema, low lymphocytesLymphatic disease (12)

Complications

  • Osteoporosis and fracturesLow vitamin D and calcium
  • Kidney stonesOxalate, when fat binds calcium
  • GallstonesIleal loss (5)
  • Short bowelDehydration, liver disease from parenteral nutrition, D-lactic acidosis with confusion
  • Whipple diseaseCNS: dementia, eye movement disorder; endocarditis
  • InfectionHyposplenism, low antibodies
  • Growth failureChildren
  • Refeeding syndromeLow phosphate when feeding starts

Diagnosis

Confirm that absorption is failing, look for the common causes with blood and stool tests, then image or biopsy.

  1. Bloods, stoolDeficiencies, infection
  2. Celiac serologyMost common mucosal cause
  3. ElastasePancreas
  4. EGD with biopsyLining
  5. CT or MRIPancreas, bile ducts, bowel

Tests

  • FBC, iron, B12, folate, calcium, vitamin D, coagulation, albuminPattern of deficiency
  • tTG-IgA with total IgACeliac disease (1)
  • Fecal elastaseLow under 200 µg/g, severe under 100; watery stool can lower it falsely
  • Fecal calprotectinInflammation
  • Stool antigen or PCRGiardia
  • Fecal fat over 72 hoursOver 7 g a day proves steatorrhea; rarely needed
  • D-xyloseNormal in luminal disease; seldom used now
  • α1-antitrypsin clearanceProtein loss from the bowel (12)

Breath tests

  • LactoseHydrogen rise of 20 ppm or more means malabsorption, if symptoms match
  • Glucose or lactuloseSIBO (10): rise of 20 ppm by 90 minutes; false results are common, so a trial of treatment may be better

Biopsy findings

FindingPoints to
Flat villi, IELsCeliac disease (1); also tropical sprue (2), drugs
PAS-positive foamy macrophagesWhipple disease (3): confirm by PCR; Mycobacterium avium is acid-fast
Giardia on the surfaceGiardiasis (4)
Dilated lymphaticsLymphangiectasia (12)
Fat-filled cells with normal villiAbetalipoproteinemia (11)
No plasma cellsCVID
GranulomaCrohn disease (5)

Red flags

  • Weight loss over 10%
  • Edema or albumin under 25 g/L
  • Fever, night sweats
  • Jaundice
  • Neurological signs
  • Anemia with bleeding

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
IBSNormal weight, bloods, and calprotectin
Bile acid diarrheaWatery, after cholecystectomy
HyperthyroidismWeight loss with appetiteTFTs
Pancreatic cancerPain, new diabetesCT
Laxative useLow K+, melanosis coliScreen
Anorexia nervosaLow intakeHistory

Find the cause

  • 1Celiac diseasetTG-IgA, biopsy
  • 2Tropical sprueTravel; biopsy; exclude celiac disease and Giardia
  • 3Whipple diseaseBiopsy and PCR; CSF if neurological
  • 4GiardiasisStool antigen or PCR
  • 5Crohn disease and ileal lossIleocolonoscopy, MRE
  • 6Short bowel syndromeSurgical record, bowel length
  • 7Lactose intoleranceBreath test, or stop dairy for 2 weeks
  • 8Pancreatic insufficiencyElastase, CT
  • 9Bile salt deficiencyLFTs, ultrasound, SeHCAT or C4
  • 10SIBOBreath test or aspirate (10³ organisms per mL or more)
  • 11AbetalipoproteinemiaVery low cholesterol, acanthocytes
  • 12Lymphatic and protein lossAlbumin, α1-antitrypsin clearance, CT, biopsy

Treatment

Treat the cause, replace what is lost, and feed by the safest route, because deficiencies outlast the illness.

  1. Treat the causeInfection, diet, enzymes
  2. ReplaceVitamins, minerals
  3. DietSmall meals, MCT
  4. SupportEnteral, then parenteral
  5. RecheckBloods, bones

Replace

NutrientHow
IronPO, or IV if not absorbed
B12IM when the ileum is lost
Vitamins A, D, E, KWater-soluble forms; check levels
Calcium, magnesium, zincPO; IV magnesium if severe
EnergyMCT, which need no bile salts or lymph; avoid too much fat in steatorrhea
ProteinHigh protein, IV albumin only for symptoms

Short bowel (6)

  • DietSmall meals; complex carbohydrate and lower fat if the colon remains; ORS rather than water
  • DrugsLoperamide, PPI early, octreotide, GLP-2 analog (teduglutide)
  • SupportParenteral nutrition until the bowel adapts over 1–2 years, often for life under 100 cm without a colon or 50–60 cm with one
  • AvoidOxalate; drinking plain water in large amounts

Be careful with

  • Refeeding: phosphate, K+, Mg2+, thiamine
  • Folate before B12
  • Vitamin A excess
  • ABX repeated for SIBO
  • Opioids
  • Whipple: immune flare when treated
  • Bile acid sequestrant after long ileal loss

Treat the cause

  • 1Celiac diseaseGluten-free diet
  • 2Tropical sprueDoxycycline or TMP-SMX for 3–6 months, folic acid, B12
  • 3Whipple diseaseCeftriaxone for 2 weeks, then TMP-SMX for 12 months; both reach the CNS. Alternative: doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine
  • 4GiardiasisTinidazole or metronidazole
  • 5Crohn disease and ileal lossTreat inflammation; B12; sequestrant if short loss
  • 6Short bowel syndromeDiet, drugs, and nutrition support, as described above
  • 7Lactose intoleranceLess lactose, or lactase tablets; keep up calcium
  • 8Pancreatic insufficiencyEnzymes with every meal;
  • 9Bile salt deficiencyTreat the liver or duct; MCT, vitamins
  • 10SIBOCorrect the stasis if possible; rifaximin; rotate ABX if it returns
  • 11AbetalipoproteinemiaLow-fat diet, high-dose vitamin E and A
  • 12Lymphatic and protein lossTreat the disease; MCT, low-fat diet; octreotide in some

Guidelines differ: Some groups advise breath testing before SIBO treatment, while others treat when the risk and symptoms are clear.

Review article

Malabsorption: separating mucosal injury from failed digestion

Malabsorption syndromes divide into true malabsorption, with mucosal injury and normal enzyme function, and maldigestion, with altered enzyme function and no mucosal injury. Celiac disease, Whipple disease, and tropical sprue injure the mucosa, whereas pancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency, and lactose intolerance impair digestion. Here, we review their mechanisms, nutrient-specific consequences, and treatment, and consider how they relate to diarrhea and IBD.

Key points

  • The D-xylose test differentiates malabsorption from maldigestion.
  • Celiac disease is confirmed by EGD with biopsy after serology.
  • Consequences follow the lost nutrient: carbohydrate, protein, fat, or micronutrient.
  • Micronutrient deficiency is treated by replacement and IV fluids.

Pathophysiology

Mucosal injury blunts the villi and decreases absorption in true malabsorption, whereas decreased enzymes or bile salts leave food undigested in maldigestion. Either way, nutrients stay in the lumen. Undigested carbohydrate causes osmotic diarrhea and gas from bacterial digestion, with abdominal pain and flatulence; undigested fat causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies; and iron, B12, and folate deficiency cause anemia.

Etiology and mechanisms

Celiac disease is associated with HLA DQ2/8 and triggered by gliadin from gluten in wheat, rye, and barley. Gliadin binds antigen-presenting cells, which activate T helper cells and then B cells, producing IgA antibodies: tTG, DGP, and EMA. Whipple disease is Tropheryma whipplei infection with mucosal damage. Tropical sprue is E. coli and Klebsiella overgrowth in tropical areas with mucosal injury. Pancreatic insufficiency follows acute or chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, and pancreatic cancer or surgery. Bile salt deficiency, a partial maldigestion, follows cirrhosis, hepatocellular injury, biliary tree obstruction, and impaired enterohepatic circulation. Lactose intolerance, also a partial maldigestion, follows genetic mutations and gastroenteritis. Celiac disease is associated with type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune disease, IgA deficiency, and dermatitis herpetiformis. Tropheryma whipplei is a gram-positive bacillus that infects macrophages and also involves the joints, heart, and CNS, and tropical sprue follows coliform overgrowth (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) after over 1 month in tropical areas. In SIBO, colonic bacteria grow in the small bowel because of stasis, from motility disorders or blind loops, or low acid, and they deconjugate bile salts and damage the mucosa. Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive MTTP mutation that prevents apo B lipoproteins from forming, so enterocytes cannot export chylomicrons and fat stays in the mucosa.

Clinical presentation and complications

Carbohydrate malabsorption causes osmotic diarrhea, bowel distention, and increased gas production from bacterial digestion, with abdominal pain and flatulence. Protein malabsorption causes muscle atrophy and weight loss. Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies: vitamin A (night blindness), vitamin D (hypocalcemia, osteomalacia, osteoporosis), vitamin E (neuropathy, hemolytic anemia), and vitamin K (coagulopathy). Micronutrient malabsorption causes iron, B12, and folate deficiency, leading to anemia. Celiac disease causes iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, fatigue, and arthralgia, and dermatitis herpetiformis, intensely itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces, is pathognomonic. Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is a rare complication, more likely in refractory disease, and a gluten-free diet lowers the risk. Whipple disease causes weight loss, diarrhea, fever, and migratory large-joint arthralgia, often first, with endocarditis and CNS signs. Tropical sprue causes chronic diarrhea after a traveler's diarrhea-like illness, with B12 and folate deficiency and anemia. SIBO causes bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea or steatorrhea, with low B12 and normal or high folate. Abetalipoproteinemia presents in infancy with failure to thrive and steatorrhea, and vitamin E deficiency causes acanthocytes, retinitis pigmentosa, and ataxia.

Diagnosis

The D-xylose test first differentiates malabsorption from maldigestion. Celiac disease is evaluated by serology (tTG, DGP, EMA, HLA), infectious causes by history taking, and confirmation is by EGD with biopsy. Pancreatic function is assessed by fecal elastase, lactose intolerance by hydrogen breath test, and bile salt deficiency by LFTs or biopsy. Celiac serology is done on a gluten diet for 6–8 weeks, measuring tTG-IgA with total IgA, since IgA deficiency gives a false negative and IgG tests are used instead. Duodenal biopsies, 1–2 from the bulb and 4 from the distal duodenum, show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Whipple disease shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages on small bowel biopsy, and tropical sprue is diagnosed from the travel history after excluding other causes. Fecal elastase is unaffected by enzyme replacement. SIBO is shown by a glucose or lactulose breath test, abetalipoproteinemia by acanthocytes with very low cholesterol, LDL, and VLDL, and dermatitis herpetiformis by direct immunofluorescence of skin beside a lesion.

Management

Micronutrient deficiency is treated by replacing the micronutrients and giving IV fluids. Celiac disease is treated with a gluten-free diet; Whipple disease and tropical sprue with ABX; pancreatic insufficiency with enzyme replacement; bile salt deficiency by treating the liver disease or cholestasis; and lactose intolerance with lactase replacement or a lactose-free diet. The gluten-free diet is strict and lifelong, with dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. Whipple disease is treated with ceftriaxone or penicillin G for 2 weeks, then TMP-SMX for at least 12 months, and tropical sprue with tetracycline, TMP-SMX, or a quinolone, plus folic acid and iron, for 3–6 months, with parenteral B12. SIBO is treated with rifaximin for 2 weeks, treatment of the cause, and B12 replacement, and abetalipoproteinemia with a low-fat diet and very large doses of oral vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamins.

Relationships to other conditions

. Every cause here produces chronic osmotic diarrhea, which has a high osmotic gap and stops with fasting, unlike secretory diarrhea.

. Ileal Crohn disease reproduces malabsorption: fat, B12, and bile salts are lost, with oxalate stones and gallstones as consequences.

. PBC and PSC cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies through the same bile salt mechanism.

. Repeated attacks link pancreatitis to pancreatic insufficiency, which fecal elastase identifies.

Diverticular Diseases

Pathophysiology

Pressure in the colon pushes mucosa through weak points where vessels enter, and the pouches may then become inflamed or bleed.

  1. Weak pointsWhere vasa recta enter
  2. Pressure and stiff wallSigmoid, altered collagen
  3. PouchesMucosa and submucosa
  4. InflammationMicroperforation
  5. Or bleedingVessel worn thin

What happens to the wall

  • APressureNarrow sigmoid, segmenting contractions
  • BFalse diverticulumNo muscle layer; next to vasa recta
  • CBleedingVessel stretched over the dome, worn thin; arterial
  • DDiverticulitisErosion by pressure, altered flora, and inflammation → microperforation
  • EPerforationAbscess, peritonitis, fistula

Two kinds of pouch

ColonicMeckel
WallFalse: mucosa and submucosaTrue: all layers
OriginAcquiredCongenital, vitelline duct
SiteSigmoid most; right colon in AsiaIleum, antimesenteric
BleedingWorn arteryAcid ulcer

Note: Fiber is not proven to prevent diverticula, though a high-fiber diet is linked with less diverticulitis, and nuts and seeds do not cause it.

Etiology

Diverticulosis is common and usually silent; inflammation, bleeding, and a congenital pouch are different problems.

Causes

  • 1DiverticulosisAge, genes, connective tissue disease, obesity, low activity; over half of people over 60
  • 2DiverticulitisFewer than 5% of people with pouches
  • 3Diverticular bleedingRight colon in half or more of bleeds
  • 4Meckel diverticulumVitelline duct fails to close; 2% of people

Risks for diverticulitis

  • LifestyleObesity, smoking, red meat, low fiber, inactivity
  • DrugsNSAIDs, corticosteroids, opioids; aspirin less so
  • GenesAbout half the risk
  • BleedingNSAIDs, antiplatelets, anticoagulants, hypertension
  • MeckelMale sex for symptoms

Symptoms and complications

  1. SilentMost
  2. LLQ painOver days
  3. FeverHigh CRP, WBC
  4. Abscess or free perforationAbout 12% complicated
  5. RecurrenceFirst year most

The pattern

  • Diverticulosis (1)None; some have cramps and bloating
  • Diverticulitis (2)Steady LLQ pain, fever, constipation or diarrhea; RLQ if right-sided
  • Bleeding (3)Sudden painless maroon or bright red blood; stops in about 80%
  • Meckel (4)Child: painless bleeding. Adult: obstruction or inflammation like appendicitis
  • Chronic painIn up to half after an attack; mostly visceral hypersensitivity

Complicated diverticulitis

  • FPericolic abscessSmall: ABX
  • GPelvic abscessLarge: drain
  • HPurulent peritonitisPus, no stool
  • JFecal peritonitisOpen hole; highest mortality

These are the stages of the Hinchey classification, which guides treatment.

Rule of 2s in Meckel

  • KPouch2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2% of people
  • LEctopic tissue2 types: gastric most, pancreatic
  • MUlcerAcid on the ileum → bleeding, usually under age 2
  • NBandCan twist the bowel; 2% have symptoms, male 2 to 1

Complications

  • AbscessFever that persists
  • FistulaBladder most: pneumaturia, fecaluria
  • ObstructionStricture or spasm
  • PerforationFirst attack most often
  • PylephlebitisPortal vein, liver abscess
  • RecurrenceAbout 15–20% at 5 years; mostly uncomplicated
  • SCADSegment of inflamed colon between pouches
  • Cancer foundAbout 2%; about 8% if complicated

Diagnosis

CT with contrast makes the diagnosis of diverticulitis and stages it; colonoscopy waits, and bleeding is worked up by its own ladder.

  1. Examination, bloodsFBC, CRP, urine, β-hCG
  2. CT APConfirm and stage
  3. Complicated or notAdmit or home
  4. Colonoscopy later6–8 weeks
  5. BleedingCTA or colonoscopy

Key test

  • CT APPouches, wall over 4 mm, fat stranding; abscess, gas, fistula
  • UltrasoundIf expert, or pregnant
  • MRIPregnancy
  • CRPOver 140 mg/L, or persistent, predicts complicated disease
  • ColonoscopyNot in the acute phase; then after complicated or first attack, sooner with alarm symptoms

Bleeding (3)

If there isObtain
StableColonoscopy, with bowel preparation; not urgent
Unstable, continuingCTA, then embolization
Upper source possibleEGD first
Repeated, no sourceColonoscopy, capsule, Meckel scan in the young

Other tests

  • Meckel scanTechnetium in gastric lining; sensitive in children, less in adults; H2 blocker helps
  • CT, capsule, laparoscopyAdult Meckel
  • CT cystogramBladder fistula
  • Stool testsIf diarrhea
  • CalprotectinHigh in SCAD and diverticulitis

Red flags

  • Peritonitis
  • Sepsis
  • Free gas
  • Immunosuppressed
  • Shock with bleeding
  • Weight loss
  • Anemia

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Colon cancerWeight loss, anemia, short segment, nodesColonoscopy
IBDDiarrhea over weeks
Ischemic colitisSudden, bleeding, over 60
IBSNo fever, normal CRPCalprotectin
Ovary or ectopic pregnancyPelvic pain, missed periodβ-hCG, pelvic ultrasound
Kidney stoneColic, hematuriaCT
AppendicitisMigrating pain; long sigmoid over the RLQ

Find the cause

  • 1DiverticulosisSeen on colonoscopy or CT
  • 2DiverticulitisCT AP
  • 3Diverticular bleedingColonoscopy, CTA if unstable
  • 4Meckel diverticulumMeckel scan; laparoscopy

Treatment

Uncomplicated diverticulitis often needs no antibiotics, complicated disease needs drainage or surgery, and surgery is chosen by patient rather than by count of attacks.

  1. StageCT
  2. Home if mildLiquids, paracetamol
  3. ABX if at riskOral first
  4. Drain or operateAbscess, peritonitis
  5. PreventLifestyle, colonoscopy

Diverticulitis (2)

If there isTreat with
Uncomplicated, immunocompetent, mildNo ABX: liquids, paracetamol, review within 7 days (AVOD, DIABOLO)
Uncomplicated at riskABX: CRP over 140 mg/L, WBC over 15 × 10⁹/L, vomiting, symptoms over 5 days, long segment or fluid on CT
Immunosuppression or frailtyABX, with a low threshold to admit and operate
Abscess under 4–5 cmABX
Abscess 4–5 cm or moreABX and percutaneous drainage
Gas by the colonABX, observe
Purulent or fecal peritonitisResection: anastomosis with or without a stoma if stable; Hartmann procedure if critical
Fistula or strictureElective resection

Antibiotics

  • OralAmoxicillin-clavulanate; a fluoroquinolone with metronidazole only if it cannot be used
  • IVCeftriaxone with metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam
  • Why not a fluoroquinolone firstC. difficile, tendon, aortic, and nerve harm, without better outcomes

Elective surgery

  • Not forNumber of attacks or young age alone
  • ForPersistent symptoms, fistula, stricture, immunosuppression, quality of life
  • After an abscessOffer, not routine; recurrence is higher
  • WhichResect to the upper rectum, minimally invasive

Bleeding (3)

  • ResuscitateTransfuse to hemoglobin of 70–80 g/L or more; reverse as needed
  • Stop itClip or band at colonoscopy; embolize; colectomy if not
  • Stop drugsNSAIDs for good; keep aspirin only for secondary prevention
  • RecursIn about a third

Prevention

  • DoFiber, activity, normal weight, no smoking
  • AvoidNSAIDs when possible; mesalazine and rifaximin do not prevent it
  • EatNuts, seeds, and popcorn are safe
  • ColonoscopyAfter 6–8 weeks if not done recently
  • SCADMesalazine if symptoms, usually settles

Be careful with

  • NSAIDs
  • Opioids
  • Colonoscopy in an attack
  • Immunosuppression
  • Fluoroquinolones
  • Enemas

Treat the cause

  • 1DiverticulosisNo treatment needed; a high-fiber diet is reasonable
  • 2DiverticulitisBy stage, as above
  • 3Diverticular bleedingEndoscopy, embolization, surgery
  • 4Meckel diverticulumResect if it causes symptoms; if found by chance, favored by age under 50, male sex, length over 2 cm, a band, or palpable ectopic tissue

Guidelines differ: The WSES and AGA omit antibiotics in selected uncomplicated cases, and many surgeons still prescribe them.
