Review article

Diverticular diseases: from pressure-driven outpouching to inflammation

Increased sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure pushes the mucosa and submucosa out through the muscularis externa, forming diverticula. Diverticulitis follows when a fecalith obstructs a diverticulum. LLQ pain is the main symptom, and complications include LGIB, abscess, enterovesical fistula, and perforation. Here, we review their mechanisms and management, and consider how they relate to ischemic colitis, IBD, and IBS.

Key points

  • Low-fiber diet, constipation, obesity, and older age raise sigmoid pressure.
  • Suspected diverticulitis is evaluated with CT AP with contrast.
  • Avoid colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis; perform it 6–8 weeks after recovery.
  • Treatment follows the complication, and severity is monitored for potential colectomy.

Pathophysiology

Low fiber and constipation increase sigmoid intraluminal pressure, which pushes mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis externa where the vasa recta enter, forming false diverticula. A vessel beside a diverticulum can bleed, causing LGIB with hematochezia. A fecalith can obstruct a diverticulum, and the back pressure and bacterial colonization that follow cause diverticulitis with LLQ pain. An inflamed diverticulum can rupture, causing abscess, pneumoperitoneum, and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Diverticulosis follows a low-fiber diet, constipation, obesity, and older age, which increase sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure and form diverticula. In diverticulitis, a fecalith obstructs a diverticulum, causing increased back pressure and bacterial colonization, with LLQ pain and inflammation. Diverticulosis affects over half of people over 60 and is left-sided in up to 90% in Western countries, but only ~4% develop diverticulitis. Meckel diverticulum forms when the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct fails to close and is the most common congenital GI anomaly. Its rule of 2s is 2% of people, 2% symptomatic, under age 2, males twice as often, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, up to 2 inches long, and 2 types of ectopic tissue. Acid from ectopic gastric mucosa causes painless rectal bleeding, currant jelly or brick-colored in children, and accounts for ~50% of LGIB under age 2; in adults, small bowel obstruction is the most common complication, and intussusception also occurs.

Clinical presentation and complications

The main symptom is LLQ pain. Complications are LGIB (hematochezia), abscess (persistent pain and fever refractory to treatment), enterovesical fistula (pneumaturia, fecaluria, UTI), and perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis). Diverticulosis is usually asymptomatic, while diverticulitis causes LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Diverticular bleeding is painless and comes from the right colon in 50–90%. Pylephlebitis, a septic portal or mesenteric vein clot, carries a mortality of up to 25%, and up to 30% have a recurrence after a first episode.

Diagnosis

Perforation is evaluated by abdominal x-ray and CT AP, bleeding by colonoscopy, and suspected diverticulitis by CT AP with contrast. Colonoscopy is avoided during acute diverticulitis and performed 6–8 weeks after recovery. Diverticulitis shows leukocytosis and high CRP. Meckel diverticulum is shown by a Meckel scan, in which technetium-99m is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa.

Management

Perforation is treated by laparotomy, bleeding by colonoscopy, abscess by ABX, percutaneous drainage, and surgery, fistula by surgery, and infection by ABX. Otherwise, fiber intake is increased. Severity is monitored for potential colectomy. Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated as an outpatient with a liquid diet and paracetamol rather than NSAIDs, with ABX (amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a fluoroquinolone with metronidazole, for 7–10 days) if the patient is immunocompromised, comorbid, or has a CRP over 140. Fever, inability to keep hydrated, immunocompromise, or comorbidity calls for admission and IV ABX. Perforation is treated by laparotomy with a Hartmann procedure or primary anastomosis. Nuts and seeds are safe, and a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is excised.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause LLQ pain and hematochezia, but diverticular bleeding is typically painless, whereas ischemic colitis causes pain with bleeding after hypoperfusion.

. Enterovesical fistula with pneumaturia, fecaluria, and UTI occurs in both.

. The mechanisms mirror each other: a fecalith obstructs a blind pouch, and pressure and infection follow. Diverticulitis causes LLQ pain, and appendicitis RLQ pain.

. Both can cause pain and altered bowel habit, but IBS has no structural damage.

Both are lifelong, relapsing inflammation in people with genetic risk; goes through the wall in patches anywhere, and stays in the mucosa in one sheet from the rectum.

Review article

Inflammatory bowel disease: contrasting Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis

IBD comprises Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, which differ in location, depth, and lesion pattern. Crohn disease occurs anywhere in the GIT with transmural skip lesions, whereas ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and confined to the colon. Their complications therefore differ, while extraintestinal features overlap. Here, we review their pathology, etiology, complications, and stepwise treatment, and consider how they relate to IBS, malabsorption, and PSC.

Key points

  • Crohn disease is transmural with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum.
  • Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn disease and decreases the risk of ulcerative colitis.
  • Fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP rule out IBS.
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis occurs only in ulcerative colitis among the extraintestinal features listed.

Pathophysiology

Genes and environment cause immune dysregulation, with Th1 predominating in Crohn disease and Th2 in ulcerative colitis, and the result is chronic inflammation. Crohn disease involves every layer of the wall, in skip lesions, so tracts through the wall form enterovesical, enteroenteral, and enterocutaneous fistulas, and scarring causes small bowel obstruction. Ulcerative colitis spreads continuously from the rectum, causing bloody diarrhea. Chronic inflammation raises the risk of colorectal cancer.

Pathology

Crohn disease occurs anywhere in the GIT, most commonly in the ileum, is rectum-sparing, and causes RLQ pain. Lesions skip, diarrhea is watery and bloody in flare-ups, ulcers are transmural with deep fissures, mesenteric fat creeps around the bowel (fat wrapping), granulomas may be present, and there is Th1 dysregulation. Ulcerative colitis involves the colon only, starts at the rectum, and causes LLQ pain. Lesions are continuous, diarrhea is bloody (hematochezia), ulcers are submucosal, there are no granulomas, and there is Th2 dysregulation.

Etiology and mechanisms

Crohn disease is associated with family history, NOD-2 mutations, Western diet, and smoking. Ulcerative colitis is associated with family history, HLA DRB1, and Western diet, and smoking decreases risk, so the risk rises in recent ex-smokers, whereas smoking raises the risk of Crohn disease.

Clinical presentation and complications

In Crohn disease, malabsorption is especially marked when the ileum is involved. Decreased fat absorption causes steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, and increased free oxalate levels with nephrolithiasis from oxalate. Decreased B12 absorption causes anemia. Decreased enterohepatic circulation decreases bile salt recycling and increases cholesterol, causing cholelithiasis. Fistulas and abscesses include enterovesical fistula (pneumaturia, fecaluria, UTI), enteroenteral fistula (diarrhea), enterocutaneous fistula (increased drainage), and perianal abscesses. Strictures cause small bowel obstruction with cramping, abdominal pain and distention, vomiting, and obstipation. In ulcerative colitis, colitis causes pain, fever, and bloody stools, and decreased myenteric plexus activity leads to megacolon, tenesmus, and perforation; chronic inflammation leads to colorectal cancer. Extraintestinal features are arthralgia, uveitis, pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, hypercoagulability (VTE, DVT, PE), and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Crohn disease also causes oral aphthous ulcers, and at least 5% of patients with ulcerative colitis develop colorectal cancer over time. Toxic megacolon follows severe colitis, usually ulcerative colitis or C. difficile, and can be precipitated by opioids, anticholinergics, and antimotility drugs. It requires a colon over 6 cm on x-ray, at least 3 of fever over 38 °C, heart rate over 120, neutrophilia, or anemia, and 1 of dehydration, confusion, electrolyte disturbance, or hypotension; it is the leading cause of death in ulcerative colitis.

Diagnosis

Perforation and small bowel obstruction are evaluated by abdominal x-ray, and nephrolithiasis or cholelithiasis by ultrasound. IBS is ruled out with fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP, and infectious diarrhea with stool culture, O&P, and C. diff. Otherwise, ileocolonoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy is obtained. In Crohn disease, colonoscopy shows skip lesions and cobblestone mucosa, noncaseating granulomas are found in up to 33%, small bowel follow-through shows a string sign from stricture or spasm, and ASCA is more common. In ulcerative colitis, colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum, friable mucosa, and pseudopolyps, biopsy shows cryptitis, crypt distortion, and crypt abscesses, a barium enema in longstanding disease shows a stove-pipe, or lead-pipe, colon, and p-ANCA is positive in 60–70%. Colonoscopy surveillance for colorectal cancer is done every 1–2 years in ulcerative colitis.

Management

Treatment moves up a pyramid with severity. 5-ASA and sulfasalazine are maintenance for ulcerative colitis; corticosteroids (prednisone, budesonide) are for induction and flare-ups; immunomodulators (AZA, 6-MP, MTX) are maintenance for Crohn disease; biological therapy comprises certolizumab, infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, and vedolizumab; and surgery is the top tier. Colectomy cures ulcerative colitis and is used for failed medical therapy, fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, or dysplasia. Toxic megacolon is treated with an IV corticosteroid for 3 days, then infliximab or cyclosporine for 3 days, and subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy if this fails. Crohn disease is treated surgically by resection or stricturoplasty for complications, and recurs at the anastomosis in ~90%.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause pain and altered bowel habit, but IBS has no structural damage and normal inflammatory markers.

. Ileal Crohn disease produces the same fat, B12, and bile salt losses.

. Most PSC patients have IBD, usually ulcerative colitis, and the combination raises colorectal cancer risk.

. Bloody diarrhea overlaps, so infection is excluded before IBD is diagnosed.

. Ileal disease leads to cholesterol gallstones through lost bile salts.

Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)

Pathophysiology

The bowel looks normal, but signals between gut and brain are disturbed: nerves are oversensitive, motility and secretion change, and the microbiome is altered.

  1. TriggerFood, infection, stress
  2. Sensitive nervesNormal gas hurts
  3. Brain amplifiesPain, worry
  4. Motility changesDiarrhea or constipation
  5. SymptomsPain tied to stool

The gut-brain loop

  • AGas and contentsPoorly absorbed sugars ferment and stretch the bowel
  • BVisceral hypersensitivityMast cells and serotonin near nerves make them fire early
  • CBrainStress, anxiety, and attention turn up the signal
  • DMotility and secretionFast in IBS-D, slow in IBS-C

What else contributes

  • InfectionAbout 1 in 10 after gastroenteritis
  • MicrobiomeLess varied; methane slows transit
  • Bile saltsIn up to a third of IBS-D
  • BarrierMore leaky after infection
  • Genes and early lifeFamily history, adverse events

Note: IBS is a real disorder with a normal colonoscopy, so it is neither imagined nor a diagnosis by exclusion.

Etiology

There is no single cause; the subtype, set by stool form on days with abnormal stools, guides treatment.

Subtypes

  • 1IBS-DLoose stools in over a quarter, hard in under a quarter
  • 2IBS-CHard stools in over a quarter, loose in under a quarter
  • 3IBS-MBoth in over a quarter
  • 4IBS-UMeets the criteria, but the pattern fits none
  • 5PostinfectiousStarts after gastroenteritis, often diarrhea

  • Age and sexUsually under 50; women more
  • ConditionsAnxiety, depression, fibromyalgia, migraine, reflux, dyspepsia
  • GastroenteritisSevere, prolonged, or in anxious people
  • FoodFODMAPs, fat, caffeine, alcohol
  • Life eventsStress, childhood adversity

Symptoms and complications

  1. Recurrent painTied to stool
  2. Change in stoolFrequency or form
  3. BloatingWorse by evening
  4. FlaresStress, food
  5. Chronic, not harmfulNormal life span

The pattern

  • PainLower abdomen, better or worse with defecation
  • StoolUrgency, mucus, incomplete emptying
  • BloatingDistention through the day
  • Outside the gutFatigue, back pain, headache, urinary urgency
  • Not typicalWaking at night, weight loss, blood

Alarm features

  • Onset at 50 or older
  • Blood in the stool
  • Fever
  • Nocturnal diarrhea
  • Weight loss
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • High CRP or calprotectin
  • Family history of cancer, IBD, or celiac disease

How severe

  • IBS severity scoreTracks pain, bloating, and life impact
  • MildDiet and advice
  • ModerateAdd drugs
  • SevereTeam care, psychology

Complications

  • Quality of lifeWork loss, isolation
  • Anxiety and depressionBoth directions
  • Restrictive eatingOver-strict diets
  • Needless surgeryGallbladder, appendix, or uterus removed without relief
  • Opioid harmNarcotic bowel syndrome
  • No cancer riskLife span is normal

Diagnosis

Make a positive diagnosis by symptoms with a few tests, not by excluding everything.

  1. SymptomsRome V
  2. Alarm featuresColonoscopy if any
  3. Few testsFBC, CRP, celiac, calprotectin
  4. SubtypeStool chart
  5. ExplainThen treat

  • Pain or discomfortRecurrent, not continuous, at least 3 days a month
  • With 2 or moreRelated to defecation; a change in stool frequency; a change in stool form
  • DurationFor 3 months, with onset at least 6 months earlier
  • In womenNot only with periods
  • In clinical practiceNot part of Rome V: a diagnosis can be made after weeks of typical symptoms once alarm features and first tests are clear

Explain the disorder, start with diet and simple drugs for the worst symptom, then add gut-brain treatment.

Review article

Irritable bowel syndrome: a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural damage

IBS is a type of DGBI that stems from visceral hypersensitivity, altered microbiome, and hypermotility, with a lack of structural damage. Patients have recurrent abdominal pain with a predominant bowel pattern of diarrhea, constipation, or both. Diagnosis uses the Rome V criteria. Here, we review its mechanisms, diagnosis, and symptom-directed treatment, and consider how it is distinguished from IBD.

Key points

  • IBS has no structural damage.
  • Rome V requires recurrent pain for at least 3 days per month with 2 of 3 criteria.
  • Treatment is directed at the dominant symptom.

Pathophysiology

There is no structural damage. An altered microbiome turns carbohydrates into gas, and gas and osmotic effects stimulate stretch receptors, causing reflex contraction. Visceral hypersensitivity means the CNS amplifies these signals, causing abdominal pain, and hypermotility causes diarrhea.

Etiology and mechanisms

In visceral hypersensitivity, psychiatric disorders, fibromyalgia, depression, and anxiety increase CNS amplification of stretch receptor stimulation from osmotic effects of carbohydrates, causing abdominal pain. In altered microbiome, the gut microbiome metabolizes carbohydrates into gas, which stimulates stretch receptors and reflex contraction, causing abdominal pain. In hypermotility, increased gut motility causes diarrhea.

Clinical presentation and complications

The predominant bowel pattern is abdominal pain with diarrhea, constipation, or mixed. Alarm features that point to another cause are onset at 50 or older, blood in the stool, fever or night sweats, nocturnal diarrhea, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, high CRP or fecal calprotectin, a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD, or celiac disease, and recent ABX.

Diagnosis

The Rome V criteria require recurrent but not continuous abdominal pain or discomfort for at least 3 days per month, and 2 of the following: related to defecation, changes in stool frequency, and changes in stool appearance. Diarrhea is evaluated by fecal calprotectin, ESR/CRP, O&P, C. diff, and colonoscopy with biopsy. Diarrhea also calls for celiac serology with total IgA, and alarm features call for colonoscopy with random biopsies of the left and right colon.

Management

Triggers are reduced with a low FODMAP diet. Abdominal pain is treated with antispasmodics such as dicyclomine first, then peppermint oil, then TCAs, with rifaximin if these fail. Constipation is treated with PEG first, then lubiprostone, linaclotide, or plecanitide. Diarrhea is treated with loperamide, then rifaximin or eluxadoline, which is avoided after cholecystectomy, and alosetron for women with severe disease, which carries a risk of ischemic colitis. Soluble fiber such as psyllium, not insoluble fiber, improves global symptoms, and psychological therapy helps refractory disease.

Relationships to other conditions

. Inflammatory markers separate them: fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP are normal in IBS.

. Carbohydrates drive symptoms in both, through osmotic effects and gas. Celiac disease must be excluded when symptoms suggest IBS.

. Alarm features (iron-deficiency anemia, rectal bleeding, weight loss, and nocturnal symptoms) call for further investigation.

Acute Diarrhea

Pathophysiology

An organism or its toxin makes the bowel secrete water, stop absorbing it, or bleed, and which of these happens shapes the illness.

  1. Ingested organism or toxinFood, water, hands, or soil
  2. Toxin, villus damage, or invasionSmall bowel or colon
  3. DiarrheaWatery or bloody
FeatureNon-inflammatoryInflammatory
SiteSmall bowelColon
StoolsWatery, large volumeSmall volume, with blood and mucus (dysentery)
Fever and tenesmusUncommonCommon
Fecal WBC and calprotectinNormalIncreased
MechanismToxins (A) or villus damage (B)Invasion or cell-killing toxins (C)
Causes1, 2, 3, and some 74, 5, 6, and some 7

How pathogens bring water into the stool

  • AToxinsCholera toxin and ETEC toxins increase cAMP or cGMP → CFTR opens and Na+ absorption falls → Cl− and water pour into the lumen → painless watery stools
  • BVillus damageViruses, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium damage or cover the villi → fewer absorptive cells and brush border enzymes → water and lactose stay in the lumen → watery stools
  • CInvasionBacteria or amebae invade the colonic mucosa, or Shiga toxin kills its cells → neutrophils, ulcers, and bleeding → bloody, mucoid stools with fever

Note: Diarrhea is 3 or more loose stools in 24 hours: acute under 2 weeks, persistent at 2–4 weeks, and chronic from 4 weeks, which is covered on Chronic Diarrhea.

Etiology

The time from exposure to symptoms points to the organism: toxins already in food act within hours, organisms that must grow first take days, and parasites take weeks.

  • 1Preformed toxinS. aureus and B. cereus (vomiting type): toxin already in the food (A), so vomiting starts within hours
  • 2Toxin made in the gutB. cereus (diarrheal type), ETEC, and V. cholerae: bacteria colonize, then secrete toxin (A)
  • 3VirusesNorovirus and rotavirus: villus damage (B)
  • 4Invasive bacteriaNontyphoidal Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter invade the mucosa (C); Salmonella Typhi causes enteric fever
  • 5STECShiga toxin kills colonic and glomerular endothelial cells (C)
  • 6C. difficileToxins A and B (C) after ABX disturb the colonic flora; a gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing anaerobic bacillus
  • 7ParasitesGiardia and Cryptosporidium (B), E. histolytica (C), and Strongyloides

Symptoms and complications

  1. ExposureHours to weeks
  2. Vomiting or diarrheaWatery or bloody
  3. Fluid lossWorst at 1–3 days
  4. RecoveryWithin 1–2 weeks
  5. ComplicationUncommon

Patterns of illness

  • Vomiting within hours, without feverPreformed toxin (1)
  • Vomiting and watery diarrhea in an outbreakNorovirus or rotavirus (3)
  • Large, watery stools without blood or feverToxins made in the gut (2), Giardia, or Cryptosporidium (7)
  • Fever, tenesmus, and small, bloody stoolsInvasion (4, 6) or E. histolytica (7)
  • Bloody diarrhea with little or no feverSTEC (5)
  • Bloating, flatulence, and greasy stoolsGiardia (7)

Complications

  • Fluid lossHypovolemia, hypokalemia, and NAGMA from HCO3− lost in stool, worst in infants and older adults
  • Severe colitis (4, 5, 6)Toxic megacolon and perforation
  • Reactive arthritis (4, 5)A sterile arthritis that follows Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or STEC, sometimes with conjunctivitis and urethritis; most patients are HLA-B27-positive
  • After the infectionPostinfectious IBS, and lactose intolerance until the brush border recovers

Complications by cause

  • 2CholeraIsotonic fluid loss causes shock within hours, hypokalemia with cramps, metabolic acidosis with Kussmaul breathing, and hypoglycemia with seizures in children; over half die untreated, and under 1% with treatment
  • 3Norovirus and rotavirusDehydration in infants and older adults; illness lasting months in immunocompromised patients; rotavirus occasionally causes seizures or encephalopathy
  • 4CampylobacterGuillain-Barré syndrome: antibodies against the organism cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerves (molecular mimicry), causing ascending weakness with lost reflexes weeks later; inflammation of the terminal ileum and cecum mimics appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis)
  • 4Nontyphoidal SalmonellaBacteremia in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised patients, seeding bone (osteomyelitis, typically in sickle cell disease), heart valves (endocarditis), and atherosclerotic arteries (mycotic aneurysm)
  • 4Enteric feverIntestinal perforation, sepsis, and meningitis if treatment is delayed; chronic carriers keep the organism in the gallbladder, spreading it and raising their risk of gallbladder cancer
  • 4ShigellaFebrile seizures in young children; HUS from Shiga toxin, mainly S. dysenteriae type 1; rectal prolapse, toxic megacolon, and a leukemoid reaction
  • 5STECHUS 5–13 days after the diarrhea starts, mostly in children under 5: Shiga toxin injures glomerular endothelium, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI
  • 6C. difficilePseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, and septic shock; about 25% recur within 30 days; 3–5% of healthy adults carry it without disease
  • 7GiardiaChronic infection with malabsorption and weight loss; lactose intolerance for weeks after the parasite clears
  • 7CryptosporidiumIn HIV with a CD4 count under 50/µL, spread to the bile ducts and pancreas (sclerosing cholangitis, acalculous cholecystitis, and pancreatitis)
  • 7E. histolyticaAmebic liver abscess 2–4 weeks later, with fever and RUQ pain, mostly in men aged 18–50 and often without diarrhea; colitis mistaken for IBD worsens with corticosteroids
  • 7StrongyloidesHyperinfection syndrome: corticosteroids, other immunosuppressants, or HTLV-1 speed up autoinfection, and masses of larvae leave the bowel carrying gut bacteria, causing gram-negative sepsis, meningitis, and periumbilical purpura, often without eosinophilia; mortality is high

Diagnosis

Most acute diarrhea needs no tests; the history, the stool, and how sick the patient is decide who does.

  1. How sick?Dehydration, sepsis
  2. Exposure and onsetFood, travel, ABX
  3. Blood or fever?Test
  4. Right testPCR, culture, toxin
  5. Treat or watchMost settle

Who to test

  • Mild watery diarrhea, eating and drinkingNo tests; most settle by themselves
  • Fever, blood, severe illness, dehydration, persistent symptoms, immunocompromise, or an outbreakStool multiplex PCR or culture, fecal WBC or calprotectin, and O&P
  • Bloody stoolsShiga toxin testing as well, with FBC and BMP for HUS
  • Recent ABX or a hospital stay, or diarrhea starting after 3 days in hospitalC. difficile testing instead of a routine stool culture
  • HypovolemiaBMP for K+, HCO3−, and creatinine

SevereDrowsy, cold, weak pulse, no urine, hypotension

Red flags

  • Shock
  • Bloody stool
  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Severe pain
  • Age over 70 or infant
  • Immune deficiency
  • Over 7 days

ForFavored byObtain

Find the cause

  • 1Preformed toxinOnset after a shared meal is enough; food or vomit is tested only in outbreaks
  • 2Toxin made in the gutCholera: stool culture, the gold standard, or rapid tests in outbreaks; ETEC: molecular tests for its toxin genes
  • 3VirusesStool PCR or antigen, mainly to control outbreaks
  • 4Invasive bacteriaStool culture or PCR, with culture for sensitivities; blood cultures if Salmonella and high risk (infant, over 50, immunosuppressed); enteric fever: blood or bone marrow culture
  • 5STECShiga toxin testing of every bloody stool; FBC, blood film, and creatinine over the following days for HUS
  • 6C. difficileLiquid stool only, in 2 steps: GDH or NAAT, such as a stool multiplex PCR, then toxin A and B, since carriers are positive on the first step alone
  • 7ParasitesGiardia and E. histolytica: antigen or PCR; Cryptosporidium: modified acid-fast stain or PCR; Strongyloides: serology, and screen before immunosuppression; liver abscess: imaging and serology

Note: Routine O&P misses Cryptosporidium, so it is requested specifically.

Treatment

Replace fluid first, use antibiotics only when the organism or the illness calls for them, and stop spread.

  1. RehydrateORS first
  2. ElectrolytesK+, HCO3−
  3. ABX?Severe, dysentery, some organisms
  4. Antimotility?Only watery, no fever
  5. PreventSoap, vaccine

For every cause

  • HypovolemiaORS (salt, water, and glucose, absorbed together by the sodium-glucose cotransporter), or IV fluids if severe or vomiting prevents drinking
  • Watery diarrhea without fever or bloodLoperamide if needed; in dysentery, STEC, or C. difficile it holds organisms and toxins in the colon
  • Dysentery, high fever, severe illness, older age, or immunocompromiseEmpirical ABX: azithromycin first-line, because fluoroquinolone resistance is common; children get ceftriaxone or azithromycin
  • Traveler's diarrheaMild: ORS and loperamide; severe or dysentery: azithromycin
  • Preventing spreadHand washing with soap and water, and contact precautions until 48 hours after symptoms stop

C. difficile (6) by severity

LevelPictureTreatment
NonsevereWBC 15 × 10⁹/L or less and creatinine stablePO fidaxomicin, or PO vancomycin
SevereWBC over 15 × 10⁹/L or creatinine over 1.5 times baselinePO fidaxomicin, or PO vancomycin
FulminantShock, ileus, or megacolonHigh-dose PO vancomycin with IV metronidazole, rectal vancomycin if ileus, and a surgeon early
First recurrenceWithin 8 weeksFidaxomicin, or vancomycin taper
Second recurrenceThird episodeFecal microbiota treatment after ABX

Be careful with

  • Loperamide in dysentery
  • ABX in STEC
  • Fluoroquinolone: resistance, tendon
  • Alcohol gel: not for spores or norovirus
  • PPIs increase the risk of C. difficile
  • No test of cure for C. difficile

Treat the cause

  • 1Preformed toxinFluids alone; ABX do not help, since the toxin is already formed
  • 2Toxin made in the gutCholera: rapid ORS, or IV Hartmann solution in shock, replacing the deficit within 3–4 hours, plus doxycycline (azithromycin as an alternative) and zinc for children; ETEC: as for traveler's diarrhea
  • 3VirusesSupportive; soap and water, since alcohol gel works poorly against norovirus, and bleach for surfaces; rotavirus vaccine prevents disease in infants
  • 4Invasive bacteriaNontyphoidal Salmonella: no ABX if healthy; enteric fever: ceftriaxone or azithromycin; Shigella: azithromycin or ciprofloxacin, guided by resistance; Campylobacter: azithromycin if severe
  • 5STECNo ABX or loperamide, which raise the risk of HUS; fluids, with blood or dialysis if HUS develops
  • 6C. difficileStop unnecessary ABX; PO fidaxomicin is first-line, or PO vancomycin; metronidazole only in fulminant disease; by severity as above; wash hands with soap, since alcohol gel does not kill spores
  • 7ParasitesGiardia: tinidazole or metronidazole; Cryptosporidium: support, and ART in HIV; E. histolytica: metronidazole, then paromomycin for cysts; Strongyloides: ivermectin

Guidelines differ: For C. difficile, the AGA favors fidaxomicin, while the ASID uses vancomycin in place of metronidazole and gives fidaxomicin an emerging role.

Review article

Acute diarrhea: timing, mechanism, and the organisms behind infectious gastroenteritis

Acute diarrhea lasts under 2 weeks and is mostly infectious. The interval from exposure to symptoms separates preformed toxins, which act within hours, from toxins made in the gut, viruses, and invasive bacteria, which take days, and from parasites, which take weeks. Non-inflammatory disease of the small bowel produces large, watery stools, whereas inflammatory disease of the colon produces dysentery with increased fecal WBC and calprotectin. Most illness settles with rehydration alone, but specific organisms carry distinctive complications, from HUS after STEC to hyperinfection after Strongyloides. Here, we review the organisms, their acquisition, incubation, and presentation, and the workup and management of acute diarrhea.

Key points

  • Onset within hours points to a preformed toxin, onset after days to toxins made in the gut, viruses, or invasive bacteria, and onset after weeks to parasites.
  • Watery, large-volume stools come from toxins or villus damage in the small bowel; dysentery comes from invasion of the colon.
  • STEC causes bloody diarrhea with little fever, and ABX and loperamide are avoided because they increase the risk of HUS.
  • Campylobacter can be followed by Guillain-Barré syndrome, and Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, and STEC by reactive arthritis.
  • Strongyloides persists for decades by autoinfection and can cause fatal hyperinfection when corticosteroids are given, so people at risk are screened first.

Pathophysiology

Diarrhea is 3 or more loose stools in 24 hours; it is acute under 2 weeks, persistent at 2–4 weeks, and chronic from 4 weeks. An ingested organism or toxin brings water into the stool in one of three ways. Toxins such as cholera toxin and the ETEC toxins increase cAMP or cGMP, opening CFTR and decreasing Na+ absorption, so that Cl− and water pour into the lumen and painless watery stools follow. Viruses, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium damage or cover the villi, leaving fewer absorptive cells and brush border enzymes, so that water and lactose stay in the lumen. Invasive bacteria and amebae enter the colonic mucosa, or Shiga toxin kills its cells, bringing neutrophils, ulcers, and bleeding, with bloody, mucoid stools and fever.

The first two mechanisms produce non-inflammatory diarrhea, which arises in the small bowel, with watery, large-volume stools, uncommon fever and tenesmus, and normal fecal WBC and calprotectin. The third produces inflammatory diarrhea, which arises in the colon, with small-volume stools containing blood and mucus (dysentery), common fever and tenesmus, and increased fecal WBC and calprotectin.

Etiology and mechanisms

The time from exposure to symptoms points to the organism, because a toxin already in food acts within hours, an organism that must grow first takes days, and a parasite takes weeks. Seven groups follow in order of onset.

Preformed toxin. S. aureus contaminates food handled by a carrier and then left unrefrigerated, such as processed meats, mayonnaise salads, and cream pastries; sudden vomiting and cramps without fever begin 30 minutes to 8 hours later and settle within 24 hours. The vomiting type of B. cereus comes from rice or other starchy food left at room temperature, even when reheated, and causes nausea and vomiting 30 minutes to 6 hours later, also settling within 24 hours.

Toxin made in the gut. Here bacteria colonize and then secrete toxin. The diarrheal type of B. cereus comes from meat, vegetables, and sauces left at room temperature and causes watery diarrhea and cramps, with little vomiting, after 6–15 hours. ETEC, the most common cause of traveler's diarrhea, is acquired from fecally contaminated food and water and causes watery diarrhea and cramps for a few days after 16 hours to 3 days. V. cholerae is acquired from contaminated water and seafood, after disasters and in crowded camps; because gastric acid kills it, a large dose is needed. After a few hours to 5 days it causes painless rice-water stools and vomiting without fever, with shock within hours in severe cases.

Viruses. Norovirus, the most common cause of gastroenteritis, spreads person to person, through contaminated food (oysters, fruit, and vegetables), and on surfaces, with outbreaks on cruise ships and in hospitals, schools, and nursing homes; a few particles infect. Sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea begin after 1–2 days and settle in 1–3 days. Rotavirus spreads on hands and surfaces among unvaccinated children under 5, often in childcare, and after 1–3 days causes vomiting first, then profuse watery diarrhea, with fever in a third, lasting 5–7 days.

Invasive bacteria. Nontyphoidal Salmonella comes from undercooked poultry and eggs, unpasteurized milk, and reptiles and other pets, and after 8–72 hours causes fever, cramps, and diarrhea, sometimes bloody; fever settles in 2–3 days and diarrhea in 4–10. Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi are spread through food and water contaminated by human carriers, in or after travel to South Asia or sub-Saharan Africa, and after 6–30 days cause enteric fever, with gradual fever, headache, abdominal pain, rose spots, relative bradycardia, and hepatosplenomegaly, and diarrhea in only some patients. Shigella has humans as its only reservoir and spreads person to person (childcare, crowding, and sex between men) and through food and water; 10–100 organisms cause disease, and after 1–4 days fever, cramps, and tenesmus are followed by bloody, mucoid diarrhea that settles in 5–7 days. Campylobacter comes from undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, untreated water, and sick puppies, and after 1–3 days, or up to a week, a prodrome of high fever and aches is followed by cramps and up to 10 stools a day, often bloody, for about 7 days.

STEC. STEC, such as O157:H7, is carried without illness by cattle and acquired from undercooked beef, unpasteurized milk, and produce or water contaminated by their manure, and at petting zoos. After 3–4 days (range 1–10), painful watery diarrhea turns bloody over 1–3 days, with little or no fever, and settles in about a week. Its Shiga toxin kills colonic and glomerular endothelial cells.

C. difficile. C. difficile, a gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing anaerobic bacillus, spreads as spores on hands and surfaces in hospitals and takes hold when ABX disturb the colonic flora, especially clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and penicillins. During or within 2 weeks of the course, its toxins A and B cause watery diarrhea, cramps, fever, and leukocytosis, ranging from mild diarrhea to pseudomembranous colitis.

Parasites. Giardia is acquired from untreated stream water, swimming, childcare, and sex between men, and as few as 10 cysts infect; after 1–2 weeks it causes bloating, flatulence, and foul, greasy stools without blood that can last weeks. Cryptosporidium is acquired from swimming pools, because its oocysts resist chlorine, as well as from farm animals, childcare, and sex between men; after about 7 days (2–28) it causes watery diarrhea that is self-limited in healthy people but chronic and wasting in advanced HIV. E. histolytica is acquired from food and water contaminated with cysts in endemic regions (India, Africa, Mexico, and Central and South America) and through oral-anal sex; 90% of infections cause no symptoms, and colitis develops gradually over several weeks, with cramps, weight loss, and watery or bloody diarrhea. Strongyloides larvae in soil penetrate bare skin in the tropics, and infection is seen in migrants, refugees, and returned travelers and soldiers; autoinfection lets it persist for decades, often with eosinophilia alone, or with epigastric pain, diarrhea, a creeping rash (larva currens), and cough.

Clinical presentation and complications

The pattern of illness narrows the cause. Vomiting within hours without fever suggests a preformed toxin, and vomiting with watery diarrhea in an outbreak suggests norovirus or rotavirus. Large, watery stools without blood or fever suggest a toxin made in the gut, Giardia, or Cryptosporidium. Fever, tenesmus, and small, bloody stools suggest an invasive organism, C. difficile, or E. histolytica, whereas bloody diarrhea with little or no fever suggests STEC. Bloating, flatulence, and greasy stools suggest Giardia.

Any cause can produce hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and NAGMA from HCO3− lost in stool, worst in infants and older adults. Severe colitis from invasive bacteria, STEC, or C. difficile can lead to toxic megacolon and perforation. Reactive arthritis, a sterile arthritis sometimes accompanied by conjunctivitis and urethritis, follows Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or STEC, and most patients are HLA-B27-positive. After the infection, postinfectious IBS can persist, and lactose intolerance lasts until the brush border recovers.

Each organism also has its own complications. Cholera causes isotonic fluid loss with shock within hours, hypokalemia with cramps, metabolic acidosis with Kussmaul breathing, and hypoglycemia with seizures in children; over half of untreated patients die, and under 1% with treatment. Norovirus and rotavirus dehydrate infants and older adults, illness can last months in immunocompromised patients, and rotavirus occasionally causes seizures or encephalopathy. Campylobacter can be followed weeks later by Guillain-Barré syndrome, because antibodies against the organism cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerves (molecular mimicry), causing ascending weakness with lost reflexes; inflammation of the terminal ileum and cecum can also mimic appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis). Nontyphoidal Salmonella causes bacteremia in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised patients, seeding bone (osteomyelitis, typically in sickle cell disease), heart valves (endocarditis), and atherosclerotic arteries (mycotic aneurysm). Delayed treatment of enteric fever risks intestinal perforation, sepsis, and meningitis, and chronic carriers keep the organism in the gallbladder, spreading it and increasing their risk of gallbladder cancer. Shigella causes febrile seizures in young children, HUS from Shiga toxin, mainly S. dysenteriae type 1, rectal prolapse, toxic megacolon, and a leukemoid reaction.

STEC causes HUS 5–13 days after the diarrhea starts, mostly in children under 5, as Shiga toxin injures glomerular endothelium, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI. C. difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, and septic shock; about 25% of patients relapse within 30 days, and 3–5% of healthy adults carry it without disease. Giardia can become chronic, with malabsorption and weight loss, and leaves lactose intolerance for weeks after it clears. In HIV with a CD4 count under 50/µL, Cryptosporidium spreads to the bile ducts and pancreas, causing sclerosing cholangitis, acalculous cholecystitis, and pancreatitis. E. histolytica causes amebic liver abscess 2–4 weeks later, with fever and RUQ pain, mostly in men aged 18–50 and often without diarrhea, and amebic colitis mistaken for IBD worsens with corticosteroids. In Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome, corticosteroids, other immunosuppressants, or HTLV-1 speed up autoinfection, and masses of larvae leave the bowel carrying gut bacteria, causing gram-negative sepsis, meningitis, and periumbilical purpura, often without eosinophilia and with high mortality.

Diagnosis

Mild watery diarrhea in a patient who is eating and drinking needs no tests, because most cases settle by themselves. Fever, blood, severe illness, dehydration, persistent symptoms, immunocompromise, or an outbreak call for a stool multiplex PCR or culture, fecal WBC or calprotectin, and O&P; routine O&P misses Cryptosporidium, so it is requested specifically. Bloody stools are also tested for Shiga toxin, with FBC and BMP for HUS. Recent ABX or a hospital stay, or diarrhea starting after 3 days in hospital, calls for C. difficile testing instead of a routine stool culture, and hypovolemia for a BMP to measure K+, HCO3−, and creatinine.

For a preformed toxin, onset after a shared meal is enough, and food or vomit is tested only in outbreaks. Cholera is confirmed by stool culture, the gold standard, or by rapid tests in outbreaks, and ETEC by molecular tests for its toxin genes. Viruses are found by stool PCR or antigen, mainly to control outbreaks. Invasive bacteria are found by stool culture or PCR, confirmed by culture since PCR also detects dead organisms; blood cultures are taken for Salmonella at high risk (age under 12 months or over 50, hemoglobinopathy, atherosclerosis, or immunosuppression), and enteric fever is diagnosed by blood cultures, or by bone marrow culture, which is more sensitive. Every bloody stool is tested for Shiga toxin, with FBC, blood film, and creatinine over the following days to detect HUS. C. difficile is tested in liquid stool only, in 2 steps, with GDH or NAAT, such as a stool multiplex PCR, then toxin A and B, since carriers are positive on the first step alone. Giardia is found by stool antigen or PCR, and Cryptosporidium by modified acid-fast stain or PCR. E. histolytica is found by stool antigen or PCR, which separate it from the harmless E. dispar, with imaging and serology for a liver abscess. Strongyloides is found by serology, the most sensitive test, and by stool examination for larvae, and people from endemic areas are screened before corticosteroids or other immunosuppression.

Management

Hypovolemia is treated with ORS, whose salt, water, and glucose are absorbed together by the sodium-glucose cotransporter, or with IV fluids if it is severe or vomiting prevents drinking. Loperamide can be used for watery diarrhea without fever or blood, but it is avoided with fever or bloody stools, in STEC and C. difficile, and in toxic megacolon, since slowing the bowel keeps invasive organisms and toxins in the colon. Empirical ABX are reserved for dysentery, high fever, severe illness, older age, or immunocompromise, using azithromycin or ciprofloxacin in adults and ceftriaxone or azithromycin in children. Mild traveler's diarrhea is treated with ORS and loperamide, and severe traveler's diarrhea or dysentery with azithromycin. Spread is prevented by hand washing with soap and water and by contact precautions until 48 hours after symptoms stop.

Preformed toxins are treated with fluids alone, because the toxin is already formed and ABX do not help. Cholera needs rapid ORS, or IV Hartmann solution in shock, replacing the deficit within 3–4 hours, with doxycycline (or azithromycin) and zinc for children; ETEC is treated as traveler's diarrhea. Viral gastroenteritis is supportive; hands are washed with soap and water, since alcohol gel works poorly against norovirus, surfaces are cleaned with bleach, and rotavirus vaccine prevents disease in infants. Nontyphoidal Salmonella is not treated with ABX in healthy adults, but bacteremia is treated with ceftriaxone. Enteric fever is treated with ceftriaxone or azithromycin, or a fluoroquinolone if the organism is susceptible, for 10–14 days, and travelers are vaccinated. Shigella is treated with azithromycin or ciprofloxacin, guided by resistance, which shortens illness and spread, and severe Campylobacter infection with azithromycin. STEC is not treated with ABX or loperamide, which increase the risk of HUS; fluids are given, with blood or dialysis if HUS develops. C. difficile is treated by stopping unnecessary ABX and giving oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin for 10 days, with metronidazole only if neither is available; recurrence is treated with fidaxomicin, bezlotoxumab, or fecal microbiota transplant, and hands are washed with soap, since alcohol gel does not kill spores. Giardia is treated with tinidazole or metronidazole. Cryptosporidium is managed supportively, with ART to restore the CD4 count in HIV. E. histolytica is treated with metronidazole or tinidazole, then a luminal agent such as paromomycin to clear cysts, and carriers without symptoms take the luminal agent alone. Strongyloides is treated with ivermectin, given daily until stools are clear in hyperinfection, with ABX for gram-negative sepsis.

Relationships to other conditions

. Diarrhea lasting 4 weeks or more is classified by stool type rather than organism, but chronic infection with Giardia, Cryptosporidium, E. histolytica, or recurrent C. difficile bridges the two; travel, water exposure, HIV, or recent ABX favor an infectious cause.

. Giardia damages the villi and causes greasy stools and lactose intolerance, mimicking malabsorption; a water exposure and a positive stool antigen favor it over celiac disease.

. Bloody diarrhea is shared, so infection, including C. difficile and E. histolytica, is excluded before IBD is diagnosed; an acute onset after a food or travel exposure favors infection, and corticosteroids given for presumed IBD worsen amebic colitis.

. Campylobacter ileocecitis can mimic appendicitis; diarrhea and a preceding febrile prodrome favor infection.

. Amebic liver abscess follows E. histolytica colitis by 2–4 weeks, often after the diarrhea has gone, so travel history and serology separate it from a pyogenic abscess.

. Bloody diarrhea with pain in an older patient after hypotension suggests ischemic colitis rather than infection.

Chronic Diarrhea

Pathophysiology

Stool is loose when water is secreted, held by solutes, or not given time to be absorbed, and the pattern shows which.

  1. Loose for 4 weeksOr longer
  2. Sort the stoolWatery, fatty, inflammatory
  3. Secreted, held, or rushedWater stays in the lumen
  4. Volume and lossDehydration, acidosis

Mechanisms

  • ASecretoryHormones, laxatives, or bile salts open Cl− channels; continues with fasting
  • BOsmoticUnabsorbed solutes pull in water; stops with fasting
  • CInflammatoryInjured mucosa leaks blood, mucus, and protein
  • DMotilityFast transit leaves too little time

What the pattern tells

TypeStoolOsmotic gapWith fasting
Secretory (A)Large, watery, also at nightLow under 50 mOsm/kgContinues
Osmotic (B)Watery with gasHigh over 125 mOsm/kgStops
Motility (D)Small, frequent, looseVariableImproves
FattyPale, greasy, foulOften highStops
Inflammatory (C)Blood, mucus, or pus; watery in microscopic colitisVariableContinues

A gap of 50–125 mOsm/kg is not decisive; older sources call it osmotic from 75.

Bile salts and the colon

  • ELiverMakes bile salts from cholesterol
  • FTerminal ileumTakes back about 95% and releases FGF19
  • GFGF19Tells the liver to make less; if low, it makes too much
  • HColonExcess bile salts open Cl− channels and speed transit

Note: Frequent small stools or leakage can be overflow from constipation or fecal incontinence, so ask and examine.

Etiology

Sort the stool first, because each group has its own causes and tests.

Sort first

Causes

  • Secretory (A)
  • 1Bile acid diarrheaIleal resection or disease, cholecystectomy, or no cause found (primary)
  • 2Hormone-secreting tumorsVIP, gastrin, serotonin; rare
  • 3Stimulant laxatives and drugsSenna, bisacodyl, metformin, SSRIs, digoxin, colchicine
  • Osmotic (B)
  • 4Lactose and other sugarsLactose, fructose, sorbitol, polyols in sugar-free foods
  • 5Osmotic laxatives and magnesiumLactulose, PEG, magnesium antacids
  • Motility (D)
  • 6HyperthyroidismFast transit; also weight loss and tremor
  • 7Diabetic diarrheaAutonomic neuropathy, SIBO, EPI, metformin, sugar-free sweeteners
  • 8IBS-D and functional diarrheaDisorder of gut-brain interaction
  • Fatty
  • 9Mucosal malabsorptionCeliac disease, giardiasis, Whipple disease, tropical sprue
  • 10MaldigestionPancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency, SIBO
  • Inflammatory (C)
  • 11IBDUlcerative colitis, Crohn disease
  • 12Microscopic colitisCollagenous, lymphocytic; older women; NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, smoking
  • 13Chronic infectionGiardia, C. difficile, HIV, E. histolytica, TB
  • 14Other inflammation and cancerRadiation, ischemia, immune checkpoint inhibitors, cancer, lymphoma

Symptoms and complications

  1. Ask the stoolWatery, fatty, bloody
  2. Night and fastingOrganic if they persist
  3. Drugs, diet, travelOften the cause
  4. Weight, bloodAlarm
  5. ElectrolytesLow K+, acidosis

Clues in the history

  • Nocturnal or fasting diarrheaSecretory or inflammatory, not IBS
  • After dairy or sweetenerOsmotic (4)
  • After cholecystectomy or ileal surgeryBile acid diarrhea (1)
  • Flushing, wheezeCarcinoid syndrome (2)
  • Older woman, watery, normal colonoscopyMicroscopic colitis (12)
  • Tremor, weight lossHyperthyroidism (6)
  • Long diabetes, night diarrheaDiabetic diarrhea (7)
  • Pale, greasyFatty (9, 10)
  • Blood, tenesmusInflammatory (11, 13)
  • New drug within weeksDrug (3, 5, 12)

Specific causes

  • Vipoma (2)Liters a day, low K+, low acid
  • Laxative use (3)Low K+, melanosis coli, hidden history
  • Microscopic colitis (12)4–9 watery stools, night stools, weight loss, joint pain; no cancer risk
  • Bile acid diarrhea (1)Urgency, incontinence, after meals

Complications

  • Volume and electrolytesLow K+, Mg2+, NAGMA
  • AKIDehydration
  • NutritionWeight loss, deficiency
  • Anal skinSoreness, incontinence
  • Missed cancerAbove all after 50
  • Quality of lifeUrgency, isolation
  • PellagraCarcinoid syndrome (2)
  • Drug levelsOral contraceptive, antiepileptics

Diagnosis

History, drugs, and a small set of tests find most causes, and alarm features or persistence lead to colonoscopy with biopsies.

  1. History and drugsStop the likely one
  2. First testsBloods, stool
  3. Alarm?Colonoscopy with biopsies
  4. Osmotic gapIf watery and unclear
  5. Targeted testsOr a trial of treatment

First tests

  • BloodsFBC, CRP, electrolytes, calcium, albumin, TFTs, glucose, ferritin, B12, folate
  • Celiac serologytTG-IgA with total IgA
  • StoolCalprotectin; culture or PCR and C. difficile; Giardia
  • Fecal immunochemical testOver 40 or any alarm
  • Bile acid testSeHCAT or serum C4; a trial of sequestrant if not available

Colonoscopy with biopsies

  • WhenOver 45–50, blood, weight loss, night stools, high calprotectin, family history
  • Biopsy normal mucosaRight and left colon, for microscopic colitis
  • CollagenousCollagen band over 10 µm
  • Lymphocytic20 or more lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells

Bile acid tests

TestMeans
SeHCAT retention at 7 daysUnder 15% mild, under 10% moderate, under 5% severe
Serum C4High: synthesis increased
FGF19Low
Trial of cholestyramineResponse supports it; failure does not exclude it

Red flags

  • Weight loss
  • Blood
  • Nocturnal stools
  • Age over 50
  • Fever
  • Anemia
  • Family history of IBD or cancer

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
OverflowConstipation, impaction, frailExamination, x-ray
Fecal incontinenceLeakage of formed stoolHistory, anal tone
Caffeine or alcoholIntake each dayA trial without them
Factitious diarrheaInconsistent history, low K+Laxative screen, low stool osmolality
ProctitisFrequent small stools with urgencySigmoidoscopy

Find the cause

  • 1Bile acid diarrheaSeHCAT, C4, or trial
  • 2Hormone-secreting tumorsOsmotic gap under 50; VIP, gastrin, 5-HIAA, chromogranin A, imaging
  • 3Stimulant laxatives and drugsDrug review, laxative screen
  • 4Lactose and other sugarsStop for 2 weeks; hydrogen breath test
  • 5Osmotic laxatives and magnesiumStool Mg2+, osmotic gap high
  • 6HyperthyroidismTFTs
  • 7Diabetic diarrheaGlucose, SIBO, elastase, drugs
  • 8IBS-D and functional diarrheaRome V, normal tests
  • 9Mucosal malabsorptionCeliac serology, biopsy, stool PCR
  • 10MaldigestionElastase, LFTs, breath test
  • 11IBDCalprotectin, colonoscopy
  • 12Microscopic colitisColonoscopy with biopsies
  • 13Chronic infectionStool PCR, C. difficile, HIV
  • 14Other inflammation and cancerColonoscopy, CT

Note: A measured stool osmolality well below plasma means water or urine was added, which points to factitious diarrhea.

Treatment

Treat the cause, replace fluid, and use an antidiarrheal only once infection and colitis are excluded.

  1. Fluids, electrolytesORS, K+, Mg2+
  2. Stop the culpritDrug, food
  3. Treat the causeBy group
  4. AntidiarrhealLoperamide if safe
  5. RecheckWeight, bloods

For every cause

  • FluidORS, IV if severe
  • DietLess caffeine, alcohol, polyols
  • LoperamideSlows transit; avoid in severe colitis or fever
  • CholestyramineBinds bile salts; take other drugs an hour before or 4–6 hours after
  • SkinBarrier cream

Bile acid diarrhea (1)

  • First-lineCholestyramine
  • If not toleratedColestipol or colesevelam
  • Long ileal lossDo not use: it worsens steatorrhea; use antidiarrheals, low-fat diet
  • PrimaryMay relapse; lowest dose

Microscopic colitis (12)

  • StopTriggering drugs, smoking
  • InduceBudesonide, effective in most
  • RelapseCommon, so low-dose budesonide to maintain
  • MildLoperamide
  • Bile saltsAdd cholestyramine if bile acid diarrhea coexists
  • RefractoryBismuth, then TNF inhibitor, vedolizumab, or thiopurine; 5-ASA is not recommended

Be careful with

  • Loperamide in colitis
  • Cholestyramine and drug absorption
  • Long PPI
  • Opioids
  • Octreotide and gallstones
  • Budesonide and bone

Treat the cause

  • 1Bile acid diarrheaCholestyramine or another sequestrant
  • 2Hormone-secreting tumorsOctreotide and resection;
  • 3Stimulant laxatives and drugsStop or change the drug
  • 4Lactose and other sugarsReduce the sugar that causes it
  • 5Osmotic laxatives and magnesiumStop the laxative or antacid
  • 6HyperthyroidismAntithyroid drugs
  • 7Diabetic diarrheaGlucose control, treat SIBO, loperamide, clonidine or octreotide
  • 8IBS-D and functional diarrhea
  • 9Mucosal malabsorption
  • 10MaldigestionEnzymes, bile salt or SIBO treatment
  • 11IBD
  • 12Microscopic colitisBudesonide
  • 13Chronic infection
  • 14Other inflammation and cancerTreat the disease; corticosteroid for checkpoint colitis

Guidelines differ: Testing for bile acid diarrhea is preferred in Europe and Canada, while a trial of sequestrant is common where SeHCAT is not available.

Review article

Chronic diarrhea: sorting secretory, osmotic, motility, fatty, and inflammatory disease

Chronic diarrhea lasts 4 weeks or more and is sorted by the stool into watery, fatty, and inflammatory disease, with watery disease divided into secretory, osmotic, and motility causes. Secretory diarrhea continues with fasting and has a low stool osmotic gap, whereas osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting and has a high gap. Inflammatory diarrhea has increased fecal calprotectin and needs colonoscopy, and microscopic colitis is found only on biopsy. Here, we review the causes, clues, workup, and treatment of chronic diarrhea, and consider how it relates to malabsorption, IBD, IBS, and PUD.

Key points

  • The stool sorts chronic diarrhea into watery (secretory, osmotic, or motility), fatty, and inflammatory disease before any test.
  • A stool osmotic gap under 50 mOsm/kg indicates secretory diarrhea and over 75 mOsm/kg osmotic diarrhea, and only osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting.
  • Vipomas, gastrinomas, carcinoid syndrome, stimulant laxatives, and bile salts cause secretory diarrhea.
  • Alarm features call for colonoscopy with biopsies, which also finds microscopic colitis in a normal-looking colon.

Pathophysiology

Chronic diarrhea lasts 4 weeks or more, and the stool sorts it into watery, fatty, or inflammatory disease before any test. A hormone, solute, fast transit, fat, or inflammation causes water to be secreted, held, or not absorbed. In secretory diarrhea, hormones, stimulant laxatives, or bile salts stimulate channels so that Cl− and water are secreted, producing large, watery stools, also at night, that continue with fasting, with a low stool osmotic gap, under 50 mOsm/kg. In osmotic diarrhea, unabsorbed solutes, such as lactose or magnesium, pull water into the lumen, producing watery stools with bloating after the culprit food or drug that stop with fasting, with a high gap, over 75 mOsm/kg. In inflammatory diarrhea, mucosal damage brings neutrophils or lymphocytes into the mucosa, producing bloody, mucoid stools, or watery stools in microscopic colitis, that continue with fasting. In motility disorders, fast transit leaves too little time to absorb water, producing frequent, loose stools with a variable gap and a variable response to fasting. Fatty stools are pale, greasy, foul, and hard to flush, and stop with fasting; the osmotic gap is not used in fatty or inflammatory diarrhea.

Etiology and mechanisms

Secretory causes are hormonal, with increased VIP from vipomas, gastrin from gastrinomas, and serotonin from carcinoid syndrome stimulating channels; stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl, and sodium picosulfate); and bile acid diarrhea, in which unabsorbed bile salts reach the colon after limited ileal resection or disease, such as Crohn disease, or after cholecystectomy, and stimulate Cl− secretion. Osmotic causes are lactose intolerance, osmotic laxatives (lactulose, PEG, and magnesium citrate), and magnesium antacids. Motility causes are hyperthyroidism and IBS with diarrhea, through fast transit. Fatty diarrhea comes from malabsorption and maldigestion (celiac disease, EPI, bile salt deficiency, SIBO, and extensive ileal resection). Inflammatory causes are IBD, microscopic colitis, which is associated with NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins, and smoking, and chronic infection with Giardia, Cryptosporidium in HIV, E. histolytica, or recurrent C. difficile. Drugs therefore act in several ways: laxatives through secretion or osmosis, magnesium antacids through osmosis, NSAIDs, PPIs, and SSRIs through microscopic colitis, and metformin.

Clinical presentation and complications

Diarrhea at night or during a fast suggests a secretory or inflammatory cause rather than IBS. Diarrhea after dairy that settles with fasting suggests lactose intolerance, and pain relieved by defecation without alarm features suggests IBS. Tremor, heat intolerance, and weight loss suggest hyperthyroidism, pale, greasy stools with weight loss suggest fatty diarrhea, and blood, mucus, fever, or weight loss suggest inflammatory disease. Complications are hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and NAGMA, and weight loss with vitamin and mineral deficiencies, especially in fatty diarrhea.

A vipoma is a pancreatic tumor whose VIP stimulates intestinal secretion and inhibits gastric acid, causing profuse watery diarrhea that continues with fasting, with hypokalemia and achlorhydria (WDHA). In a gastrinoma, acid floods the small bowel, damaging the mucosa and inactivating pancreatic enzymes and bile salts, with refractory peptic ulcers (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). Carcinoid syndrome appears once a midgut neuroendocrine tumor reaches the liver, which otherwise breaks down serotonin, causing flushing, wheezing, and right-sided heart valve disease; tryptophan is diverted to serotonin, causing niacin deficiency (pellagra). Hidden stimulant laxative use causes secretory diarrhea with hypokalemia, and anthraquinones such as senna leave pigment-laden macrophages in the colon (melanosis coli), which fade once they stop. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery, nonbloody diarrhea, 4–9 stools a day and often at night, mostly in older women, with a normal-looking colonoscopy.

Diagnosis

The history covers the stool type, nocturnal symptoms, drugs, surgery, and alarm features. Initial tests are FBC, CRP, TFTs, celiac serology, fecal calprotectin, FOBT, and stool tests for infection. Alarm features (onset after 50, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, fever, iron deficiency anemia, high CRP or calprotectin, positive FOBT, or a family history of IBD or colorectal cancer) call for colonoscopy with biopsies. Watery stools are sent for stool Na+ and K+ to calculate the osmotic gap, 290 − 2 × (stool Na+ + stool K+); a low gap means electrolytes hold the water, and a high gap means unabsorbed solutes do.

Secretory diarrhea has a gap under 50 mOsm/kg and is investigated with VIP, gastrin, and urine 5-HIAA, a laxative screen of stool or urine, and colonoscopy for melanosis coli, and a response to cholestyramine supports bile acid diarrhea. Osmotic diarrhea has a gap over 75 mOsm/kg and stops with fasting, and lactose intolerance is confirmed by a hydrogen breath test. Motility causes are investigated with TFTs, and IBS is diagnosed by Rome V criteria once alarm features are excluded. Fatty diarrhea is investigated with fecal elastase and fecal fat. Inflammatory diarrhea is investigated with fecal calprotectin, stool tests for infection, and colonoscopy, and microscopic colitis needs biopsies, showing a collagen band over 10 µm in collagenous colitis or 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 cells in lymphocytic colitis.

Management

Hypovolemia and electrolyte loss are treated with ORS or IV fluids, with K+ replacement, and non-inflammatory diarrhea can be treated with loperamide once the cause is known. Vipomas and carcinoid syndrome are treated with octreotide or lanreotide and resection, gastrinomas with high-dose PPIs and resection, stimulant laxative misuse by stopping the laxatives, and bile acid diarrhea with cholestyramine, which binds bile salts in the lumen. Lactose intolerance is treated with a lactose-free diet or lactase, and osmotic laxatives and magnesium antacids are stopped. Hyperthyroidism and IBS are treated as on their own pages. Fatty diarrhea is treated by its cause, and cholestyramine does not help after extensive ileal resection, since the bile salt pool is already depleted. IBD is treated as on its own page, microscopic colitis by stopping culprit drugs and then giving budesonide for 6–8 weeks, and chronic infection as for acute diarrhea.

Relationships to other conditions

. Persistent infection with Giardia, Cryptosporidium, E. histolytica, or C. difficile can pass the 4-week mark; travel, water exposure, HIV, or recent ABX favor infection over the other chronic causes.

. Fatty diarrhea is the shared endpoint, and lactose intolerance is its osmotic form; a high stool osmotic gap and resolution with fasting favor an osmotic or fatty cause over secretory disease.

and . Fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP separate inflammatory disease from IBS, and nocturnal or fasting diarrhea argues against IBS. Infectious diarrhea is excluded before IBD is diagnosed, and microscopic colitis, unlike IBD, leaves the colon looking normal.

. Gastrinomas cause both refractory ulcers and secretory diarrhea, so the two together suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Intestinal Ischemia

Pathophysiology

Flow to the bowel falls below what it needs, so the mucosa dies first and then the whole wall, and the bacteria it held back enter the blood.

  1. Flow fallsArtery, vein, or low output
  2. Mucosa hypoxicVillus tips first, within hours
  3. Barrier failsBacteria and fluid cross
  4. Transmural infarctionBy about 6–12 hours
  5. Perforation, sepsisReperfusion adds injury

What ischemia does

  • ALess oxygenSpasm and colicky pain with a soft abdomen
  • BAnaerobic respirationLactate, AGMA
  • CLeaky vesselsEdema, fluid loss, hematochezia
  • DInfarctionConstant pain; signs appear late
  • EPerforationPneumoperitoneum, peritonitis

Why these places

  • SMA takes emboliWide, leaves the aorta at a narrow angle; they lodge past its first branches, sparing proximal jejunum
  • Thrombus at the originPlaque sits there, so the whole midgut suffers
  • Watershed colonSplenic flexure and rectosigmoid, where two arteries meet
  • Rectum sparedDouble supply, from the IMA and iliac arteries
  • CollateralsSlow narrowing is tolerated until two vessels are narrow

Colon or small bowel

Acute mesentericIschemic colitis
CauseBlocked vessel or low flowLow flow, vessel usually open
PainSevere, out of proportionMild, crampy, left
BleedingLateWithin a day
TestCTA nowCT, then colonoscopy
OutcomeOften fatalUsually heals

Note: Reperfusion releases oxygen radicals and K+, so the patient can worsen just after flow returns.

Etiology

Each cause differs in who, how fast, and how it is treated, so ask which one at the bedside.

Sites

  • Acute mesenteric ischemia
  • 1Arterial embolismA-fib, MI, valve disease, endocarditis; sudden
  • 2Arterial thrombosisAtherosclerosis; often a history of pain after meals
  • 3Nonocclusive (NOMI)Shock, heart failure, dialysis, vasopressors, digoxin, cocaine
  • 4Venous thrombosisClotting disorder, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, cancer, estrogen; over days
  • Chronic
  • 5Chronic mesenteric ischemiaPlaque in two or more vessels; women, smokers
  • Colon
  • 6Ischemic colitisLow flow, aortic surgery, constipating drugs, thrombophilia

Note: Median arcuate ligament compression, vasculitis, and dissection are rarer causes, and sickle cell disease can cause any of them.

Symptoms and complications

  1. Pain firstSoft abdomen
  2. EmptyingVomiting, diarrhea
  3. Quiet intervalMisleading
  4. PeritonitisInfarcted
  5. ShockSepsis, acidosis

The pattern

  • Acute (1, 2)Severe pain out of proportion, vomiting, diarrhea, and an embolic source or vascular disease
  • NOMI (3)Distention, feeding intolerance, or rising lactate in the ICU, where pain may be masked
  • Venous (4)Vague pain over days, anorexia, low fever
  • Chronic (5)Pain 15–30 minutes after meals, fear of eating, weight loss, epigastric bruit
  • Colitis (6)Sudden left cramps and urge, then blood or bloody diarrhea within 24 hours

Signs of infarction

  • Peritonitis
  • Hypotension
  • Lactate over 2 mmol/L and rising
  • Acidosis
  • Fever
  • Melena or blood
  • Organ failure

Colitis severity (6)

LevelPicture
MildTypical, no risk factors
Moderate1–3 risk factors: male, pulse over 100, systolic BP under 90 mmHg, pain without bleeding, urea over 7.1 mmol/L, hemoglobin under 120 g/L, LDH over 350 U/L, Na+ under 136 mmol/L, WBC over 15 × 10⁹/L
SevereMore than 3 risk factors, peritonitis, pneumatosis, portal venous gas, gangrene, or pancolonic or right-sided disease

Complications

  • Infarction and perforationPeritonitis, pneumoperitoneum
  • Sepsis and shockTranslocated bacteria
  • Short bowelAfter long resection
  • Reperfusion injuryLung and kidney failure
  • StrictureWeeks after colitis (6)
  • DeathAbout 30–70% in acute mesenteric ischemia, under 5% in nongangrenous colitis
  • RecurrenceWithout anticoagulation (1, 4)
  • Chronic to acutePlaque clots (5)

Diagnosis

Pain out of proportion in someone at risk is mesenteric ischemia until CTA shows otherwise; do not wait for lactate or an x-ray.

  1. Suspect earlyPain, risk, age
  2. CTA nowArterial and venous phase
  3. Cause and viabilityWhich vessel, dead bowel?
  4. Surgeon and vascularCall together
  5. Flow firstThen resect

What CT shows

  • FNormalWall enhances evenly
  • GArterial (1, 2)Filling defect; thin wall with little enhancement
  • HVenous (4)Vein clot, thick wall, target, ascites
  • JInfarctedGas in wall, portal venous gas, no enhancement; gas alone is not proof

Other tests

  • CTADo not delay for AKI; no oral contrast
  • LactateNormal early; does not exclude
  • D-dimerSensitive, not specific
  • FBC, gas, electrolytesHigh WBC, acidosis; K+ rises after necrosis
  • ECG and echoA-fib, MI, clot (1)
  • Thrombophilia screenVenous (4), if no local cause
  • Duplex ultrasoundChronic (5), fasting
  • X-rayLate: ileus, thumbprinting, free gas

Colonoscopy (6)

  • WhenWithin 48 hours, gently, not in peritonitis or gangrene
  • ShowsSegment spared at the rectum, pale with petechiae, hemorrhagic nodules, single linear ulcer
  • BiopsyGhost cells, hyalinized lamina propria, fibrosis
  • CTA as well ifRight-sided, isolated, or pain out of proportion

Red flags

  • Peritonitis
  • Portal venous gas
  • Free gas

Review article

Intestinal ischemia: arterial, venous, and low-flow injury to the bowel

Arterial occlusion, venous occlusion, or hypoperfusion causes loss of blood supply to the intestines. Acute mesenteric ischemia presents with out-of-proportion abdominal pain, chronic mesenteric ischemia with postprandial pain, and ischemic colitis with LLQ pain and hematochezia. Here, we review these three patterns, their workup, and their treatment, and consider how they relate to other causes of abdominal pain and bloody stools.

Key points

  • The SMA is the most commonly affected vessel in acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Chronic mesenteric ischemia requires atherosclerosis of 2 of the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA.
  • CT angiogram evaluates mesenteric ischemia; CT AP and colonoscopy evaluate ischemic colitis.
  • Treatment combines bowel decompression, ABX, heparin, and revascularization.

Pathophysiology

Arterial occlusion, venous occlusion, or hypoperfusion decreases oxygen supply to the bowel, causing abdominal pain, and increased demand after eating makes this worse in chronic disease. Anaerobic respiration causes AGMA, and increased vascular permeability causes hematochezia. Prolonged ischemia causes infarction and necrosis, with out-of-proportion abdominal pain, and full-thickness necrosis perforates, causing pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Acute arterial ischemia follows thrombosis (atherosclerosis), embolism (history of A-fib or AAA), or hypoperfusion (shock), which decrease perfusion or block the SMA, most commonly, or IMA, causing infarction and necrosis with out-of-proportion abdominal pain. Acute venous ischemia follows mesenteric thrombosis (hypercoagulation) or portal thrombosis (cirrhosis), with venous occlusion of the portal vein, SMV, or IMV, venous congestion, and decreased oxygen supply. Chronic mesenteric ischemia follows atherosclerosis of 2 of the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA; decreased oxygen supply cannot meet increased oxygen demand when eating, causing postprandial abdominal pain. Ischemic colitis follows shock or a history of vasopressor usage, with hypoperfusion of the IMA and decreased oxygen supply to the splenic flexure, descending colon, and rectosigmoid junction, causing LLQ pain and hematochezia. Of acute mesenteric ischemia, embolism, usually cardiac, accounts for 40–50%, thrombosis for 25–30%, and nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI) for ~20%, from vasospasm in critically ill patients on vasopressors. Venous thrombosis follows malignancy, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, factor V Leiden, or protein C or S deficiency. In chronic mesenteric ischemia, pain begins 15–30 minutes after meals and lasts up to 4 hours, causing fear of eating and weight loss. Ischemic colitis mostly affects the watershed areas, the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point), which account for ~70%.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are abdominal pain and hematochezia. Complications are AGMA, from lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration in ischemic bowel, worsened as increased vascular permeability adds fluid loss and hypoperfusion, and perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis). Acute ischemia causes pain out of proportion to examination, and chronic ischemia postprandial pain and weight loss. Mortality is 60–80% in acute mesenteric ischemia, and under 5% in nongangrenous ischemic colitis.

Diagnosis

Acute or chronic mesenteric ischemia is evaluated by CT angiogram, and ischemic colitis by CT AP and colonoscopy. CT angiography is preferred even with renal impairment, and lactate and LDH rise only late. Ischemic colitis is confirmed by colonoscopy with biopsy within 48 hours.

Management

Bowel decompression uses NPO, IV fluids, and NGT. ABX prevent sepsis, heparin prevents clotting, and revascularization uses endovascular procedures and surgery. Vasopressors and alpha-agonists are avoided, since they cause vasospasm. NOMI is treated by correcting the low-flow state, with catheter-directed papaverine, and venous thrombosis with anticoagulation. Mild ischemic colitis is managed supportively, moderate disease with broad-spectrum ABX and surgical review, and severe disease with surgery.

Relationships to other conditions

. The same low-flow logic applies: shock injures the watershed splenic flexure in the colon and zone 3 in the liver.

. Both cause LLQ pain and hematochezia. Painless, large-volume bleeding favors diverticulosis, whereas ischemic colitis causes pain with bleeding.

and infectious colitis. Bloody diarrhea is shared, but a recent episode of hypotension or vasopressor use points to ischemia.

Embolic disease. A-fib embolizes to both the SMA and the brain, so the same source explains both.

Review article

Vascular liver injury: inflow failure, outflow congestion, and zone 3 hypoxia

Decreased blood flow into or out of the liver leads to hypoxia of zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, causing hepatocellular injury. Ischemic hepatitis reflects failed arterial inflow, whereas congestive hepatopathy and Budd-Chiari syndrome reflect impaired venous outflow. Each has a distinct tempo and enzyme pattern. Here, we review their mechanisms, differentiation, and treatment, and consider how they relate to other causes of very high aminotransferases.

Key points

  • Ischemic hepatitis causes a massive AST/ALT rise that falls within 7–10 days.
  • JVD is present in HF and absent in Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins is first-line for Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Budd-Chiari treatment steps up from anticoagulation to transplant.

Pathophysiology

Shock or cardiac arrest decreases hepatic perfusion, whereas RHF or a clot blocks outflow, raising sinusoidal pressure and causing sinusoidal congestion. Either way, zone 3 hepatocytes receive the least oxygen and die first, releasing AST and ALT, which often exceed 1000 U/L. Chronic congestion causes zone 3 atrophy, leading to nutmeg liver and cardiac cirrhosis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver") follows shock (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic) or cardiac arrest: decreased hepatic perfusion causes zone 3 hypoxia and centrilobular necrosis, with increased AST/ALT, often over 1000 U/L. Congestive hepatopathy follows RHF, as well as tricuspid regurgitation and constrictive pericarditis: increased CVP and hepatic venous pressure cause sinusoidal congestion, zone 3 atrophy, and necrosis, producing nutmeg liver and, if chronic, cardiac cirrhosis. Budd-Chiari syndrome is thrombosis of the hepatic veins or IVC, most commonly from myeloproliferative neoplasms (polycythemia vera, JAK2), and also from pregnancy, OCPs, PNH, and malignancy such as HCC. Blocked hepatic outflow and increased sinusoidal pressure cause hepatomegaly, ascites, and RUQ pain. Portal vein thrombosis is most often due to cirrhosis, and otherwise to myeloproliferative and other prothrombotic states or abdominal inflammation such as pancreatitis; it blocks portal inflow and causes portal hypertension, with varices and splenomegaly but near-normal liver function unless the liver is cirrhotic. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, or veno-occlusive disease, follows conditioning for hematopoietic cell transplant, especially with busulfan, or drugs such as cyclophosphamide and oxaliplatin, which damage the zone 3 sinusoidal endothelium and obstruct the sinusoids, causing jaundice, painful hepatomegaly, and ascites or weight gain.

Clinical presentation and complications

Ischemic hepatitis is acute, 1–3 days after hypotension, often with no symptoms or with nausea and RUQ pain; JVD depends on the cause of shock, and AST/ALT shows a massive rise, often over 1000 U/L, falling within 7–10 days. Congestive hepatopathy is usually chronic, with RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema; JVD is present with hepatojugular reflux, and there is a mild rise, often with increased bilirubin. Budd-Chiari syndrome is acute or chronic, with a triad of RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, and ascites; JVD is absent, and the rise is variable and very high in acute disease. General symptoms are RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, jaundice, and nausea. Complications are acute liver failure (coagulopathy with increased INR, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia), cardiac cirrhosis from long-standing congestion, and portal hypertension (ascites, varices, splenomegaly).

Diagnosis

Any vascular cause is assessed with LFTs and INR. Ischemic hepatitis is supported by a history of hypotension, serial LFTs with a rapid rise then rapid fall, and markedly increased LDH. Congestive hepatopathy is evaluated by echocardiogram and BNP. Budd-Chiari syndrome is evaluated by Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins first, CT or MR venography to confirm, and a hypercoagulability workup (JAK2 V617F). JVD is present in HF and absent in Budd-Chiari syndrome. Portal vein thrombosis is shown by Doppler ultrasound, with normal or near-normal LFTs unless the liver is cirrhotic, and a chronic clot forms a portal cavernoma. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome is diagnosed clinically by a bilirubin of 34 µmol/L or more with 2 of painful hepatomegaly, weight gain over 5%, or ascites, usually within 21 days of transplant, and Doppler shows decreased or reversed portal flow.

Management

Ischemic hepatitis is treated by restoring perfusion and treating the cause of shock (fluids, vasopressors, cardiac support); LFTs normalize within 7–10 days once blood flow is restored. Congestive hepatopathy is treated by treating HF, such as with diuretics. Budd-Chiari syndrome is treated in all patients with anticoagulation and treatment of the underlying cause, then angioplasty or stenting for short venous narrowing, TIPS, and liver transplant for fulminant failure or cirrhosis. Portal vein thrombosis is treated with early anticoagulation, with management of portal hypertension and the cause, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome with defibrotide, the only approved drug, started early.

Relationships to other conditions

. Low flow injures vulnerable zones in both organs: zone 3 in the liver and the watershed splenic flexure in the colon.

. Both can raise aminotransferases above 1000 U/L, but ischemic hepatitis rises and falls within days with a very high LDH, whereas viral hepatitis rises and falls more slowly.

. Both injure zone 3, so the history separates them.

. Congestion and Budd-Chiari syndrome share portal hypertension with cirrhosis, and SAAG of 11 g/L or more does not separate them.

Viral Hepatitis

Pathophysiology

A virus infects hepatocytes, and the T cells that kill infected cells cause the hepatitis; failure to clear the virus leaves chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and cancer.

  1. Virus enters hepatocytesFrom the gut or the blood
  2. Innate responseType I interferons
  3. Cytotoxic T cellsKill infected cells
  4. Acute hepatitisALT rises, jaundice
  5. Clears or persistsImmunity, or chronic infection
  6. Fibrosis and HCCOver decades
