Review article

Infectious liver injury: the hepatitis viruses and their clinical divergence

Viral infection of hepatocytes triggers a cytotoxic T-cell response, which destroys infected cells and causes hepatic inflammation. Hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral and acute, whereas hepatitis B, C, and D are bloodborne and can become chronic, leading to cirrhosis and HCC. CMV, HSV, and EBV also cause hepatitis. Here, we review their virology, phases, serology, and treatment, and consider how they relate to other liver injuries.

Key points

  • "The vowels hit your bowels": hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral, acute only, and naked.
  • HDV needs HBsAg from HBV as its envelope.
  • In the window period, IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker, and anti-HBc never comes from vaccination.
  • Anti-HCV stays positive for life, so HCV RNA confirms current infection.
  • Screen for HCC every 6 months in chronic HBV, or HCV with cirrhosis.

Pathophysiology

Viruses replicate inside hepatocytes, where type I interferons (IFN-α and β) are the first, innate antiviral defense, and cytotoxic T cells destroy the infected cells, causing hepatic inflammation and increased AST and ALT. Chronic infection leads to fibrosis and then cirrhosis, and HBV integrates into host DNA, so it can cause HCC without cirrhosis.

Virology

HAV is a naked +ssRNA picornavirus spread by the fecal-oral route, with 2–6 weeks of incubation; it is acute only, has no carrier state, and has an inactivated vaccine. HBV is an enveloped, partially double-stranded, circular DNA (pdsDNA) hepadnavirus spread by sex, blood, and perinatally, with 1–6 months of incubation; it becomes chronic in ~90% of infants and under 5% of adults, integrates into host DNA so can cause HCC without cirrhosis, and has a recombinant HBsAg vaccine. HCV is an enveloped +ssRNA flavivirus spread by blood, mainly IV drug use, with 2 weeks–6 months of incubation; it becomes chronic in 75–85%, and high antigenic variation means no vaccine and frequent chronicity. HDV is a circular −ssRNA deltavirus with an HBsAg envelope borrowed from HBV, spread by sex, blood, and perinatally, with incubation similar to HBV; the HBV vaccine protects. HEV is a naked +ssRNA hepevirus spread by the fecal-oral route through contaminated water and undercooked pork, with 2–9 weeks of incubation; it is acute, chronic only if immunocompromised, rarely chronic overall, has no widely available vaccine, and causes fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy with high mortality.

Coinfection and superinfection

HDV only infects people who also have HBV. In coinfection, HBV and HDV are acquired at the same time; disease is usually acute and self-limited, and both viruses are usually cleared. In superinfection, HDV is acquired by someone with chronic HBV; disease is more severe, with a risk of fulminant hepatitis, and usually becomes chronic with faster progression to cirrhosis.

Viral life cycles

+ssRNA viruses (HAV, HCV, HEV) attach, enter the hepatocyte, and uncoat; +ssRNA acts directly as mRNA, is translated into a polyprotein that viral proteases cleave, and viral RdRp copies a −RNA template that makes new genomes, followed by assembly and release. They replicate in the cytoplasm, and HCV drugs target NS3/4A, NS5A, and NS5B. HBV attaches and enters via the NTCP receptor, its nucleocapsid carries pdsDNA into the nucleus, pdsDNA is repaired into cccDNA, host RNA polymerase II makes mRNAs and pregenomic RNA, viral reverse transcriptase converts pregenomic RNA into new pdsDNA, and assembly with an HBsAg envelope is followed by release. cccDNA persists, so HBV is hard to cure, and tenofovir and entecavir block reverse transcriptase. HDV replicates in the nucleus using host RNA polymerase.

Other viruses

CMV affects immunocompromised patients (transplant, AIDS), with a mono-like illness, a negative heterophile test, and usually mild hepatitis. HSV affects pregnancy (third trimester), neonates, and immunocompromised patients; it is rare, and can be fulminant and anicteric. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis in adolescents and young adults, with common mild transaminase rise and hepatosplenomegaly. Beyond viruses, pyogenic liver abscesses are usually polymicrobial, with E. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes, spreading from the biliary tract or through the portal vein, and half of solitary abscesses lie in the right lobe. Amebic abscesses follow Entamoeba histolytica infection from contaminated food or water, most often in men aged 18–50 who live in or travel to endemic areas. Hydatid cysts come from Echinococcus granulosus eggs shed by dogs, whose intermediate hosts are sheep and other livestock, and grow slowly, forming daughter cysts. Schistosoma mansoni and japonicum, acquired from freshwater, send eggs to the liver, where granulomas lead to Symmers pipe-stem periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and varices.

Clinical presentation and complications

Acute viral hepatitis passes through an asymptomatic incubation phase; a prodromal phase with flu-like illness, RUQ pain, arthralgia, and increased ALT more than AST; an icteric phase with jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and increased bilirubin; and a convalescent phase resolving over weeks to months. Many infections are anicteric, especially HAV in young children and acute HCV. Outcomes are recovery (HAV, HEV, most adult HBV), fulminant hepatitis (HBV, HDV, HEV in pregnancy), and chronic infection (HBV, HCV, HDV), in which ongoing inflammation causes fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC, and liver failure; in chronic HBV, DNA integrates into the host genome and causes HCC even without cirrhosis. Extrahepatic manifestations, mostly from immune complexes (HBV) and cryoglobulins (HCV), are arthritis and arthralgia (serum sickness-like in HBV); polyarteritis nodosa (HBV) and mixed cryoglobulinemia vasculitis (HCV); rare myocarditis and pericarditis; glomerulonephritis, including membranous nephropathy (HBV) and MPGN (HCV and HBV); thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and neutropenia; B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (HCV); and porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus (HCV).

Diagnosis

IgM means current or recent infection, and IgG means past infection or immunity. Acute HAV shows IgM anti-HAV, and IgG anti-HAV is also positive after vaccination. Acute HDV shows IgM anti-HDV or HDV RNA with positive HBsAg, and past infection shows IgG anti-HDV; IgM anti-HBc is positive in coinfection and negative in superinfection. Acute HEV shows IgM anti-HEV, or HEV RNA if immunocompromised, and past infection shows IgG anti-HEV; it should be considered in pregnant patients with acute hepatitis. For HBV, acute infection shows positive HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA, with IgM anti-HBc. The window period shows negative HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA, and anti-HBs, anti-HBe that may be positive, and IgM anti-HBc. Recovery shows positive anti-HBs and anti-HBe, with IgG anti-HBc. Immunized patients have only anti-HBs. Chronic, replicative infection (high infectivity) shows positive HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA with IgG anti-HBc, and chronic, non-replicative infection (low infectivity) shows positive HBsAg and anti-HBe, low or undetectable HBV DNA, and IgG anti-HBc. HBsAg for 6 months or more means chronic infection. HCV is screened with anti-HCV antibody; if positive, HCV RNA (PCR) checks for active virus. RNA-negative patients have resolved past infection or a false-positive antibody, and RNA-positive patients have current infection and need fibrosis assessed before treatment using APRI (above 1.0 suggests cirrhosis), FIB-4, or elastography. CMV is evaluated by CMV PCR (blood), with "owl's eye" inclusions on biopsy; HSV by HSV PCR (blood); and EBV by heterophile antibody (Monospot) and EBV serology. A pyogenic abscess is imaged with ultrasound and then contrast CT, with guided aspiration for stains and cultures; an amebic abscess is diagnosed by imaging and serology, and aspiration, if done, yields odorless, brown anchovy paste. Hydatid cysts are staged by ultrasound, with a detached membrane, the water lily sign, or daughter cysts, often with eosinophilia, and schistosomiasis by eggs or antigen in stool and periportal fibrosis on imaging.

Management

HAV is treated supportively, with vaccine or immunoglobulin post-exposure. Acute HBV is treated supportively, with antivirals if severe; chronic HBV is treated with tenofovir or entecavir, or peginterferon-α; and post-exposure and newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers receive vaccine and HBIG. The vaccine is given to all infants and unvaccinated children and to adults at risk: sex partners and household contacts of HBsAg-positive people, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, health care workers, people on dialysis, and people with diabetes, chronic liver disease, HCV, or HIV, and travelers to endemic areas. HCV is treated with direct-acting antivirals for 8–12 weeks, such as sofosbuvir-based regimens, with cure over 95%. HDV is treated with peginterferon-α and treatment of the HBV. HEV is treated supportively, with ribavirin if chronic. CMV is treated with ganciclovir if immunocompromised, HSV with IV acyclovir started as soon as HSV hepatitis is suspected, and EBV supportively, avoiding contact sports while the spleen is enlarged. HCC screening with ultrasound every 6 months applies in chronic HBV, or HCV with cirrhosis. Pyogenic abscesses are drained and treated with ABX; amebic abscesses with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin, with drainage only in select cases; hydatid cysts with albendazole, adding PAIR or surgery for larger cysts while avoiding spillage, which can cause anaphylaxis; and schistosomiasis with praziquantel.

Relationships to other conditions

. Viral hepatitis rises and falls more slowly, and a very high LDH favors ischemia.

. HEV and HSV both cause severe hepatitis in the third trimester, so viral causes are considered alongside AFLP.

. Autoimmune hepatitis also has a hepatocellular pattern, but viral serologies are negative and ANA, ASMA, and IgG are high.

. CMV and HSV also cause esophagitis in immunocompromised patients.

Primary Biliary Cholangitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis

Pathophysiology

Immune attack destroys small ducts in PBC or scars large ones in PSC, so bile salts stay in the liver, injure hepatocytes, and reach the skin as itch.

Review article

Autoimmune liver disease: bile duct injury in PBC and PSC, and autoimmune hepatitis

Immune-mediated bile duct damage leads to cholestasis, and retained bile salts cause hepatocellular injury. PBC destroys small intrahepatic ducts, whereas PSC, which is not strictly autoimmune, scars medium and large ducts. Autoimmune hepatitis and IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis complete the group. Here, we review their mechanisms, cholestatic consequences, and treatment, and consider how they relate to IBD and cholangiocarcinoma.

Key points

  • PBC: middle-aged women, AMA-positive, small intrahepatic ducts.
  • PSC: young to middle-aged men, p-ANCA, beaded ducts on MRCP, and most patients have IBD.
  • A cholestatic pattern is first evaluated with RUQ ultrasound, then serology.
  • PSC needs surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer.

Pathophysiology

T cells destroy small intrahepatic bile ducts in PBC, whereas onion-skin fibrosis causes strictures of medium and large ducts in PSC. In both, bile builds up, increasing bile salts in blood, with pruritus, and conjugated bilirubin, with jaundice. Retained bile salts then damage hepatocytes, and ongoing injury leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Etiology and mechanisms

In PBC, AMA is positive in over 90%; T cells destroy small intrahepatic bile ducts, with granulomas around the ducts ("florid duct lesion"), causing loss of bile ducts (ductopenia) and cholestasis. It affects middle-aged women and is associated with other autoimmune diseases: scleroderma (CREST), Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren syndrome. Cancer risk is HCC once cirrhotic. In PSC, p-ANCA is positive in many patients; inflammation and fibrosis of medium and large, intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, with "onion-skin" fibrosis, cause strictures alternating with dilations ("beaded" ducts on MRCP) and cholestasis. It affects young to middle-aged men and is associated with other p-ANCA-associated diseases: ulcerative colitis, glomerulonephritis, and vasculitis. Cancer risks are HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer. Autoimmune hepatitis type 1 has ANA and ASMA, in young women with high IgG; type 2 has anti-LKM1, mostly in children. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis mimics PSC and is corticosteroid-responsive.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are fatigue, pruritus (often the first symptom), jaundice, RUQ discomfort, and xanthomas. Duct destruction or stricture causes cholestasis, with increased bile salts in blood (pruritus), increased conjugated bilirubin (jaundice, dark urine), and increased cholesterol (xanthomas). Decreased bile reaching the gut causes fat malabsorption, with steatorrhea, pale stools, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K), and osteoporosis. Toxic bile salts retained in the liver cause hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, biliary cirrhosis, HCC, portal hypertension, and liver failure. In PSC only, chronic bile duct inflammation causes cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent bacterial cholangitis, as bile stagnates behind strictures.

Diagnosis

The cholestatic LFT pattern is markedly increased ALP, increased GGT, increased conjugated bilirubin later, and mildly increased AST/ALT. RUQ ultrasound first rules out extrahepatic obstruction such as gallstones or a mass. Serology follows: AMA, p-ANCA, ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM1, and IgG4. A positive AMA means PBC, with biopsy only if AMA-negative or unclear. p-ANCA or IBD prompts MRCP, in which "beaded" bile ducts mean PSC.

Management

UDCA decreases liver injury and is first-line in PBC. Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, relieves pruritus. Deficiencies are corrected with fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and calcium and vitamin D for bone health. A dominant stricture in PSC is opened by ERCP with balloon dilation, and end-stage disease is treated by liver transplant. Autoimmune hepatitis is treated with corticosteroids with or without azathioprine, and IgG4-related disease with corticosteroids. PSC needs surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer. In PBC that does not respond to UDCA, obeticholic acid, a farnesoid X receptor agonist, is added.

Relationships to other conditions

. Most PSC patients have IBD, usually ulcerative colitis, so PSC prompts colonoscopy.

. A new dominant stricture with rising CA 19-9 in PSC suggests cholangiocarcinoma. This risk is specific to PSC, not PBC.

. Bile salt deficiency causes fat malabsorption here as it does in other cholestatic disease.

. Both give a cholestatic LFT pattern, but ultrasound finds dilated ducts with stones and non-dilated ducts in PBC.

. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis can occur with autoimmune pancreatitis.

Hemochromatosis, Wilson Disease, and Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency

Pathophysiology

An inherited fault lets iron or copper build up, or a misfolded protein stick, inside hepatocytes, which stresses them until they scar.

  1. Gene faultHFE, ATP7B, or SERPINA1
  2. Iron, copper, or protein builds upIn hepatocytes
  3. Free radicals or ER stressCell death
  4. FibrosisOver decades, or in childhood
  5. Cirrhosis and HCCOther organs too

Three buildups

  • AIron (1)Low hepcidin → ferroportin stays open → free radicals
  • BCopper (2)ATP7B fails → no excretion into bile
  • CMisfolded protein (3)A1AT polymers trapped in the ER
  • DFibrosisRepeated stress → cirrhosis

Iron: hepcidin holds the gate (1)

  • EDuodenal cellAbsorbs iron, exports by ferroportin
  • FMacrophageRecycles red cells, exports by ferroportin
  • GHepcidinFrom the liver; high with iron and inflammation, and closes ferroportin

Copper: two jobs of ATP7B (2)

  • HCeruloplasminCopper loaded for the blood: low if it fails
  • JBileThe only real exit: closed if it fails
  • KFree copperBrain, cornea, kidney, red cells

A1AT (3)

  • LiverToo much protein inside: globules, cirrhosis
  • LungToo little in blood: elastase destroys alveoli
  • Why they differNull genotypes have no liver disease, but lung disease

Etiology

  • 1Hereditary hemochromatosisAutosomal recessive; HFE C282Y homozygous in most; also HJV, HAMP, and TFR2, and ferroportin (dominant)
  • 2Wilson diseaseAutosomal recessive; ATP7B, chromosome 13
  • 3Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyCodominant; SERPINA1; PiZZ is severe, PiMZ is a cofactor

Review article

Metabolic liver disease: iron, copper, misfolded protein, and fat

Buildup of iron, copper, misfolded protein, or fat in hepatocytes causes cellular stress, leading to hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Hereditary hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, A1AT deficiency, and MASLD share this path to HCC but differ widely beyond the liver. Here, we review their inheritance, mechanisms, multisystem features, and treatment.

Key points

  • All four can progress through hepatitis and fibrosis to cirrhosis and HCC.
  • Hemochromatosis: decreased hepcidin and increased iron absorption.
  • Wilson disease: ATP7B mutation, low ceruloplasmin, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
  • A1AT deficiency: protein builds up in the liver and is missing from the lungs.
  • MASLD: cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death.

Pathophysiology

An inherited or acquired defect causes buildup in hepatocytes. In hemochromatosis, decreased hepcidin increases ferroportin activity, and iron causes free radical damage. In Wilson disease, an ATP7B mutation decreases copper excretion into bile, so copper builds up in the liver. In A1AT deficiency, the misfolded protein polymerizes and is trapped in the hepatocyte ER, causing hepatocellular injury. In MASLD, triglycerides accumulate, causing steatosis. Repeated cellular stress leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Hereditary hemochromatosis

Inheritance is autosomal recessive, except ferroportin disease, which is autosomal dominant. Type 1 (HFE, C282Y homozygosity) is most common; type 2A (HJV, hemojuvelin) and type 2B (HAMP, hepcidin) are juvenile, severe, and early in onset; type 3 (TFR2, transferrin receptor 2) is rare; and type 4 (SLC40A1, FPN, ferroportin) resists hepcidin or fails to export iron. HFE, HJV, HAMP, and TFR2 mutations decrease hepcidin, and FPN mutation makes ferroportin resist hepcidin. Increased ferroportin activity increases duodenal iron absorption; iron deposits in the liver, heart, pancreas, and skin, causing free radical damage by the Fenton reaction. Hepcidin normally blocks ferroportin, the only cellular iron exporter.

Wilson disease

Inheritance is autosomal recessive. ATP7B mutation on chromosome 13 decreases copper excretion into bile and loading onto ceruloplasmin; copper builds up in the liver, and free copper in the blood reaches the brain, cornea, kidneys, and RBCs.

A1AT deficiency

Inheritance is autosomal codominant. SERPINA1 mutation (PiZZ genotype) makes misfolded A1AT polymerize. In the liver, it is trapped in the hepatocyte ER (PAS-positive globules), causing hepatocellular injury and cirrhosis. In the lungs, decreased A1AT in blood leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed, causing alveolar wall destruction.

MASLD

MASLD is acquired, and is steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, without significant alcohol use (formerly NAFLD). Metabolic syndrome is the main risk factor: central obesity, T2DM, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia (increased TG, decreased HDL), and hypertension. Increased fatty acids reaching the liver and increased fat production cause triglycerides to build up in hepatocytes (steatosis), then lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, and MASH (steatohepatitis). Alcohol-related steatohepatitis shares these histological features, so the history of alcohol use separates them.

Clinical presentation and complications

All four can progress from hepatotoxicity to hepatomegaly and hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, with risk especially high in hemochromatosis. Wilson disease can present as acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Beyond the liver, hemochromatosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy (which can become dilated) and arrhythmias, diabetes mellitus from pancreatic iron, hypogonadism from pituitary iron, hyperpigmentation ("bronze diabetes"), arthropathy of the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, and infections (Vibrio vulnificus, Yersinia). Wilson disease causes Kayser-Fleischer rings, sunflower cataract, basal ganglia (putamen) disease with tremor, parkinsonism, and psychiatric symptoms, Fanconi syndrome, and Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. A1AT deficiency causes panniculitis (rare), panacinar emphysema (lower lobes, worse with smoking), and neonatal cholestasis. MASLD causes cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death, T2DM, CKD, and extrahepatic cancers such as colorectal cancer.

Diagnosis

Hemochromatosis is evaluated first by increased transferrin saturation (over 45%), then increased ferritin, HFE genetic testing (C282Y), and liver MRI or biopsy (Prussian blue) if unclear. Wilson disease is evaluated by decreased serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-hour urine copper, slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver biopsy (hepatic copper) or ATP7B testing if unclear. A1AT deficiency is evaluated by decreased serum A1AT level, phenotyping or genotyping (PiZZ), liver biopsy showing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules, and pulmonary function tests and chest CT for emphysema. MASLD shows mildly increased ALT more than AST (AST:ALT over 2:1 suggests alcohol) and a bright (echogenic) liver on ultrasound; fibrosis is assessed by FIB-4, then elastography, after excluding alcohol, viral hepatitis, and other causes.

Management

Hemochromatosis is treated by therapeutic phlebotomy first, with iron chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox) if phlebotomy is not possible, and by avoiding iron, vitamin C, alcohol, and raw shellfish. Wilson disease is treated by copper chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine, zinc for maintenance, which blocks intestinal copper absorption, and a low-copper diet that avoids shellfish, liver, nuts, and chocolate. A1AT deficiency is treated by stopping smoking and IV A1AT augmentation therapy for emphysema. MASLD is treated by 7–10% weight loss through diet and exercise first, treating metabolic risk factors (diabetes, lipids, blood pressure), GLP-1 receptor agonists or resmetirom for MASH with fibrosis, and bariatric surgery for severe obesity. Liver transplant treats end-stage disease, and cures the defect in Wilson disease and A1AT deficiency.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both MASLD and alcohol cause steatosis, but ALT exceeds AST in MASLD and AST:ALT is over 2:1 in alcohol.

. Wilson disease is a cause of acute liver failure, and all four feed into cirrhosis.

. A1AT deficiency can cause neonatal cholestasis, and cholestasis itself is the hallmark of PBC and PSC.

Movement disorders. Wilson disease causes parkinsonism and tremor in young patients.

Drug-Induced Liver Injury and Paracetamol Overdose

Pathophysiology

A drug, herb, or its metabolite injures hepatocytes or bile ducts by direct toxicity, predictably and by dose, or by an unpredictable reaction in a susceptible person.

  1. Drug or metaboliteCYP enzymes

  3. Cell or duct injuryHepatocellular, cholestatic, mixed

  • ADirect toxicityNAPQI uses up glutathione → zone 3 necrosis

Review article

Iatrogenic and toxic liver injury: postoperative, paracetamol, and alcohol

Drugs, toxins, and complications of medical care injure hepatocytes through direct toxicity or immune reactions. Postoperative causes, paracetamol overdose, alcoholic liver disease, and other hepatotoxic drugs each follow a distinct path. Here, we review their mechanisms, staged presentations, and treatment, and consider how they relate to metabolic and vascular liver disease.

Key points

  • The toxic paracetamol dose is over 150 mg/kg, and risk is higher with chronic alcohol use and malnutrition.
  • Always check a paracetamol level after an overdose, even if the patient looks well.
  • NAC replenishes glutathione and works best within 8 hours.
  • Alcoholic liver disease has AST:ALT over 2:1, with AST usually under 300 U/L.

Pathophysiology

Drugs, toxins, and medical care injure hepatocytes directly or through immune reactions. In paracetamol overdose, increased NAPQI uses up glutathione, causing zone 3 necrosis. In halothane hepatitis, altered liver proteins provoke an immune reaction after repeat exposure. In alcohol use, an increased NADH:NAD+ ratio increases fatty acid synthesis, causing steatosis, and acetaldehyde adducts act as new antigens, causing immune activation and alcoholic hepatitis.

Postoperative complications

Intraoperative hypotension causes ischemic hepatitis. Inhaled anesthetics cause halothane hepatitis, which is immune-mediated and follows repeat exposure. Bile duct injury, such as during cholecystectomy causes bile leak and bile duct stricture. Blood transfusions and hematoma resorption cause an increased bilirubin load and jaundice. Sepsis and TPN cause cholestasis.

Paracetamol overdose

At a normal dose, ~90% undergoes glucuronidation and sulfation and is safely excreted, and ~5–10% is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes, so there is no liver injury. In overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation are saturated, more drug goes through CYP2E1, glutathione is used up, and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins, causing zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis. Toxicity is staged: at 0–24 hours, nausea, vomiting, or no symptoms; at 24–72 hours, RUQ pain and rising AST/ALT; at 72–96 hours, peak AST/ALT and liver failure; and at 4 days–2 weeks, recovery or death.

Alcoholic liver disease

Three pathways lead to the same result: alcohol dehydrogenase (cytosol, main pathway), CYP2E1 (induced by chronic drinking), and catalase (peroxisomes, minor). They produce acetaldehyde with an increased NADH:NAD+ ratio, followed by acetate via aldehyde dehydrogenase. The increased NADH:NAD+ ratio increases fatty acid synthesis and decreases fatty acid breakdown, causing fatty liver (steatosis), which is reversible with abstinence. Acetaldehyde binds proteins, and these acetaldehyde adducts act as new antigens, causing immune activation and free radical damage, leading to alcoholic hepatitis (neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies), fibrosis, and cirrhosis. The spectrum runs from fatty liver (usually no symptoms; hepatomegaly) through alcoholic hepatitis (fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly) to cirrhosis.

Other hepatotoxic drugs

These include isoniazid, amiodarone, methotrexate, valproate, amoxicillin-clavulanate (cholestatic), flucloxacillin (cholestatic), and statins (rare). Intrinsic injury, as with paracetamol, is dose-dependent and predictable, whereas idiosyncratic injury is unpredictable and can be inherited through HLA type: flucloxacillin injury is associated with HLA-B*57:01, so a relative's liver injury from the same drug is a warning. Aspirin given to children during a viral illness, most often influenza or varicella, causes Reye syndrome, an acute encephalopathy with fatty liver failure that begins with vomiting and confusion.

Diagnosis

Postoperative liver injury is judged by its timing after surgery and its LFTs pattern: very high AST and ALT after hypotension, or cholestasis with sepsis or TPN, with MRCP for a bile leak or stricture. Paracetamol overdose is evaluated with a 4-hour paracetamol level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, with LFTs, INR, creatinine, and glucose. Alcoholic liver disease shows AST:ALT over 2:1, with AST usually under 300 U/L, increased GGT, and macrocytosis, with an alcohol history. Drug-induced liver injury rests on the timing of the drug, exclusion of other causes, and improvement after stopping it.

Management

Paracetamol overdose is treated with the antidote NAC, which replenishes glutathione and is best within 8 hours, activated charcoal if within 1–2 hours of ingestion, and transplant evaluation if acute liver failure develops. Alcoholic liver disease is treated by abstinence, the most important measure, nutrition and thiamine, and prednisolone for severe alcoholic hepatitis if the Maddrey score is 32 or more. Postoperative and drug-induced injury is treated by stopping the offending drug, supportive care, and treating the underlying complication.

Relationships to other conditions

. Paracetamol and hypoperfusion both injure zone 3, and intraoperative hypotension links this page to vascular injury.

. Steatosis is shared, and the AST:ALT ratio and alcohol history separate them.

. Paracetamol is a leading cause of acute liver failure, and alcohol of cirrhosis.

. Ethanol and valproate cause pancreatitis as well as liver injury.

Review article

Liver tumors: distinguishing benign lesions, primary cancers, and metastases

Benign or malignant tumors replace and compress normal liver tissue, and metastases are the most common liver malignancy. Hemangioma, hepatic adenoma, and FNH are benign, whereas HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, and angiosarcoma are primary malignancies. Here, we review their features, complications, imaging, and treatment, and consider how they relate to cirrhosis and PSC.

Key points

  • Metastases are the most common liver malignancy, and HCC the most common primary liver cancer.
  • Do not biopsy a hemangioma, because of bleeding risk.
  • In cirrhosis, arterial-phase enhancement with washout diagnoses HCC without biopsy.
  • Hepatic adenoma can rupture, so resect if large (over 5 cm) or bleeding.

Pathophysiology

Tumors replace normal liver, which can cause liver failure, and press on bile ducts, causing obstructive jaundice. Hepatic adenoma and HCC can rupture, causing hemoperitoneum, and HCC can cause polycythemia, hypoglycemia, and hypercalcemia as paraneoplastic effects.

Etiology and mechanisms

Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and should not be biopsied, because of bleeding risk. Hepatic adenoma occurs in young women on oral contraceptives and anabolic steroid users, and can rupture and bleed. FNH has a central stellate scar and no malignant potential. Metastases are the most common liver malignancy, from the colon, breast, lung, and pancreas. HCC is the most common primary liver cancer, associated with cirrhosis, HBV, HCV, and aflatoxin. Cholangiocarcinoma is bile duct cancer, associated with PSC, liver flukes, choledochal cysts, hepatitis B or C, and cirrhosis. Angiosarcoma is rare, associated with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. A fibrolamellar variant of HCC affects young patients without cirrhosis.

Clinical presentation and complications

Tumors are often found incidentally, or cause RUQ pain or mass, weight loss, and worsening of known cirrhosis (HCC). Complications are rupture and hemoperitoneum (hepatic adenoma, HCC), paraneoplastic syndromes (HCC: polycythemia, hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia), obstructive jaundice (cholangiocarcinoma), and liver failure.

Diagnosis

Any liver mass is evaluated with multiphase contrast CT or MRI. HCC shows arterial-phase enhancement with washout, with no biopsy needed in cirrhosis, and increased AFP. For metastases, the primary tumor is sought, such as with colonoscopy and CEA. Hepatic adenoma is best characterized by MRI with a liver-specific contrast agent, and AFP stays normal unless it transforms into HCC. Cholangiocarcinoma is imaged with MRI and MRCP to show a stricture or mass, with CA 19-9 and tissue from brushings or biopsy. Angiosarcoma is a heterogeneous, hemorrhagic mass with progressive enhancement and no washout, and its tumor markers are normal, so biopsy confirms it. Unclear imaging is biopsied, but not for hemangioma. Hemangiomas show peripheral, nodular arterial enhancement that fills in toward the center on later phases, and FNH, mostly in women aged 20–50, has a central scar. Patients with cirrhosis or chronic HBV are surveyed for HCC with ultrasound every 6 months.

Management

Hemangioma and FNH usually need no treatment. Hepatic adenoma is treated by stopping oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids, with resection if large (over 5 cm) or bleeding. HCC is treated by resection, transplant (Milan criteria), or ablation if early, and TACE or systemic therapy if advanced. Metastases and cholangiocarcinoma depend on the primary tumor and stage, with resection if possible. Angiosarcoma is resected if confined to the liver and otherwise treated with chemotherapy or TACE; transplant is not used because it recurs quickly. Adenomas are resected in all men, and in women if over 5 cm or bleeding, because of the risks of rupture and malignant transformation.

Relationships to other conditions

. Cirrhosis is the main setting for HCC, and HCC screening every 6 months with ultrasound is part of its care.

. HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.

. PSC is a major risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

. HCC is among the malignancies that can cause hepatic vein thrombosis.

Pathophysiology

A previously healthy liver is destroyed within weeks, so it stops making clotting factors and clearing ammonia, and the brain swells.

Review article

Acute liver failure and cirrhosis: sudden and chronic loss of hepatic function

Acute liver failure is a sudden loss of function in a previously healthy liver, whereas cirrhosis is chronic scarring in which repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules. Their consequences reflect lost liver function and, in cirrhosis, portal hypertension. Child-Pugh scoring grades cirrhosis severity. Here, we review their causes, complications, workup, and treatment, and consider how every cause of liver injury converges on them.

Key points

  • Acute liver failure is encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks in a previously healthy liver.
  • Its big 4 are encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and infection.
  • Cirrhosis has two arms: portal hypertension and loss of liver function.
  • Child-Pugh rows spell ABCDE: albumin, bilirubin, coagulation, distention (ascites), and encephalopathy.

Pathophysiology

Severe acute injury causes hepatocyte loss in acute liver failure, whereas repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules that distort the architecture in cirrhosis. Increased sinusoidal pressure causes portal hypertension, with varices, ascites, and splenomegaly. Decreased albumin and clotting factor synthesis cause ascites, edema, and coagulopathy, and decreased ammonia clearance causes hepatic encephalopathy.

Etiology and mechanisms

Acute liver failure is severe acute injury in a previously healthy liver, with encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks; main causes are paracetamol, viral hepatitis, ischemic injury, Wilson disease, and AFLP. In cirrhosis, repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules, and distorted architecture raises portal pressure and reduces liver function; main causes are alcohol, MASLD, HBV, HCV, PBC, PSC, and hemochromatosis.

Acute liver failure: the big 4

Encephalopathy causes altered mental status, asterixis, and increased ICP from cerebral edema. Coagulopathy causes increased PT/INR, intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, and mucocutaneous bleeding. Hypoglycemia follows decreased gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores. Infection includes pneumonia, UTI, and sepsis.

Cirrhosis: portal hypertension

Blood diverts into portosystemic collaterals, causing esophageal varices with life-threatening bleeding, caput medusae, and rectal varices. Increased sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure and low albumin cause transudative ascites (SAAG 11 g/L or more), sustained by sodium and water retention as splanchnic vasodilation activates RAAS, the sympathetic nervous system, and ADH, and ascites can lead to SBP (ascitic neutrophils 250/µL or more). Splanchnic vasodilation from nitric oxide decreases effective arterial volume, with RAAS activation and renal vasoconstriction, causing hepatorenal syndrome (functional kidney failure) and sodium and water retention, worsening ascites. Portosystemic shunting lets ammonia bypass the liver, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and hepatic encephalopathy. Splenomegaly causes thrombocytopenia as platelets pool in the spleen.

Cirrhosis: loss of liver function

Decreased ammonia clearance causes hepatic encephalopathy. Decreased clotting factor synthesis causes coagulopathy (increased INR) and bleeding. Decreased bilirubin and bile salt excretion causes jaundice and pruritus. Decreased glucose production causes hypoglycemia. Decreased immune function raises infection risk (SBP, pneumonia, sepsis). Decreased vitamin A, D, E, K processing causes fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, with complications such as osteoporosis and bleeding. Damaged hepatocytes release stored B12, increasing serum B12, which is mostly inactive and rises with severity. Decreased estrogen breakdown increases estrogen, causing spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, and testicular atrophy. Decreased albumin synthesis decreases oncotic pressure, causing ascites and edema.

Child-Pugh score

Points of 1, 2, and 3 are given for albumin (over 35, 28–35, under 28 g/L), bilirubin (under 34, 34–50, over 50 µmol/L), INR (under 1.7, 1.7–2.3, over 2.3), ascites (none, mild, moderate to severe), and encephalopathy (none, grade 1–2, grade 3–4). Class A is 5–6 points (1-year survival about 100%), class B is 7–9 points (about 80%), and class C is 10–15 points (about 45%).

Diagnosis

Acute liver failure is evaluated with LFTs (AST/ALT, bilirubin), complications are checked with INR, glucose, ammonia, and cultures, and the cause is sought with paracetamol, viral and autoimmune serology, and Doppler. Cirrhosis is evaluated with bloods (FBC with low platelets, LFTs, INR, albumin) and ultrasound with elastography showing a nodular, stiff liver, with biopsy as the gold standard if unclear. Complications are screened with EGD and diagnostic paracentesis, and HCC screening is every 6 months with ultrasound. The MELD score, from bilirubin, creatinine, and INR, predicts short-term mortality and ranks patients for transplant. Hepatopulmonary syndrome is hypoxemia from intrapulmonary vasodilation, with dyspnea and platypnea, confirmed by contrast echocardiography and treated by transplant.

Management

Acute liver failure is managed with ICU care, treating the cause, such as with NAC, managing the big 4, and early transplant referral. Varices are treated with a non-selective beta-blocker or band ligation. Variceal bleeding is treated with octreotide or terlipressin, IV ABX, and endoscopic banding within 12 hours, with TIPS if refractory. Ascites is treated with sodium restriction, spironolactone with furosemide, and large-volume paracentesis with albumin. SBP is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin, with long-term prophylaxis afterwards. Hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose, then rifaximin. Hepatorenal syndrome is treated with albumin plus a vasoconstrictor such as terlipressin and transplant. End-stage disease is treated by liver transplant.

Relationships to other conditions

. Paracetamol leads to acute liver failure, whereas alcohol leads to cirrhosis.

. Wilson disease can present as acute liver failure, and hemochromatosis and MASLD lead to cirrhosis.

. Budd-Chiari syndrome and congestion also cause portal hypertension, so portal hypertension alone does not mean cirrhosis.

. Cirrhosis is the main setting for HCC.

Gallstones, Cholecystitis, and Biliary Fistulas

Pathophysiology

Bile that holds too much cholesterol or bilirubin, or sits still, forms stones; a brief cystic duct block is colic, a lasting one is cholecystitis, and years of pressure can open a fistula into the bowel.

  1. Supersaturated or still bileCrystals form
  2. StonesMost stay silent
  3. Brief blockBiliary colic
  4. Lasting blockDistension, ischemia, infection
  5. Gangrene or fistulaPerforation, or gallstone ileus

How a stone forms and blocks

  • ASupersaturationMore cholesterol, or fewer bile salts and phospholipids
  • BNucleationMucin and too few inhibitors: crystals grow
  • CHypomotilityBile stays still: pregnancy, fasting, TPN
  • DCystic duct blockBrief → colic; lasting → cholecystitis

  • Fever and guardingInfection and peritoneal irritation

Review article

Gallstones, cholecystitis, and biliary fistulas: from stone formation to erosion

Excess cholesterol or bilirubin in bile, or bile stasis, forms gallstones, most of which never cause symptoms. A stone that briefly blocks the cystic duct causes biliary colic, a persistent block causes cholecystitis, with Mirizzi syndrome and acalculous cholecystitis as important variants, and chronic inflammation around a large stone can erode into a neighboring organ, forming a fistula through which the stone can obstruct the bowel. Here, we review stone types and risk factors, the forms and complications of cholecystitis, fistula types, and their diagnosis and treatment, and consider how gallbladder disease relates to bile duct stones, pancreatitis, and other conditions.

Key points

  • Cholesterol stones are ~75% of gallstones; their triad is supersaturation, accelerated nucleation, and gallbladder hypomotility.
  • Biliary colic has normal LFTs and no fever; pain over 6 hours or fever suggests cholecystitis.
  • RUQ ultrasound is first-line, and HIDA scan is used if ultrasound is unclear; jaundice suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome.
  • Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients, with a high risk of gangrene and perforation.
  • Cholecystoduodenal fistula is the most common type and the main route for gallstone ileus; pneumobilia and Rigler triad on CT suggest it.
  • Asymptomatic gallstones need no treatment; colic and cholecystitis are treated by cholecystectomy, and gallstone ileus by enterolithotomy first.

Pathophysiology

Increased cholesterol, or decreased bile salts or phospholipids, supersaturates bile and forms crystals, excess nucleation factors help them grow, and hypomotility keeps bile in the gallbladder long enough for them to become stones. A stone that briefly blocks the cystic duct causes biliary colic, and a persistent block causes cholecystitis.

A stone obstructs the cystic duct, causing RUQ pain over 6 hours, and increased back pressure distends the gallbladder. Bacterial colonization with E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus causes fever and sepsis, and the inflamed wall causes RUQ tenderness and Murphy sign. Wall necrosis leads to gangrene, with perforation, abscess, and peritonitis.

Chronic inflammation weakens the gallbladder wall, a large stone presses on it, and a tract opens into a neighboring organ. A stone that enters the bowel can cause gallstone ileus, and gut bacteria that enter the bile ducts cause ascending cholangitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Cholesterol stones are most common (~75%), arise from cholesterol supersaturation, nucleation, and gallbladder hypomotility, and form in the gallbladder. Black pigment stones are less common, arise from chronic hemolysis with increased unconjugated bilirubin, in conditions such as sickle cell disease and spherocytosis, cirrhosis, or ileal disease such as Crohn disease, and form in the gallbladder as calcium bilirubinate. Brown pigment stones are less common, though more common in East Asia, arise from bile duct infection with bacteria or parasites (Clonorchis) or from strictures, and form in the bile ducts. Only ~10% of gallstones show on x-ray, depending on their calcium content. The cholesterol triad comprises supersaturation (increased cholesterol secretion into bile, and decreased bile salts or phospholipids to dissolve it), accelerated nucleation (excess nucleation factors such as mucin, and no nucleation inhibitors to stop crystals forming), and gallbladder hypomotility (stasis, giving crystals time to grow into stones). Risk factors are the 6 Fs: female (estrogen raises cholesterol secretion), fat (obesity), fertile (pregnancy, multiparity), forty (age 40 or older), fair (white or Indigenous American ancestry), and family history. Others are rapid weight loss, bariatric surgery, oral contraceptives, estrogen therapy, fibrates, octreotide, fasting, TPN (hypomotility), Crohn disease, and ileal resection (bile salt loss).

In calculous cholecystitis (~90–95%), a stone obstructs the cystic duct, causing increased back pressure and gallbladder distention, then bacterial colonization (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) and gallbladder wall inflammation. In Mirizzi syndrome, a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck presses on the common hepatic duct from outside, causing cholecystitis plus obstructive jaundice, with cholestatic LFTs unlike simple cholecystitis. Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients (ICU, burns, sepsis, TPN), with gallbladder stasis and ischemia without a stone, causing inflammation with a high risk of gangrene and perforation. Acalculous disease accounts for ~10% of acute cholecystitis.

Cholecystoduodenal fistula connects the gallbladder and duodenum and is the main route for gallstone ileus, with Bouveret syndrome if the stone blocks the pylorus or duodenum. Cholecystocolic fistula connects the gallbladder and colon, causing bile acid diarrhea, and stones may pass in the stool. Cholecystogastric fistula connects the gallbladder and stomach and can cause gastric outlet obstruction. Cholecystocholedochal fistula connects the gallbladder and common bile duct, as in advanced Mirizzi syndrome. Choledochoduodenal fistula connects the common bile duct and duodenum, from a penetrating duodenal ulcer or CBD stones. Causes are gallstones (most cases, especially large stones), peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, trauma or surgery, and Crohn disease. Of biliary-enteric fistulas, ~68% are cholecystoduodenal, ~17% cholecystocolic, and ~5% cholecystogastric.

Clinical presentation and complications

Cholelithiasis is mostly asymptomatic and often found by chance on imaging. In biliary colic, a heavy, fatty meal triggers CCK release, the gallbladder contracts against an impacted stone, and epigastric or RUQ pain radiates to the back or right scapula, resolving within 6 hours as the stone dislodges. Stones cause disease by location: in the gallbladder, cholelithiasis; in the cystic duct, biliary colic with a brief block or cholecystitis with a persistent block; in the common bile duct, choledocholithiasis, which can lead to cholangitis; and at the ampulla, gallstone pancreatitis, all covered under bile duct stones. About 1–2% of people with gallstones develop symptoms each year. Complications are acute cholecystitis from a persistent cystic duct block; chronic cholecystitis from repeated colic, which can calcify the wall as porcelain gallbladder; choledocholithiasis, which can lead to cholangitis; gallstone pancreatitis; gallstone ileus, when a large stone passes through a fistula; and gallbladder carcinoma, whose risk rises with stone size and is highest over 3 cm.

Symptoms are RUQ pain over 6 hours, RUQ tenderness, Murphy sign, fever, and nausea and vomiting. LFTs are usually normal, and jaundice suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome. Complications are sepsis, gallbladder empyema (pus-filled gallbladder), gangrenous cholecystitis (leading to perforation, abscess, and peritonitis), emphysematous cholecystitis (gas-forming bacteria, in diabetics), and cholecystoenteric fistula, leading to gallstone ileus. A chronically inflamed gallbladder with a large stone forms a fistula, the stone passes into the bowel, and it lodges at the terminal ileum or ileocecal valve, causing small bowel obstruction (CAVO: colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, obstipation). Emphysematous cholecystitis follows wall ischemia with gas-forming bacteria, especially Clostridium perfringens, mostly in men and diabetics, and carries a high mortality. Chronic cholecystitis follows repeated biliary colic, with stones in over 90%, and causes ongoing inflammation and fibrosis of the wall; it gives dull RUQ or epigastric pain after meals for weeks to months, and fever is rare. Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, mucosa herniated into the thickened wall, are found in ~90% of specimens. Porcelain gallbladder is a wall calcified by chronic inflammation, often found by chance on x-ray or CT, and its cancer risk is lower than once thought.

Fistulas often cause no symptoms, or recurrent cholangitis, and diarrhea in cholecystocolic disease. Complications are gallstone ileus (small bowel obstruction, CAVO), Bouveret syndrome (gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting and epigastric fullness), ascending cholangitis as gut bacteria enter the bile ducts, and GI bleeding. Gallstone ileus usually impacts at the terminal ileum, mostly with stones over 2 cm, and mainly affects older women.

Diagnosis

Gallstones are evaluated by RUQ ultrasound, which is first-line and shows mobile, shadowing stones. LFTs and FBC assess complications and are normal in biliary colic. Plain x-ray misses most stones, since only ~10% contain enough calcium to show.

Acute cholecystitis is evaluated by RUQ ultrasound, first-line, showing a thick wall, pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy sign. An unclear ultrasound is followed by HIDA scan, in which the gallbladder does not fill. FBC and LFTs assess inflammation, showing leukocytosis with usually normal LFTs. Mirizzi syndrome is evaluated by MRCP or ERCP, and gallstone ileus by CT, showing Rigler triad. Emphysematous cholecystitis shows gas in the gallbladder wall or lumen on CT. Chronic cholecystitis shows a thick wall and stones on ultrasound, and a HIDA scan with CCK shows an ejection fraction under 35%.

A suspected fistula is evaluated by CT abdomen, showing pneumobilia. Gallstone ileus is evaluated by CT, showing Rigler triad. The fistula opening is evaluated by ERCP or upper endoscopy. CT detects Rigler triad with a sensitivity of ~93%, and an x-ray may also show it.

Management

Asymptomatic gallstones need no treatment. Biliary colic is treated with pain relief such as NSAIDs, then elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Patients not fit for surgery can have ursodeoxycholic acid, for small cholesterol stones only. Ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves fewer than half of stones.

Acute cholecystitis is treated with NPO, IV fluids, pain relief, and IV ABX, then early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours. Patients too unwell for surgery, or with acalculous disease, have percutaneous cholecystostomy (drain) with ABX. Gangrene or perforation requires emergency cholecystectomy. Gallstone ileus is treated by enterolithotomy (removing the stone from the bowel), with fistula repair later if needed. Mirizzi syndrome is treated by cholecystectomy (often open), with ERCP stenting if needed. Emphysematous cholecystitis also needs emergency cholecystectomy. Chronic cholecystitis is treated with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, or a low-fat diet if the patient is not fit for surgery. Porcelain gallbladder is removed if it causes symptoms or shows selective mucosal calcification; otherwise, observation is discussed with the patient.

A symptomatic fistula is treated by cholecystectomy with fistula repair. Gallstone ileus is treated by enterolithotomy first, with fistula repair later if needed. Bouveret syndrome is treated by endoscopic stone removal, with surgery if this fails. Enterolithotomy is usually open.

Relationships to other conditions

. Most bile duct stones start in the gallbladder. Jaundice and a cholestatic pattern move the stone from the cystic duct to the CBD, Mirizzi syndrome mimics this from outside the duct, and fever with RUQ pain becomes cholangitis once jaundice completes Charcot triad.

. Ileal disease causes gallstones by losing bile salts.

. A penetrating duodenal ulcer can form a choledochoduodenal fistula, and both can cause gastric outlet obstruction.

. Bile acid diarrhea from a cholecystocolic fistula is a rare cause to remember in older patients with gallstones.

Choledocholithiasis and Ascending Cholangitis

Pathophysiology

A stone or stricture stops bile, so bilirubin backs up; when bacteria climb into the still bile under pressure, they enter the blood.

  1. BlockStone, stricture, stent
  2. CholestasisPale stool, dark urine
  3. Bacteria ascendFrom the duodenum
  4. PressureBile and bacteria leak to blood
  5. SepsisShock if undrained

  • ACBD obstructionBile cannot reach the duodenum

  • Pain without feverStone moving

  • 2Stone at the ampullaBlocks both ducts: pancreatitis

Stones pass: about a third of duct stones pass without treatment, but they are offered removal because some cause cholangitis or pancreatitis.

Review article

Choledocholithiasis and ascending cholangitis: obstruction of the common bile duct, with and without infection

A stone in the CBD blocks bile flow and causes cholestasis, a stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts and causes gallstone pancreatitis, and bacteria ascending into the stagnant bile cause ascending cholangitis, in which infected bile under pressure enters the blood and causes sepsis. Lipase separates gallstone pancreatitis, fever separates cholangitis, and the likelihood of a stone decides between MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound and going straight to ERCP. Here, we review the mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of all three, and consider how they relate to gallbladder disease, pancreatitis, PSC, and malignant obstruction.

Key points

  • Lipase is normal in choledocholithiasis and increased 3 or more times in gallstone pancreatitis.
  • Up to 90% of duct stones form in the gallbladder; primary brown pigment stones form in the ducts and cause recurrent cholangitis.
  • High likelihood of a stone goes to ERCP; intermediate likelihood goes to MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound.
  • Charcot triad is fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice; Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion and means septic shock.
  • Cholangitis is treated with IV ABX and drainage, usually by ERCP, urgently when severe.
  • Cholecystectomy follows during the same admission, or once recovered, when gallstones were the cause.

Pathophysiology

A stone in the CBD stops bile draining into the duodenum. Back pressure increases conjugated bilirubin and bile salts, causing jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine, and decreased bile reaching the gut causes pale stools. A stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts, causing gallstone pancreatitis, and bacteria behind the blockage cause ascending cholangitis.

A blocked duct holds bile still, and E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus ascend from the duodenum into it. Infected bile under pressure causes fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice, and bacteria and toxins that enter the blood cause a cytokine storm and sepsis.

Etiology and mechanisms

A stone in the CBD means bile cannot drain into the duodenum, increasing conjugated bilirubin and bile salts, with jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine, and decreasing bile reaching the gut, with pale stools. A stone at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts, so pancreatic enzymes activate inside the pancreas. Gallstones are the most common cause of pancreatitis. Up to 90% of stones are secondary, forming in the gallbladder and migrating into the CBD, usually as cholesterol stones. Primary stones form in the ducts with bile stasis and infection, as brown pigment stones; they are more common in Asia and cause recurrent cholangitis.

Ascending cholangitis follows any bile duct obstruction: a CBD stone, the most common cause, a benign or malignant stricture, a blocked biliary stent after ERCP, or PSC. Stasis allows bacteria to ascend from the duodenum (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus), and infected bile under pressure lets bacteria and toxins enter the blood.

Clinical presentation and complications

Choledocholithiasis causes RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools, with a cholestatic pattern and normal lipase. Gallstone pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting, and may also cause jaundice, with a cholestatic pattern and lipase increased 3 or more times normal. Long-standing obstruction causes secondary biliary cirrhosis.

Charcot triad is fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice. A cytokine storm causes sepsis, leading to Reynolds pentad, which adds hypotension and confusion. Reynolds pentad means septic shock and needs urgent biliary drainage. Charcot triad is specific, but only ~25% of patients have all three features.

Diagnosis

The cholestatic LFT pattern is increased ALP and GGT, increased conjugated bilirubin, and AST/ALT that can spike early, then fall. RUQ ultrasound comes first, showing a dilated CBD (over 6 mm), although the stone itself is often not seen. Intermediate likelihood, such as abnormal LFTs or a dilated CBD alone, is evaluated by MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound. High likelihood (stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin over 68 µmol/L with a dilated CBD) proceeds to ERCP, which diagnoses and removes the stone. A dilated CBD is over 6 mm, or over 8 mm after cholecystectomy, and ultrasound shows the stone itself in only 15–40%. Age over 55 is an intermediate predictor, and patients with no predictors proceed to cholecystectomy, with intraoperative cholangiography if needed.

Inflammation is evaluated with FBC (leukocytosis), CRP, and blood cultures; cholestasis with LFTs, showing a cholestatic pattern with increased bilirubin; and obstruction and its cause with ultrasound or CT (dilated bile ducts), with MRCP if unclear. The Tokyo Guidelines combine these three findings to diagnose and grade cholangitis.

Management

Choledocholithiasis is treated with ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone removal, then cholecystectomy during the same admission. Gallstone pancreatitis is treated with IV fluids, pain relief, and early feeding, with ERCP only if there is cholangitis or ongoing obstruction, and cholecystectomy during the same admission if mild. Alternatively, laparoscopic CBD exploration clears the duct during the cholecystectomy itself.

Resuscitation uses IV fluids, with vasopressors if in shock. Infection is treated with broad-spectrum IV ABX such as piperacillin-tazobactam. Bile is drained by ERCP with stone removal or stent, which is definitive, with percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails. Recurrence is prevented by cholecystectomy once recovered, if gallstones were the cause. Severe disease, with shock or organ failure, needs urgent drainage, while 80–90% of mild cases respond to ABX and are drained before discharge.

Relationships to other conditions

. Most duct stones start in the gallbladder. Cystic duct stones leave LFTs normal, whereas CBD stones produce a cholestatic pattern, and RUQ pain with fever but no jaundice suggests cholecystitis rather than cholangitis.

. Stones usually cause painful jaundice, whereas tumors cause painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder.

. Gallstones are the leading cause; the pancreatitis page covers its systemic and local complications.

. Strictures in PSC cause recurrent bacterial cholangitis as bile stagnates behind them.

Review article

Biliary tract and periampullary malignancies: painless obstruction of bile flow

Tumors in or around the bile ducts gradually obstruct bile flow, causing painless obstructive jaundice. Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common periampullary cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma arise within the biliary tree. Courvoisier law separates malignant from gallstone obstruction. Here, we review their features, workup, and treatment, and consider how they relate to gallstone disease and PSC.

Key points

  • Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignancy.
  • The double duct sign supports a periampullary tumor.
  • CA 19-9 and CEA are not for screening.
  • Resectable periampullary tumors are treated by pancreaticoduodenectomy.

Pathophysiology

A tumor below the cystic duct causes a slow, steady blockage of bile flow. Bile cannot reach the gut, causing pale stools, and builds up behind the block, causing painless jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine. Because the gallbladder wall is healthy and stretchy, it enlarges into a palpable, nontender gallbladder.

Etiology and mechanisms

Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common periampullary cancer, with risk factors of smoking, chronic pancreatitis, and diabetes. Ampullary adenocarcinoma blocks bile early, so it is found earlier and has a better prognosis, may cause intermittent jaundice, and is linked to FAP. Duodenal adenocarcinoma is rare, may also cause GI bleeding or obstruction, and is linked to FAP, Lynch syndrome, and celiac disease. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet cells and may secrete hormones (insulinoma, gastrinoma, vipoma, glucagonoma), with MEN1 as a risk factor. Bile duct adenocarcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma) is intrahepatic, perihilar, or distal, with perihilar (Klatskin) most common, and risk factors of PSC, liver flukes (Clonorchis), choledochal cysts, hepatitis B or C, and cirrhosis. Gallbladder carcinoma is often found late, or by chance after cholecystectomy, in older women, with risk factors of gallstones (especially large), porcelain gallbladder, polyps over 1 cm, and PSC. Lynch syndrome also raises the risk of ampullary cancer. Of cholangiocarcinomas, ~50% are perihilar, ~40% distal, and ~10% intrahepatic, and hepatitis B or C and cirrhosis also raise the risk. More than half of gallbladder carcinomas are found by chance at cholecystectomy; the risk is highest with stones over 3 cm, and the risk from porcelain gallbladder is lower than once thought.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are painless jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss, and a palpable, nontender gallbladder. In malignant obstruction, a tumor below the cystic duct (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD) causes slow, steady blockage of a healthy, stretchy gallbladder, producing an enlarged, palpable, nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice. In gallstone obstruction, a stone in the CBD meets a gallbladder already scarred by repeated inflammation, which cannot distend, usually with pain. Courvoisier law states that painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be caused by gallstones, so malignancy is suspected. Complications are ascending cholangitis, liver metastases, and gastric outlet obstruction.

Diagnosis

Cholestasis is evaluated by LFTs. Tumor markers are CA 19-9 and CEA, which are not for screening. Imaging is ultrasound, then CT or MRCP, which may show the double duct sign. Tissue diagnosis is by ERCP brushings or endoscopic ultrasound biopsy. Periampullary tumors show the double duct sign on CT and are sampled by EUS biopsy. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are found by hormone levels that match the syndrome, such as insulin during hypoglycemia or a fasting gastrin, with chromogranin A and CT, MRI, or EUS. Cholangiocarcinoma appears on MRCP as a stricture or mass, and because ERCP brushings can miss it, surgery may proceed without tissue. Gallbladder carcinoma shows a mass or wall thickening on ultrasound and is often found on histology after cholecystectomy.

Management

Periampullary tumors are treated by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) if resectable. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are resected if localized and treated with somatostatin analogs such as octreotide, targeted therapy, or chemotherapy if advanced. Cholangiocarcinoma is treated by resection (bile duct, often with part of the liver), with transplant in selected cases. Gallbladder carcinoma is treated by cholecystectomy with liver resection and lymph node removal. Unresectable disease is treated with a biliary stent to relieve jaundice, and chemotherapy. Gallbladder carcinoma confined to the mucosa needs only cholecystectomy.

Relationships to other conditions

. Pain and a shrunken gallbladder favor stones; painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder favors malignancy.

. PSC raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma.

. Chronic pancreatitis is a risk factor for pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.

. Gastrinomas and vipomas link pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors to chronic secretory diarrhea.

. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma overlaps with primary liver malignancy.

Review article

Acute pancreatitis: autodigestion and its local and systemic consequences

Premature activation of trypsin inside the pancreas leads to autodigestion, causing local and systemic inflammation. Gallstones and ethanol are the leading causes in the I GET SMASHED mnemonic. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 criteria, and severity is graded by organ failure and local complications. Here, we review its causes, complications, and management, and consider how it relates to biliary disease and malabsorption.

Key points

  • Gallstones are the most common cause, and ethanol the second.
  • Diagnosis requires any 2 of pain, enzymes, and imaging.
  • RUQ ultrasound is obtained in every patient.
  • CT too early can miss necrosis.
  • Prophylactic ABX are not given.

Pathophysiology

Trypsin is activated inside the pancreas, and the enzymes digest the gland, causing epigastric pain. Increased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α cause SIRS. Increased capillary permeability causes third spacing, with hypovolemia and shock, and lipase digests surrounding fat, releasing fatty acids that bind calcium and cause hypocalcemia.

Etiology and mechanisms

I GET SMASHED covers idiopathic disease, with no cause found in about 10–20%; gallstones, the most common cause, in which a stone blocks the ampulla; ethanol, the second most common, through direct acinar toxicity and protein plugs in ducts; trauma, such as blunt abdominal trauma from a bicycle handlebar injury; corticosteroids; mumps and other infections, such as coxsackievirus and CMV; autoimmune causes, including IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis, SLE, and polyarteritis nodosa; scorpion sting (Tityus trinitatis, Trinidad); hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia (usually over 11.3 mmol/L), and hypothermia; ERCP, of which it is the most common complication; and drugs, including azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, furosemide, sulfonamides, and didanosine.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients have severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting, fever, tachycardia, and epigastric tenderness and guarding. Trypsin activated inside the pancreas causes autodigestion, with epigastric pain and increased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, leading to SIRS and local complications. Systemically, increased capillary permeability causes third spacing, with hypovolemia and fluid in the lungs and abdomen, leading to shock, AKI, ARDS, exudative ascites, and abdominal compartment syndrome. Increased tissue factor causes clotting throughout small vessels, consuming platelets and clotting factors and shearing red cells (schistocytes), leading to DIC. Lipase digests surrounding fat, and fatty acids bind calcium (fat saponification), causing hypocalcemia; islet damage causes hyperglycemia. Locally, interstitial edematous pancreatitis causes pancreatic edema and fluid around the pancreas, forming a pseudocyst after 4 weeks, with no epithelium, which can cause infection, rupture, and compression with small bowel or gastric outlet obstruction. Necrotizing pancreatitis causes tissue necrosis and an acute necrotic collection, becoming walled-off necrosis after 4 weeks; enzymes erode blood vessels, causing retroperitoneal bleeding (Cullen and Grey Turner signs). Repeated attacks can lead to chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis is most often caused by alcohol in adults, though under 10% of heavy drinkers develop it, and by smoking; in children, cystic fibrosis and genes such as PRSS1, SPINK1, and CFTR are responsible. Protein plugs in the ducts calcify and form stones, and fibrosis replaces the gland. It causes chronic epigastric pain, often better leaning forward, with pain-free periods; steatorrhea and weight loss once over 90% of the gland is damaged; pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes; and an increased risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis

Any 2 of 3 criteria are required: acute, severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back; lipase (or amylase) at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, with lipase more specific; and typical findings on contrast CT abdomen, MRI, or ultrasound. The cause is sought with RUQ ultrasound for gallstones in every patient, LFTs (ALT over 150 suggests gallstones), triglycerides, calcium, alcohol history, and medications. Contrast CT is obtained if the diagnosis is unclear, or after 48–72 hours if the patient is not improving, as CT too early can miss necrosis. Severity is assessed with FBC, creatinine, BUN, oxygen saturation, and scores such as BISAP. By the revised Atlanta classification, mild disease has no organ failure and no local complications, moderately severe disease has organ failure lasting under 48 hours or local complications, and severe disease has organ failure lasting over 48 hours. Chronic pancreatitis is shown by calcifications, its hallmark, on CT or MRCP, with duct dilation, strictures, or stones, and exocrine function is assessed with fecal elastase (normal over 500 µg/g) or a 72-hour fecal fat over 7 g a day, the most definitive test.

Management

Supportive care comprises goal-directed IV fluids such as Hartmann solution, pain relief, and early oral feeding, with enteral feeding if severe. The cause is treated: cholecystectomy during the same admission for gallstones, stopping drinking for alcohol, insulin infusion for hypertriglyceridemia, and stopping the offending drug. Infected necrosis is treated with ABX such as a carbapenem and delayed drainage or necrosectomy, ideally after 4 weeks, with no prophylactic ABX. Pseudocysts are observed, and drained only if symptomatic or complicated. In chronic pancreatitis, every patient stops alcohol and smoking. Pain is treated with paracetamol, NSAIDs, or pregabalin first and opioids only if these fail, with celiac plexus block, and ERCP or shock wave lithotripsy for obstructing stones or strictures. Steatorrhea is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals, which does not relieve pain.

Relationships to other conditions

. A stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts. A cholestatic LFT pattern and ALT over 150 favor a gallstone cause.

. Repeated attacks lead to chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency.

. Epigastric pain overlaps; radiation to the back and increased lipase favor pancreatitis, and pain that changes with meals favors PUD.

. Autoimmune pancreatitis can occur with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.

. Painless jaundice favors a pancreatic head tumor over pancreatitis.

Appendicitis

Pathophysiology

Obstruction or inflammation of the lumen raises pressure within it, so bacteria multiply and the wall becomes ischemic, inflamed, and at risk of perforation.

  1. Lumen blockedOr mucosa inflamed
  2. DistentionMucus and bacteria
  3. IschemiaVenous, then arterial
  4. Inflamed serosaPain localizes
  5. PerforationAbscess or peritonitis

Review article

Appendicitis: luminal obstruction, migrating pain, and perforation

Obstruction of the appendix lumen leads to increased pressure, infection, and ischemia, causing inflammation and eventually perforation. Pain classically migrates from the periumbilical region to the RLQ as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum. Here, we review its causes, examination signs, age-specific imaging, and treatment, and consider how it relates to diverticulitis and other causes of abdominal pain.

Key points

  • Fecalith is the most common cause in adults, and lymphoid hyperplasia in children.
  • Pain migrates from visceral (T8–T10) to parietal over 12–24 hours.
  • Imaging depends on the patient: CT AP in adults, and ultrasound first in children and pregnancy.
  • Diagnosis is often clinical.

Pathophysiology

A fecalith or lymphoid tissue blocks the lumen, and increased intraluminal pressure causes distention and infection, with periumbilical visceral pain. Pressure then compresses the wall, causing ischemia and infarction, inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, causing sharp RLQ pain, and the dead wall ruptures, causing abscess and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Obstruction arises from a fecalith, most common in adults; lymphoid hyperplasia, in children and after viral infection; or a neoplasm, such as carcinoid, in older adults. Increased intraluminal pressure causes distention and infection, then ischemia and infarction, then perforation and abscess.

Clinical presentation and complications

Periumbilical visceral pain (T8–T10) moves to sharp, localized RLQ pain as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum over 12–24 hours, with anorexia, nausea and vomiting after the pain, and low-grade fever. McBurney point is tenderness one-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus and suggests typical appendix position. Rovsing sign is pain in the RLQ on pressing the LLQ, suggesting peritoneal irritation in the RLQ. Psoas sign is pain on extending the right hip with the patient lying on the left side, suggesting a retrocecal appendix irritating the iliopsoas. Obturator sign is pain on internally rotating the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix irritating the obturator internus. Rebound tenderness and guarding, with pain when pressure is released and a tense abdominal wall, suggest peritonitis. Complications are perforation after 48–72 hours, particularly in young children and older adults; abscess or phlegmon; and generalized peritonitis and sepsis.

Diagnosis

Bloods show leukocytosis with left shift and CRP, β-hCG is obtained in anyone who could be pregnant to rule out ectopic pregnancy, and urinalysis is performed. Adults have CT AP with contrast, showing an appendix over 6 mm and fat stranding. Children and pregnant patients have ultrasound first to avoid radiation, with MRI if unclear in pregnancy. Diagnosis is often clinical, using scores such as the Alvarado score.

Management

Uncomplicated appendicitis is treated by laparoscopic appendectomy with perioperative ABX, or ABX alone in selected cases. Perforation with generalized peritonitis requires emergency appendectomy with IV ABX. Perforation with a contained abscess is treated with IV ABX and percutaneous drainage, with appendectomy later if needed.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are blind pouches obstructed by a fecalith, with abscess and perforation as complications. Appendicitis causes RLQ pain, and diverticulitis LLQ pain.

. RLQ pain is shared; a longer history with diarrhea and weight loss favors Crohn disease.

. Carcinoid is a cause of appendiceal obstruction in older adults, and can cause secretory diarrhea.

Ectopic pregnancy. This is the mimic to exclude, so β-hCG is obtained in anyone who could be pregnant.

Localizing GI Bleeding

The question

Blood in or from the gut asks four questions: how much is missing, how fast is it going, how far has it traveled, and could it be something else? The source comes last, because the first two decide what happens in the next hour.

  1. How much is missing?Pulse and posture, not hemoglobin
  2. How fast?Color, clots, and clinical change
  3. How far has it come?Vomited, black, maroon, or red
  4. Is it blood, and from the gut?Iron, nose, vagina, bladder
  5. Then the sourceEndoscopy or CTA

Why color comes after the pulse

  • Color is a clockIt records time spent in the bowel, not the place it came from
  • A clock can be outrunA fast upper bleed reaches the rectum red in under an hour
  • The pulse does not lie about rateRed stool with shock is an upper bleed until shown otherwise

The mechanism

Blood changes color as acid and bacteria turn hemoglobin into dark pigment, so color depends on transit, rate, and where it starts.

Color is a clock

  • ABright redFresh: anorectal or left colon if small in amount
  • BMaroon, or with clotsHours in the bowel: right colon or small bowel, or a brisk upper bleed; clots make an upper source unlikely
  • CBlack, sticky, foul (melena)Digested for about 8–14 hours: usually upper, but a slow right colon can do it; as little as 50–100 mL is enough
  • DRed and fastOutruns digestion: an upper source with shock

The route

  • 1–2EsophagusVarices, esophagitis
  • 3JunctionMallory-Weiss tear
  • 4–5Stomach and duodenumUlcer, gastritis, Dieulafoy lesion
  • 6Third part of the duodenumAortoenteric fistula
  • 7Small bowelAngiodysplasia, tumor, Crohn disease, Meckel diverticulum
  • 8–10Colon above the sigmoidAngiodysplasia, cancer, ischemia
  • 11–12Sigmoid and rectumDiverticula, colitis, radiation
  • 13AnusHemorrhoids, fissure

What the body shows, and when

  • EPulseRises first; β-blockers and pacemakers hide it
  • FHemoglobinWhole blood is lost, so concentration is normal until fluid moves in: 24–72 hours
  • GUreaRises as digested blood is absorbed, and as a poorly perfused kidney reabsorbs more; creatinine changes little
  • HBlood pressureHolds until about a third of the blood volume is gone; a fall on standing comes earlier

Note: Low MCV at the first visit means the bleeding is old, whatever the color today, because iron takes weeks to run out.

Discriminators

These findings move the odds between an upper and a lower source, or between a bleed that can wait and one that cannot.

Upper or lower

Melena by historyLR 5–6 for upper
UCR over about 120 (urea-to-creatinine over 30 in older units)LR 7.5 for upper
Blood or coffee grounds from a nasogastric tubeLR 9.6 for upper; a clear aspirate does not exclude a duodenal source
Clots in the stoolLR 0.05 for upper, so strongly lower
HematemesisUpper, or swallowed blood
Blood on the paper onlyAnorectal

Severe or not (upper)

FindingWorth
TachycardiaLR 4.9 for a bleed needing urgent treatment
Hemoglobin under 80 g/LLR 4.5–6.2

If there isThink of

Differentials

What else it could be, and why it is missed: not blood, not the gut, a body that hides loss, or a number that reassures.

Not GI blood

If there isConsiderObtain

Who hides it

WhoWhat is lostSo
