Reassurance that misleads

  • A normal hemoglobinIn the first hours it says nothing about loss
  • A clear nasogastric aspirateA closed pylorus hides a duodenal ulcer
  • Bright red bloodCan be upper if fast
  • MelenaCan be the right colon; it lasts 3–5 days after bleeding stops
  • Hemorrhoids on examinationCommon, and they coexist with cancer
  • A normal EGDDieulafoy lesions come and go, and the third part of the duodenum may not have been seen
  • Iron givenTurns stool black and hides melena
  • A negative stool testSampling; use only for screening, not in overt bleeding

Guidelines differ: Most do not advise routine nasogastric lavage now, because it does not change outcome despite its value for locating the source.

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The red stool

  1. A 64-year-old passes a large amount of bright red blood per rectum

    What it changes

    The color suggests the colon, and at this age diverticular bleeding is the first thought. Bright red only means the blood spent little time in the bowel, however. That can be because the source is near the rectum or because the bleeding is very fast.

  2. Pulse is 128 and blood pressure is 88/50 mmHg

    What it changes

    Shock changes the meaning of the color. A lower source that causes shock is possible, but a brisk upper bleed is common enough that it must be excluded first. Two large-bore lines, blood, and a call to endoscopy now come before any reasoning about the source.

  3. They take ibuprofen each day for a knee

    What it changes

    An NSAID raises the chance of an ulcer, especially a duodenal one over the gastroduodenal artery, which bleeds hard. The upper source moves ahead of diverticular bleeding. Iron deficiency or a change in bowel habit would have pulled the other way.

  4. Urea is 18 mmol/L (2.5–7.1) and creatinine is 90 µmol/L (45–90)

    What it changes

    The UCR is 200, which is well over the level that points to an upper source. Digested blood has been absorbed as protein, and kidney function is normal, so it is not from the kidney. This supports doing EGD before colonoscopy.

  5. EGD shows a spurting posterior duodenal ulcer

    What it changes

    The color was right about the time in the bowel and wrong about the place. The lesson is to read color together with the pulse, and to look up before down whenever there is shock. The ulcer is on .

Case 2: The normal hemoglobin

  1. A 45-year-old has vomited bright red blood twice; they feel dizzy on standing

    What it changes

    Fresh red vomit means bleeding above the ligament of Treitz that is recent and not yet digested. Dizziness on standing is a sign of volume loss, though it is less reliable than a measured fall.

  2. Hemoglobin is 138 g/L (120–160)

    What it changes

    This does not reassure, because the hemoglobin is a concentration. Red cells and plasma left together, so the number is unchanged until fluid moves in from the tissues over a day or more. It will be a baseline, not a measure of loss.

  3. Standing raises the pulse from 92 to 130

    What it changes

    A rise of 30 or more on standing is a real sign of loss, and it appears before the blood pressure falls. It tells more than the hemoglobin. Fluid and cross-matched blood should be ready before it is needed.

  4. Platelets are 72 × 10⁹/L (150–400) and the spleen is palpable

    What it changes

    Low platelets with a large spleen point to portal hypertension, which makes varices likely. A variceal bleed is treated differently from the start: early vasoactive drug and antibiotics, a cautious transfusion target, and airway protection. The same story with normal platelets would have pointed to an ulcer or a tear.

  5. They have not drunk alcohol, and ferritin is 1600 µg/L (30–300)

    What it changes

    Cirrhosis need not come from alcohol, and a ferritin this high suggests hemochromatosis, so family history and diabetes are worth asking about later. The cause of the cirrhosis does not change the first hour; holds the rest.

Case 3: The black stool

  1. A 70-year-old mentions black stool for a week

    What it changes

    Black stool asks first whether it is blood. Melena is sticky, tarry, and foul, and black stool that is none of these is often iron or bismuth. Asking the patient to describe the smell and consistency splits them quickly.

  2. They started iron tablets two weeks ago for anemia

    What it changes

    Iron makes stool dark green to black, but formed and not foul, so this may be all. But iron also means that someone found anemia, and that has to be explained. The tablets can hide new melena, so the question is what made them anemic.

  3. MCV is 72 fL (80–100) and ferritin is 8 µg/L (30–300)

    What it changes

    Small cells and a very low ferritin mean the loss has been going on for weeks or months. In a 70-year-old, that is a bleeding source in the gut until shown otherwise, and a slow right-sided colon cancer is the one not to miss. The black color is now beside the point.

  4. The stool on the glove is dark green, formed, and not foul

    What it changes

    That fits iron rather than melena, so there is probably no active upper bleed today. It does not answer the anemia. Both endoscopies are still needed, because a normal stool test on one day cannot exclude a slow source.

  5. Colonoscopy finds a cecal cancer

    What it changes

    The black stool was a false alarm, and it led to a true finding because the anemia was not accepted as the answer. Iron deficiency at 70 deserves a full look at both ends. holds the treatment.

Where it leads

Stabilize first, decide where to look, and leave the treatment to the page that owns the source.

  1. Two lines, crossmatchBlood if under 70 g/L, higher in heart disease
  2. Stop and reverseAnticoagulants if life-threatening
  3. Score itGlasgow-Blatchford or Oakland
  4. EGD or CTABy site and rate
  5. Second lookIf no source

Which test first

If there isObtain
Upper bleed, stableEGD within 24 hours, earlier if variceal
Red blood with shockEGD, or CTA if too unstable, then embolization
Lower bleed, stableColonoscopy after preparation, not urgent
Lower bleed, ongoing and severeCTA
Two normal endoscopiesCapsule; CT enterography if obstruction is possible
A young person with painless bloodMeckel scan
Iron deficiency without overt bloodEGD with duodenal biopsy, and colonoscopy

Angiodysplasia, which has no page of its own

  • WhereRight colon and small bowel; aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome, from lost von Willebrand multimers), kidney failure, and heart pumps increase the risk
  • First moveArgon plasma coagulation; iron; octreotide, thalidomide, or bevacizumab for refractory bleeding

Review article

GI bleeding and obstruction: locating the source from the blood, the patient, and the pattern of symptoms

Gastrointestinal bleeding is divided by the ligament of Treitz into upper and lower GI bleeding, which differ in how the blood appears, which causes dominate, how the bleeding is scored, and which test comes first. Obstruction presents with colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation, and its level and cause shape both the presentation and the danger. Here, we review the causes, signs, and initial management of upper and lower GI bleeding and of small and large bowel obstruction, and consider how they relate to the condition pages that describe each cause.

Key points

  • Upper GI bleeding, above the ligament of Treitz, makes up 75% of acute GI bleeds and presents with hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melena; a BUN:creatinine ratio over 30 points upward.
  • Peptic ulcer disease is the most common upper source, followed by esophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis, varices, and Mallory-Weiss tears.
  • Diverticulosis is the most common lower source in older adults, hemorrhoids and fissures in younger adults, and anal fissure in infants and toddlers; brisk upper GI bleeding can also cause hematochezia.
  • Upper bleeding is scored with the Glasgow-Blatchford score and investigated by EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal; lower GI bleeding is scored with the Oakland score and investigated by colonoscopy, with CTA for brisk bleeding.
  • Obstruction presents with CAVO; adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction and colorectal cancer of large bowel obstruction, and strangulation or a closed loop with a competent ileocecal valve is the main danger.

Approach

The ligament of Treitz, at the duodenojejunal flexure, divides upper from lower GI bleeding. Bleeding above it causes hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melena and accounts for 75% of acute GI bleeds, whereas bleeding below it, from the small bowel beyond the third part of the duodenum, the colon, the rectum, or the anus, causes hematochezia. Hematochezia usually means a lower source, but brisk upper GI bleeding can cause it too, so hemodynamics matter as much as the color of the blood. Obstruction announces itself with CAVO, colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation, and the level of the blockage sets both the pattern and the likely cause.

Upper versus lower GI bleeding

Among upper sources, peptic ulcer disease is the most common, at 32–36%, driven by H. pylori and NSAIDs, followed by esophagitis at 24%, gastritis at 18–22%, duodenitis at 13%, esophageal varices at 11%, which form when portal pressure exceeds 12 mmHg, and Mallory-Weiss tears at 5–15%. An aortoenteric fistula, in which an aortic aneurysm or graft erodes into the bowel, is rare but dangerous. Among lower sources, the small bowel accounts for 5–10% of bleeds, from angiodysplasia, the most common cause over 50, tumors, Crohn disease, NSAID ulcers, and Meckel diverticulum. In the colon, angiodysplasia affects the right colon of older adults and is linked to aortic stenosis in Heyde syndrome, to ESRD, and to von Willebrand disease; colorectal cancer and polyps bleed occultly, causing iron deficiency anemia on the right and obstruction on the left; ischemic colitis causes pain and then bloody diarrhea at the watershed areas; diverticulosis causes painless, large bleeds and accounts for about 64% of rectal bleeding over 50; and colitis from IBD, infection, or radiation causes bloody diarrhea. Hemorrhoids and anal fissures cause bright red blood and are the most common causes in young and middle-aged adults.

The two differ in other ways too. Upper bleeding raises the BUN:creatinine ratio above 30, because blood is digested and absorbed, whereas lower GI bleeding usually leaves it normal. Upper bleeding is scored with the Glasgow-Blatchford score, on which 0–1 can go home and 6 or more predicts intervention in over half, and is investigated first by EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal. Lower bleeding is scored with the Oakland score, on which 8 or less is low risk, and is investigated by colonoscopy, best at 24–72 hours after bowel preparation. When the first test fails or bleeding is brisk, CTA localizes the source in either.

Upper GI bleeding

Patients present with hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melena (black, sticky, tarry stool), hematochezia if bleeding is brisk, syncope, or shock, and chronic bleeding causes iron deficiency anemia with a low MCV. The history points to the cause: epigastric pain, NSAIDs, or H. pylori to peptic ulcer disease; cirrhosis, alcohol use, splenomegaly, or ascites to varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy; retching or vomiting followed by hematemesis, with alcohol use or a hiatal hernia, to a Mallory-Weiss tear; odynophagia, heartburn, or pills taken lying down to esophagitis; a prior aortic graft or aneurysm with back pain to an aortoenteric fistula; and weight loss and early satiety to a gastric tumor. Aspirin with clopidogrel or anticoagulants makes any lesion bleed more, with a risk of up to 17% a year on combined treatment at 75 or older. When no cause is seen, a Dieulafoy lesion, GAVE, hemobilia, or hemosuccus pancreaticus is considered.

Management begins with resuscitation through 2 large-bore IV lines, intubation if the airway is at risk, and transfusion when hemoglobin falls below 70 g/L. The Glasgow-Blatchford score then guides care. An IV PPI is given before endoscopy, and when varices are suspected, octreotide or terlipressin with ABX in cirrhosis. EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal, achieves hemostasis, after which high-risk ulcers receive high-dose PPI for 72 hours, and CTA is used if EGD finds no source.

Lower GI bleeding

Patients present with hematochezia, maroon stool or clots, or blood on the paper or dripping from an anorectal source; pain on defecation suggests a fissure, a change in bowel habit or weight loss suggests cancer, tenesmus suggests proctitis, and occult bleeding causes iron deficiency anemia. A large, painless bleed in an older adult suggests diverticulosis; an older adult with aortic stenosis, ESRD, or von Willebrand disease suggests angiodysplasia, mostly in the right colon; iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or a change in bowel habit suggests colorectal cancer; pain and then bloody diarrhea in someone with vascular disease or shock suggests ischemic colitis; bloody diarrhea with fever, travel, or a food source suggests infectious colitis; and bloody diarrhea with tenesmus in a young adult suggests IBD. Painless bright red blood on the paper suggests hemorrhoids, and pain on defecation with constipation or straining suggests an anal fissure, the most common cause in infants and toddlers. In children, painless bleeding suggests Meckel diverticulum, and red currant jelly stool with colicky pain at 6–36 months suggests intussusception. When EGD and colonoscopy find nothing, the source is usually in the small bowel, most often angiodysplasia over 50, and capsule endoscopy follows; massive hematochezia with shock should also raise the possibility of a brisk upper source.

Management again begins with restoring volume and checking the blood count and clotting. The Oakland score guides admission, colonoscopy in stable patients, best performed at 24–72 hours after preparation, diagnoses and treats the source by hemostasis or polypectomy, and CTA is used for ongoing or severe bleeding.

Obstruction

Obstruction causes colicky, crampy pain as peristalsis works against the blockage, which becomes constant and severe if the bowel strangulates; abdominal distention from gas and fluid above the blockage; vomiting, which comes early in proximal obstruction, gastric at first and bilious as the blockage lies further down, and late in colonic obstruction; and obstipation, though partial obstruction may still let some stool and flatus through. Above the blockage, rising pressure causes distention and vomiting, with loud, high-pitched bowel sounds early. Vomiting and third-spacing of fluid cause dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Beyond the blockage, the bowel empties, causing obstipation and an absence of rectal gas on x-ray. If the bowel strangulates, venous outflow fails and then arterial inflow, leading to ischemia, necrosis, perforation, and sepsis.

Small bowel obstruction is most often caused by postoperative adhesions, in up to 74%, and then hernias; vomiting comes early, especially when the blockage is proximal; distention is common and marked when obstruction is complete; strangulation is the main danger; and CT is the gold standard, showing the transition point, ischemia, and perforation. Large bowel obstruction is most often caused by colorectal cancer, followed by volvulus and diverticulitis; vomiting comes late, once an incompetent ileocecal valve lets contents back into the small bowel; distention is marked and progressive when the valve is competent, creating a closed loop at risk of cecal perforation; and x-rays show a dilated colon without rectal gas, followed by CT.

Causes of obstruction

Prior abdominal surgery points to adhesions, the leading cause of small bowel obstruction, and a tender lump in the groin or abdominal wall to an incarcerated or strangulated hernia, which accounts for 2–10%. An older adult with weight loss, anemia, or alternating diarrhea and constipation suggests colorectal cancer, usually of the descending or sigmoid colon. A bedbound older adult with chronic constipation and a coffee bean sign on x-ray suggests sigmoid volvulus, at an average age of 70, whereas a distended right colon in middle age suggests cecal volvulus, typically in the fifth decade. Pneumobilia with a gallstone in the bowel suggests gallstone ileus; Crohn disease, diverticulitis, ischemia, or radiation can cause inflammatory or fibrotic strictures; red currant jelly stool at 6–36 months suggests intussusception; and bilious vomiting in a newborn suggests malrotation with volvulus. Ileus, a functional obstruction without a transition point, follows surgery, opioids, or low potassium and gives sparse or absent bowel sounds, and acute colonic pseudo-obstruction causes massive colonic distention without a blockage in sick inpatients, with cecal perforation in 15%.

Management begins with isotonic IV fluids, correction of hypokalemia and alkalosis, and decompression by nasogastric tube, which also relieves vomiting and lowers the risk of aspiration. Strangulation is sought through constant pain, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, acidosis, or peritonitis. Surgery is needed for strangulation, ischemia, perforation, or complete obstruction, whereas partial obstruction often settles without it. Sigmoid volvulus is decompressed endoscopically and then resected electively, because it recurs; cecal volvulus is treated by right hemicolectomy or ileocolic resection; and ileus is treated by addressing its cause, stopping opioids and correcting electrolytes. In ileus, bowel sounds are sparse or absent, whereas mechanical obstruction gives loud, high-pitched sounds early.

Relationships to other conditions

and . Both cause upper GI bleeding with hematemesis and melena and are both investigated by urgent EGD, but their drugs differ: ulcers are treated with high-dose PPI, whereas suspected varices add octreotide or terlipressin and ABX in cirrhosis. Cirrhosis, alcohol use, and splenomegaly favor varices, and NSAIDs and epigastric pain favor ulcers.

and . Both cause lower GI bleeding in older adults, but diverticular bleeding is painless and large, whereas ischemic colitis brings pain first and then bloody diarrhea at the watershed areas, often after shock or in vascular disease.

. Colicky pain with distention, vomiting, and obstipation points to obstruction, whereas constant, severe pain with peritonitis signals strangulation or perforation, the same features that turn the approach to abdominal pain toward surgery.

Localizing Abdominal Pain

The question

Abdominal pain asks three questions in order: which nerve is carrying it, which length of gut feeds that nerve, and how fast is the tissue failing? The name of the disease comes last.

  1. Which nerve?Visceral, parietal, or referred
  2. Which level?Foregut, midgut, or hindgut
  3. How fast?Seconds, hours, or days
  4. What could hide it?Age, drugs, pregnancy
  5. Then name itAnd test

Why this order works

  • The nerveSeparates stretch, which can wait, from an inflamed lining, which may not
  • The levelNarrows the organ before the pain has settled in one place
  • The speedSeparates rupture and lost blood supply from inflammation

The mechanism

The gut is cut, burned, and handled without pain; it feels stretch, traction, and lost blood supply, and the body reports each through a different wire.

Three wires

  • AVisceralC fibers from both sides, over several levels: dull, midline, hard to point to, with sweating and nausea
  • BParietalAδ fibers from one side and one level: sharp, pointed at with a finger, worse with any movement
  • CReferredTwo inputs meet in one segment, and the brain blames the skin

Three lengths of gut, and where they are referred

  • DForegut (T5–T9)Lower esophagus to the second part of the duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas → epigastrium
  • EMidgut (T8–T11)Duodenum to two-thirds along the transverse colon, with the appendix → umbilicus
  • FHindgut (T11–L1)The rest of the colon to the rectum → below the umbilicus
  • GShoulder tip (C3–C5)Diaphragm: blood, gas, or pus beneath it
  • HRight shoulder bladeGallbladder and bile duct
  • JBackPancreas, posterior ulcer, aorta
  • KGroinUreter; a loin-to-groin pain over 60 is the aorta until shown otherwise

The change that matters

  • Visceral to parietalVague and central becomes sharp and local: inflammation has reached the lining, as in appendicitis
  • Colic to constantWaves stop going back to zero: the blood supply is failing
  • Local to generalOne spot becomes the whole abdomen: perforation
  • Severe to silentPain eases while the patient looks worse: necrosis or rupture

How fast it came

  • LSecondsRupture, perforation, embolism, torsion: patients can say what they were doing
  • MWaves back to nothingBowel or ureter squeezing against a block
  • NBuilds, then staysBiliary pain, pancreatitis, ischemia; biliary “colic” is really this
  • ODaysDiverticulitis, abscess, cancer

Note: Nausea before pain suggests a stomach or body-wide illness, and pain before nausea suggests a surgical one.

Discriminators

A useful finding splits two groups; most classic findings do not, so each row gives what it splits and how far.

Where, once it has settled

  • 1Right upper quadrantGallbladder, bile duct, liver; or
  • 2EpigastricStomach, pancreas, heart; or
  • 3Left upper quadrantSpleen, tail of the pancreas, splenic flexure
  • 4PeriumbilicalMidgut before it settles: early appendix, small bowel, aorta
  • 5Right lower quadrantAppendix, ileum, cecum, ovary;
  • 6SuprapubicBladder, uterus, ovary, rectum
  • 7Left lower quadrantSigmoid, ovary, ureter;
  • 8Everywhere (not marked)Peritonitis, , , or a body-wide cause

Reassurance that misleads

  • A soft abdomenEarly ischemia, and anyone above

  • A normal x-ray in obstructionA poor test (LR 1.6), and fluid-filled loops show no gas
  • A high lipaseAlso perforation, ischemia, and kidney failure

Note: Opioids do not harm diagnosis in acute abdominal pain (Cochrane), so treat pain while you think.

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The pain that moved

  1. A 24-year-old has had dull pain around the umbilicus since the morning

    What it changes

    Dull pain that cannot be pointed to is visceral, and the umbilicus is where the midgut is felt. That leaves the small bowel, the appendix, and the right colon, but it cannot separate them yet, and the early hours of gastroenteritis or obstruction look the same.

  2. By evening it is sharp in the right lower quadrant

    What it changes

    Sharp pain that can be pointed to means the parietal peritoneum is now inflamed, so the process has reached the surface of the organ. Midgut pain settling in the right lower quadrant makes appendicitis the leading answer, but anything that irritates the lining there would do this, including the ovary and tube.

  3. They feel faint when they stand

    What it changes

    Uncomplicated appendicitis does not cause faintness on standing this early. A fall in blood pressure on standing means volume is missing, and with little vomiting the missing volume is probably blood. The question changes from what is inflamed to what is bleeding.

  4. The right shoulder tip aches lying flat

    What it changes

    The diaphragm and the shoulder share C3–C5, so something is irritating the underside of the diaphragm. It is worse lying flat because fluid tracks up from the pelvis. Gas would do the same, but with faintness, blood is more likely than a perforation.

  5. β-hCG is positive

    What it changes

    Pregnancy with pain and signs of free blood is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until ultrasound shows otherwise. The first reasoning was sound about the place and the peritoneum, but it stopped at the first organ that fitted. Testing β-hCG at the start would have reordered the list, and an unstable patient goes to theater without waiting for a formal scan.

Case 2: The soft abdomen

  1. A 72-year-old has sudden severe central pain and has vomited

    What it changes

    Pain at full strength within seconds means something ruptured, perforated, twisted, or blocked an artery. Central pain places it in the midgut or the aorta. At 72, vascular causes move to the top, so an ECG and a look at the aorta with bedside ultrasound belong in the first minutes.

  2. The abdomen is soft, with little tenderness

    What it changes

    A perforation would already have given a rigid abdomen, so a soft one argues against it. Pain far worse than the examination is the pattern of ischemia before infarction: the muscle is in spasm, but the lining is not yet inflamed. The soft abdomen is therefore a warning, and the best time to act.

  3. The pulse is irregular

    What it changes

    An irregular pulse suggests A-fib, and a clot from the left atrium is the most common source of a mesenteric embolus. The SMA is the usual target because it leaves the aorta at a narrow angle. Age, sudden onset, pain out of proportion, and a source now all point the same way.

  4. Lactate is 1.4 mmol/L (under 2)

    What it changes

    Lactate rises once enough bowel is dying for the liver to be overwhelmed, so a normal value is expected while the bowel can still be saved. It does not lower the probability enough to stop. Repeating it and waiting for it to rise would mean waiting for infarction.

  5. Creatinine is 160 µmol/L (high)

    What it changes

    Contrast may worsen the kidney function a little, and that can be managed afterward. A missed embolus is usually fatal, and each hour of delay costs bowel. The balance favors a CT angiogram now, without oral contrast, while the surgical and vascular teams are called.

  6. The SMA has a filling defect

    What it changes

    The filling defect confirms an embolus, and bowel that still enhances can be saved by restoring flow. Heparin and broad ABX start while that is arranged. The diagnosis came from the story and the examination, and the blood tests added nothing to it: .

Case 3: The quiet one

  1. A 58-year-old on prednisolone for months has three days of vague lower pain

    What it changes

    Pain building over days is inflammation or a tumor rather than a vessel, and lower abdominal pain is the hindgut. Diverticulitis, colorectal cancer, and colitis lead. Corticosteroids are themselves a risk for diverticular perforation, and they blunt the signs that would show it.

  2. Temperature is 37.4 °C, and the abdomen is soft

    What it changes

    Fever and guarding are made by the inflammatory response that prednisolone suppresses, so their absence carries little information here. The same examination in someone not taking corticosteroids would be reassuring. The right response is to lower the threshold for imaging, not to send them home.

  3. Pulse is 118, and they look unwell

    What it changes

    Tachycardia is not suppressed by corticosteroids, so it is the sign to trust. A pulse of 118 in someone who looks unwell does not fit a soft abdomen, and when the patient and the abdomen disagree, believe the patient. Sepsis, bleeding, and adrenal insufficiency from missed doses all need considering.

  4. WBC is 15 × 10⁹/L (4–11)

    What it changes

    Corticosteroids release neutrophils from vessel walls, so they increase WBC without any infection. A normal value would not have excluded infection either. The result cannot move the decision in either direction, and CT is needed whatever it shows.

  5. CT shows gas outside the sigmoid and fluid

    What it changes

    Free gas and fluid confirm a perforated sigmoid with none of the expected peritonitis. Resuscitation, ABX, and a surgeon come next, with extra corticosteroid to cover the stress, because the adrenal glands are suppressed. The lesson is to ask what the patient is taking before trusting the examination: .

Where it leads

Make the patient safe, choose the test that splits the leading two possibilities, and go to the page that owns the answer.

  1. Unstable?Resuscitate, bedside ultrasound, surgeon
  2. β-hCG, ECGIf either could apply
  3. Pain reliefNow
  4. One splitting testNot every test
  5. Look againExamine in hours

Review article

Localizing abdominal pain: from where it hurts to the test that confirms it

Abdominal pain is localized by its site, its character and triggers, the signs it brings beyond the abdomen, and specific examination findings, and is confirmed by targeted bloods, stool tests, imaging, and endoscopy. Dangerous causes outside the gut must be excluded early. Here, we review how each step narrows the differential and which test answers each question.

Key points

  • Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized; somatoparietal pain from the parietal peritoneum is sharp and localized.
  • Pain out of proportion to the examination suggests acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Myocardial infarction, ruptured AAA, aortic dissection, ectopic pregnancy, and torsion must be excluded early.
  • An upright CXR is the first test for suspected perforation, and RUQ ultrasound for RUQ pain.

Approach

The location of pain narrows the organs involved, its character and triggers narrow the process, signs beyond the abdomen and specific examination findings point to particular conditions, and tests confirm the leading diagnosis. Visceral pain arises from stretch of hollow organs, with receptors in the serosa, mesentery, muscle, and mucosa, and is dull and poorly localized. Somatoparietal pain arises from inflamed or stretched parietal peritoneum and is sharp and localized, as when appendicitis reaches the RLQ. Referred pain occurs when visceral and somatic nerves share a spinal level, as in left shoulder pain with splenic rupture.

Location

Right upper quadrant pain suggests biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, acute hepatitis and liver abscess, and Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis. Epigastric pain suggests peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, GERD, and acute and chronic pancreatitis; exclude myocardial infarction. Left upper quadrant pain suggests splenic infarct, abscess, or rupture (Kehr sign: left shoulder pain); pancreatitis. Periumbilical pain suggests early appendicitis, before it localizes; embolism to the proximal SMA (mesenteric ischemia). Right lower quadrant pain suggests appendicitis at McBurney point, terminal ileal Crohn disease, and right-sided diverticulitis; ectopic pregnancy and ovarian torsion. Suprapubic and pelvic pain suggests ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian or testicular torsion, urinary tract infection or obstruction, and incarcerated hernia. Left lower quadrant pain suggests diverticulitis, ischemic colitis, and ulcerative colitis. Diffuse pain suggests acute mesenteric ischemia, bowel obstruction, perforation with peritonitis, and ruptured AAA; pneumonia or PE can cause diffuse upper pain.

Character of pain

Colicky RUQ or epigastric pain after a fatty meal, gone within 6 hours; normal LFTs, no fever points to biliary colic. RUQ pain over 6 hours, fever, and Murphy sign points to acute cholecystitis. Fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice (Charcot triad), with hypotension and confusion in Reynolds pentad points to ascending cholangitis. Burning epigastric pain, worse with eating points to gastric ulcer. Burning epigastric pain, better with eating, worse fasting and at night points to duodenal ulcer. Heartburn and regurgitation points to GERD. Severe epigastric or LUQ pain radiating to the back, with vomiting points to acute pancreatitis. Chronic epigastric pain, better leaning forward, with steatorrhea points to chronic pancreatitis. Periumbilical pain moving to the RLQ over 12–24 hours, anorexia, then vomiting points to appendicitis. Sudden, severe pain out of proportion to the examination; the patient writhes points to acute mesenteric ischemia. Pain 15–30 minutes after meals, lasting up to 4 hours, with fear of eating and weight loss points to chronic mesenteric ischemia. LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis points to diverticulitis. LLQ pain and hematochezia after shock or vasopressors points to ischemic colitis. RLQ pain, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and perianal disease points to crohn disease. Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus points to ulcerative colitis. Recurrent pain related to defecation, with changes in stool frequency or appearance points to IBS. Pain, vomiting, obstipation, and distention points to bowel obstruction, including gallstone ileus. Sudden pain, then a rigid abdomen; the patient lies still points to perforation with peritonitis, such as a perforated ulcer. Painless rectal bleeding points to diverticular bleeding; under age 2, Meckel diverticulum.

Causes outside the gut

Epigastric pain with cardiac risk factors, dyspnea, sweating, or exertional symptoms suggests myocardial infarction, evaluated with ECG and troponin. Abdominal, back, or flank pain with hypotension and a pulsatile mass suggests ruptured AAA, evaluated with bedside ultrasound if unstable; CT if stable. Sharp, tearing pain with pulse deficits suggests aortic dissection, evaluated with CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Pain and vaginal bleeding 6–8 weeks after the last period suggests ectopic pregnancy, evaluated with β-hCG, then transvaginal ultrasound. Severe pelvic pain and vomiting with an adnexal mass suggests ovarian torsion, evaluated with pelvic ultrasound. Severe testicular and lower abdominal pain in a young male suggests testicular torsion, evaluated with testicular examination; scrotal ultrasound. LUQ pain after trauma, referred to the left shoulder suggests splenic rupture (Kehr sign), evaluated with imaging, with resuscitation.

Signs beyond the abdomen

Jaundice points to biliary obstruction, hepatitis, or hemolysis; see Reading Liver Function Tests. Painless jaundice with a palpable, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier law) points to periampullary or biliary malignancy. Dark urine, pale stools, and pruritus points to cholestasis, such as a bile duct stone. Pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, uveitis, arthralgia, or oral aphthous ulcers points to IBD; pyoderma gangrenosum accompanies ulcerative colitis in 5–12% and Crohn disease in 1–2%. Dermatitis herpetiformis points to celiac disease. Angular cheilitis or a smooth, pale tongue; a beefy, red tongue points to iron deficiency; B12 or folate deficiency, as in malabsorption or autoimmune gastritis. Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, or Krukenberg tumor points to metastatic gastric cancer. Acanthosis nigricans or Trousseau syndrome points to gastric cancer, as a paraneoplastic sign. Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) or Grey Turner sign (flank bruising) points to intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding, as in necrotizing pancreatitis. Asterixis, fetor hepaticus, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, ascites, or caput medusae points to cirrhosis and liver failure. Kayser-Fleischer rings points to wilson disease. Bronze skin with diabetes points to hemochromatosis. Xanthelasma points to chronic cholestasis, such as PBC. Flushing, wheezing, and tricuspid valve disease points to carcinoid syndrome. Migratory large-joint arthralgia with weight loss and diarrhea points to whipple disease. Pneumaturia and fecaluria points to enterovesical fistula, from diverticulitis or Crohn disease.

Examination

Distention and visible peristalsis suggests bowel obstruction. Dilated veins draining away from the umbilicus suggests portal hypertension. Pulsatile mass suggests AAA. High-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds suggest early small bowel obstruction. Absent bowel sounds suggests late obstruction, intestinal ischemia, ileus, or peritonitis. Shifting dullness suggests ascites. Murphy sign: inspiration stops as the gallbladder meets the hand suggests acute cholecystitis. Tenderness at McBurney point, a third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus suggests appendicitis. Rovsing sign: LLQ pressure causes RLQ pain suggests appendicitis. Psoas sign: pain on passive extension of the right hip suggests retrocecal appendicitis. Obturator sign: pain on internally rotating the flexed right hip; sensitivity only 8% suggests pelvic appendicitis or abscess. Rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding, or rigidity suggests peritonitis. Succussion splash suggests delayed gastric emptying, as in gastric outlet obstruction. Rectal examination suggests GI bleeding; adds little in appendicitis. Pelvic or testicular examination suggests pelvic disease or torsion in lower abdominal pain.

Investigations

For any significant abdominal pain, obtain FBC, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, calcium, LFTs, and lipase; β-hCG if pregnancy is possible; urinalysis. For peritonitis, sepsis, or suspected perforation, obtain upright CXR first, for free air; blood cultures; then CT AP with contrast. For RUQ pain, obtain LFTs and lipase; RUQ ultrasound first; HIDA if cholecystitis is unclear; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound for a bile duct stone. For epigastric pain, obtain ECG and troponin if cardiac risk; lipase; EGD for suspected ulcer; urea breath test or stool antigen for H. pylori. For suspected appendicitis, diverticulitis, or obstruction, obtain CT AP with contrast in adults; ultrasound first in children and pregnancy. For suspected mesenteric ischemia, obtain CT angiogram; lactate rises only late (Intestinal Ischemia). For chronic diarrhea or suspected IBD, obtain fecal calprotectin and CRP; stool culture, O&P, and C. difficile; colonoscopy with biopsy (IBD). For suspected malabsorption, obtain tTG-IgA with total IgA, then duodenal biopsy; fecal elastase; hydrogen breath test (Malabsorption). For painless rectal bleeding in a young child, obtain meckel scan (Diverticular Diseases). EGD is used for persistent upper abdominal pain or pain with alarm features; persistent vomiting; dysphagia or odynophagia; refractory GERD and Barrett surveillance; upper GI bleeding; chronic diarrhea or malabsorption; iron deficiency anemia with a suspected upper source. Colonoscopy is used for rectal bleeding, changed bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, positive FOBT, and chronic diarrhea (with biopsies); screening from age 45–50. Not needed for uncomplicated abdominal pain or diarrhea under 4 weeks; avoided in peritonitis and acute diverticulitis. ERCP is used for mainly therapeutic: removing bile duct stones, stenting strictures, and draining cholangitis.

Relationships to other conditions

. Jaundice and RUQ pain lead to the LFT pattern, which separates hepatocellular, cholestatic, and hemolytic causes.

. Its migrating pain shows the shift from visceral to somatoparietal pain.

. Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen distinguishes it from peritonitis, where the abdomen is rigid.

Reading Liver Function Tests

The question

A panel of liver tests asks four questions in order: which cell is hurt, is bile flowing, is the liver still working, and which way is it moving? One set of numbers is a photograph, so the fourth needs a second set.

  1. Which cell?Pattern: AST and ALT, or ALP and GGT
  2. Is bile flowing?ALP, GGT, bilirubin split
  3. Is it still working?INR, albumin, glucose
  4. Which way?Compare with the last
  5. Then the causeHistory first

Why this order

  • Injury is not functionEnzymes measure cells breaking, and say nothing about whether the rest can cope
  • Function is the emergencyAn increasing INR with confusion matters more than any enzyme
  • The trend outranks the levelThe same ALT means opposite things on the way up and on the way down

The mechanism

Each test lives in a different part of the cell, and each leaves the blood at its own speed. Those two facts explain nearly every pattern.

Where each test lives

  • AHepatocyte fluidALT, nearly all from the liver; a leaky membrane is enough to release it
  • BMitochondriaMost AST, also in muscle, heart, kidney, and red cells; deeper injury or alcohol releases it
  • CCanaliculusALP and GGT; pressure and bile salts make cells produce more, so they rise over days, not hours
  • DMade for the bloodClotting factors and albumin: the only true function tests here
  • EBilirubinCrosses from blood to bile; the stops along its path are on

Each test is a clock

  • FINRFactor VII lasts hours, so it shows today's liver
  • GASTFalls by half about every 15 hours after paracetamol injury
  • HALTFalls by half about every 40 hours, so it outlasts AST
  • JBilirubinLags, and bilirubin bound to albumin lingers for weeks
  • KAlbuminAbout 3 weeks, so it shows last month's liver

Normal values, and what they come from

TestNormalComes from
ALT4–36 U/LLiver
AST5–30 U/LLiver, muscle, heart, red cells
ALP30–120 U/LBile ducts, bone, placenta, gut
GGT6–50 U/LBile ducts; induced by alcohol and drugs
Bilirubin2–17 µmol/LHeme
Albumin35–50 g/LLiver only
INR0.9–1.1Liver, with vitamin K

Note: A laboratory range is set by people who may have fatty liver, and the ACG puts a truly healthy ALT at 29–33 U/L in men and 19–25 U/L in women.

Discriminators

Pattern first, then height, then ratios, and then speed; each narrows what the one before left open.

The pattern

PatternMeans
AST and ALT far more than ALPHepatocytes broken: virus, drug, ischemia, autoimmune, fat
ALP and GGT far more than AST and ALTBile not flowing, in a duct or in the liver
BothMixed: drugs, or a pattern on its way from one to the other
Bilirubin aloneSplit it: unconjugated is hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome
ALP aloneGGT normal → bone, pregnancy, growth; GGT high → infiltration or early duct disease
INR and bilirubin, enzymes fallingFailure

How high

  • Over 1000 U/LA short list: ischemia, paracetamol or another toxin, virus, autoimmune, and a stone that has just passed
  • Over 10000 U/LParacetamol or profound ischemia
  • Alcohol-associated hepatitisRarely over 300–500 U/L; higher means a second cause

Ratios and rates that split

FindingSplits
ALT to LDH ratio over 1.5Viral hepatitis from ischemia and paracetamol (sensitivity 94%, specificity 84%)
AST over twice ALTAlcohol, if AST is under about 400; otherwise muscle, or cirrhosis
AST over twice ALT after paracetamolUncommon, and a sign of the sickest
GGT with a high ALPLiver from bone; not alcohol by itself
R value ()Hepatocellular 5 or more, cholestatic 2 or less
ALT halves in a day or twoThe injury has stopped: ischemia, a passed stone, a toxin
ALT steady for weeksOngoing: virus, autoimmune, fat
INR corrects with vitamin KBile salts missing, not a failing liver
Factor V low, VIII normalLiver, not DIC

Signs far from the numbers

If there isThink of
Confusion or asterixisFailure, whatever the enzymes

What else it could be, and why it is missed: not the liver, a liver that hides its disease, or a number that reassures.

AST alone, high LDHHemolysis, or a hemolyzed sampleRepeat; haptoglobin

Who hides it

WhoWhat is lostSo
CirrhosisEnzymes: few cells left to breakPlatelets, albumin, elastography

Reassurance that misleads

  • Enzymes are fallingGood only if INR and bilirubin fall too
  • Normal enzymesDo not exclude cirrhosis
  • A normal ultrasoundDoes not exclude fibrosis, and a duct may not have dilated yet
  • A high INR after a day of ABX and fastingOften vitamin K: give it and repeat
  • Plasma has been givenThe INR no longer measures the liver
  • “It's the alcohol”ALT over 300–500 needs another answer
  • “It's the statin”Mild increases settle; jaundice does not belong to it
  • A single abnormal resultRepeat if mild, but do not only repeat: look for a cause (BSG)

Guidelines differ: The BSG advises a cause screen whatever the level and duration, while many pathways repeat a mild abnormality first.

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: Better numbers, worse patient

  1. Day 1: ALT is 6200 U/L (4–36) and INR is 1.8 (0.9–1.1) after an uncertain overdose

    What it changes

    A level this high has a short list, and paracetamol and ischemia head it. NAC starts on suspicion, because waiting for a history costs liver. The INR is already up, so this is severe injury with some loss of function.

  2. Day 3: ALT is 2700 U/L, and INR is 3.1

    What it changes

    ALT has fallen by more than half, which matches its half-life once the injury stops. If the liver were recovering, the INR would have turned by now, because factor VII is replaced in hours. The two are moving in opposite directions, and the INR is the one that measures function.

  3. Bilirubin has increased from 40 to 130 µmol/L (2–17)

    What it changes

    Increasing bilirubin with falling enzymes means there are fewer cells left to break and fewer to clear bile. It is the pattern of collapse rather than repair. A chart that plots only ALT would look like good news.

  4. They are drowsy, and glucose is 2.9 mmol/L (4–7.8)

    What it changes

    Drowsiness makes this acute liver failure, and a low glucose adds that the liver has no stores left to release. These are not enzyme results, and both are more urgent than any of them. Plasma is withheld unless there is bleeding, so that the INR can still be read.

  5. Day 5: ALT is 900 U/L, and INR is 4.6

    What it changes

    The enzyme column has improved every day, and the patient has got worse every day. The trend to follow is the one that measures function, beside the patient. holds transplant referral.

Case 2: Three thousand, gone in three days

  1. Day 1: ALT is 3000 U/L (4–36) in a 58-year-old with one night of upper abdominal pain

    What it changes

    Three thousand suggests hepatitis, ischemia, or a toxin, and a virus is usually the first thought. Pain for a single night does not fit a virus well, as hepatitis aches rather than strikes. Ask about paracetamol and about low blood pressure as well.

  2. There was no hypotension, no drug, and paracetamol is undetectable

    What it changes

    Ischemia needs a fall in flow, usually with heart failure or shock, so it is now unlikely. A toxin needs an exposure. Two of the three common causes have gone, and the rate of fall can separate the rest.

  3. Day 2: ALT is 1600 U/L

    What it changes

    A halving in a day means the injury has already stopped. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis go on for weeks and would not fall like this. Something happened once and ended.

  4. ALP is 160 U/L (30–120), and bilirubin is 48 µmol/L (2–17)

    What it changes

    ALP is only slightly up because cells need days to make more of it, so early obstruction can look like hepatitis. The pattern on the first morning was misleading, and it will turn cholestatic if the block stays. Its smallness is about timing, not about the cause.

  5. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a 7 mm duct, with the pain gone

    What it changes

    A stone passed through the duct, and the pressure pulse broke hepatocytes before ALP could respond. The falling rate made the diagnosis. The stones remain, so decides what next.

Case 3: One number

  1. A well 63-year-old has ALP of 260 U/L (30–120) on a routine panel; everything else is normal

    What it changes

    ALP has three main homes: bile ducts, bone, and placenta. With normal AST, ALT, and bilirubin, none is proved. The first job is to find the organ, not the disease.

  2. GGT is 24 U/L (6–50)

    What it changes

    Biliary cells make GGT alongside ALP, so a normal GGT points away from the liver. The answer is probably bone, and at this age bone has an important list. A high GGT would have led to ultrasound and AMA instead.

  3. They need a larger hat and have had hip pain for a year

    What it changes

    Paget disease enlarges the skull and bows bone, and it produces an isolated high ALP. Metastases from prostate or breast must be excluded, because they can also increase ALP silently. Calcium and an x-ray come next.

  4. Calcium is 2.3 mmol/L (2.1–2.6) and vitamin D is normal

    What it changes

    Normal calcium argues against hyperparathyroidism and makes extensive metastasis less likely, though it does not exclude it. Normal vitamin D makes osteomalacia unlikely. The list is now short.

  5. X-ray of the pelvis shows thick, coarse bone

    What it changes

    The film is typical of Paget disease, so the abnormal “liver test” was never a liver test. The lesson is that GGT should have been the first question. The panel is only as good as the organ it came from.

Where it leads

Treat failure first, then let pattern, height, and trend choose one next test.

  1. Failing?INR with confusion: call
  2. NAC?If paracetamol is possible
  3. History and drugsBefore tests
  4. PatternScreen or image
  5. RepeatTo see direction

Review article

Reading liver function tests: patterns of injury, cholestasis, and failing function

The liver panel mostly measures injury and cholestasis rather than function: AST and ALT reflect hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT reflect bile flow, and bilirubin, albumin, and INR reflect synthetic reserve. The pattern, the degree of rise, and the trend, read with the clinical picture, point to the cause. Here, we review each test, the main patterns, the bilirubin pathway, and how combinations of results and signs narrow the differential.

Key points

  • ALT is the most liver-specific enzyme; AST also comes from muscle, heart, and red cells.
  • A high ALP with a normal GGT suggests bone rather than liver.
  • Massive rises over 10000 IU/L suggest paracetamol toxicity or profound ischemia.
  • Falling AST and ALT with rising bilirubin and INR mean a failing liver, not recovery.

Approach

Most of the panel measures injury or cholestasis rather than function: AST and ALT reflect hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT reflect bile flow, and bilirubin, albumin, and INR reflect what the liver can still do. The pattern matters more than any single value, and trends more than a single result. Normal LFTs do not exclude liver disease, since MASLD, fibrosis, and compensated cirrhosis can all have normal enzymes.

The tests

ALT comes from hepatocyte cytosol, is the most liver-specific enzyme, rises in hepatocellular injury, and has a normal range of 4–36 IU/L. AST comes from the cytosol and mitochondria of the liver, muscle, heart, kidney, brain, and red cells, rises in hepatocellular injury, alcohol use, muscle injury, and hemolysis, and has a normal range of 5–30 IU/L. ALP comes from the canalicular membrane and bile duct epithelium, and also from bone, placenta, and intestine, rises in cholestasis, bone disease, pregnancy, and growth, and has a normal range of 30–120 IU/L. GGT comes from bile ducts, is induced by alcohol and drugs, confirms that a high ALP comes from the liver, and has a normal range of 6–50 IU/L. Bilirubin comes from heme breakdown and is conjugated by UGT1A1 in hepatocytes; it rises in hemolysis, conjugation defects, liver injury, and obstruction, and has a normal range of 2–17 µmol/L, with direct bilirubin 0–6. Albumin is made only by the liver, has a half-life of 14–21 days, falls slowly in chronic liver disease, and has a normal range of 35–50 g/L. PT/INR reflects clotting factors made by the liver, of which II, VII, IX, and X need vitamin K, rises quickly when synthesis fails, and has a normal PT range of 10.9–12.5 s.

Patterns

In the hepatocellular pattern, AST and ALT rise much more than ALP; causes include ALT higher: viral hepatitis, MASLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, ischemic hepatitis and acute Budd-Chiari syndrome, autoimmune hepatitis, drugs and toxins, and celiac disease. AST higher: alcohol, cirrhosis, and nonhepatic causes (hemolysis, myopathy, thyroid disease, exercise). In the cholestatic pattern, ALP and GGT rise, often with bilirubin, more than AST and ALT; causes include bile duct obstruction, PBC and PSC, drugs, infiltration (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, lymphoma), which can raise ALP and GGT while bilirubin stays normal, metastases, and cystic fibrosis. In the mixed pattern, both rise; causes include overlapping processes, or a pattern changing over time. In the isolated bilirubin pattern, bilirubin alone; fractionate it; causes include unconjugated: hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. Conjugated: Dubin-Johnson or Rotor syndrome. In the isolated ALP pattern, ALP alone; check GGT; causes include normal GGT: bone, pregnancy, or growth. High GGT: a hepatobiliary source. In the synthetic failure pattern, low albumin, high INR, and rising bilirubin; causes include acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis; AST and ALT may already be falling. Falling AST and ALT with rising bilirubin and INR mean a failing liver, not recovery.

Degree of rise

A mild rise, under 5 × ULN suggests MASLD; alcohol, often with AST:ALT of 2:1 or more; chronic hepatitis B or C; drugs such as statins, NSAIDs, and antiepileptics; early hemochromatosis; muscle and thyroid disease. A moderate rise, 5–15 × ULN suggests acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and drug-induced injury; alcoholic hepatitis rarely exceeds 300–500 IU/L. A severe rise, over 15 × ULN suggests acute hepatitis A, B, or E; severe drug injury; toxins such as Amanita phalloides; ischemic hepatitis. A massive rise, over 10000 IU/L suggests paracetamol toxicity, profound ischemia after cardiac arrest or shock, and, rarely, HSV hepatitis in pregnancy or immunocompromise.

Bilirubin

Bilirubin moves from red cells to the liver, where UGT1A1 conjugates it, then into bile and the gut, where bacteria form urobilinogen and stercobilin. Excess heme from hemolysis, a large hematoma, or ineffective erythropoiesis raises unconjugated bilirubin, rarely above 68 µmol/L. Defective uptake and conjugation also raise unconjugated bilirubin, as in Gilbert syndrome, with UGT1A1 at 30–50% and jaundice after fasting, illness, menstruation, or exertion that needs no treatment, in Crigler-Najjar syndrome, and with drugs that block UGT1A1. Hepatocyte injury and defective excretion raise conjugated, often mixed, bilirubin, as in hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, and PBC, and in Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2, with a black liver) and Rotor syndrome (without pigment). Bile duct obstruction by stones, strictures, PSC, or tumors raises conjugated bilirubin with ALP and GGT, causing pale stools, dark urine, and pruritus. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and darkens urine, whereas unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and does not, so bilirubin in urine means a conjugated rise.

In the distal ileum and colon, bacteria deconjugate and reduce conjugated bilirubin to colorless urobilinogen, which is oxidized to urobilin and stercobilin and turns stool orange-brown; 10–20% is reabsorbed, and some urobilin reaches the urine, giving it its yellow color. Urine and stool color therefore point to where bilirubin handling fails. Jaundice with normal urine and stool, acholuric jaundice, means an unconjugated rise from hemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, or Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine with normal or slightly pale stool means a conjugated rise from hepatocyte injury, as in hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, and the Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes, whereas dark urine with pale, clay-colored or light gray acholic stool and pruritus means bile duct obstruction or cholestasis from stones, strictures, PSC, or tumors, with high ALP and GGT. Pale, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats is steatorrhea, from too few bile salts in obstruction or from pancreatic insufficiency. On urine dipstick, bilirubin means a conjugated rise, often before jaundice is visible; more urobilinogen means more bilirubin made, as in hemolysis, more reabsorbed from the colon, or less cleared by a diseased liver; and absent urobilinogen means complete obstruction, since no bilirubin reaches the gut to form it. Red or brown urine that is negative for bilirubin suggests hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis. Black, tarry stool is melena from upper GI bleeding rather than a liver test pattern, and pale stool with dark urine beyond 2 weeks of age in an infant suggests biliary atresia.

Synthetic function

Albumin: half-life 14–21 days, so it falls in chronic, not acute, liver disease; also low in malnutrition, inflammation, nephrotic syndrome, burns, sepsis, and protein-losing enteropathy. Pre-albumin, or transthyretin, has a half-life of 2–3 days, so it shows changes in nutrition faster than albumin. PT/INR: clotting factors have short half-lives, so it rises quickly; also prolonged by vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, DIC, and antiphospholipid antibodies. With a vitamin K test, INR that corrects with parenteral vitamin K points to deficiency, as in malabsorption; failure to correct means severe hepatocellular dysfunction. Bilirubin, albumin, and INR feed the Child-Pugh and MELD scores.

Combining results with the picture

Cholestatic pattern with fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice suggests ascending cholangitis, and calls for blood cultures, ultrasound, then ERCP. Cholestatic pattern with RUQ pain and a dilated CBD suggests choledocholithiasis, and calls for MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound; ERCP if likelihood is high. Cholestatic pattern with painless jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable gallbladder suggests periampullary or biliary malignancy, and calls for CT or MRCP; CA 19-9. Cholestatic pattern with itch and fatigue in a middle-aged woman suggests PBC, and calls for AMA, positive in over 90%. Cholestatic pattern with ulcerative colitis suggests PSC, and calls for MRCP: beaded ducts; p-ANCA. AST:ALT of 2:1 or more with high GGT and heavy drinking suggests alcohol-related liver disease, and calls for maddrey score if alcoholic hepatitis. Very high ALT after paracetamol ingestion suggests paracetamol toxicity, and calls for paracetamol level; NAC. ALT over 1000 after shock, cardiac arrest, or HF suggests ischemic hepatitis, and calls for treat the low-flow state. ALT-predominant rise with viral risk factors suggests viral hepatitis, and calls for HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, and HCV antibody. ALT-predominant rise in a young woman with high IgG suggests autoimmune hepatitis, and calls for ANA and ASMA (type 1); anti-LKM1 (type 2). Mild rise with obesity, diabetes, or dyslipidemia suggests MASLD, and calls for ultrasound; fibrosis score such as FIB-4. Hepatocellular rise with diabetes, bronze skin, or arthropathy suggests hemochromatosis, and calls for transferrin saturation over 45%, then ferritin and HFE testing. Hepatocellular rise in a young patient with tremor, psychiatric change, or Kayser-Fleischer rings suggests wilson disease, and calls for ceruloplasmin. Hepatocellular rise with early lower-lobe emphysema suggests α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and calls for α1-antitrypsin level. High transaminases and hypoglycemia in the third trimester suggests acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and calls for swansea criteria. Isolated unconjugated bilirubin after fasting or illness, with normal enzymes and FBC suggests gilbert syndrome, and calls for no treatment needed. Unconjugated bilirubin with anemia suggests hemolysis, and calls for FBC and blood film. High INR and encephalopathy within 26 weeks, with no prior liver disease suggests acute liver failure, and calls for find the cause; transplant referral. Low albumin, high INR, ascites, and varices suggests cirrhosis, and calls for child-Pugh and MELD scores.

Relationships to other conditions

. RUQ pain and jaundice lead here, and the LFT pattern decides between imaging the ducts and testing for hepatitis.

. Bilirubin, albumin, and INR measure the failing liver and feed the Child-Pugh and MELD scores.

. A cholestatic pattern with a dilated duct is its signature.

Barrett Esophagus and Esophageal Cancer

Pathophysiology

Reflux turns squamous lining into intestinal metaplasia that can become adenocarcinoma, while smoke, alcohol, and chronic irritation turn squamous lining directly into squamous cell carcinoma.

  1. InjuryAcid and bile, or smoke and alcohol
  2. Metaplasia or dysplasiaBarrett, or squamous dysplasia
  3. TP53 lostAn early, shared step
  4. High-grade dysplasiaStill above the basement membrane
  5. InvasionRich lymphatics: early nodes
  6. ObstructionDysphagia once the lumen is under about half

From reflux to adenocarcinoma

  • BarrettColumnar cells with goblet cells, resisting acid
  • Low-grade dysplasiaAbout 0.7% a year progress
  • High-grade dysplasiaTreat: much higher
  • OverallFewer than 5% with Barrett develop cancer, well under 1% a year without dysplasia

The two cancers

FeatureAdenocarcinomaSquamous cell carcinoma
WhereLower third, EGJMiddle and upper thirds
WorldHigh-income countries, risingAbout 85% worldwide: eastern Asia and Africa

Main risksReflux, obesity, smoking, menSmoking and alcohol
GenesTP53, CDKN2A, HER2TP53, CDKN2A, ALDH2 variants
Chemoradiation clears itAbout 23%About 49%

Note: With no serosa and with lymphatics in the mucosa, esophageal cancer spreads to nodes and neighbors early.

Etiology

  • Adenocarcinoma
  • 1Reflux and Barrett esophagusLong, frequent reflux; longer Barrett segments carry more risk
  • 2Obesity, smoking, sex, and ageCentral obesity, smoking, men, over 50, White people, and a family history
  • Squamous cell carcinoma
  • 3Tobacco and alcoholMultiply each other; worse with ALDH2 deficiency (flushing)
  • 4Chronic injuryAchalasia, caustic stricture, radiation, and very hot drinks
  • 5Inherited and associated diseasePlummer-Vinson syndrome, tylosis, Fanconi anemia, and head and neck cancer
  • 6Diet and environmentPoor diet and oral hygiene, smoke from fuel, and HPV in some regions

Note: Alcohol is a strong risk for squamous cell carcinoma and little or none for adenocarcinoma.

Symptoms and complications

  1. SilentBarrett and early cancer
  2. Solids stickMeat and bread
  3. Liquids tooOver weeks to months
  4. Weight lossOften more than dysphagia explains
  5. SpreadVoice, cough, liver, and bone

The pattern

  • DysphagiaProgressive and painless; solids, then liquids
  • Weight lossWith dysphagia, cancer until proven otherwise
  • RefluxMay improve as Barrett forms
  • BleedingIron deficiency; rarely large
  • PainOdynophagia, or back pain: invasion

Diagnosis

EGD with biopsy diagnoses both Barrett esophagus and cancer, and CT, PET-CT, and EUS then stage cancer to choose between endoscopy, surgery, and palliation.

  1. Dysphagia or bleedingEGD within 2 weeks
  2. BiopsySeveral
  3. CTChest and abdomen
  4. PET-CTDistant spread

Esophageal Tears and Varices

Pathophysiology

Sudden pressure or an instrument tears the esophagus, shallow enough to bleed or deep enough to leak, while portal hypertension swells its veins until they burst.

  1. Pressure or injuryRetching, instrument, or portal hypertension
  2. Wall gives wayMucosa, vein, or all layers
  3. BleedingMallory-Weiss and varices
  4. LeakPerforation: mediastinitis within hours
  5. ShockBlood loss or sepsis

How deep it goes

  • AMallory-WeissA lengthwise split of 1–2 cm, one in 90%
  • BIntramural hematomaPain and dysphagia; anticoagulants or instruments; settles
  • CPerforationAir, food, and acid reach the mediastinum; no serosa to seal it
  • DVarixWall tension rises with pressure and width, and falls with thickness (Laplace)

Why varices form

  • EResistanceFibrosis, and too little NO within the liver
  • FFlowSplanchnic vasodilation, from NO, adds more
  • GCollateralBack through the left gastric vein
  • HVaricesHVPG 10 mmHg or more to form, 12 or more to bleed

What makes a varix bleed

  • Large (5 mm or more)
  • Red marks
  • Child-Pugh C
  • Active alcohol use
  • High HVPG

Note: Bleeding without pain suggests a tear or varix, and pain without much bleeding suggests a perforation.

Etiology

  • Tears
  • 1Mallory-Weiss tearRetching, from alcohol (50–70%), pregnancy, bulimia, or chemotherapy; cough, straining, or endoscopy
  • 2Boerhaave syndromeForceful vomiting against a closed cricopharyngeus; weights, childbirth, seizure; about 15% of perforations
  • 3Iatrogenic perforationThe most common perforation: dilation, stent, resection, or echo probe
  • 4Foreign body, caustic, or traumaFish bone, button battery, caustic, stab, or cancer
  • Varices
  • 5Varices from cirrhosisMost: alcohol, viral, and steatotic liver disease
  • 6Varices without cirrhosisPortal or splenic vein thrombosis, schistosomiasis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome

Note: Isolated gastric varices with a normal liver suggest splenic vein thrombosis, as after pancreatitis.

Symptoms and complications

  1. TriggerVomiting, instrument, or liver disease
  2. BleedHematemesis or melena
  3. Or painChest, neck, or abdomen
  4. DeteriorationShock or sepsis

Telling them apart

FeatureMallory-WeissPerforationVarices
BeforeRetching, then bloodVomiting or an instrument; none in 25–45%Liver disease; no warning
PainLittleSevere, suddenNone
BloodSmall to moderateLittleLarge
SignsFewCrepitus, fever, shock, effusionJaundice, spiders, ascites, spleen
CourseStops in mostDeath if delayedEach bleed may kill; rebleeds

Perforation by level

  • NeckPain, hoarseness, crepitus; mildest
  • ChestRetrosternal pain; left effusion if low, right if mid
  • AbdomenRigid abdomen, back or shoulder pain
  • Mackler triadVomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema: seldom complete
  • Hamman signCrunch with each heartbeat

Complications

  • Hemorrhagic shockVarices above all
  • Mediastinitis and empyemaPerforation
  • SepsisPerforation; infection after variceal bleeding
  • Hepatic encephalopathyBlood as a protein load
  • Acute kidney injuryLow volume; hepatorenal syndrome
  • AspirationAirway and bleeding
  • RebleedingVarices, within 6 weeks
  • Fistula and strictureAfter perforation or banding

Diagnosis

Bleeding is diagnosed and treated by EGD, within 12 hours if varices are likely, but suspected perforation goes to CT with contrast first.

  1. Airway and circulationBefore any test
  2. Bleeding or leak?Pain, crepitus, effusion
  3. BleedingEGD after resuscitation
  4. LeakCT with oral water-soluble contrast
  5. CauseLiver, drugs, and procedure

  • CTAir, fluid, and leak; the best first test
  • CXRPneumomediastinum, effusion, V sign; may be normal early
  • Contrast swallowWater-soluble first; barium if negative; misses 10–38%
  • Pleural fluidpH below 6, high amylase, food
  • EGDOnly if unclear or to treat

  • EGDLongitudinal tear at the junction; or varices with red marks
  • FBC and clottingHemoglobin lags; low platelets suggest portal hypertension; INR does not predict bleeding
  • UreaHigh for creatinine

  • BeforeBiopsy; off anticoagulants if possible
  • HowSmall steps over sessions, toward 13–15 mm or more
  • AfterPain, fever, or crepitus: CT
  • RefractoryCorticosteroid injection, stent, or review for cancer

Feeding and safety

  • Soft, moist food
  • Upright to eat
  • Small bites, chew well
  • Speech pathology if oropharyngeal
  • Dietitian
  • Medicines as liquid
  • Dental care

When to refer

If there isThen
Drooling, battery, or leakEmergency

Functional Dyspepsia and Gastroparesis

Pathophysiology

The stomach relaxes poorly, senses too much, or empties too slowly, so meals cause fullness, nausea, or pain without a visible cause; functional dyspepsia and gastroparesis are overlapping ends of this spectrum.

  1. TriggerInfection, diabetes, vagal injury, drugs, or stress
  2. Nerves, pacemakers, muscleCells of Cajal and inhibitory neurons lost
  3. Poor relaxation or emptyingOr a sensitive gut
  4. Meal symptomsFullness, nausea, pain
  5. Less eatingWeight and glucose suffer

What the stomach should do

  • AAccommodationThe fundus relaxes by the vagus and nitric oxide; failure → early satiation
  • BPacemakerCells of Cajal, 3 waves a minute; loss → weak, uneven waves
  • CGrindingAntral waves break solids; weak antrum → slow emptying
  • DPylorusOpens to small particles; spasm → retention
  • EDuodenumFat, acid, and eosinophils signal back → fullness, hypersensitivity

Two ends of a spectrum

FeatureFunctional dyspepsiaGastroparesis
Main symptomFullness, satiation, or painNausea and vomiting
EmptyingNormal, or mildly slow in someSlow, by definition
MechanismAccommodation, sensitivity, duodenal inflammationNerve and Cajal cell loss
Weight lossUncommonIn the severe
EGDNormalNormal, or retained food

Note: symptoms track poorly with the emptying rate, and one diagnosis can become the other over time.

Etiology

  • Functional dyspepsia
  • 1Postprandial distress syndromePDS: bothersome fullness or early satiation with meals
  • 2Epigastric pain syndromeEPS: bothersome epigastric pain or burning, not only with meals
  • Gastroparesis
  • 3DiabeticLong type 1 or 2, with neuropathy and poor control
  • 4IdiopathicThe most common; young women; can follow a viral illness
  • 5PostsurgicalVagal injury: fundoplication, gastrectomy, lung or heart surgery
  • 6DrugsOpioids, GLP-1 agonists, anticholinergics, cannabis
  • 7NeurologicParkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, stroke, dysautonomia
  • 8Connective tissue and infiltrativeSystemic sclerosis, SLE, amyloid
  • 9OtherHypothyroidism, paraneoplastic, mesenteric ischemia, critical illness

What raises the risk of dyspepsia

  • Acute gastroenteritis
  • H. pylori
  • Anxiety and depression
  • NSAIDs
  • Smoking
  • Female sex
  • IBS or GERD

High glucose itself

  • Acute hyperglycemiaSlows emptying within hours, so test only when controlled
  • Slow emptyingInsulin acts before food arrives → early hypoglycemia, late hyperglycemia

Symptoms and complications

Rome V functional dyspepsia

  • One or moreBothersome fullness after meals, early satiation, epigastric pain, or epigastric burning
  • Clinical diagnosisBothersomeness is enough; no fixed frequency or 6-month wait
  • EGDNot needed without alarm features; needed for research
  • Research criteriaPDS on 2 or more days a week (3 in Rome IV), with onset over 6 months before
  • PDS and EPSCan overlap

The pattern

FeaturePDS (1)EPS (2)Gastroparesis (3–9)
TriggerMealsAny time, or fastingMeals, worse late in the day
VomitingRareRareUndigested food, hours later
PainMildMainCommon, not main
ReliefSmall mealsPPI in someVomiting
WeightStableStableCan fall

Signs to seek

  • Succussion splashRetention: obstruction until excluded
  • DiabetesRetinopathy, neuropathy, postural fall in BP
  • Skin and jointsSystemic sclerosis
  • Teeth and handsSelf-induced vomiting
  • Hot showersCannabinoid hyperemesis

Severity of gastroparesis

GradeMeans
1, mildEats normally
2, compensatedAltered diet, weight kept
3, failureVomiting, admission, or feeding tube

Complications

  • Dehydration and alkalosisLow potassium and chloride
  • MalnutritionWeight loss over 5–10%
  • Labile glucoseHypoglycemia after insulin
  • BezoarRetained fiber
  • Mallory-Weiss tearRetching
  • AspirationAt anesthesia too
  • Drug failureOral tablets absorbed late
  • Anxiety and food avoidanceRestrictive eating

Diagnosis

Functional dyspepsia is a positive diagnosis from symptoms without alarm features; gastroparesis needs slow emptying on a 4-hour solid test after obstruction is excluded.

  1. Alarm or age 60EGD
  2. H. pylori testTreat if positive
  3. Stop drugsOpioid, GLP-1, cannabis
  4. Exclude obstructionEGD; CT or MR enterography
  5. Emptying testIf vomiting or refractory

Gastric emptying

  • FNormal60% or less at 2 hours, 10% or less at 4 hours
  • GGastroparesisAt 4 hours: 11–20% mild, 21–35% moderate, 36–50% severe, and over 50% very severe
  • HRapidUnder 30% at 1 hour: dumping

Doing it properly

  • MealLow-fat egg meal, 4 hours of images; 2 hours misses cases
  • Stop for 2–3 daysOpioids, prokinetics, anticholinergics, cannabis
  • GlucoseBelow about 15 mmol/L
  • GLP-1 agonistExplain or stop; hold with the prescriber
  • AlternativeStable isotope breath test
  • Not enoughA single scan: results vary

Other tests

  • AllFBC, electrolytes, glucose, HbA1c, TSH, celiac serology
  • Autoimmune or neurologic clueANA, centromere and Scl-70, autonomic tests
  • PylorusFunctional lumen imaging, in centers
  • Not routineEmptying test in typical dyspepsia

Red flags

  • Weight loss
  • Dysphagia
  • Bleeding or anemia
  • New at 60 or older
  • Family history of gastric cancer
  • Mass
  • Persistent vomiting
  • Night vomiting

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Outlet obstructionSuccussion splash, weight lossEGD, CT
Cyclic vomitingAttacks with well weeks between; migraineHistory
Cannabinoid hyperemesisDaily cannabis, hot showers; ends on stoppingHistory
RuminationEffortless, within minutes, no nausea or retchingHistory, manometry
SMA syndromeRapid weight loss, relief lying proneCT
Eating disorderWeight fear, purgingAssessment
Adrenal insufficiencyLow sodium, postural fallCortisol
PregnancyMissed periodPregnancy test
VolvulusRetching, pain, tube will not passCT

Find the cause

  • 1Postprandial distress syndromeHistory; H. pylori; EGD if alarm
  • 2Epigastric pain syndromeThe same; ultrasound if biliary pain
  • 3Diabetic gastroparesisHbA1c, eyes, feet; emptying test
  • 4Idiopathic gastroparesisExcluded others; viral onset
  • 5Postsurgical gastroparesisOperation list
  • 6DrugsDrug list, then retest off it
  • 7NeurologicNeurologic and autonomic examination
  • 8Connective tissue and infiltrativeANA, Scl-70; biopsy for amyloid
  • 9OtherTSH, CT; paraneoplastic antibodies

Treatment

Explain the diagnosis, change meals, treat H. pylori and the drug list, then climb one step at a time; procedures come last and by center.

  1. ExplainGut-brain disorder, not imagined
  2. RemoveH. pylori, opioid, cannabis
  3. MealsSmall, low fat, low residue
  4. Drug by subtypePPI, TCA, or prokinetic
  5. RefractoryPylorus, feeding

Functional dyspepsia ladder

StepUse
1Eradicate H. pylori; a small effect, and prevents ulcers and cancer
2PPI at the lowest dose that works, 4–8 weeks; best for EPS
2, if fullness leadsProkinetic where available: itopride, acotiamide, mosapride
3TCA: amitriptyline 10 mg at night, rising to 30–50
4, with weight lossMirtazapine
4, painPregabalin or sulpiride, by a specialist
AnyExercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, hypnotherapy

Gastroparesis ladder

StepUse
1Fluids and potassium, small low-fat meals, blended if needed; glucose control
2Metoclopramide: lowest dose, before meals, up to 12 weeks
2, short courseErythromycin: tachyphylaxis in weeks; QT
3Domperidone or a 5-HT4 agonist, shared decision
3, nauseaOndansetron, prochlorperazine, or hyoscine hydrobromide: relief, no faster emptying
4G-POEM or stimulation in selected, refractory patients
5Jejunal feeding; venting gastrostomy; parenteral last

Be careful

  • Metoclopramide: tardive dyskinesia, Parkinson disease
  • Domperidone: QT
  • Erythromycin: CYP3A4
  • Opioids: never for this pain
  • Botulinum: not recommended
  • TCA: can slow emptying
  • Anesthesia: full stomach

Diabetes

  • GlucosePump or sensor; insulin after the meal if needed
  • AvoidGLP-1 agonists and pramlintide
  • DKA with vomitingTreat first; test later

Admit if

  • Dehydration
  • Low potassium
  • DKA
  • Weight loss over 10%
  • Hematemesis
  • Cannot keep drugs down

Treat the cause

  • 1Postprandial distress syndromeMeals, prokinetic, then TCA or mirtazapine
  • 2Epigastric pain syndromePPI, then TCA
  • 3Diabetic gastroparesisGlucose, then the ladder
  • 4Idiopathic gastroparesisThe ladder; often improves after a viral illness
  • 5Postsurgical gastroparesisThe ladder; G-POEM or pyloroplasty
  • 6DrugsStop or change
  • 7NeurologicTreat the disease; avoid metoclopramide in Parkinson disease: domperidone
  • 8Connective tissue and infiltrativeTreat the disease; early nutrition
  • 9OtherLevothyroxine; treat the tumor or vessel

Guidelines differ: ACG 2022 supports domperidone and 5-HT4 agonists, and AGA 2025 suggests against them, and G-POEM, as first treatment.

Stomach Disease: Comparison and Workup

Comparison

Most dyspepsia has a normal EGD; the tests exist to find an ulcer, H. pylori, cancer, or a slow stomach among the rest.

Six views

  • ADrugs, alcohol, or stress: shallow breaks
  • BBenign gastric ulcerRound, smooth, folds reach the edge; biopsy
  • CDuodenal ulcerIn the bulb; biopsy not needed
  • DAtrophyPale, vessels show; body only if autoimmune
  • EIrregular, heaped edge, folds stop short
  • FSubepithelial bulgeGIST, leiomyoma, lipoma, NET, or a neighbor: EUS

Side by side

FeatureDuodenal ulcerGastric ulcerCancerDyspepsiaGastroparesis

VomitingIf obstructedIf obstructedIf obstructedRareMain
WeightStableDownDownStableCan fall

First treatmentH. pylori, PPIH. pylori, PPI, recheckStageH. pylori, PPI, TCADiet, metoclopramide

CauseSiteAcidGastrinCancer risk

NSAIDAntrumNormalNormalNone

Age, alarm features, and one H. pylori test sort almost every patient; EGD, gastrin, and emptying answer what is left.

  1. Not gastric?Heart, gallbladder, pancreas
  2. Alarm or age 60EGD
  3. H. pylori test and treatBreath or stool
  4. PPI 4–8 weeksIf negative or still ill
  5. TCA or prokineticFunctional
  6. EGD or emptyingIf refractory

Which test first

If there isObtain
Under 60, no alarmH. pylori breath or stool test
60 or older, new symptoms, or alarmEGD
Hematemesis or melenaGlasgow-Blatchford, EGD within 24 hours

Vomiting old foodDecompress, then EGD and CT

Submucosal bulgeEUS

Where to biopsy

  • GAntrum, lesser curvatureWithin 2–3 cm of the pylorus
  • HAntrum, greater curvatureThe same level
  • JIncisuraWhere metaplasia starts
  • KBody, lesser curvatureAbout 4 cm above the incisura
  • LBody, greater curvatureAbout 8 cm from the cardia; separate jars for antrum and body

Reading gastrin

GastrinpHMeans

If there isUse

Do not miss

  • Perforation
  • Aortoenteric fistula after a graft
  • Gastric cancer behind an ulcer
  • Volvulus
  • Cancer hidden by a PPI
  • Mesenteric ischemia

Treatment

The same few tools recur: suppress acid, eradicate H. pylori, protect from drugs, stop bleeding, move the stomach, and replace what is lost.

  1. EmergenciesBleed, hole, obstruction
  2. CauseH. pylori and NSAIDs
  3. AcidLowest dose that works
  4. FunctionDiet, TCA, prokinetic
  5. Follow upCure, ulcer, atrophy
