Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease

Pathophysiology

Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde, which fills hepatocytes with fat, makes the gut leak endotoxin, and calls neutrophils, until stellate cells lay down scar.

  1. AlcoholAlcohol dehydrogenase, CYP2E1, catalase
  2. Acetaldehyde, NADHFat made, not burned
  3. Leaky gutEndotoxin to Kupffer cells
  4. NeutrophilsNecrosis, ballooning
  5. Stellate cellsScar around cells

How alcohol injures the liver

  • AFatty liverIncreased NADH : NAD+ → more fat made, less burned
  • BAcetaldehyde adductsNew antigens → immune attack, neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies

Where it starts

  • CZone 1Most oxygen, around the portal tract
  • DZone 2Between
  • EZone 3Most CYP2E1, least oxygen: fat, necrosis, then scar around cells

Three enzymes make acetaldehyde, and one clears it

  • Alcohol dehydrogenaseMakes it: cytosol, the main route
  • CYP2E1Makes it: induced by drinking, with free radicals, and more NAPQI from paracetamol
  • CatalaseMakes it: peroxisomes, minor
  • Aldehyde dehydrogenaseClears it to acetate: blocked by disulfiram, weak in the ALDH2 variant

Note: fat clears in weeks of abstinence, and scar can regress over years.

Etiology

  • Stages, which overlap
  • 1SteatosisIn about 90% who drink over 60 g a day; reversible
  • 2Alcohol-associated hepatitisBallooning and neutrophils; often with cirrhosis
  • 3CirrhosisIn 10–20% of heavy drinkers over years

Who gets it

  • AmountOver about 30–50 g a day for 5 years or more
  • PatternDaily, without food, spirits; binge on top
  • WomenLess drink, more injury
  • GenesPNPLA3 raises risk
  • Other liver diseaseObesity, HCV, HBV, iron overload
  • SurgeryGastric bypass: faster absorption
  • SmokingMore cirrhosis

MetALD

  • Metabolic risk with more alcohol than MASLD allowsMetALD, between MASLD and alcohol-associated disease
  • Alcohol alone above thatAlcohol-associated liver disease

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. SteatosisSilent, large liver
  2. HepatitisWeeks after heavy drinking
  3. Fibrosis10–20% a year with hepatitis
  4. CirrhosisDecompensation
  5. HCC1–3% a year

The pattern

StageFeatures
1 SteatosisNone; smooth hepatomegaly
2 Alcohol-associated hepatitisRapid jaundice, fever, tender liver, ascites, muscle loss
3 CirrhosisSpider nevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, small testes, parotids, Dupuytren

Alcohol beyond the liver

  • BrainWernicke encephalopathy, withdrawal
  • PancreasPancreatitis
  • HeartDilated cardiomyopathy, A-fib
  • Nerve and muscleNeuropathy, myopathy
  • BloodMacrocytosis, low platelets, folate
  • MetabolicKetoacidosis, low sugar, low phosphate

Signs of severity

  • Maddrey 32 or more
  • MELD over 20
  • Encephalopathy
  • AKI
  • Infection
  • GI bleeding

Complications

  • InfectionA leading cause of death
  • Hepatorenal AKI
  • Acute-on-chronic failureOrgan failures
  • Variceal bleeding
  • EncephalopathyInfection, bleed, constipation
  • RefeedingLow phosphate, thiamine first
  • HCCUltrasound every 6 months if cirrhosis

Diagnosis

Heavy drinking with AST above ALT, both under 400 U/L, high bilirubin, and no other cause makes alcohol-associated hepatitis likely; biopsy is for doubt.

  1. Ask without blameAUDIT-C, PEth
  2. LFTs, FBC, INRAST above ALT
  3. ExcludeViruses, drugs, biliary, MASLD
  4. Look for infectionCultures, urine, CXR, ascitic tap
  5. ScoreMaddrey, MELD

Alcohol-associated hepatitis (NIAAA)

  • Jaundice within 60 days of drinking
  • Over 60 g a day (men), 40 g (women), for 6 months
  • Bilirubin over 50 µmol/L
  • AST 50–400 U/L
  • AST : ALT over 1.5
  • No other cause

Other tests

  • GGT, MCVSupport alcohol, not specific
  • PEthDrinking in past 2–4 weeks; not changed by liver disease
  • FIB-4, elastographyFibrosis; falsely high in active inflammation
  • UltrasoundFat, cirrhosis, ducts, HCC, portal vein
  • Biopsy, transjugularUnclear, or atypical
  • AscitesTap at admission, before antibiotics

How bad is it

ScoreSevereUses
Maddrey32 or morePT and bilirubin
MELDOver 20Bilirubin, INR, creatinine
LilleOver 0.45 at day 4 or 7Corticosteroid failing: stop
Glasgow9 or moreAge, white cells, urea, INR, bilirubin

Red flags

  • Confusion
  • Fever or low BP
  • AKI
  • GI bleeding
  • AST over 500: think paracetamol or ischemia

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
MASLDALT above AST, diabetesHistory, PEth
ParacetamolAST in thousandsLevel, NAC first
Ischemic hepatitisShockEchocardiogram
CholangitisPain, dilated ductsUltrasound
Viral or autoimmuneALT above ASTSerology, IgG
Wernicke encephalopathyEye signs, ataxiaThiamine first

Find the cause

  • 1SteatosisHistory, ultrasound, PEth
  • 2Alcohol-associated hepatitisNIAAA criteria; infection screen
  • 3CirrhosisElastography, ultrasound, EGD

Treatment

Abstinence changes everything; feed the patient, seek infection, try corticosteroid for a week in severe disease, and refer early for transplant.

  1. Thiamine before glucoseAnd electrolytes
  2. WithdrawalCareful benzodiazepine
  3. Nutrition35 kcal/kg, protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg
  4. Severe?Prednisolone 40 mg
  5. LilleDay 4 or 7
  6. AbstinenceDrug and team

Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis

If there isThen
Maddrey 32 or more, MELD over 20, no contraindicationPrednisolone 40 mg for 28 days
AddIV NAC as an adjunct
Lille over 0.45Stop corticosteroid; palliative or transplant
Lille 0.45 or lessFinish 28 days

PentoxifyllineNo longer
AntibioticOnly for proven or suspected infection

No corticosteroid if

  • Active infection, until controlled
  • GI bleeding
  • AKI or hepatorenal
  • HBV untreated
  • TB
  • Uncontrolled diabetes

Alcohol use disorder

DrugPlace in liver disease
BaclofenFirst in compensated disease; avoid with encephalopathy
AcamprosateSafe; dose by kidney
NaltrexoneCompensated; avoid in acute hepatitis
Gabapentin, topiramateOptions; watch sedation
DisulfiramNever

Feed and protect

Nutrition
  • Night snack
  • Nasogastric tube if below target
  • No protein limit
  • Zinc, thiamine, folate
Protect
  • HAV, HBV, pneumococcal vaccine
  • Stop smoking
  • No NSAIDs
  • Paracetamol 2 g a day at most
Withdrawal
  • Lorazepam or oxazepam
  • Score and monitor
  • Avoid long-acting

Treat the cause

  • 1SteatosisAbstain; weight and diabetes
  • 2Alcohol-associated hepatitisAbstain, feed, corticosteroid if severe, infection
  • 3CirrhosisAbstain; varices, ascites, HCC; transplant if decompensated

Guidelines differ: some centers still require 6 months of abstinence before transplant, whereas 2024 guidance accepts early transplant in selected first episodes.

Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD)

Pathophysiology

Insulin resistance floods the liver with fat, which overwhelms its handling, injures hepatocytes, and drives inflammation and scar from the central vein outward.

  1. Insulin resistanceFat tissue keeps releasing fatty acids
  2. Fat made in the liverGlucose turned to fat
  3. SteatosisTriglyceride stores it safely
  4. LipotoxicityFree fatty acids, oxidative stress, gut endotoxin
  5. MASHBallooning and inflammation
  6. FibrosisStellate cells

What the buildup does

  • AFatTriglycerides accumulate → steatosis
  • BFibrosisRepeated stress → fibrosis → cirrhosis

Stages of scar

  • CF0None
  • DF1Around the central vein or portal tract
  • EF2Both
  • FF3Bridges between them
  • GF4Nodules: cirrhosis

Why the risk is in the heart

  • Shared causeInsulin resistance drives liver, vessels, and kidney
  • Fibrosis stagePredicts death better than inflammation
  • CancerHCC can come before cirrhosis, rarely

Etiology

  • 1Insulin resistance and obesityCentral obesity, T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidemia
  • 2Lean MASLDNormal BMI with visceral fat or genes
  • 3GeneticPNPLA3 and TM6SF2; lipodystrophy
  • 4Other steatosisDrugs, HIV, TPN, rapid weight loss, gastric bypass: not MASLD, but part of steatotic liver disease

The criteria

  • MASLDSteatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic factor, no other cause, and little alcohol
  • Alcohol limitUnder 20 g a day (women) or 30 g (men)
  • MetALDOver that, up to 50 or 60 g a day
  • Alcohol-associatedAbove that
  • CryptogenicCirrhosis with past risk factors but no fat left: often burned-out MASLD

Cardiometabolic factors

  • BMI 25 or more (23 in Asian people)
  • Waist over 94 cm (men) or 80 cm (women)
  • Fasting glucose 5.6 mmol/L or more
  • BP 130/85 mmHg or more
  • Triglycerides 1.7 mmol/L or more
  • Low HDL

Raise the risk of progression

  • Age over 50
  • T2DM
  • Obesity
  • Alcohol
  • PNPLA3
  • Menopause
  • Sleep apnea

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. SteatosisMost stay here
  2. MASHAbout a fifth
  3. FibrosisAbout a stage in 7–14 years
  4. CirrhosisThen decompensation
  5. HCC1–2% a year with cirrhosis

The pattern

  • MostNone, or fatigue and an ache
  • ExaminationCentral obesity, hepatomegaly, acanthosis nigricans
  • AdvancedSpider nevi, splenomegaly, ascites
  • Clue to lookAny T2DM, obesity with one more risk, or high ALT

Beyond the liver

  • Heart and vesselsLeading cause of death
  • KidneyCKD
  • DiabetesBoth ways
  • CancerColorectal, breast
  • Sleep apneaCommon
  • BrainFatigue, mood

Complications

  • Cirrhosis
  • HCCCirrhosis mostly; also F3
  • Portal hypertension
  • Acute liver failureNot from MASLD alone
  • Drug harmStatins are safe

Diagnosis

Steatosis on imaging with a metabolic factor makes the diagnosis; the real question is who has advanced fibrosis.

  1. UltrasoundBright liver
  2. Other causesAlcohol, viruses, iron, drugs
  3. FIB-4Below 1.3: stop
  4. ElastographyIndeterminate
  5. MASH testsELF, MR elastography
  6. BiopsyOnly if unclear

Who to check

  • T2DM
  • Obesity with one risk factor
  • High ALT
  • Family of MASLD cirrhosis
  • PMOS
  • Sleep apnea

Fibrosis pathway

FIB-4ElastographyThen
Below 1.3 (2.0 if over 65)Not neededRepeat in 1–3 years
1.3–2.67Below 8 kPaPrimary care
1.3–2.678–12 kPaHepatology; second test
Above 2.67Above 12 kPaHepatology; advanced

Other tests

  • ALTNormal in many; AST : ALT above 1 suggests cirrhosis
  • FerritinHigh in a third with normal saturation: inflammation, not iron
  • ANALow titer is common
  • BiopsyBallooning, steatosis, inflammation, scar
  • CardiovascularLipids, HbA1c, BP, smoking, risk score

Red flags

  • Platelets below 150
  • Splenomegaly
  • AST above ALT
  • Ascites
  • Weight loss
  • Jaundice

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Alcohol-associatedAST above ALT, macrocytosisPEth, history
DrugAmiodarone, methotrexate, corticosteroidList
HCVGenotype 3 causes fatRNA
Wilson diseaseYoungCeruloplasmin
Celiac diseaseIron deficiencytTG IgA
HemochromatosisSaturation over 45%HFE

Find the cause

  • 1Insulin resistance and obesityWaist, BMI, glucose, lipids, BP
  • 2Lean MASLDWaist and visceral fat; metabolic risk despite BMI
  • 3GeneticFamily, young age; gene test if severe or lean
  • 4Other steatosisDrug and TPN history, weight change, HIV test

Treatment

Weight loss treats every stage; drugs are for significant fibrosis, and heart, diabetes, and cirrhosis care come with it.

  1. Weight 7–10%Diet and exercise
  2. Metabolic riskDiabetes, lipids, BP
  3. No alcoholOr minimal
  4. DrugsF2–F3
  5. Cirrhosis careVarices, HCC

How much weight

Weight lossGain
3–5%Less fat
7–10%MASH improves
10% or moreFibrosis can improve
No lossExercise still helps; coffee and Mediterranean diet too

Drugs by stage

If there isTreat with
F2–F3 MASH, no cirrhosis (elastography 8–15 kPa)Resmetirom or semaglutide
T2DM or obesityGLP-1 agonist or tirzepatide, chosen for that
T2DM, heart failure, or CKDSGLT2 inhibitor
T2DM, no heart failurePioglitazone: MASH improves, weight rises
MASH without diabetesVitamin E, selected; prostate and stroke concerns
BMI 35 or more, or 30 with comorbidityBariatric surgery, unless decompensated

For everyone

Heart
  • Statin, safe in compensated cirrhosis
  • BP and smoking
Liver
  • Vaccinate HAV and HBV
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Coffee is fine
Cirrhosis
  • Ultrasound and AFP every 6 months
  • EGD by platelets and stiffness
  • Carvedilol if portal hypertension
End stage
  • Transplant; MASLD can recur
  • Weight first

Treat the cause

  • 1Insulin resistance and obesityWeight loss, glucose, lipids, BP
  • 2Lean MASLDThe same; modest loss helps
  • 3GeneticWeight loss; metreleptin for lipodystrophy
  • 4Other steatosisStop the drug, treat HIV, feed

Guidelines differ: resmetirom and semaglutide are licensed for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis in the US, and licensing elsewhere varies.

Liver Abscess and Trauma

Pathophysiology

Force tears liver and vessels, so the danger is bleeding and later bile leak; infection seeds the liver through the portal vein, bile ducts, or blood, and makes pus or a cyst.

  1. Force or microbeTrauma, gut, bile, or blood
  2. Torn tissue or inflammationLaceration or abscess
  3. Bleed, bile, or pusIn the liver or peritoneum
  4. Sepsis or shockIf untreated
  5. HealingMost, without surgery

What trauma does

  • ALacerationRUQ pain
  • BHemorrhageHemoperitoneum, shock
  • CBile leakBiloma, peritonitis
  • DHemobiliaRUQ pain, jaundice, and GI bleeding, later
  • EDiaphragm irritationRight shoulder pain

How germs reach the liver

  • Bile ductsCholangitis, the most common route
  • Portal veinColon: diverticulitis, appendicitis, IBD, cancer
  • ArteryBacteremia, endocarditis, dental
  • DirectGallbladder, perforated ulcer
  • Gut parasitesAmeba, Echinococcus

Etiology

  • Trauma
  • 1Blunt traumaRoad crash, fall, or assault
  • 2Penetrating traumaStab or gunshot; check chest and bowel
  • Abscess and parasites
  • 3Pyogenic abscessE. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, anaerobes; often more than one
  • 4Amebic abscessEntamoeba histolytica; travel, men 18–50
  • 5Hydatid cystEchinococcus granulosus; dogs and sheep
  • 6SchistosomiasisS. mansoni or japonicum; freshwater snails

Abscess at a glance

  • FPyogenic (3)Often several
  • GAmebic (4)Usually one, right lobe
  • HHydatid (5)Cyst within cyst
  • JSchistosomiasis (6)Pipe-stem portal scar

Who gets a pyogenic abscess

  • Diabetes
  • Biliary disease or stent
  • Colon cancer or diverticulitis
  • Transplant
  • Cirrhosis
  • Klebsiella in East Asia

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. TraumaBleeding in hours; delayed to days
  2. AbscessDays to weeks of fever
  3. CystYears, then rupture
  4. HealingWith drainage or time

The pattern

  • TraumaRUQ pain, right shoulder pain, distension, shock
  • Pyogenic (3)Fever, RUQ pain, weight loss; jaundice if biliary; one or many
  • Amebic (4)Fever, RUQ pain, recent travel; diarrhea in a third
  • Hydatid (5)Silent; then pain, rupture, or anaphylaxis
  • Schistosomiasis (6)Portal hypertension with good liver function

Klebsiella (3)

  • HypervirulentLiver abscess with metastatic spread: eye, meninges, lung
  • EyePain, red, or lost vision: endophthalmitis, same day
  • Gas in abscessThink diabetes

Signs of severity

  • Hypotension
  • FAST positive
  • Rigors and sepsis
  • Rupture into chest or abdomen
  • Anaphylaxis
  • Vision change

Complications

  • HemorrhageFirst hours; delayed at 1–2 weeks
  • Bile leakBiloma, peritonitis
  • Hemobilia and pseudoaneurysmDays to weeks
  • Abscess after traumaFever
  • RuptureInto chest, pericardium, or abdomen
  • SepsisPyogenic
  • Cyst spillageAnaphylaxis, spread
  • Portal hypertensionSchistosomiasis

Diagnosis

In trauma, FAST and then CT grade the injury if the patient is stable; in fever with RUQ pain, imaging finds the cavity and serology or aspiration names it.

  1. Unstable traumaFAST, then operate
  2. Stable traumaContrast CT
  3. Fever, RUQ painUltrasound or CT
  4. SerologyAmeba, hydatid, schistosomiasis
  5. AspirateNot a hydatid cyst

Grading trauma (1–2)

Since 2018, a pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula on CT raises the grade.

Other tests

  • TraumaFBC, lactate, crossmatch; chest and head as needed
  • PyogenicBlood cultures before ABX; colonoscopy after recovery; MRCP if biliary
  • KlebsiellaEye examination
  • HydatidUltrasound WHO stage; chest CT
  • SchistosomiasisStool eggs, serology, portal fibrosis on ultrasound

Red flags

  • Shock
  • Peritonitis
  • Pulsatile mass with bleed
  • New eye symptoms
  • Abscess near the heart
  • Hydatid with sudden pain

Mimics

CholecystitisMurphy signUltrasound

Find the cause

  • 1Blunt traumaFAST, CT, other injuries
  • 2Penetrating traumaCT, wound track, chest and bowel
  • 3Pyogenic abscessCulture; biliary and colon search
  • 4Amebic abscessSerology, stool antigen, travel
  • 5Hydatid cystSerology, stage; no blind aspiration
  • 6SchistosomiasisEgg, serology, ultrasound

Treatment

Most stable liver injuries heal with watching; pus needs drainage and antibiotics, amoebae need metronidazole then a gut drug, and a hydatid cyst is never punctured carelessly.

  1. Stable or not?Operate if unstable
  2. Watch or embolizeGrade and bleed
  3. DrainPyogenic, 5 cm or over
  4. DrugBy cause

Review article

Traumatic liver injury: hemodynamic stability as the decision point

Blunt or penetrating force causes liver lacerations and hematomas, leading to bleeding. Management turns on hemodynamic stability rather than the mechanism alone. Here, we review its causes, complications, and management, and consider how it relates to other causes of RUQ pain.

Key points

  • Hemodynamic stability determines the next test and treatment.
  • Unstable patients have a FAST exam, and stable patients have CT abdomen with IV contrast.
  • Most stable liver injuries heal without surgery.

Pathophysiology

Blunt or penetrating force tears liver tissue, causing RUQ pain. Torn vessels bleed, causing hemoperitoneum and hypovolemic shock, and torn ducts leak, causing biloma and bile peritonitis. Blood that enters the bile ducts causes hemobilia, with RUQ pain, jaundice, and GI bleeding, and blood under the diaphragm causes right shoulder pain.

Etiology and mechanisms

Blunt trauma follows motor vehicle collisions, falls, and assault. Penetrating trauma follows stab wounds and gunshot wounds.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are RUQ pain, right shoulder pain from diaphragm irritation, abdominal distention, and signs of shock. Complications are hemorrhage (hemoperitoneum, hypovolemic shock), bile leak (biloma, bile peritonitis), hemobilia (RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding), and liver abscess.

Diagnosis

Unstable patients have a FAST exam to look for free fluid. Stable patients have CT abdomen with IV contrast to grade the injury. Injuries are graded on the AAST scale from I to VI, and grades I and II make up over half.

Management

Hemodynamically stable patients have nonoperative management with close monitoring, with angioembolization if actively bleeding. Unstable patients with a positive FAST have emergency laparotomy. Most stable liver injuries heal without surgery.

Relationships to other conditions

. Hemobilia can resemble biliary disease, with RUQ pain and jaundice, but GI bleeding after liver trauma points to it.

. Hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage can itself cause ischemic liver injury.

Cirrhosis

Pathophysiology

Repeated injury turns stellate cells into scar makers, and bands of scar around regenerating nodules raise portal pressure and starve the liver of function.

  1. Injury for yearsAny cause
  2. Stellate cellsCollagen
  3. Nodules and bandsDistorted vessels
  4. Portal pressureResistance, then more flow
  5. CompensatedNo symptoms
  6. DecompensatedAscites, bleed, or confusion

What the scarred liver does

  • AFibrosis and nodulesDistorted architecture
  • BPortal hypertensionVarices, ascites, splenomegaly
  • CLost synthesisLow albumin and clotting factors
  • DLost clearanceAmmonia, drugs, estrogen

Stages

  • ECompensatedNo portal hypertension; live many years
  • FPortal hypertensionVarices form; still no symptoms
  • GFirst decompensationAscites, variceal bleed, encephalopathy
  • HFurtherInfection, AKI, ACLF, HCC

Why each sign appears

  • Spider nevi, gynecomastiaEstrogen not cleared
  • Muscle lossAmmonia used by muscle, poor diet
  • Bleeding and clottingBoth factors fall: balanced, but can tip
  • InfectionKupffer cells lost, gut leak
  • VasodilationNitric oxide: low BP, fluid kept

Etiology

  • Common
  • 1MASLDMetabolic risk; may have no fat left
  • 2AlcoholOften with obesity or HCV
  • 3ViralHBV, HCV, HDV
  • Others
  • 4Autoimmune and biliaryAutoimmune hepatitis, PBC, PSC
  • 5MetabolicIron, copper, A1AT, cystic fibrosis
  • 6Vascular and cardiacBudd-Chiari, heart failure
  • 7DrugsMethotrexate, amiodarone
  • 8CryptogenicOften burned-out MASLD

What speeds it

  • Alcohol
  • Obesity and diabetes
  • Coinfection
  • Iron overload
  • Smoking
  • Older age
  • Male sex

Stopping the cause: can let scar regress, and recompensation is now a treatment aim.

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. SilentFound on tests
  2. SignsSpider nevi, spleen
  3. DecompensationAscites in most first
  4. Second eventHigher death
  5. ACLF or HCCTransplant

Examination

  • HandsPalmar erythema, clubbing, asterixis, white nails
  • Face and chestJaundice, spider nevi, gynecomastia, parotids
  • AbdomenAscites, caput medusae, big spleen, small liver
  • LegsEdema, bruising
  • GenitalTesticular atrophy, loss of hair
  • NerveAsterixis, confusion

Loss of function

  • Ammonia
  • ClottingHigh INR, low platelets; not protected from clot
  • Bile salts and bilirubinItch, jaundice
  • GlucoseLow late; diabetes common
  • Vitamins A, D, E, KOsteoporosis, bleeding
  • AlbuminEdema
  • MuscleSarcopenia and frailty
  • Stored B12Serum B12 high, not useful

Portal hypertension

  • Varices and ascites
  • SpleenLow platelets and white cells
  • LungHepatopulmonary and portopulmonary

Acute-on-chronic liver failure

  • WhatCirrhosis with a trigger and new organ failure; short-term death is high
  • TriggersInfection, alcohol, bleeding, drug, HBV flare
  • GradesBy number of failing organs, 1–3
  • DoICU, treat trigger, early transplant

Signs of severity

  • Bilirubin rising
  • INR rising
  • Ascites
  • Encephalopathy
  • AKI
  • Infection
  • Frailty

Complications

  • Ascites and SBPMost common first
  • Variceal bleeding
  • EncephalopathyTriggers
  • Hepatorenal AKIPrerenal AKI
  • HCC
  • Portal vein clotAlso worsens
  • InfectionOften the trigger
  • Osteoporosis, sarcopeniaFalls

Grades cirrhosis severity. Select one option per row:

Measure 1 point 2 points 3 points

Diagnosis

A stiff, nodular liver with low platelets or a big spleen is enough; the next question is whether portal hypertension is significant, because that decides carvedilol and endoscopy.

  1. ElastographyStiff liver
  2. Platelets and spleenPortal hypertension
  3. Find the causeTreat it
  4. VaricesEGD if not excluded
  5. HCCUltrasound every 6 months
  6. MELDTransplant

Stiffness and platelets (×10⁹/L)Then

Spleen stiffness over 55 kPa (100 Hz)Present
Risk model 75% or morePresent: ANTICIPATE (stiffness, platelets), ANTICIPATE-NASH (adds BMI, for obese MASLD), or NICER (adds spleen)

  • Child-PughGrades cirrhosis severity

Treatment

Treat the cause to let the liver recover, prevent the first decompensation with carvedilol, and look for cancer, malnutrition, and transplant at every visit.

  1. CauseCure HCV, suppress HBV, abstain
  2. CarvedilolIf significant portal hypertension
  3. NutritionProtein, snack
  4. Cancer and varicesScreening

Every visit

Portal Hypertension and Ascites

Pathophysiology

Resistance to portal flow rises, then splanchnic vessels dilate and send more blood, so pressure forces collaterals, spleen enlargement, and fluid into the abdomen.

  1. ResistanceScar, clot, or pressure
  2. Splanchnic dilationNitric oxide: more inflow
  3. Pressure over 10 mmHgVarices and ascites start
  4. Low effective volumeRAAS, SNS, ADH
  5. Salt and water keptAscites, low sodium, hepatorenal

What portal pressure does

  • ACollateralsEsophageal and gastric varices, caput, rectal varices
  • BAscitesSinusoid leaks; kidneys keep sodium
  • CSplenomegalyLow platelets and white cells

Two steps to ascites

  • Sinusoidal pressureForces lymph out
  • Arterial underfillingVasodilation → RAAS, SNS, ADH → sodium and water kept
  • Low albuminAdds, but does not start it
  • Gradient over 12 mmHgNeeded for bleeding or ascites

SAAG: a wide serum to ascites albumin gap, 11 g/L or more, means the pressure is portal.

Etiology

  • By level
  • 1PrehepaticPortal or splenic vein clot or stenosis; splenic AV fistula
  • 2PresinusoidalSchistosomiasis, PSVD, early PBC, sarcoidosis
  • 3SinusoidalCirrhosis: by far the most common; alcohol-associated hepatitis, MASLD
  • 4Post-sinusoidalSinusoidal obstruction syndrome, venous sclerosis
  • 5PosthepaticBudd-Chiari, IVC web, right heart failure, constriction

Clue to the level

LevelLiver functionWedged pressureGradient
1, 2GoodNormalNormal
3PoorHighHigh: 10 mmHg is significant, 12 bleeds
4PoorHighHigh
5VariableHigh, as is the free pressureNormal or near

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. SilentSpleen, low platelets
  2. VaricesForm, then enlarge
  3. AscitesHalf decompensate within 10 years
  4. SBP, AKI, hyponatremiaLater
  5. TransplantOr death

The pattern

  • VaricesSilent until hematemesis or melena
  • AscitesDistension, weight gain, shifting dullness; umbilical hernia
  • SplenomegalyLow platelets, early satiety
  • HydrothoraxRight-sided effusion, dyspnea
  • Portal vein clotSudden ascites or pain

Grades of ascites

GradeMeansFirst
1Ultrasound onlyTreat cause, no diuretic
2ModerateSalt limit, diuretic
3Large or tenseTap, then diuretic
RefractoryNo response, or drugs not toleratedTaps, TIPS, transplant

Lung in portal hypertension

  • HepatopulmonaryDilated lung vessels → low oxygen, worse upright; bubble echo late bubbles; oxygen, transplant
  • PortopulmonaryPulmonary hypertension; pulmonary vasodilator first, then transplant; no TIPS or beta-blocker if moderate or severe
  • Hepatic hydrothoraxAscites crosses the diaphragm; as ascites, avoid chest drain

Signs of severity

  • Fever or abdominal pain
  • Encephalopathy
  • Creatinine rising
  • Sodium below 130
  • Bleeding
  • Oxygen falling when upright

Complications

  • Variceal bleeding
  • SBPNeutrophils 250/µL or more
  • Hepatorenal AKIAfter SBP, bleed, or tap
  • HyponatremiaToo much water kept
  • Hernia ruptureUmbilical; leak
  • Hydrothorax and empyemaRight side
  • Lung syndromesAbove
  • Splenic infarctRare

Diagnosis

Every new ascites is tapped: SAAG says portal or not, and neutrophils say infected; HVPG is the gold standard but Doppler and stiffness usually do.

  1. Ultrasound and DopplerAscites, flow, liver
  2. TapCount, albumin, protein, culture
  3. SAAG11 g/L or more portal
  4. Neutrophils250/µL or more SBP
  5. VaricesEGD or exclude

Reading ascites

SAAG=serum albumin−ascites albuminSAAG, serum-ascites albumin gradient, g/L; measured the same day
SAAG and proteinThink of
11 or more, protein under 25 g/LCirrhosis
11 or more, protein 25 or moreHeart failure, Budd-Chiari early
Under 11, protein highCancer, tuberculosis, pancreatitis
Under 11, protein lowNephrotic syndrome, malnutrition

What else to send

TestMeans
Neutrophils 250/µL or moreSBP: treat now
Culture in blood bottlesGrows 1 in 2
Glucose low, LDH high, many germsSecondary peritonitis: CT
CytologyCancer in peritoneum
Adenosine deaminaseTuberculosis
AmylasePancreatic
TriglycerideChylous
BacterascitesGrows, under 250: repeat and treat if symptoms

SBP types

  • ClassicOne germ, gut Gram-negative or streptococcus
  • Culture-negativeSame treatment
  • SecondaryPerforation: surgery
  • NosocomialResistant: broader

Red flags

  • Fever, pain, or confusion in ascites
  • Tense and dyspneic
  • Hypotension
  • Low urine
  • Bloody tap

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Heart failureHigh JVP, effusionEchocardiogram
Cancer ascitesWeight loss, low SAAGCytology
Nephrotic syndromeProteinuriaUrine
TuberculosisFever, travelAdenosine deaminase, culture
PancreaticHigh amylaseAmylase
OvarianPelvic mass, CA 125CT

Find the cause

  • 1PrehepaticDoppler: portal, splenic clot
  • 2PresinusoidalTravel, biopsy, drugs
  • 3SinusoidalStiffness, biopsy
  • 4Post-sinusoidalTransplant drugs; biopsy
  • 5PosthepaticDoppler, echocardiogram, JVP

Treatment

Tap, limit salt, and add spironolactone; infection is treated within hours; and TIPS and transplant come in when drugs and taps fail.

  1. Salt and diureticSpironolactone, furosemide
  2. TapLarge: albumin
  3. SBPABX and albumin
  4. TIPSRefractory
  5. TransplantRefer early

Ascites ladder

StepUse
1Salt under about 5 g a day, stop NSAID and ACE inhibitor
2Spironolactone, then add furosemide, 100 : 40 ratio
3Aim 0.5 kg a day, or 1 kg with edema
4Large-volume tap with albumin if over 5 L
Stop diuretic ifEncephalopathy, sodium below 125, AKI, or potassium high
RefractoryRepeated taps, TIPS, transplant

TIPS

If there isThen
Refractory ascites, good functionTIPS early; reduces ascites, raises encephalopathy
Bilirubin over 50 µmol/L or MELD over 18Weigh by team: higher early death, not an absolute bar; avoid in heart failure or severe encephalopathy
Variceal bleed not stoppedSalvage TIPS
High risk after a bleedEarly TIPS within 72 hours

SBP

If there isTreat with
Community, no resistanceCefotaxime or ceftriaxone for 5–7 days
Hospital or resistant areaPiperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem by local pattern
All SBPAlbumin day 1 and 3: less AKI and death
No better at 48 hoursRepeat tap: secondary?
After first SBPLifelong prophylaxis
Variceal bleedCeftriaxone for 5–7 days
Ascites protein under 15 with renal or liver failurePrimary prophylaxis, selected

Other complications

If there isTreat with
Sodium 126–135Watch, fluid by need
Sodium below 125Stop diuretic, limit water; albumin
Umbilical herniaControl ascites, then repair
HydrothoraxAs ascites; no chest drain; TIPS
HepatopulmonaryOxygen, transplant
PortopulmonaryAs above

Varices

  • Primary and secondary prevention
  • Beta-blockerCarvedilol if significant portal hypertension

Treat the cause

  • 1PrehepaticAnticoagulate, or splenectomy for splenic vein bleeding
  • 2PresinusoidalPraziquantel; treat disease
  • 3SinusoidalTreat cirrhosis
  • 4Post-sinusoidalDefibrotide
  • 5PosthepaticStent, TIPS, heart treatment

Guidelines differ: Baveno VIII (2026) keeps most earlier cutoffs, but no longer applies 25 kPa alone to MASLD with obesity.

Hepatic Encephalopathy and Hepatorenal Syndrome

Pathophysiology

Ammonia and other toxins skip the failing or bypassed liver and swell the brain; widened gut vessels leave the kidney underfilled and constricted, with no damage to its structure.

  1. Portal blood bypasses liverShunts, or lost function
  2. Ammonia reaches the brainAstrocytes swell
  3. Splanchnic vessels dilateNitric oxide
  4. Effective volume fallsRAAS, SNS, ADH
  5. Kidney arteries constrictFunctional AKI

Brain and kidney

  • ABrainAmmonia → astrocyte swelling, inflammation, GABA tone
  • BKidneyVasoconstriction without injury

Hepatorenal, step by step

  • CSplanchnic dilationNitric oxide
  • DLow effective volumeThough total is high
  • ERAAS and SNSSalt and water kept
  • FKidney artery constrictionGFR falls

Ammonia's limits

  • LevelDoes not track with grade: treat the patient
  • NormalMakes encephalopathy doubtful
  • Rising muscle useSarcopenia worsens it

Etiology

  • Encephalopathy: look for a trigger
  • 1InfectionSBP, chest, urine, skin, C. difficile
  • 2GI bleedingProtein load in the gut
  • 3Constipation and dehydrationOver-diuresis
  • 4DrugsBenzodiazepine, opioid, alcohol
  • 5Electrolytes and kidneyLow potassium or sodium, alkalosis, AKI
  • 6Shunt or TIPSLarge bypass
  • Hepatorenal: what tips it
  • 7SBP or infectionThe most common
  • 8Large tap, diuretic, or bleedWithout albumin

Types of encephalopathy

  • Type AAcute liver failure
  • Type BBypass, no liver disease
  • Type CCirrhosis
  • Episodic, recurrent, persistentCourse
  • Covert or overtGrade 0–1, or 2–4

No trigger found: in some, so look again and check for a large shunt.

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. CovertSlow thinking, poor driving
  2. OvertConfusion, asterixis
  3. ComaTrigger or failure
  4. HepatorenalDays after trigger
  5. Recovery or transplantOr death

West Haven grades

GradeFeatures
0 or minimalFound only by tests
1Short attention, sleep reversal
2Drowsy, disoriented, asterixis
3Stupor, confused, rousable
4Coma

Hepatorenal

  • OnsetCreatinine rises, urine low, bland sediment
  • SettingAscites, low BP, low sodium
  • Two formsHRS-AKI, fast; HRS-CKD, slow
  • Mimics of itAcute tubular injury, volume loss, nephrotoxin

Signs of severity

  • Grade 3 or 4
  • Airway
  • Creatinine doubling
  • Lactate
  • Infection
  • Bilirubin high

Complications

  • AspirationGrade 3–4
  • Falls and accidentsCovert too
  • ComaAcute liver failure swells
  • AKI to dialysisHepatorenal
  • RecurrenceCommon
  • DeathWeeks to months without transplant in HRS-AKI
  • Cognitive declineRepeated episodes

Diagnosis

Encephalopathy is clinical: cirrhosis, confusion, and no other cause, then a search for a trigger; hepatorenal is AKI with ascites that no volume or other cause explains.

  1. Grade itWest Haven
  2. Find a triggerTap, cultures, bleed, drugs
  3. Exclude othersGlucose, CT, B12, alcohol
  4. KidneyStop drugs, volume
  5. HepatorenalIf no improvement

Find the trigger

  • Diagnostic tap
  • Blood, urine, and chest cultures
  • Rectal exam: bleed, stool
  • Drug list
  • Electrolytes, creatinine
  • Glucose
  • Head CT if focal, fall, or new

Hepatorenal AKI

Cirrhosis with ascites, AKI that does not improve within 24 hours of adequate volume when volume was needed, and no other explanation. The full criteria and treatment are in renal.

Prerenal Acute Kidney Injury

TestHepatorenalTubular injury
SedimentBlandMuddy casts
Urine sodiumLowHigh
Response to volumeNoneNone
TriggerSBP, tap, bleedSepsis, nephrotoxin

Other tests

  • AmmoniaNot for grade; normal argues against
  • Covert testingAnimal naming, psychometric, if driving matters
  • Brain CTFocal, fall, or first episode
  • EEGUnclear coma
  • UrineSodium, protein, sediment; kidney ultrasound

Red flags

  • Fever or abdominal pain
  • Focal sign
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Creatinine rising after a tap
  • Grade 3 or 4

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Alcohol withdrawalTremor, sweating, last drinkHistory
Wernicke encephalopathyEyes, ataxiaThiamine
Subdural hematomaFall, focalCT
HypoglycemiaLow glucoseGlucose
SepsisFeverCultures
UremiaHigh ureaCreatinine
Drug effectSedativeList

Find the cause

  • 1InfectionTap, cultures
  • 2GI bleedingMelena, hematemesis, rectal exam
  • 3Constipation and dehydrationStool history, diuretic
  • 4DrugsDrug list, toxicology
  • 5Electrolytes and kidneyPotassium, sodium, creatinine, gas
  • 6Shunt or TIPSTIPS date; CT for shunt
  • 7SBP or infectionTap, cultures
  • 8Large tap, diuretic, or bleedRecord of tap and diuretic

Treatment

Treat the trigger first, clear the gut with lactulose, add rifaximin for prevention, and give albumin with a vasoconstrictor for hepatorenal AKI while transplant is planned.

  1. TriggerTreat it
  2. Lactulose2–3 soft stools
  3. RifaximinTo prevent
  4. Albumin and vasoconstrictorHepatorenal
  5. TransplantRefer

Encephalopathy ladder

StepUse
1Trigger; airway if grade 3 or 4
2Lactulose by mouth or enema, to 2–3 soft stools; excess makes dehydration
3Rifaximin added after the second episode, or if lactulose fails
4L-ornithine L-aspartate, branched-chain amino acids, selected
NeverProtein restriction, benzodiazepine, sedating antihistamine

Nutrition and safety

Feed
  • 1.2–1.5 g/kg protein
  • Vegetable protein if needed
  • Late snack
Safety
  • Falls, driving advice
  • Airway if grade 3
Prevent
  • Lactulose after first episode
  • Prophylaxis for SBP
  • Stop drugs

Hepatorenal AKI

  • FirstStop diuretics and nephrotoxins; treat infection
  • AlbuminGuided by volume; avoid overload

  • TransplantThe cure

Not proven

  • Protein restriction
  • Routine ammonia tests
  • Neomycin: ear and kidney harm
  • Albumin for a low level
  • Diuretics in hepatorenal

Treat the cause

  • 1InfectionABX by source; albumin if SBP
  • 2GI bleedingStop the bleed, ceftriaxone
  • 3Constipation and dehydrationLaxative, fluid
  • 4DrugsStop; naloxone or flumazenil only if needed
  • 5Electrolytes and kidneyReplace potassium; treat AKI

Comparison

Every liver disease ends in a few patterns, so name the pattern (hepatocellular, cholestatic, infiltrative, vascular, or cirrhotic) and the tests follow.

By zone

  • AZone 1Portal tract: virus, autoimmune, iron, cholestasis
  • BZone 2Yellow fever
  • CZone 3Central vein: paracetamol, shock, congestion, alcohol, MASLD

Judge function first (INR, bilirubin, albumin, confusion), then pattern, then a short panel, then fibrosis; biopsy answers only what remains.

Remove stones that hurt, drain ducts that block, give antibiotics for infection, and operate on the gallbladder early.

  3. GallbladderEarly
  4. CauseStone or tumor
  5. FollowHistology

Chronic Pancreatitis

Pathophysiology

Repeated injury turns acini into scar and the duct into stones and strictures, so enzymes and then insulin fail, and trapped nerves make pain outlast the cause.

  1. Injury for yearsAlcohol, smoke, gene, or block
  2. Protein plugsStones
  3. FibrosisStellate cells
  4. Enzymes failOver 90% lost
  5. Islets failDiabetes
  6. CancerSome

What the scar does

  • APlugs and stonesWide, beaded duct
  • BAcini lostLittle enzyme: fat malabsorption
  • CNervesInflamed and large: pain
  • DIsletsLate loss: diabetes type 3c

Why pain stays

  • PressureDuct blocked: endoscopy or surgery can help
  • NeuropathyScar around nerves
  • Central sensitizationOutlasts the gland
  • OpioidHyperalgesia

Etiology

  • Toxic
  • 1AlcoholUnder 10% of heavy drinkers; adults
  • 2SmokingIndependent; speeds all others
  • Inherited or immune
  • 3GeneticPRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC
  • 4AutoimmuneType 1 (IgG4) and type 2 (with IBD)
  • Structural and other
  • 5ObstructiveStricture, tumor, divisum, sphincter
  • 6Recurrent acuteRepeated attacks
  • 7MetabolicHigh calcium or triglyceride
  • 8IdiopathicEarly (under 35) and late

Two autoimmune types (4)

FeatureType 1Type 2
AgeOlder menYounger
IgG4HighNormal
Other organsBile duct, kidney, salivaryIBD
MassSausage gland, like cancerFocal
RelapseCommonRare

Check for cancer

  • New weight loss
  • New diabetes over 50
  • Painless jaundice
  • Duct cut-off
  • Single stricture

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. AttacksYears
  2. Pain or notSome painless
  3. SteatorrheaOver 90% lost
  4. DiabetesLater
  5. CancerRisk rises

The pattern

  • PainEpigastric to back, better leaning forward, worse with meals
  • Weight lossFear of eating, malabsorption
  • StoolPale, bulky, floats
  • DiabetesEasy hypoglycemia (no glucagon)
  • BonesOsteoporosis, vitamin D low

Signs of severity

  • Opioid need
  • Weight loss
  • Steatorrhea
  • Jaundice
  • Splenomegaly, varices
  • Low albumin
  • New diabetes

Complications

  • Exocrine failureEnzyme, fat vitamins
  • Diabetes type 3cInsulin, hypoglycemia
  • PseudocystPain, infection
  • Bile or duodenal strictureJaundice, vomiting
  • Splenic vein thrombosisGastric varices
  • PseudoaneurysmBleeding
  • Duct leakAscites, pleural
  • CancerPancreatic
  • OsteoporosisAnd falls
  • Opioid dependenceAnd mood

Diagnosis

CT or MRI with MRCP shows calcification and a beaded duct; EUS and function tests add only when doubt stays, and cancer is always on the list.

  1. CT or MRI and MRCPCalcification, duct
  2. EUSIf unclear
  3. ElastaseFunction
  4. CauseGenes, IgG4, calcium, lipid
  5. CancerMass, stricture

TestFinding

Glucose, HbA1cDiabetes

Vitamins and bones

  • A, D, E, K
  • B12, zinc, magnesium
  • INR
  • DXA every 2 years

Red flags

  • Jaundice
  • Weight loss over 10%
  • Mass
  • New diabetes over 50
  • Bleeding

  • 6Recurrent acutePast attacks

Treatment

Stop alcohol and smoking, treat pain stepwise, open or drain a blocked duct early, replace enzymes with every meal, and check for diabetes and cancer.

  1. StopAlcohol and smoking
  2. PainStep by step
  3. EnzymesWith food
  4. DiabetesInsulin or metformin
  5. DuctEndoscopy or surgery
  6. CancerWatch

Pain ladder

StepUse
1Paracetamol, NSAID
2Pregabalin or TCA; antioxidants, modest
3Weak opioid, short and reviewed
4Endoscopy: stones, stricture, stent
5Surgery: drain or resect; better than endoscopy first with a duct of 5 mm or more and recent opioids (ESCAPE)
6Celiac block; total pancreatectomy with islets in selected

Enzymes (PERT)

  • WhoElastase low, weight loss, steatorrhea
  • DoseFat meals need more; with the first bite
  • Not betterAdd PPI, check dose, bacterial overgrowth, giardia
  • FollowWeight, vitamins, not pain

Diabetes 3c

  • MetforminIf mild
  • InsulinOften needed, low dose, hypoglycemia
  • GLP-1Avoid incretin drugs: pancreatitis
  • NutritionEnzymes with meals help glucose

Complications

If there isTreat with
Stone or strictureLithotripsy, ERCP, stent, or surgery
Bile strictureStent or bypass
PseudocystDrain if symptomatic
PseudoaneurysmEmbolize
Varices from splenic clotSplenectomy if bleeding
AutoimmunePrednisolone, then azathioprine or rituximab

Treat the cause

  • 1AlcoholAbstain
  • 2SmokingStop
  • 3GeneticSupport, counseling, cancer watch
  • 4AutoimmuneCorticosteroid
  • 5ObstructiveEndoscopy or surgery
  • 6Recurrent acutePrevent attacks
  • 7MetabolicCalcium, triglyceride
  • 8IdiopathicSupport

Guidelines differ: enzymes do not relieve pain, though some patients are given a trial.

Pancreatic Cancer

Pathophysiology

Duct cells gather mutations over a decade or more, so by the time they invade vessels and nerves, most tumors cannot be removed.

  1. KRASEarly lesion (PanIN)
  2. CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4Invasion
  3. Dense scarPoor drug entry
  4. Nerves and vesselsPain, encasement
  5. Liver, peritoneumEarly spread

From duct to cancer

  • ANormal ductOne cell layer
  • BLow-grade PanINKRAS
  • CHigh-grade PanINCDKN2A
  • DCarcinomaTP53 and SMAD4; scar around it

Why it kills

  • Early spreadMicrometastases
  • Dense stromaDrugs get in poorly
  • Nerve invasionBack pain
  • ClotsTrousseau syndrome
  • WastingCachexia and enzyme loss

Etiology

  • Cancer
  • 1Ductal adenocarcinomaAbout 90%; head in two-thirds
  • Cysts that can become cancer
  • 2IPMNMucin in the main or branch duct; older men
  • 3Mucinous cystic neoplasmBody and tail; women; ovarian stroma
  • 4Other cystsSerous (benign), solid pseudopapillary (young women), pseudocyst
  • 5HereditaryBRCA2, PALB2, CDKN2A, Lynch, PRSS1, Peutz-Jeghers

Who is at risk

  • Smoking
  • New diabetes over 50
  • Chronic pancreatitis
  • Obesity
  • Family: two first-degree
  • Older age
  • Alcohol, heavy
  • Mucinous cysts

Where it sits

SitePresents
Head (E)Painless jaundice, Courvoisier gallbladder, weight loss
Body (F)Back pain, late
Tail (G)Late, weight loss, splenic vein clot
UncinateVessel invasion, no jaundice

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. SilentNew diabetes or vague pain
  2. Jaundice or weight lossMonths
  3. Back painNerves
  4. AscitesPeritoneum
  5. Weeks to monthsIf untreated

The pattern

  • Painless jaundiceDark urine, pale stool, itch
  • Weight lossOver 10%
  • New diabetesOver 50, with weight loss
  • Back painWorse lying
  • SteatorrheaDuct blocked
  • Migratory clotTrousseau
  • DepressionEarly

IPMN branch (2)Grape-like, joins ductWatch or remove by feature

PseudocystAfter pancreatitisNone
Solid pseudopapillary (4)Young woman, solid and cysticRemove

Signs of severity

  • Bilirubin high
  • Vessel encased
  • Ascites
  • Weight loss
  • CA 19-9 over 1000
  • Uncontrolled pain

Complications

  • CholangitisAfter stent
  • Duodenal obstructionVomiting
  • VTECommon
  • MalabsorptionEnzymes
  • Diabetes3c
  • PainCeliac plexus
  • CachexiaPoor outcome
  • BleedingDuodenum, varices

Diagnosis

Pancreas-protocol CT names and stages a mass; EUS biopsy gives tissue, CA 19-9 follows it, and resectability is decided by vessels before any stent.

  1. Pancreas-protocol CTMass and vessels
  2. EUS biopsyIf treatment needs it
  3. CA 19-9Follow, not screen
  4. LaparoscopyCA 19-9 over 150–500, over 3 cm, body or tail, or unclear CT
  5. Germline testEvery patient

FeatureThen

Surgery is the only cure for about one in five; give chemotherapy with it, and treat pain, enzymes, clots, and mood in everyone.

Neuroendocrine Tumors and Carcinoid Syndrome

Pathophysiology

Neuroendocrine cells in the pancreas and gut grow slowly and can secrete hormones; carcinoid syndrome appears only once liver spread lets serotonin skip the liver.

  1. Neuroendocrine cellSporadic or gene
  2. Growth, graded by Ki-67Slow to fast
  3. Hormone or noneSyndrome or mass
  4. Liver spreadCarcinoid syndrome
  5. Valves and bowelFibrosis

Why carcinoid needs liver spread

  • ASmall bowel tumorMakes serotonin
  • BLiverClears it, normally
  • CLiver metastasesSend it on
  • DRight heartValves thicken: tricuspid leak, pulmonary stenosis
  • EBodyFlush, diarrhea, wheeze

Grade

GradeKi-67Behaves
G1Under 3%Slow
G23–20%Moderate
G3 NETOver 20%, well differentiatedFaster
NEC (9)Over 20%, poorly differentiatedLike small-cell cancer

Etiology

  • Functioning pancreas
  • 1InsulinomaFasting low glucose; usually single and benign
  • 2GastrinomaUlcers, diarrhea; duodenum often
  • 3GlucagonomaRash, diabetes, weight loss, clots
  • 4VipomaWatery diarrhea, low potassium, low acid
  • 5SomatostatinomaDiabetes, stones, steatorrhea
  • Others
  • 6Nonfunctioning pancreaticMass or chance
  • 7Small bowel with carcinoid syndromeIleum; often multiple
  • 8Appendix and rectumUsually small and found by chance
  • 9Neuroendocrine carcinomaPoorly differentiated

Genes

  • MEN1Pancreas, parathyroid, pituitary; gastrinoma and insulinoma
  • VHLPancreatic cysts and NET, kidney, eye
  • NF1Somatostatinoma at the ampulla
  • TSCPancreatic NET
  • SporadicMost

  1. Silent or hormoneYears
  2. SyndromeOften mistaken
  3. MassOr found by chance

Whipple triad (1)

  • Symptoms of low glucose
  • Glucose low
  • Relieved by glucose

Celiac Disease

Pathophysiology

In people with HLA-DQ2 or DQ8, gluten peptides set off a T cell and antibody response in the duodenum, which kills the epithelium and flattens the villi.

  1. Gluten eatenGliadin resists digestion
  2. tTG changes itBinds HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 better
  3. T helper cellsRelease interferon-γ
  4. Villi flattenCrypts lengthen
  5. MalabsorptionIron first, then others

From gluten to injury

  • AGliadin crossesThrough a leaky epithelium into the lamina propria
  • BtTGDeamidates gliadin, which makes it negatively charged
  • CPresentationHLA-DQ2 or DQ8 holds it tightly and shows it to T cells
  • DT helper cellsInterferon-γ and IL-21 drive inflammation
  • EB cellsMake antibodies to tTG, DGP, and endomysium
  • FIELsIL-15 arms them to kill stressed epithelial cells

Stages on biopsy (Marsh)

  • GNormalVilli at least 3 times as tall as the crypts are deep
  • HInfiltrative25 or more IELs per 100 epithelial cells; not specific
  • JHyperplasticCrypts lengthen as well
  • KDestructiveVilli are partly, mostly, or completely lost

Why each feature appears

  • Duodenum worstIron, folate, and calcium are absorbed there
  • Long disease reaches the jejunumFat, sugar, and protein malabsorption → diarrhea and weight loss
  • Lost brush border enzymesSecondary lactose intolerance
  • Low vitamin D and calciumSecondary hyperparathyroidism, osteoporosis
  • Antibodies to transglutaminase 3 in skinDermatitis herpetiformis
  • Spleen shrinksRisk from encapsulated bacteria

Note: About a third of people carry HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 and only a few develop the disease, so a negative result rules it out but a positive one means little.

Etiology

The cause is gluten in wheat, barley, and rye acting on the right genes, and the disease is classed by how it shows itself.

Forms

  • 1ClassicalMalabsorption: diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, edema, or poor growth
  • 2NonclassicalAnemia, osteoporosis, bloating, or high transaminases without malabsorption; the most common form in adults
  • 3SubclinicalNo symptoms, found by screening; villi are flat
  • 4PotentialPositive serology with normal or near-normal villi
  • 5RefractoryVilli stay flat with symptoms after 12 months of a strict diet, with other causes excluded

Who is at risk

  • RelativesAbout 10% of first-degree relatives
  • Autoimmune diseaseType 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, autoimmune hepatitis
  • ChromosomesDown, Turner, and Williams syndromes
  • IgA deficiency10–15 times more common, and it hides the usual test
  • TriggersEnteric infection in childhood may contribute

Who to test

  • Chronic diarrhea or bloating
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Osteoporosis when young
  • High transaminases
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Type 1 diabetes
  • First-degree relatives
  • Infertility or miscarriage
  • Ataxia or neuropathy

Symptoms and complications

  1. SilentAntibodies, then flat villi
  2. Iron deficiencyOften the only sign
  3. Bloating, diarrheaOr constipation
  4. MalabsorptionWeight loss, edema
  5. Refractory diseaseUncommon

The pattern

  • BowelDiarrhea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain, or constipation
  • BloodIron deficiency anemia that does not respond to oral iron; folate deficiency
  • BoneOsteopenia, fractures
  • SkinDermatitis herpetiformis: intensely itchy vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks
  • MouthAphthous ulcers, enamel defects
  • NervesGluten ataxia, neuropathy, headache
  • ReproductiveInfertility, miscarriage, late puberty
  • ChildrenPoor growth, irritability, wasted buttocks

Deficiencies to look for

NutrientCauses
IronMicrocytic anemia, fatigue
Folate, B12Macrocytic anemia; B12 less often, as the ileum is spared
Vitamin D, calciumOsteomalacia, osteoporosis, tetany
Vitamin KBruising, long prothrombin time
Zinc, copperRash, poor taste, neuropathy

Complications

  • OsteoporosisFracture risk falls on the diet
  • HyposplenismPneumococcal sepsis
  • Refractory disease (5)Type 1 has normal IELs; type 2 has clonal IELs and behaves like early lymphoma
  • Ulcerative jejunoileitisPain, bleeding, stricture; usually type 2
  • EATLWeight loss, pain, fever, obstruction; rare, and more common in type 2
  • Small bowel adenocarcinomaRare
  • Celiac crisisSevere diarrhea, acidosis, low K+ and Ca2+; rare
  • Microscopic colitisPersistent watery diarrhea

Diagnosis

Positive tTG-IgA on a gluten diet with villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy makes the diagnosis in adults.

  1. Keep eating glutenUntil testing is complete
  2. tTG-IgA and total IgAOne test for most
  3. Duodenal biopsyDistal duodenum and bulb
  4. Baseline testsDeficiencies, bone, thyroid
  5. Diet, then recheckAntibodies fall

Serology

  • tTG-IgAFirst-line at any age; the titer rises with the damage
  • Total IgAIf deficient, use tTG-IgG or DGP-IgG, and biopsy if suspicion remains
  • EMAVery specific; kept for uncertain results
  • HLA typingRules out the disease when results conflict or gluten has already stopped
  • Already gluten-freeCheck HLA first; if positive, a gluten challenge for several weeks before testing

Biopsy

  • WhereAt least 4 from the distal duodenum and 2 from the bulb, whether or not the lining looks abnormal
  • EndoscopyScalloped folds, mosaic pattern, fewer folds; can look normal
  • FindingsIELs, long crypts, flat villi; not specific alone
  • Dermatitis herpetiformisSkin biopsy beside a lesion: granular IgA in the dermal papillae

When results disagree

If there isThen
Positive tTG-IgA, normal villiPotential disease (4): check the samples, HLA, and EMA; repeat over time
Flat villi, negative serologyExclude the mimics below, check IgA and HLA, then judge the response to the diet
Low positive tTG-IgARepeat on gluten, then biopsy
Symptoms only, all negativeNonceliac gluten or wheat sensitivity, often due to fructans

Other tests at diagnosis

  • FBC, ferritin, folate, B12
  • Vitamin D, calcium, ALP, PTH
  • LFTs
  • TFTs, glucose
  • Coagulation
  • DXA if at risk

Red flags

  • Relapse on a strict diet
  • Weight loss
  • Fever or night sweats
  • Pain or obstruction
  • Low albumin
  • GI bleeding

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Tropical sprueResidence in the tropics; folate and B12 both low
GiardiasisTravel, camping, CVIDStool antigen or PCR
Drug enteropathyOlmesartan, mycophenolate, immune checkpoint inhibitorsStop the drug
CVIDInfections; no plasma cells on biopsyIgG, IgA, IgM
Autoimmune enteropathySevere, resists the diet; no goblet cellsAnti-enterocyte antibodies
Crohn diseasePain, ulcers, high calprotectin
SIBOSurgery, motility disorderBreath test
IBSNormal serology and biopsy

Find the cause

  • 1ClassicalSerology and biopsy
  • 2NonclassicalSerology in anemia, bone disease, or high transaminases
  • 3SubclinicalScreen relatives and people with linked disease
  • 4PotentialTwo positive results, HLA, and repeat biopsy over time
  • 5RefractoryDiet review, stool or urine gluten peptides, repeat biopsy with IEL typing, then capsule and CT or MRE

Guidelines differ: The ESsCD conditionally allows diagnosis without biopsy under age 45 when tTG-IgA is at least 10 times the limit on two samples, while biopsy remains the standard elsewhere.

Treatment

A strict lifelong gluten-free diet heals the bowel and lowers the risk of complications, so most of the work is teaching it and checking it.

  1. DietitianDiagnosis first, then diet
  2. Gluten-free for lifeWheat, barley, rye
  3. Replace deficienciesIron, vitamin D, folate
  4. RecheckAntibodies at 6–12 months
  5. Still unwell?Look for gluten first

The diet

  • AvoidWheat, barley, rye, and malt; hidden gluten in sauces, medicines, and shared kitchens
  • SafeRice, corn, potato, quinoa, buckwheat, meat, fruit, plain dairy
  • OatsCertified gluten-free only; a few people react to them
  • LactoseAvoid for some months if it causes symptoms
  • GapsFiber, B vitamins, and iron; watch weight gain

Follow-up

MeasureWhen
Symptoms, dietitianAt 3–6 months, then every year
tTG-IgA6 and 12 months, then yearly; normal values do not prove healing
FBC, ferritin, vitamin D, TFTsYearly or as needed
DXAAt diagnosis if at risk; repeat if low
Repeat biopsyPersistent symptoms, or to prove healing in older adults at 1–2 years
VaccinesPneumococcal if hyposplenic, over 65, or with refractory type 2 disease

Still unwell on the diet

If there isThen
Gluten exposure, the most common causeDietitian, gluten peptides in stool or urine
Wrong diagnosisReview serology and biopsies
Healed villiIBS, lactose intolerance, microscopic colitis, EPI, SIBO, bile acid diarrhea
Villi still flat after 12 monthsRefractory disease (5): IEL typing in a center

Refractory disease (5)

  • Type 1Open-capsule budesonide, sometimes AZA; good outlook
  • Type 2Budesonide, then cladribine or other specialist treatment; about half survive 5 years
  • BothNutrition, exclude EATL, specialist center

Be careful with

  • Diet before testing
  • Cosmetics and medicines
  • Dapsone: check G6PD, FBC
  • Iron: IV if oral fails
  • Calcium and vitamin D gaps
  • Iodine in food can flare the rash

Treat the cause

  • 1ClassicalDiet, nutrients, IV fluid and electrolytes if severe
  • 2NonclassicalDiet; treat bone and iron
  • 3SubclinicalDiet is advised, even without symptoms
  • 4PotentialWatch, or treat if symptoms; diet if they progress
  • 5RefractoryFind gluten, then budesonide and a specialist center

Dermatitis herpetiformis

  • DietHeals skin over months to years, and the bowel
  • DapsoneRelieves itch within days; does not treat the bowel

Note: Larazotide and other drugs remain under study, so no medicine replaces the diet.

  • ASecretoryGap under 50 mOsm/kg: electrolytes hold the water

Crohn Disease

Pathophysiology

In people with genetic risk, gut bacteria cross a weak barrier and drive a T cell response that does not switch off, so inflammation runs through the whole wall in patches, then scars or tunnels.

  1. Genes and environmentNOD2, smoking, diet
  2. Barrier and bacteriaFewer defenses, altered flora
  3. IL-23 and TNFTh1 and Th17 cells
  4. Transmural inflammationSkip lesions
  5. Stricture or fistulaOver years

Why the immune system stays on

  • AWeak barrierNOD2 and ATG16L1 variants weaken Paneth cell defenses and autophagy
  • BBacteria crossLess varied flora, with fewer protective bacteria
  • CDendritic cellsRelease IL-12 and IL-23
  • DT cellsTh1 (interferon-γ) and Th17 (IL-17) cells; α4β7 integrin brings more to the gut
  • EInflammationTNF keeps it going and triggers granulomas

What it does to the wall

  • FTransmural inflammationDeep fissures, lymphoid aggregates
  • GFistulas and abscessesA fissure reaches the serosa and tunnels
  • HStrictureMyofibroblasts lay down collagen; the muscle thickens
  • IGranulomaNoncaseating; found in about a third, so absence does not exclude it
  • JCreeping fatMesenteric fat wraps the inflamed bowel

Why each feature appears

  • Ileal inflammationRLQ pain, low B12, bile salt loss
  • Bile salt lossWatery diarrhea, gallstones; fat binds calcium → free oxalate → kidney stones
  • Protein loss and low intakeLow albumin, weight loss, poor growth
  • Deep inflammationFever, mass, abscess
  • CytokinesFatigue, anemia of inflammation, clots

Note: The Th1 and Th2 split between the two diseases is the classic teaching, but Th17 cells and IL-23 drive both.

Etiology

The cause is unknown, so the disease is classed by location, which predicts its symptoms and course.

By location

  • 1Ileal (L1)About a third; strictures, low B12, bile salt diarrhea
  • 2Colonic (L2)About a quarter; bloody diarrhea, rectum often spared
  • 3Ileocolonic (L3)About 40%; most surgery
  • 4Upper GI (L4)Alone in under 5%, with another site in 10–15%; more in children
  • 5Perianal (p)About a quarter over time; can come first

Who gets it

  • Family historyFirst-degree relative; NOD2 is the strongest single gene, mainly for ileal disease
  • SmokingIncreases the risk, flares, and surgery
  • Early life and dietABX in childhood, ultra-processed food, urban life
  • DrugsNSAIDs can trigger flares
  • AgePeak at 15–35; a smaller second peak later

Note: Smoking worsens Crohn disease but appears to protect from ulcerative colitis.

Symptoms and complications

  1. InflammationPain, diarrhea, weight loss
  2. Relapse and remissionSilent activity continues
  3. Stricture or penetrationAbout half within 20 years
  4. SurgeryRecurs near the join

The pattern

  • CardinalRLQ pain, nonbloody diarrhea over 4–6 weeks, weight loss, fatigue, fever
  • Colonic (2)Bloody diarrhea, urgency
  • Upper GI (4)Epigastric pain, vomiting, outlet obstruction
  • Perianal (5)Pain, discharge, skin tags, off-midline fissure
  • ChildrenGrowth failure and late puberty, sometimes alone
  • ExaminationRLQ mass, mouth ulcers, perianal disease, skin, eyes, joints

Behavior

  • KInflammatory (B1)Most at diagnosis; responds to drugs
  • LStricturing (B2)Pain after meals, vomiting, distention
  • MPenetrating (B3)Abscess or fistula; often with a stricture beyond it

Fistulas and their symptoms

Between bowel andCauses
BladderPneumaturia, fecaluria, repeated UTI
BowelDiarrhea, bacterial overgrowth
SkinDrainage, skin damage, fluid loss
VaginaAir or stool from the vagina
RetroperitoneumPsoas abscess: hip pain on extension

A worse course is likely with

  • Diagnosis under 40
  • Extensive small bowel disease
  • Deep ulcers
  • Perianal disease
  • Stricture or fistula at diagnosis
  • Upper GI disease
  • Smoking

Complications

  • ObstructionInflamed or scarred stricture
  • Abscess and perforationFree perforation is uncommon
  • MalabsorptionB12, iron, vitamin D, zinc; short bowel after resections
  • StonesOxalate kidney stones, gallstones
  • CancerColorectal in colonic disease; small bowel, rare
  • VTEHighest during flares
  • BoneOsteoporosis from inflammation and corticosteroids
  • ExtraintestinalJoints, skin, eyes, bile ducts

Diagnosis

No single test makes the diagnosis: it rests on symptoms, ileocolonoscopy with biopsies, and small bowel imaging together, after infection is excluded.

  1. Calprotectin and bloodsAnd stool tests
  2. IleocolonoscopyBiopsy normal areas too
  3. Small bowel imagingMRE, CT, or ultrasound
  4. Location and behaviorClass and severity
  5. Risk of a poor courseDecides the first drug

Key tests

  • IleocolonoscopySkip lesions, aphthous to deep linear ulcers, cobblestones, strictures
  • BiopsyPatchy chronic inflammation, focal cryptitis, sometimes noncaseating granulomas
  • MREWall thickening, enhancement, engorged vessels (comb sign), strictures, fistulas; no radiation
  • Intestinal ultrasoundWall over 3 mm with increased blood flow; repeatable
  • CTEmergency: abscess, obstruction, perforation

Other tests

  • BloodsFBC, CRP, albumin, ferritin, B12, folate, vitamin D, LFTs
  • Fecal calprotectinHigh with inflammation; can be normal in ileal disease
  • Pelvic MRI and examination under anesthesiaPerianal disease (5)
  • EGDUpper symptoms, and in every child
  • CapsuleIf other tests are normal; patency capsule first, as it can lodge in a stricture
  • ASCAMore often positive, but not diagnostic

How severe

MeasureWhat it captures
Symptom indexesPain, stools, well-being; correlate poorly with ulcers
CRP and calprotectinInflammation between scopes
Endoscopic scoreUlcer size and extent; predicts surgery
ImagingThe wall and beyond

Red flags

  • Fever with a mass
  • Peritonitis
  • Vomiting and distention
  • Perianal pain with fever
  • Weight loss over 10%
  • Growth failure

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Intestinal TBTravel or birth in an endemic area, night sweats, ascites, patulous ileocecal valveBiopsy culture and PCR, chest x-ray, interferon-γ release assay
Infection (Yersinia)Acute onsetStool PCR
AppendicitisMigrating pain over a dayCT
LymphomaMass, night sweatsBiopsy
Behçet diseaseOral and genital ulcers; large round ileocecal ulcersClinical criteria
NSAID enteropathyThin diaphragm stricturesStop NSAIDs
Ulcerative colitisContinuous from the rectum

Find the cause

  • 1Ileal (L1)Ileoscopy and MRE
  • 2Colonic (L2)Colonoscopy with segmental biopsies
  • 3Ileocolonic (L3)Both
  • 4Upper GI (L4)EGD with biopsies
  • 5Perianal (p)Examination, pelvic MRI

Note: Never start a corticosteroid or a TNF inhibitor for ileocecal disease without considering TB and an abscess.

Treatment

Treat early and to a target of healed mucosa without corticosteroids, choosing the first drug by the risk of damage rather than climbing a pyramid.

  1. Stop smoking, nutritionVaccines and screening
  2. InduceAdvanced therapy or a short corticosteroid course
  3. Check the targetSymptoms, CRP, calprotectin, scope
  4. AdjustOptimize or switch
  5. MaintainNever with corticosteroids

Inducing remission

If there isTreat with
Mild ileal or right colon diseaseIleal-release budesonide; 5-ASA is not effective
Moderate to severe diseaseAdvanced therapy early; a corticosteroid only as a bridge
Poor-prognosis featuresTop-down: infliximab with a thiopurine from the start
A child with luminal diseaseEEN, as effective as corticosteroids without harming growth

Advanced therapies

DrugTargetPlace
Infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumabTNFFirst-line; infliximab has the best evidence in fistulas
Risankizumab, guselkumab, mirikizumabIL-23First-line or later; risankizumab beat ustekinumab after TNF inhibitors failed
UstekinumabIL-12 and IL-23Safe; first-line or later
Vedolizumabα4β7 integrinGut-selective; slow; low infection risk
UpadacitinibJAK1Oral, fast; usually after a TNF inhibitor

Older drugs

  • AZA, 6-MPMaintain remission or reduce antibodies to infliximab; not for induction. Check TPMT and NUDT15
  • MTXMaintains; teratogenic
  • CorticosteroidsFlares only
  • CombinationInfliximab with a thiopurine works better than either alone, with more infection and lymphoma

Be careful with

  • Abscess not drained
  • Latent TB or HBV
  • Heart failure (TNF inhibitors)
  • Demyelination (TNF inhibitors)
  • Young EBV-negative men (thiopurines)
  • Pregnancy (MTX, JAK inhibitors)
  • Opioids
  • NSAIDs

Perianal disease

  • NInternal sphincterInvoluntary
  • OExternal sphincterVoluntary; spare it
  • PSimpleLow, single opening
  • QComplexHigh, branching, or with an abscess: drain first
  • RSetonLoop that keeps the tract draining
  • FirstDrain sepsis under anesthesia, place a seton, ABX (metronidazole, ciprofloxacin)
  • ThenInfliximab, ideally at higher drug levels
  • LaterSurgical closure after a TNF inhibitor heals more on MRI than the drug alone
  • RefractoryDiverting stoma; proctectomy

Complications

If there isTreat with
AbscessABX and percutaneous drainage; then advanced therapy or elective resection
Inflamed strictureMedical treatment, bowel rest
Short scarred strictureBalloon dilation if up to 5 cm, reachable, with no fistula
Long or multiple stricturesStricturoplasty or resection, saving bowel
Free perforationEmergency resection, often a stoma
Bile salt diarrheaBile acid sequestrant; low-fat diet if over 100 cm of ileum is lost

After surgery

  • RecurrenceEndoscopic in up to 90% by 1 year at the join; symptoms come later and in fewer
  • RiskSmoking, penetrating disease, previous resection: start a TNF inhibitor within weeks
  • EveryoneColonoscopy at 6–12 months, then treat what it shows
  • Short ileocecal diseaseUnder 40 cm, not strictured, after conventional drugs fail: resection matches infliximab for quality of life, with more drug-free remission at 10 years (LIR!C)

Treat the cause

  • 1Ileal (L1)Budesonide if mild; advanced therapy; B12
  • 2Colonic (L2)Advanced therapy; surveillance from 8 years if a third or more of the colon is involved
  • 3Ileocolonic (L3)Advanced therapy early
  • 4Upper GI (L4)PPI with advanced therapy; dilation
  • 5Perianal (p)Drain, seton, infliximab

Guidelines differ: The ACG and PROFILE favor advanced therapy from diagnosis, while funding rules in many countries still require a corticosteroid or thiopurine first.

Ulcerative Colitis

Pathophysiology

In people with genetic risk, a thin mucus layer and leaky epithelium let gut bacteria reach immune cells, so the mucosa becomes inflamed in one continuous sheet from the rectum upward.

  1. Genes and environmentHLA, stopping smoking
  2. Barrier defectThin mucus, leaky epithelium
  3. Immune responseIL-13, IL-23, TNF
  4. Continuous mucosal inflammationFrom the rectum
  5. Bleeding and diarrheaThen dysplasia over years

What happens in the mucosa

  • ABarrier defectFewer goblet cells, thin mucus, loose junctions
  • BImmune cellsNatural killer T cells release IL-13, which harms the epithelium; Th17 and TNF add to it
  • CCrypt abscessNeutrophils fill the crypts; crypts then branch and shorten
  • DShallow ulcersIslands left between them form pseudopolyps
  • EDilated vesselsFriable, bleeds on touch

How deep it goes

  • FMucosa and submucosaThe muscle and serosa are spared, so no fistulas or strictures; a stricture is cancer until proven otherwise
  • GDysplasiaOxidative damage over years; often flat and multifocal, with early TP53 mutation

Why each feature appears

  • Friable mucosaBlood and mucus
  • Inflamed rectumUrgency, tenesmus, small frequent stools
  • Lost absorption of Na+ and waterDiarrhea
  • Inflammation reaches the muscleNitric oxide paralyzes it → toxic megacolon
  • CytokinesFever, anemia, low albumin, clots

Note: Colectomy removes the target organ, so it ends the colitis, but not liver disease, axial arthritis, or the risk of pouchitis.

Etiology

The cause is unknown, so the disease is classed by extent and by severity, which set the treatment.

By extent and severity

  • 1Proctitis (E1)Rectum only; about a third
  • 2Left-sided colitis (E2)Up to the splenic flexure; about a third
  • 3Extensive colitis (E3)Past the splenic flexure; most colectomy and cancer
  • 4Acute severe colitisAny extent: 6 or more bloody stools a day with systemic toxicity
  • 5Pouch disordersAfter colectomy with IPAA

Who gets it

  • Family historyFirst-degree relative; HLA-DRB1 and other HLA genes
  • SmokingLowers the risk; stopping it can bring on the disease or a flare
  • AppendectomyFor appendicitis in youth lowers the risk
  • Triggers of a flareInfection (C. difficile, CMV), NSAIDs, missed drugs
  • AgePeak at 15–35; a smaller one at 50–70

Note: About a third of people with proctitis extend over years, so reassess extent when symptoms change.

Symptoms and complications

  1. ProctitisBlood, urgency
  2. ColitisBloody diarrhea, cramps
  3. Severe colitisFever, tachycardia, anemia
  4. Megacolon or perforationEmergency

The pattern

  • CardinalBloody diarrhea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, nocturnal stools
  • PainCramps in the LLQ, eased by passing stool
  • Proctitis (1)Blood and urgency, sometimes with constipation above
  • Extensive (3)Weight loss, fever, anemia
  • ExaminationOften normal; tenderness or distention is worrying
  • CorticosteroidsCan hide peritonitis

How severe

LevelPicture
MildFewer than 4 stools a day, little blood, well
Moderate4–6 stools a day, minimal toxicity
Severe (4)6 or more bloody stools a day, with fever, tachycardia, anemia, or a high CRP or ESR
FulminantOver 10 stools, continuous bleeding, distention

Signs of severity

  • Fever over 37.8 °C
  • Heart rate over 90
  • Hemoglobin under 105 g/L
  • High CRP
  • Low albumin
  • Distention
  • Fewer bowel sounds

Toxic megacolon

  • What it isColon over 6 cm on x-ray with systemic toxicity
  • CausesSevere colitis: ulcerative colitis, C. difficile, CMV, less often Crohn disease
  • PrecipitantsOpioids, anticholinergics, loperamide, low K+ or Mg2+, barium enema, colonoscopy
  • DangerPerforation, which greatly increases mortality

Complications

  • HemorrhageUncommon; may need colectomy
  • PerforationWith or without megacolon
  • CRCRises with time, extent, inflammation, PSC, family history
  • VTEHighest in hospital with a flare
  • PSCIn about 5%; more common than in Crohn disease but not exclusive
  • AnemiaBlood loss and inflammation
  • BoneCorticosteroids
  • Mental healthAnxiety, depression, fatigue

Diagnosis

Chronic bloody diarrhea, negative stool tests, and continuous inflammation from the rectum with chronic changes on biopsy make the diagnosis.

  1. Stool testsCulture or PCR, C. difficile
  2. Calprotectin and bloodsFBC, CRP, albumin
  3. Colonoscopy with biopsiesSigmoidoscopy if severe
  4. Extent and severitySet treatment
  5. Liver testsFor PSC

What the scope shows

  • HNormal or healedVessel pattern visible
  • JMildRed, vessel pattern blurred
  • KModerateNo vessel pattern, friable, erosions
  • LSevereUlcers, spontaneous bleeding

Other tests

  • BiopsyCrypt distortion, basal plasma cells, cryptitis, crypt abscesses; no granulomas
  • DistributionContinuous; a cecal patch or backwash ileitis can occur, and treatment can spare the rectum
  • Fecal calprotectinHigh; tracks activity
  • Abdominal x-raySevere disease: dilation, mucosal islands, free gas
  • p-ANCAIn about 60–70%; not diagnostic
  • LFTsHigh ALP: MRCP for PSC

Severe colitis (4)

  • Within 24 hoursStool C. difficile and culture, unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsies, x-ray
  • CMVTissue immunohistochemistry, above all if corticosteroids fail
  • Before rescueHBV, TB screen, Mg2+, cholesterol

Red flags

  • Colon over 6 cm
  • Peritonitis
  • Free gas
  • Hypotension
  • Hemoglobin falling
  • Stricture
  • Dysplasia

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Infectious colitisAcute, fever, contacts; normal cryptsStool PCR and culture, C. difficile
Crohn colitisSkip lesions, perianal disease, granulomas, small bowel diseaseMRE
Ischemic colitisOver 60, sudden, rectum sparedCT, colonoscopy
Radiation proctitisPelvic radiotherapySigmoidoscopy
Sexually transmitted proctitisReceptive anal sex, rectal painSwabs for gonorrhea, chlamydia, herpes, syphilis
Immune checkpoint colitisCancer immunotherapySigmoidoscopy with biopsies
CRCOver 50, change in habitColonoscopy

Find the cause

  • 1Proctitis (E1)Sigmoidoscopy, then one full colonoscopy
  • 2Left-sided colitis (E2)Colonoscopy with segmental biopsies
  • 3Extensive colitis (E3)Colonoscopy; MRCP if LFTs are abnormal
  • 4Acute severe colitisAdmit: C. difficile, sigmoidoscopy, x-ray
  • 5Pouch disordersPouchoscopy with biopsies

Surveillance: Colonoscopy from 8 years after onset in all but proctitis, every 1–5 years by risk, and every year from the diagnosis of PSC.

Treatment

Match the drug to extent and severity, aim for healed mucosa without corticosteroids, and involve surgeons early in severe colitis.

  1. Extent and severityChoose route
  2. Induce5-ASA, corticosteroid, or advanced
  3. Check the targetSymptoms, calprotectin, scope
  4. MaintainNever with corticosteroids
  5. SurveyCancer, bones, vaccines

By severity

If there isTreat with
Mild to moderate proctitis (1)5-ASA suppository; rectal corticosteroid or tacrolimus if it fails
Mild to moderate left-sided (2)5-ASA enema with oral 5-ASA
Mild to moderate extensive (3)Oral with rectal 5-ASA
No responseColonic-release budesonide, then prednisolone
Moderate to severeAdvanced therapy early, not gradual steps after 5-ASA; stop 5-ASA once on it
Acute severe (4)Admit; see below

Advanced therapies

ClassDrugsNote
TNF inhibitorsInfliximab, golimumab, adalimumabInfliximab is the most effective, better with a thiopurine
IntegrinVedolizumabGut-selective; beat adalimumab; first-line
IL-23Risankizumab, guselkumab, mirikizumabSafe; first-line
IL-12 and IL-23UstekinumabSafe; good after TNF inhibitors
JAK inhibitorsUpadacitinib, tofacitinib, filgotinibOral, fast; upadacitinib is among the most effective
S1P modulatorsOzanimod, etrasimodOral; check heart rhythm and eyes

Maintenance

  • 5-ASAAfter 5-ASA induction, long term; may lower cancer risk
  • ThiopurineAfter corticosteroids; not for induction
  • Advanced therapyContinue the drug that worked
  • MTXNot effective in ulcerative colitis
  • CorticosteroidsNot for maintenance

Acute severe colitis (4)

  • AdmitIV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone; do not wait for stool cultures
  • Prevent VTELMWH even with bleeding, unless massive
  • CorrectK+, Mg2+, fluids, feed by mouth; transfuse
  • AvoidOpioids, anticholinergics, loperamide, NSAIDs; no routine ABX
  • Day 3Over 8 stools, or 3–8 with CRP over 45 mg/L, predicts colectomy in 85%
  • RescueInfliximab or cyclosporine, equal in trials; cyclosporine not with low Mg2+ or cholesterol
  • ColectomyPerforation, massive bleeding, megacolon not settling, or failed rescue: subtotal with ileostomy

Toxic megacolon

  • At onceICU, surgeon, nasogastric decompression, IV corticosteroid, broad ABX
  • C. difficileTreat it, and avoid corticosteroids unless colitis coexists
  • No improvement in 24–72 hoursSubtotal colectomy with end ileostomy
  • Perforation or shockColectomy now

Surgery and the pouch

  • Elective colectomyFailed drugs, dysplasia that cannot be resected, cancer
  • IPAATwo or three stages; fertility may fall, so discuss timing
  • Pouchitis (5)Frequency and urgency: ABX; if repeated, probiotics or long-term ABX, then advanced therapy
  • Crohn-like pouch or cuffitisCorticosteroids and advanced therapy; topical 5-ASA for cuffitis

Be careful with

  • JAK inhibitors over 65 or with vascular risk
  • S1P with heart block
  • TB or HBV before biologics
  • Live vaccines on treatment
  • 5-ASA: check creatinine
  • Pregnancy: continue most drugs; stop JAK, S1P, MTX

Treat the cause

  • 1Proctitis (E1)5-ASA suppository
  • 2Left-sided colitis (E2)Rectal and oral 5-ASA
  • 3Extensive colitis (E3)Oral and rectal 5-ASA, or advanced therapy
  • 4Acute severe colitisIV corticosteroid, rescue by day 3–5, colectomy
  • 5Pouch disordersABX; advanced therapy if refractory

Guidelines differ: American labels keep JAK inhibitors for after TNF inhibitors, while European advice limits them by age, smoking, vascular, and cancer risk.
