Small and Large Bowel Obstruction

Pathophysiology

A blockage dilates the bowel above it with gas and fluid and empties the bowel below it, and a loop that loses its blood supply becomes ischemic within hours.

  1. BlockedMechanical or functional
  2. Bowel dilatesGas, fluid, bacteria
  3. Fluid lostVomit and third space
  4. Veins, then arteries closeStrangulation
  5. Necrosis, perforationSepsis

What the blockage does

  • AProximal distentionPeristalsis fights the block → colic and loud, high-pitched sounds; sounds fade later
  • BFluid lossDehydration and low K+; vomiting of gastric juice → metabolic alkalosis
  • CDistal collapseBowel beyond empties → no stool or flatus
  • DStrangulationConstant pain, lactic acidosis, perforation

Kinds of obstruction

  • EPartialSome gas and fluid pass; often settles
  • FCompleteNothing passes; needs closer watching, and contrast may still get through
  • GClosed loopBlocked at both ends, such as a twist, a hernia, or a blocked colon with a competent ileocecal valve; ischemia is early

Why the cecum perforates

  • Widest partWall tension rises with the radius (Laplace)
  • Competent ileocecal valveGas cannot escape back into the ileum
  • DangerRisk climbs above 12 cm, and with time

Note: Vomiting gives alkalosis, but ischemia or severe dehydration turns it into lactic acidosis, so a fall in HCO3− is a warning.

Etiology

Sort by where it is and whether anything blocks the lumen, because surgery is often needed for one and harmful in the other.

Causes

  • Small bowel
  • 1AdhesionsPrevious abdominal surgery; about 60–75% of small bowel obstruction
  • 2HerniaGroin or wall; look in every patient
  • 3TumorMetastases, lymphoma, neuroendocrine tumor, adenocarcinoma
  • 4Inflammatory or radiation strictureCrohn disease, radiation, ischemia
  • 5Contents in the lumenGallstone, bezoar, parasites, foreign body
  • Large bowel
  • 6Colorectal cancerLeft colon most; the leading cause of large bowel obstruction
  • 7Diverticular strictureRepeated inflammation; hard to tell from cancer
  • 8VolvulusSigmoid or cecal twist;
  • Functional (no blockage)
  • 9IleusAfter surgery, sepsis, low K+, opioids
  • 10Acute colonic pseudo-obstructionSick or injured inpatients, spinal surgery, opioids

Look elsewhere for

  • Newborn with bilious vomiting
  • Child with drawing up of the legs
  • Groin lump
  • Gallstone ileus

Symptoms and complications

  1. ColicWaves
  2. VomitingEarly if high
  3. DistentionMarked if low
  4. No stool or flatusLate in partial
  5. Constant painStrangulation

The cardinal four (CAVO)

  • Colicky painCrampy, every few minutes; constant if strangulated
  • Abdominal distentionMore when the block is low
  • VomitingBilious from the small bowel, feculent late; late in colonic obstruction
  • ObstipationNo stool or flatus; some may pass early from below

Small or large bowel

FeatureSmall bowelLarge bowel
CauseAdhesions, herniaCancer, volvulus, diverticular stricture
VomitingEarly, frequentLate
DistentionModerate, centralMarked, with a tympanic rim
PainCramps, periumbilicalLower, longer between waves
DangerStrangulationCecal perforation

Signs of strangulation

  • Constant or worsening pain
  • Fever
  • Tachycardia
  • Localized tenderness
  • Peritonitis
  • High lactate or WBC
  • Acidosis

Complications

  • StrangulationNecrosis and perforation
  • PerforationCecal in large bowel obstruction
  • Dehydration, AKIThird space and vomit
  • AspirationVomiting, NGT helps
  • SepsisTranslocated bacteria
  • ElectrolytesLow K+ and Mg2+
  • Short bowelAfter long resection
  • RecurrenceAdhesions: about a fifth to a third

Diagnosis

CT with IV contrast confirms obstruction, finds the transition point and cause, and shows whether the bowel is ischemic.

  1. ExamineGroins, scars, rectum
  2. Bloods, gasLactate, K+
  3. CTTransition point
  4. Ischemia?Operate
  5. If notContrast challenge

What the films show

  • HSmall bowelLoops over 3 cm, central, lines across the full width, fluid levels, no colonic gas
  • JLarge bowelColon over 6 cm, cecum over 9 cm, lines partway across, no rectal gas
  • KIleusGas in small and large bowel and rectum; no transition point
  • LPerforationGas under the diaphragm on an upright film

CT signs

SignMeans
Transition pointDilated above, collapsed below
Reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric edema, free fluidIschemia
C or U loop, beak, or whirlClosed loop or volvulus
Gas in wall or portal veinNecrosis likely
Pneumobilia and a stoneGallstone ileus
No transition pointIleus or pseudo-obstruction

Other tests

  • BloodsFBC, CRP, lactate, K+, Mg2+, creatinine, gas
  • Water-soluble contrastBy NGT in adhesive obstruction: colon on x-ray by 24 hours predicts it will settle
  • Contrast enemaRarely, for suspected pseudo-obstruction or colon cancer if CT unclear
  • ColonoscopyColon cancer biopsy, or decompression

Red flags

  • Peritonitis
  • Shock
  • Lactate rising
  • Cecum over 12 cm
  • Closed loop
  • Irreducible hernia
  • Immunosuppressed
  • No previous surgery in small bowel obstruction

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
IleusAfter surgery, silent abdomen, no transition pointCT, electrolytes
Mesenteric ischemiaPain out of proportion
Severe constipationStool in rectumExamination, x-ray
GastroenteritisDiarrhea, no distentionStool test
GastroparesisVomiting after meals, normal CT
Toxic megacolonColitis, fever

Find the cause

  • 1AdhesionsCT: no mass, sharp transition; scar
  • 2HerniaExamine groins and wall; CT
  • 3TumorCT, then histology
  • 4Inflammatory or radiation strictureCT or MRE; endoscopy
  • 5Contents in the lumenCT: stone, bezoar, or foreign body
  • 6Colorectal cancerCT, colonoscopy with biopsy, CEA
  • 7Diverticular strictureCT, colonoscopy after recovery
  • 8VolvulusX-ray or CT: coffee bean, whirl
  • 9IleusNo transition point; K+, Mg2+, drugs, sepsis
  • 10Acute colonic pseudo-obstructionCecum and right colon dilated, no block on CT

Treatment

Resuscitate and decompress first, operate at once for ischemia, perforation, or a closed loop, and otherwise give a timed trial without surgery.

  1. Fluids and K+Balanced crystalloid
  2. DecompressNGT, fasting
  3. Ischemia?Operate
  4. Wait, if safeUp to 72 hours
  5. Not settlingOperate

At once

  • FluidHartmann solution, urine output, K+ and Mg2+
  • NGTIf vomiting or distended
  • Pain and vomitingOpioid is fine; avoid metoclopramide in a mechanical block
  • ABXOnly for ischemia, perforation, or surgery
  • VTE preventionLMWH unless surgery is imminent

Adhesions (1)

If there isThen
Peritonitis, strangulation, or ischemiaOperate at once
None of theseFluids and NGT, safe for about 72 hours
Contrast reaches the colon by 24 hoursFeed and go home
Contrast does not reach itLikely to need surgery
72 hours without progressOperate; laparoscopic if selected

Large bowel

If there isTreat with
Perforation or peritonitisResection, often Hartmann procedure
Right-sided cancerRight hemicolectomy, usually with anastomosis
Left-sided cancer, curableResection, anastomosis if safe, or Hartmann; stent as a bridge if discussed, with resection after about 2 weeks
Not curableStent, or stoma
VolvulusSee its page

Ileus and pseudo-obstruction (9, 10)

  • BothStop opioids and anticholinergics, correct K+ and Mg2+, mobilize, treat sepsis, NGT
  • Postoperative ileusChewing gum, early feeding, opioid-sparing analgesia, alvimopan where available
  • Pseudo-obstruction under 12 cmConservative for 24–48 hours
  • Persistent, or over 12 cmNeostigmine with ECG monitoring and atropine ready; then colonoscopic decompression
  • Ischemia or perforationSurgery

Malignant obstruction

  • PalliativeOctreotide, dexamethasone, hyoscine butylbromide, haloperidol; venting gastrostomy
  • Selected patientsSurgery, stent, or bypass

Be careful with

  • Opioids in ileus
  • Metoclopramide in a complete block
  • Neostigmine: bradycardia, asthma, block
  • Barium if perforation possible
  • Waiting in virgin abdomen
  • Stent and bevacizumab: perforation
  • Laxatives

Treat the cause

  • 1AdhesionsTrial, then adhesiolysis
  • 2HerniaReduce or operate; repair
  • 3TumorResect, bypass, or palliate
  • 4Inflammatory or radiation strictureMedical treatment, dilation, resection
  • 5Contents in the lumenRemove stone or bezoar, treat worms
  • 6Colorectal cancerResect; stent in selected cases
  • 7Diverticular strictureResect, as cancer cannot be excluded
  • 8VolvulusDecompress or resect;
  • 9IleusCorrect the cause, wait
  • 10Acute colonic pseudo-obstructionConservative, neostigmine, decompress, surgery

Guidelines differ: Stenting before surgery for left-sided cancer is an option in the ESGE guideline after shared decisions, while others prefer emergency resection because of the risk of perforation and recurrence.

Volvulus and Intussusception

Pathophysiology

A volvulus twists bowel around its mesentery, and an intussusception pulls one segment into the next; both block the lumen and then the blood supply.

  1. Loose or narrow baseOr a lead point
  2. Twists or telescopesLumen closed
  3. Veins close firstEdema, blood
  4. Artery closesIschemia
  5. NecrosisPerforation

How it happens

  • ANarrow baseA long loop on a short, narrow mesentery
  • BTwistGas is trapped as in a closed loop
  • CVeins closeEdema, bleeding into the lumen
  • DArtery closesNecrosis within hours
  • ELead pointTumor, polyp, or swollen Peyer patch is dragged forward by peristalsis
  • FTelescopingMesentery is trapped too

Why each feature appears

  • Closed loopSevere pain and distention
  • Venous blood and mucusRed currant jelly stool, a late sign in children
  • Midgut round the SMAWhole small bowel at risk
  • Reduced by pressureAir pushed from below can unfold a child's bowel

Note: Detorsion treats the twist, not the mobile mesentery, so a sigmoid volvulus recurs in most people without resection.

Etiology

Age and the mobile segment identify the type.

Types

  • 1Sigmoid volvulusOlder, constipated, institutional, neurological or psychiatric disease; Chagas and megacolon
  • 2Cecal volvulusYounger than sigmoid, loose cecum, previous surgery, pregnancy; bascule is a fold, not a twist
  • 3Midgut volvulusMalrotation; mostly the first month of life
  • 4Intussusception in children6–36 months; usually no cause, after a viral illness; lead point over 5 years
  • 5Intussusception in adultsLead point in most: cancer in the colon more often than in the small bowel

Risks

  • Long sigmoidHigh-fiber diet, laxatives
  • Lead pointsMeckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma, IgA vasculitis, cystic fibrosis
  • After surgeryAdhesions, bypass (Petersen hernia)
  • Rotavirus vaccineVery small increase in risk; the benefit is far greater

Symptoms and complications

  1. Sudden colicDistention
  2. VomitingLate in sigmoid
  3. Closed loopConstant pain
  4. Bloody stoolIschemia
  5. ShockPerforation

The pattern

  • Sigmoid (1)Abdominal distention, obstipation, pain, often repeated
  • Cecal (2)Small bowel pattern: colic, vomiting, right or central swelling
  • Midgut (3)Bilious vomiting in a newborn, with a soft or flat abdomen at first
  • Child (4)Attacks of drawing up the legs, pallor, lethargy between them, sausage mass, late bloody stool
  • Adult (5)Vague colic, intermittent, bleeding, weight loss

Classic triad in children

  • Colicky pain
  • Vomiting
  • Bloody, mucoid stool
  • Present together in under half

Signs of ischemia

  • Peritonitis
  • Fever
  • Shock
  • Blood
  • High lactate
  • Free gas

Complications

  • Gangrene and perforationWithin hours
  • Short bowelMidgut (3)
  • RecurrenceSigmoid most; about 10% of intussusceptions after an enema
  • Sepsis and shockLate
  • Missed cancerAdult colonic type
  • AspirationVomiting
  • Compartment syndromeHuge distention
  • DeathHigh in gangrene and late midgut

Diagnosis

Bilious vomiting in a baby is malrotation until proven otherwise; in others, x-ray and CT show the twist, and ultrasound shows intussusception in children.

  1. Age and storyPick the type
  2. Peritonitis?Operate
  3. X-ray or CTUltrasound in child
  4. Confirm viabilityEnhancement, lactate
  5. Reduce or resectBy type

What imaging shows

  • GSigmoid (1)Coffee bean, apex toward the right upper abdomen; CT whirl, beak
  • HCecal (2)Single large loop, left upper or mid abdomen, small bowel dilated
  • JMidgut (3)Upper GI contrast: duodenum in a corkscrew, jejunum right of midline; ultrasound whirl, SMV left of the SMA
  • KIntussusception (4, 5)Target or doughnut across, pseudokidney along

Other tests

  • BloodsFBC, lactate, gas, K+
  • CT (adult)Diagnosis, lead point, ischemia
  • SigmoidoscopyDiagnosis and decompression (1)
  • Enema in childConfirms and treats

Red flags

  • Bilious vomiting in a newborn
  • Peritonitis
  • Shock
  • Free gas
  • Lactate rising
  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Over 48 hours

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Pseudo-obstructionNo twist, sick inpatientCT
Toxic megacolonBloody diarrheaSigmoidoscopy
Pyloric stenosisNonbilious vomiting, 3–6 weeksUltrasound
GastroenteritisDiarrhea, no lethargyStool test
IgA vasculitisRash, jointsUrine, ultrasound
Meckel bleedingPainless bleedScan
Hirschsprung diseaseDelayed meconiumRectal biopsy

Find the cause

  • 1Sigmoid volvulusX-ray or CT; sigmoidoscopy
  • 2Cecal volvulusCT
  • 3Midgut volvulusUpper GI contrast or ultrasound; do not delay surgery if sick
  • 4Intussusception in childrenUltrasound
  • 5Intussusception in adultsCT; colonoscopy if colonic and it resolves

Treatment

Untwist or reduce if the bowel is alive, resect if it is dead, and prevent recurrence in the same admission where possible.

  1. ResuscitateFluids, NGT, ABX if ischemic
  2. Dead or perforated?Operate now
  3. ReduceScope, enema, or Ladd
  4. Resect or fixPrevent recurrence
  5. Follow upCause

By type

If there isTreat with
Sigmoid, no ischemiaFlexible sigmoidoscopy decompression, leave a tube, then sigmoid resection in the same admission
Sigmoid, dead or failedUrgent resection, often Hartmann
Sigmoid with megacolonSubtotal colectomy
CecalRight hemicolectomy; scope decompression is not advised
MidgutUrgent Ladd procedure: untwist, cut bands, widen the mesentery, appendectomy
Child, stableAir or saline enema under imaging
Adult, colonicResect without reduction, as cancer is likely
Adult, small bowel, short, no lead pointMay resolve; watch

Enema reduction (4)

  • WorksIn about 80–90% of children with ileocolic intussusception; never for a midgut volvulus
  • Not ifPeritonitis, shock, or perforation
  • RepeatAfter 30 minutes to a few hours if partly resolved
  • AfterwardWatch for recurrence; most can go home after hours of observation
  • SurgeryFailed enema, lead point, or perforation

Be careful with

  • Enema with peritonitis
  • Delay in bilious vomiting
  • Detorsion without resection
  • ABX before enema: not routine
  • Reducing adult colonic tumor
  • High recurrence in the frail

Treat the cause

  • 1Sigmoid volvulusDecompress, then sigmoid resection; endoscopic fixation if unfit
  • 2Cecal volvulusResect; cecopexy is inferior
  • 3Midgut volvulusLadd procedure
  • 4Intussusception in childrenEnema; surgery if it fails
  • 5Intussusception in adultsResection by cancer rules

Guidelines differ: The WSES advises sigmoid resection as early as possible after decompression, and some surgeons delay it for weeks in frail patients.

Hernias

Pathophysiology

Abdominal contents push through a weak point in the wall, and when the neck is tight they can be trapped and lose their blood supply.

  1. Weak pointCongenital or acquired
  2. PressureCough, strain, obesity
  3. Sac and contentsFat or bowel
  4. Trapped at the neckIncarcerated
  5. Blood lostStrangulated

What can happen

  • AReducibleGoes back lying down or with pressure
  • BIncarceratedStuck; can obstruct
  • CStrangulatedVenous then arterial flow fails; tender, red, obstruction, sepsis
  • DRichterPart of the bowel wall; can die without obstruction

Why each weak point

  • InguinalCord leaves through the deep ring; weaker floor with age
  • FemoralNarrow ring beside the vein, so it strangulates early
  • UmbilicalRing closes slowly in children; stretches in adults
  • IncisionalPoor wound healing, infection, obesity

Note: The neck matters more than the size: a small femoral hernia is riskier than a large wide-necked incisional one.

Etiology

Site names the hernia; look at the groin first, then the wall.

Groin

  • 1Indirect inguinalLateral to the epigastric vessels, through the deep ring; the most common type in both sexes; a patent processus vaginalis in children
  • 2Direct inguinalMedial to the vessels, through the weak floor; older men
  • 3FemoralBelow the ligament, medial to the femoral vein; women over 50

Wall

  • 4Umbilical and paraumbilicalInfants (most close by 4–5 years), adults with obesity, pregnancy, ascites
  • 5EpigastricMidline fat above the navel; often painful
  • 6Incisional and parastomalAfter any incision, within 2 years usually; around a stoma
  • 7RareSpigelian, obturator (thin older women), lumbar, internal, Petersen

Risks

  • Male sex
  • Age
  • Family history
  • Chronic cough
  • Straining
  • Obesity
  • Pregnancy
  • Ascites
  • Smoking
  • Connective tissue disease

Symptoms and complications

  1. BulgeWorse standing, cough
  2. AcheBy evening
  3. ReducibleLying down
  4. StuckPainful, irreducible
  5. StrangulatedEmergency

The pattern

  • Inguinal (1, 2)Lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle; scrotal if indirect
  • Femoral (3)Small lump below and lateral to the tubercle; often presents as obstruction
  • Umbilical (4)Lump at the navel, worse with strain
  • Epigastric (5)Tender nodule of fat in the midline
  • Incisional (6)Wide bulge under a scar
  • Obturator (7)Thigh pain on extension and rotation (Howship-Romberg sign), obstruction, no lump

Signs of strangulation

  • Sudden severe pain
  • Irreducible, tense
  • Red, warm skin
  • Vomiting, obstipation
  • Fever, tachycardia
  • Peritonitis

Complications

  • IncarcerationObstruction
  • StrangulationFemoral most
  • Bowel necrosisResection
  • Chronic groin painAfter repair, about 1 in 10
  • RecurrenceLess with mesh
  • Mesh infectionRare; may need removal
  • Testicular atrophyAfter repair
  • Skin lossLarge umbilical hernia with ascites

Diagnosis

Most hernias are diagnosed by examining the patient standing, and imaging is for the lump that cannot be found or an emergency.

  1. Examine standingCough, then lying
  2. Reduce?Tense or tender
  3. Side and siteLigament and tubercle
  4. ImagingIf unclear
  5. Emergency?Operate

Which groin hernia

Indirect (1)Direct (2)Femoral (3)
Above or below the ligamentAboveAboveBelow
To the epigastric vesselsLateralMedialMedial to the femoral vein
ScrotumOftenRarelyNo
Cough test: pressure at deep ringStops itDoes notDoes not
StrangulatesSometimesRarelyOften
WhoAny age, boysOlder menOlder women

Other tests

  • UltrasoundUnclear groin lump
  • CTObstruction, obese, incisional, obturator
  • MRIGroin pain without lump
  • Lactate, WBCStrangulation

Red flags

  • Irreducible and painful
  • Vomiting
  • Red skin
  • Femoral in any patient
  • Ascites with skin thinning
  • Bowel obstruction without scar

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
HydroceleTransilluminates, get above itUltrasound
VaricoceleBag of worms, leftUltrasound
Undescended testisEmpty scrotumUltrasound
Lymph nodeFixed, infected, below the ligamentUltrasound
Saphena varixDisappears lying, thrill on coughDuplex
Femoral aneurysmPulsatesDuplex
Testicular torsionSudden, high testisSurgery
Rectus diastasisMidline ridge, no ringExamination

Find the cause

  • 1Indirect inguinalExamine, ultrasound if unclear
  • 2Direct inguinalExamine
  • 3FemoralExamine, CT if obstructed
  • 4Umbilical and paraumbilicalExamine; liver disease in adults
  • 5EpigastricExamine, ultrasound
  • 6Incisional and parastomalCT for size
  • 7RareCT

Treatment

Repair symptomatic hernias and all femoral hernias, use mesh in most adults, and operate at once for strangulation.

  1. Emergency?Operate now
  2. OptimizeWeight, smoking, cough
  3. Watch or repairMen with few symptoms
  4. MeshOpen or laparoscopic
  5. RecoverActivity early

Who to repair

If there isThen
Strangulation or obstructionEmergency surgery; no forced reduction if strangulated
Femoral (3)Repair soon, in everyone fit
Inguinal in womenRepair early; check for femoral
Men, few or no symptomsWatchful waiting is safe; about a third have surgery within 3 years and most eventually
Symptomatic inguinalElective repair
Umbilical in childrenWait until 4–5 years, unless large or incarcerated
Infant inguinalRepair early, as incarceration is common

How to repair

  • Inguinal, adultsMesh: open Lichtenstein or laparoscopic (TEP, TAPP); Shouldice if mesh is refused
  • Bilateral or recurrent after openLaparoscopic
  • WomenLaparoscopic, sees the femoral ring
  • FemoralMesh or suture repair
  • Umbilical, epigastricMesh, open preperitoneal; suture is an option under 1 cm, up to 2 cm in some
  • IncisionalMesh with closure of fascia; large ones in a center
  • ChildrenHigh ligation without mesh
  • Contaminated fieldSuture or slowly absorbed mesh

Reducing a stuck hernia

  • Try ifUnder 4–6 hours, no skin change, peritonitis, or sepsis
  • HowAnalgesia, legs up, gentle pressure at the neck
  • AfterObserve; repair soon
  • Never ifSkin red, toxic, or obstruction prolonged; avoid in femoral hernias, where the tight ring can hide dead bowel

After surgery

  • ActivityEarly, as pain allows
  • Pain over 3 monthsExamine, nerve block, specialist
  • RecurrenceUse the other approach

Be careful with

  • Forced reduction
  • Mesh in bowel resection
  • Ascites: treat first
  • Anticoagulants
  • Obesity BMI over 40
  • Smoking

Treat the cause

  • 1Indirect inguinalMesh, or high ligation in children
  • 2Direct inguinalMesh
  • 3FemoralRepair early, femoral mesh or suture
  • 4Umbilical and paraumbilicalMesh if over 1–2 cm; wait in children
  • 5EpigastricSmall: suture; larger: mesh
  • 6Incisional and parastomalMesh and fascia closed; loosen risk factors first
  • 7RareCT then surgery

Guidelines differ: Open and laparoscopic inguinal mesh repair have similar recurrence, and HerniaSurge leaves the choice to the surgeon's skill and the patient's needs.

Polyps and Colorectal Cancer

Pathophysiology

Cells in the crypt gather mutations over about 10 years, pass from polyp to cancer, and spread first to nodes and then to the liver.

  1. Normal cryptInjury, aging
  2. PolypFirst mutation
  3. DysplasiaMore mutations
  4. CancerInvades submucosa
  5. SpreadNodes, liver, lung

Three roads

  • AAdenomaAbout 70–85%: APC lost first, then KRAS, SMAD4, TP53; chromosomal instability
  • BSerratedAbout 15–20%: BRAF, methylation, MLH1 silenced; often right-sided
  • CMismatch repairAbout 3–5%: inherited MMR gene; errors in short repeats (MSI-high)

How deep it is

  • DT1Submucosa; nodes in about 8–15%, less if shallow and well differentiated
  • ET2Muscle
  • FT3Fat around the bowel
  • GT4Surface or another organ

Why it matters which side

  • MRightWide lumen and liquid stool → bleeds → anemia, mass; MSI-high more often
  • NLeftNarrow lumen, formed stool → change in habit, obstruction
  • ORectumBlood, tenesmus, mucus; treated differently

Note: Nodes drain along the vessels, so colon surgery removes the mesentery with the bowel and needs at least 12 nodes to stage.

Etiology

Number by what you find at the scope or in the family, because it sets the follow-up.

Polyp shapes

  • HPedunculatedRemoved whole with a snare
  • JSessileBroad base
  • KFlatEasily missed
  • LLaterally spreadingOver 10 mm; EMR

What it is

  • 1Conventional adenomaTubular, tubulovillous, or villous; risk rises with size over 10 mm, villous form, and high-grade dysplasia
  • 2Serrated lesionsSSLs, traditional serrated adenoma; hyperplastic over 10 mm
  • 3Other polypsHyperplastic (small, left, benign), inflammatory, hamartoma (Peutz-Jeghers, juvenile)
  • 4Sporadic cancerAge over 50, obesity, smoking, alcohol, red and processed meat, inactivity, diabetes
  • 5Lynch syndromeMMR genes; about 3% of cancers
  • 6FAP and other polyposisAPC, MUTYH, STK11; many polyps
  • 7IBD-associated cancerDuration, extent, PSC;

Protective

  • Fiber and whole grains
  • Activity
  • Milk and calcium
  • Aspirin (selected)
  • Polyp removal
  • Healthy weight

Symptoms and complications

  1. SilentYears
  2. Iron deficiencyRight
  3. Blood or habit changeLeft, rectal
  4. ObstructionEmergency
  5. SpreadLiver, lung

The pattern

  • RightAnemia, weight loss, mass
  • LeftAlternating habit, blood, colic
  • RectumBright blood, tenesmus, mucus, narrow stool
  • PolypsUsually none; blood or mucus, low K+ with a large villous adenoma
  • Under 50Rising; delayed because bleeding is blamed on hemorrhoids

Inherited

  • Lynch (5)Cancer under 50, right colon; uterus, ovary, stomach, ureter, small bowel
  • FAP (6)Hundreds of polyps by teens; cancer by 40 if untreated; desmoid, duodenal adenoma, retinal spots
  • MUTYH (6)Recessive; 10–100 polyps
  • Peutz-Jeghers (6)Dark lip spots, hamartomas, intussusception, many cancers
  • Juvenile polyposis (6)Hamartomas; SMAD4 with telangiectasia
  • Serrated polyposis (6)Many serrated lesions

Spread

  • LiverThrough the portal vein; most common
  • LungRectal more, through the inferior veins
  • Peritoneum, ovarySeeded
  • NodesAlong mesenteric vessels

Complications

  • ObstructionAbout 10–15%
  • PerforationAt the tumor or cecum
  • BleedingAnemia
  • FistulaBladder, vagina
  • Liver metastasesSometimes cured by surgery
  • Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditisLook for a colon lesion
  • Ureter obstructionRectosigmoid
  • After surgeryLeak, low anterior resection syndrome, sexual dysfunction

Diagnosis

Colonoscopy with biopsy makes the diagnosis, then CT stages it, and rectal cancer needs an MRI as well.

  1. Symptoms or iFOBTColonoscopy
  2. BiopsyMMR on all
  3. StageCT chest, abdomen, pelvis
  4. RectumMRI
  5. Team meetingPlan

Screening (Australia)

WhoTest
45–74, no symptomsiFOBT every 2 years; 45–49 can ask for the first kit
Positive testColonoscopy
Outside 45–74, or family historyDecide with the doctor; colonoscopy if a strong family history
SymptomsNot screening: investigate

After polyps are removed (Cancer Council Australia)

AdenomasAll under 10 mm, low grade, tubularAll under 10 mm, any high-grade or villousAny 10 mm or more, low grade, tubularAny 10 mm or more, high-grade or villous
1–210 years, or return to screening after 45 years3 years3 years
3–45 years3 years3 years1 year
5–93 years1 year1 year1 year
10 or more1 year1 year1 year1 year

In 1–2 small low-grade adenomas, consider 5 years with metabolic syndrome. Think of a genetic cause with 10 or more.

FindingFirst colonoscopy
1–2 SSLs under 10 mm without dysplasia5 years
1–2 SSLs 10 mm or more, or with dysplasia; 3–4 SSLs under 10 mm; 1–2 traditional serrated3 years
5 or more small SSLs, or 3–4 with a large or dysplastic one1 year
Large sessile, removed in piecesAbout 6 months, then 12
Large sessile, removed wholeAbout 12 months

Staging and markers

  • CTChest, abdomen, pelvis
  • MRI pelvisRectum: depth, mesorectal fascia, vein invasion
  • MRI liver, PETIf metastases may be cut out
  • CEABaseline and follow-up; not for screening
  • MMR or MSIAll cancers: Lynch, immunotherapy
  • RAS, BRAF, HER2Metastatic disease: choose drugs
  • dMMR and BRAFBRAF V600E with MLH1 loss points to sporadic, not Lynch

Red flags

  • Rectal bleeding over 45
  • Iron deficiency
  • Weight loss
  • Change in habit over 6 weeks
  • Mass
  • Obstruction
  • Family under 50

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Diverticular strictureLong, smooth, feverColonoscopy
IBDYoung, diarrhea
Ischemic colitisSudden, olderColonoscopy
HemorrhoidsBright, on paperStill scope if over 45 or alarm
Lymphoma, neuroendocrine tumorSmooth, submucosalBiopsy
EndometriosisWith periodsMRI

Find the cause

  • 1Conventional adenomaHistology: size, villous, dysplasia
  • 2Serrated lesionsHistology
  • 3Other polypsHistology
  • 4Sporadic cancerColonoscopy, biopsy, CT
  • 5Lynch syndromeMMR testing, then germline genes
  • 6FAP and other polyposisOver 10 adenomas, or under 40: gene panel
  • 7IBD-associated cancerColonoscopy with segmental biopsies

Treatment

Remove polyps whole, resect colon cancer with its mesentery, treat rectal cancer in sequence, and use molecular tests to choose drugs.

  1. PolypSnare, EMR, ESD
  2. ColonResect, then chemotherapy if stage III
  3. RectumMRI, neoadjuvant, TME
  4. MetastasesResect if possible
  5. Follow up5 years

Polyps

  • SmallCold snare
  • Large flatEMR; ESD if early cancer is possible
  • Malignant polypSurgery if deep, poor grade, vessel invasion, or margin close
  • TattooIf it may need finding
  • Hyperplastic under 5 mm, rectosigmoidNo follow-up

Colon cancer

StageTreatment
IResect; no chemotherapy
II, low riskResect; ctDNA helps choose chemotherapy
II, high risk (T4, perforation, under 12 nodes)Consider chemotherapy; not if dMMR with fluorouracil alone
IIIResect, then FOLFOX or CAPOX for 3–6 months
IV, resectableResect liver or lung, chemotherapy around it
IV, not resectableChemotherapy with EGFR or VEGF antibody

Rectal cancer

If there isTreat with
Very early (T1, good features)Local excision
EarlyTME
Locally advanced (T3–4 or nodes)TNT, then TME or watch and wait if complete response
dMMRDostarlimab; complete response in most, so surgery is often avoided
Low tumorAbdominoperineal resection if the sphincter is involved

Drugs by marker

If there isTreat with
dMMR, metastaticPembrolizumab, or nivolumab with ipilimumab, first-line
RAS wild-type, left-sidedEGFR antibody with chemotherapy
RAS mutated, or rightBevacizumab with chemotherapy
BRAF V600EEncorafenib with cetuximab
HER2 positiveTrastuzumab-based
PI3K-altered, resectedLow-dose aspirin halved recurrence (ALASCCA)

After cure

  • CEA, CTCEA every 3–6 months, CT yearly, for up to 5 years
  • ColonoscopyAt 1 year, then 5 years if normal, then 5 again
  • Exercise, diet, smokingA 3-year structured exercise program after chemotherapy improved disease-free and overall survival (CHALLENGE)
  • AspirinPI3K-altered only
  • Low anterior syndromeLoperamide, irrigation, pelvic floor work

Inherited

SyndromeDo
Lynch (5)Colonoscopy from 25 (MLH1, MSH2) or 35 (MSH6, PMS2); every 1–2 years in Australia. Discuss hysterectomy; aspirin
FAP (6)Yearly sigmoidoscopy from 10–12; colectomy before cancer; upper scope
MUTYH (6)Colonoscopy every 1–2 years from 18–20; colectomy if many
Peutz-Jeghers (6)Scope from childhood; other cancers
First-degree relativesTest the family

Be careful with

  • Oxaliplatin: neuropathy
  • Capecitabine: hand-foot syndrome
  • Bevacizumab: perforation, bleeding
  • Cetuximab: rash, low Mg2+
  • Irinotecan: diarrhea
  • Immunotherapy: colitis
  • Stopping scope follow-up early

Treat the cause

  • 1Conventional adenomaRemove whole, then surveillance
  • 2Serrated lesionsRemove all but tiny rectosigmoid hyperplastic polyps, then surveillance
  • 3Other polypsRemove if over 5–10 mm
  • 4Sporadic cancerBy stage
  • 5Lynch syndromeResect, with a wider operation discussed; immunotherapy if advanced
  • 6FAP and other polyposisSurveillance and colectomy
  • 7IBD-associated cancerColectomy for cancer or dysplasia that cannot be removed

Guidelines differ: Australia repeats colonoscopy every 1–2 years in all Lynch carriers (eviQ), while the Mallorca guidelines use 2–3 years, and up to 5 for PMS2; the ESGE returns 1–4 small low-risk adenomas to screening.

Constipation

Pathophysiology

Stool moves too slowly, or the pelvic floor does not let it out, and the drier stool left behind is harder to pass.

  1. Slow transit or outletOr drugs, disease
  2. Stool staysWater removed
  3. Hard stoolPainful, straining
  4. WithholdingWorse again
  5. ImpactionOverflow, tears

Where the delay is

  • ANormal transitMarkers gone, yet symptoms persist; often with IBS
  • BSlow transitMarkers spread; few strong contractions
  • COutletMarkers held in the rectum; pelvic floor does not relax

When the pelvic floor fails

  • DNormal pushRectum rises in pressure, muscle relaxes, angle opens
  • EDyssynergiaMuscle tightens, or push is weak
  • FRectoceleRectum bulges into the vagina; stool trapped

Why each feature appears

  • Water taken outHard, pellet stool
  • StrainingHemorrhoids, fissure, prolapse
  • Retained stoolBloating, early fullness, overflow
  • Distended rectumLoss of urge

Note: Slow transit may follow an outlet disorder and improve when it is treated, so test the outlet before the colon.

Etiology

Most is functional; the rest comes from drugs, disease, or a blockage, and these are worth finding.

Causes

  • Primary
  • 1Normal-transit (functional)Low fiber and fluid, inactivity, ignored urge
  • 2Slow-transitPoor colon contractions; young women often
  • 3Defecatory disorderDyssynergia, rectocele, prolapse, anismus
  • Secondary
  • 4Opioid-inducedMu receptors slow the gut; tolerance does not develop
  • 5Other drugsAnticholinergics, iron, calcium blockers, TCA, ondansetron, antipsychotics, GLP-1 agonists
  • 6Metabolic and endocrineHypothyroidism, high calcium, low K+, diabetes, pregnancy
  • 7NeurologicalParkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, Hirschsprung disease
  • 8StructuralCancer, stricture, hernia, stone

Who gets it

  • WomenTwice as often
  • OlderDrugs, immobility
  • PregnancyProgesterone, iron
  • ChildrenWithholding after pain
  • HospitalOpioids, bed

Symptoms and complications

  1. Infrequent or hardUnder 3 a week
  2. StrainingIncomplete
  3. BloatingPain
  4. ImpactionOverflow
  5. Anal diseaseFissure, piles

The pattern

  • Slow transit (2)Little urge, under 3 stools a week, poor response to fiber
  • Outlet (3)Straining, blocked feeling, digital help, sitting long
  • IBS-CPain tied to stool; see its page
  • ImpactionOverflow diarrhea, confusion, urine retention in older people
  • ChildrenPainful stool, soiling

Alarm features

  • Onset over 45–50
  • Blood
  • Weight loss
  • Iron deficiency
  • Family history of CRC or IBD
  • Sudden change
  • Severe pain, vomiting

Complications

  • Fecal impactionElderly, opioids
  • OverflowLooks like diarrhea
  • Stercoral ulcerSigmoid perforation
  • Hemorrhoids and fissureStraining
  • Rectal prolapseStraining
  • Urinary retentionPressure
  • Sigmoid volvulusLong colon
  • Laxative harmLow K+, melanosis coli (harmless)

Diagnosis

History, stool form, drugs, and a rectal examination with simulated push find most causes; tests follow when treatment fails.

  1. HistoryStool form, drugs
  2. Rectal examTone, push, stool
  3. BloodsIf suggested
  4. Alarm?Colonoscopy
  5. FailsManometry, transit

Examination

  • LookFissure, tags, prolapse, descent when straining
  • FeelTone, stool, mass
  • Ask to pushMuscle should relax; it tightens in dyssynergia
  • NervesPerianal feeling, reflex

Tests

If there isObtain
Anyone not settlingFBC, glucose, calcium, TFTs, creatinine
Alarm features or due screeningColonoscopy
Straining, no responseAnorectal manometry with balloon expulsion
Outlet normal, slowMarker or scintigraphic transit study
Suspected prolapse or rectoceleDefecography
OpioidStool chart
Child from birthRectal biopsy for Hirschsprung disease

Reading the tests

  • Balloon50 mL not out in 1–2 minutes (up to 3 in some laboratories): outlet disorder
  • Transit at 5 daysOver 20% of markers left (more than 5 of 24): slow
  • ManometryAnal pressure rises on push, or rectal push weak: dyssynergia

Red flags

  • Obstruction
  • Blood and anemia
  • Sudden onset over 50
  • Saddle numbness, retention
  • Fever
  • Impaction with pain

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
IBS-CPain with stool
ObstructionVomiting, distention
Colon cancerOver 50, blood
HypothyroidismCold, weight gainTFTs
Cauda equinaSaddle numbness, weak legsEmergency MRI
Depression, eating disorderLow intakeAsk

Find the cause

  • 1Normal-transit (functional)History, normal transit
  • 2Slow-transitTransit study, after outlet excluded
  • 3Defecatory disorderExamination, manometry, balloon
  • 4Opioid-inducedDrug history
  • 5Other drugsDrug list
  • 6Metabolic and endocrineCalcium, TFTs, glucose, K+
  • 7NeurologicalNeurological exam, imaging
  • 8StructuralColonoscopy, CT

Treatment

Fix drugs and habits, use fiber if it helps and osmotic laxatives if not, and send the outlet disorder to biofeedback rather than more laxatives.

  1. Habit, drugsSquat, time, move
  2. FiberPsyllium
  3. OsmoticPEG
  4. StimulantBisacodyl, senna
  5. PrescriptionLinaclotide, prucalopride

Steps

StepUsePlace
FiberPsyllium 2 weeks or moreWorse bloating in slow or outlet
OsmoticPEG, lactulose, magnesiumPEG first; magnesium not in kidney disease
StimulantBisacodyl, picosulfate, sennaSafe to use when needed
SecretagogueLinaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostoneAfter PEG
ProkineticPrucalopride (5-HT4 agonist)Slow transit
Suppository or enemaGlycerol, bisacodyl, phosphateOutlet, impaction; phosphate not in elderly with kidney disease

By cause

  • Outlet (3)Pelvic floor biofeedback, best treatment
  • Opioid (4)Osmotic and stimulant from the first dose; then naloxegol, methylnaltrexone, or naldemedine
  • PregnancyFiber, PEG, lactulose
  • ChildrenPEG, disimpact first, treat withholding
  • Cord injuryBowel routine, suppository

Impaction

  • Rectal stoolSuppository or enema, then manual disimpaction with pain relief
  • Higher upPEG by mouth in large amounts if no obstruction
  • AfterRegular laxative
  • Pain, fever, peritonitisCT: stercoral perforation

If still refractory

  • FirstOutlet excluded; combination laxatives tried
  • ThenTransanal irrigation, sacral nerve stimulation in some
  • ColectomyOnly for proven slow transit, no outlet or upper gut disorder, and psychological review
  • UncertainTemporary ileostomy first

Be careful with

  • Magnesium in CKD
  • Phosphate enema: kidney, elderly
  • Bulk laxative in impaction
  • Docusate: weak
  • Secretagogue: diarrhea
  • Opioid antagonists: not in obstruction

Treat the cause

  • 1Normal-transit (functional)Habit, fiber, PEG
  • 2Slow-transitPEG, stimulant, prucalopride; colectomy rarely
  • 3Defecatory disorderBiofeedback; repair large rectocele if trapped stool
  • 4Opioid-inducedLaxative with opioid; peripheral antagonist
  • 5Other drugsChange or reduce
  • 6Metabolic and endocrineTreat the disease
  • 7NeurologicalRoutine, PEG, suppository
  • 8StructuralRemove or bypass; no laxatives if obstructed

Guidelines differ: The AGA and ACG strongly recommend PEG, sodium picosulfate, linaclotide, plecanatide, and prucalopride, and give fiber, senna, and lactulose a weaker recommendation.

Related: Enteric Nervous System

References

  2. Staller K, Neshatian L, Lembo A, Bharucha AE. AGA clinical practice update on evaluation and management of refractory constipation: expert review. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2026;24(2):296–305. PMC12788801

  4. Sizar O, Genova R, Gupta M. Opioid-Induced Constipation. 2023. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK493184
  5. Setya A, Mathew G, Cagir B. Fecal Impaction. 2023. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK448094

Anorectal Conditions

Pathophysiology

Straining, spasm, and blocked glands in the anal canal cause most of these, and the dentate line decides whether they hurt.

  1. Canal above the lineNo pain fibers
  2. Canal belowSkin, very painful
  3. Strain, spasm, gland blockSwell, tear, infect
  4. Bleed, hurt, itchOr bulge
  5. Cancer is rareBut scope

The canal

  • ADentate lineAbove: columnar lining, painless, portal and iliac veins; below: skin, pudendal nerve
  • BInternal sphincterSmooth muscle; spasm feeds a fissure
  • CExternal sphincterVoluntary
  • DCushionsVascular; swell → internal hemorrhoids
  • EBelow the lineExternal hemorrhoid, fissure, very painful
  • FGland in the cryptBlocks → abscess → fistula

How each arises

  • HemorrhoidCushions slip down with strain, pregnancy, aging
  • FissureHard stool tears; spasm cuts blood to the posterior midline
  • AbscessGland blocked, pus tracks along planes
  • FistulaAbscess that drained leaves a tunnel; about a third to a half
  • PilonidalHair driven into the cleft
  • CancerHPV, mostly HPV 16

Note: Painless bright bleeding is usually hemorrhoids, and sharp pain with stool is a fissure, but bleeding over 45 or with alarm features still needs a scope.

Etiology

Name the problem by bleeding, pain, lump, discharge, or itch.

Conditions

  • 1HemorrhoidsInternal above the line, external below; strain, constipation, pregnancy, low fiber
  • 2Anal fissurePosterior midline, most; hard stool, childbirth, spasm
  • 3Anorectal abscessBlocked gland; Crohn disease, diabetes, HIV
  • 4Anal fistulaFollows abscess; Crohn disease, TB, radiation, cancer
  • 5Pilonidal diseaseYoung men, hair, sitting, obesity
  • 6Rectal prolapseOlder women, strain, multiparity, connective tissue
  • 7Fecal incontinenceChildbirth injury, nerve damage, loose stool, surgery
  • 8Pruritus aniSoap, moisture, worms, eczema, hemorrhoids
  • 9Anal cancerHPV, HIV, smoking, receptive anal sex, immunosuppression

Grades of internal hemorrhoid

GradeProlapse
IBleeds, no prolapse
IIOut on straining, back by itself
IIIOut, must be pushed back
IVOut and cannot go back

Fistula types (Parks)

  • MIntersphinctericMost common; between the sphincters
  • NTrans-sphinctericThrough both
  • OSuprasphinctericOver the top
  • PExtrasphinctericOutside; think pelvic disease

Symptoms and complications

  1. BloodBright
  2. PainSharp, or throbbing
  3. LumpProlapse
  4. Pus or itchInfection
  5. ChangeCancer until excluded

What it points to

SymptomPoints to
Bright blood, painlessInternal hemorrhoid
Blood with tearing painFissure
Throbbing pain, feverAbscess
Purulent discharge, recurrentFistula
Sudden hard blue lumpThrombosed external hemorrhoid
Midline pit in the cleftPilonidal disease
Red circular foldsFull-thickness prolapse; radial folds suggest hemorrhoids
LeakageIncontinence
Itch, worse at nightPruritus, threadworm
Ulcer, mass, nodesAnal cancer

Abscess spaces

  • GPerianalRed tender lump at the edge
  • HIschiorectalDeep, fever, buttock swelling
  • JIntersphinctericPain, little to see
  • KSupralevatorPelvic, urinary signs, CT
  • LFistulaCrypt to skin

Complications

  • ThrombosisHemorrhoid: 48–72 hours worst
  • Strangulated hemorrhoidGrade IV, gangrene
  • Chronic fissureSentinel tag, spasm
  • Necrotizing infectionFournier gangrene: pain, crepitus, sepsis
  • Horseshoe abscessBoth sides
  • IncontinenceAfter sphincter surgery
  • RecurrencePilonidal, fistula
  • Anal cancer spreadGroin nodes, liver

Diagnosis

Look, gently part the buttocks, then a finger and anoscope if pain allows; examine under anesthesia if it does not.

  1. HistoryBlood, pain, lump
  2. InspectPart buttocks
  3. Finger, anoscopeIf no severe pain
  4. Alarm?Colonoscopy
  5. Deep or complexMRI, EUA

Examination

  • Posterior midline tearFissure (2); off the midline: Crohn disease, TB, syphilis, HIV, cancer
  • Blue tender lumpThrombosed (1)
  • Opening near the anusFistula (4): Goodsall rule: posterior openings curve to the midline; anterior run straight, unless over 3 cm from the verge
  • Full circle on strainProlapse (6)
  • Groin nodesCancer (9)
  • Too painfulEUA

Tests

If there isObtain
Bleeding over 45, anemia, family history, changeColonoscopy
Deep or recurrent abscess, complex fistulaMRI
IncontinenceManometry, endoanal ultrasound
Ulcer, massBiopsy; MRI, CT, PET
ProlapseColonoscopy, defecography
ItchTape test for threadworm, skin biopsy if lesion
Fissure off midlineEUA and biopsy

Red flags

  • Bleeding over 45
  • Weight loss
  • Mass or ulcer
  • Fever, crepitus
  • Immunosuppressed
  • Nodes
  • Pain out of proportion
  • Off-midline fissure

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
CRCBlood mixed, anemia
IBD proctitisDiarrhea, mucus
STI proctitisDischarge, sex historySwabs: gonorrhea, chlamydia, herpes, syphilis
Perianal Crohn diseaseTags, many fistulas
HidradenitisGroin and armpit tooExamination
CondylomaWartsBiopsy if odd
Rectal varicesCirrhosisEndoscopy
Levator spasmBrief, deep rectal acheNormal exam

Find the cause

  • 1HemorrhoidsAnoscope; grade
  • 2Anal fissureInspection
  • 3Anorectal abscessInspection, MRI if deep
  • 4Anal fistulaEUA, MRI
  • 5Pilonidal diseaseInspection
  • 6Rectal prolapseStraining on toilet
  • 7Fecal incontinenceExamination, manometry, ultrasound
  • 8Pruritus aniSkin look, tape test, patch test
  • 9Anal cancerBiopsy, stage

Treatment

Soft stool is the base for most; drain pus at once, protect the sphincter, and treat cancer with chemoradiation.

  1. Soft stoolFiber, fluid, no strain
  2. Pain reliefSitz bath, topical
  3. ProcedureBand, botulinum, drain
  4. SurgeryIf it fails
  5. Follow upCancer, continence

Hemorrhoids (1)

If there isTreat with
AllFiber, no straining, short toilet time
Grade I–IITopical for under 2 weeks; band ligation if it persists
Grade IIIBand or surgery
Grade IV, or failedHemorrhoidectomy; artery ligation or stapling are alternatives
Thrombosed external, under 72 hoursExcise under local
Thrombosed, laterAnalgesia, settles
Anticoagulant, cirrhosisNo banding on warfarin, a DOAC, or clopidogrel, as the band can bleed at 7–14 days; sclerotherapy or infrared instead

Fissure (2)

  • AcuteFiber, sitz bath, topical lidocaine
  • Chronic (over 6–8 weeks)Topical GTN or diltiazem for 6–8 weeks
  • FailsBotulinum toxin
  • ThenLateral internal sphincterotomy: best healing, small incontinence risk
  • Off midlineLook for a cause

Abscess and fistula (3, 4)

If there isTreat with
AbscessDrain at once; ABX only if cellulitis, sepsis, diabetes, or immunosuppression
Fistula, low and simpleLay open (fistulotomy)
High or complex, or CrohnSeton; then LIFT, flap, or plug
Fournier gangreneEmergency debridement and broad ABX
HorseshoeDrain with counter-incisions

The rest

  • Pilonidal, acute (5)Drain off midline
  • Pilonidal, chronicExcision with off-midline closure or flap; hair removal
  • Prolapse (6)Reduce; rectopexy (abdominal) if fit; perineal (Delorme, Altemeier) if frail
  • Incontinence (7)Loperamide, fiber, biofeedback; then sacral nerve stimulation, sphincter repair
  • Pruritus (8)Keep dry, stop soaps and wipes, short corticosteroid; treat the cause
  • Anal cancer (9)Chemoradiation (fluorouracil with mitomycin); abdominoperineal resection if it persists; HPV vaccine

Be careful with

  • Steroid cream over 2 weeks
  • Sphincterotomy in women and prior injury
  • Banding on anticoagulants
  • Draining too close to the sphincter
  • ABX instead of drainage
  • Missing cancer behind hemorrhoids
  • Biopsy of tags in Crohn

Treat the cause

  • 1HemorrhoidsFiber, banding, surgery
  • 2Anal fissureFiber, diltiazem, botulinum, sphincterotomy
  • 3Anorectal abscessDrain
  • 4Anal fistulaFistulotomy or seton
  • 5Pilonidal diseaseDrain, excise
  • 6Rectal prolapseRectopexy or perineal
  • 7Fecal incontinenceBulk stool, biofeedback, stimulation, repair
  • 8Pruritus aniDry skin, treat cause
  • 9Anal cancerChemoradiation

Guidelines differ: Some surgeons choose sphincterotomy early for fissure because it heals best, while others try creams and botulinum toxin first to protect continence.

Localizing Dysphagia

The question

Difficulty swallowing asks four questions: did the swallow start, did it fail on solids, liquids, or both, is it getting worse, and is there pain or weight loss? The order places the fault in time before it names a cause.

  1. Can they start?Oral and pharyngeal, or esophageal
  2. Solids, liquids, both?Narrow, or weak
  3. How is it changing?Intermittent, steady, or sudden
  4. Alarm?Weight loss, bleeding, age
  5. Then the testEndoscopy or swallow study

Why time comes before place

  • Within the first secondFails to start, coughs, or comes back through the nose: mouth or pharynx
  • After several secondsIt sticks behind the chest: esophagus
  • Where they pointThe throat is often named when the fault is far below, so pointing high does not place it, while pointing low usually does

The mechanism

A swallow is a relay: voluntary muscle hands to a reflex, the reflex opens the upper sphincter, and a wave carries the bolus to the lower one.

The swallow, and where each step fails

  • AOral (under 1 second)Tongue and lips form the bolus; weak: drooling, food left in the cheek, dribbling
  • BPharyngeal (about 1 second)Airway closes and the UES opens; weak: cough, choking, nasal regurgitation, wet voice
  • CUpper esophagusSkeletal muscle and the nucleus ambiguus; weak: myositis, stroke
  • DBody (8–10 seconds)Smooth muscle and enteric nerves; weak: scleroderma, achalasia, spasm
  • ELower sphincterRelaxes as the wave starts; fails: achalasia

Narrow or weak

  • FWide enoughOver about 20 mm rarely causes trouble
  • GSolids onlySometimes at 13–20 mm, nearly always under 13 mm: ring, stricture, web, cancer
  • HSoft food, then liquidsUnder 10 mm: the stricture is tight, or the cancer advanced
  • JBoth from the startNo wave or no relaxation: motility

The pace

  • KIntermittent for yearsRing, web, eosinophilic esophagitis, spasm
  • LSteadily worseCancer in weeks to months; peptic stricture in months to years; achalasia slowly
  • MSuddenFood impaction, pill injury, stroke, caustic

Note: Odynophagia is pain on swallowing and means the mucosa is injured: pill, infection, caustic, or severe reflux.

Discriminators

Each row is a finding that splits two groups, with how far it splits them.

Mouth and throat, or chest

If there isPoints toward
Hesitation, repeated tries to startOral or pharyngeal
Cough or choking within a secondPharyngeal; silent in some
Nasal regurgitation, slurred or nasal voicePharyngeal, neuromuscular
Sticks seconds after swallowingEsophageal
Pressure at the sternum with painEsophageal spasm or heart
Food comes back undigested hours laterZenker diverticulum or achalasia
Constant lump, no trouble with foodGlobus
Worse with liquids than solids, with coughNeurological (pharyngeal)

Pairs that are confused

PairThe finding that splits them
Cancer or peptic strictureMonths of weight loss, age over 50 → cancer; years of heartburn → stricture
Ring or eosinophilic esophagitisYoung, atopy, impactions → eosinophilic
Achalasia or cancerBoth need a scope; achalasia has years, a widened esophagus, and pseudoachalasia from a tumor must be excluded
Achalasia or sclerodermaTight sphincter → achalasia; reflux with open sphincter, Raynaud → scleroderma
Spasm or heart painExertion → heart first, always
Myasthenia or strokeWorse through the meal, ptosis by evening → myasthenia; sudden → stroke
Zenker or pharyngeal weaknessBulge on barium swallow, gurgling, halitosis → Zenker
Infectious or pill esophagitisImmunosuppression, thrush → infectious; tablet with little water, day after → pill

Signs far from the swallow

If there isThink of
Ptosis, weakness that tiresMyasthenia: Myasthenia
Tongue wasting and twitchingALS: ALS
Tremor, slow movementParkinson disease: Parkinson disease
Facial weakness, suddenStroke: Stroke by location
Raynaud, tight skin, telangiectasiaScleroderma
Smooth tongue, spoon nails, iron deficiencyPlummer-Vinson web, and cancer risk
ThrushCandida, HIV, inhaled corticosteroid
Virchow node, hoarsenessCancer; nerve involved
Rash, proximal weaknessMyositis

Differentials

What else it could be, and why it is missed: not a swallow problem, a patient who adapts, or a test that looks normal.

Not the esophagus, or not swallowing

If there isConsiderObtain
Chest pain after food with exertionCoronary diseaseECG, troponin
Fever, neck pain, drooling, stridorEpiglottitis, deep neck infectionAirway first; CT
Pain and fever after vomiting or a scopeEsophageal perforationCT with contrast, surgeon
Cannot swallow salivaComplete food impactionUrgent endoscopy
Sudden with facial droopStrokeCT; nil by mouth until tested
Lump constant, between mealsGlobusThroat look; reassurance
Mass in the neck, long historyThyroid goiter, aorta (dysphagia lusoria or aortica)CT
Dry mouthAnticholinergic drugs, Sjögren syndromeDrug list; antibodies

Who hides it

WhoWhat is lostSo
Slow eatersThey chew, cut, drink, and avoid: ask about time at mealsWeigh them
Stroke, dementiaCough reflex, so silent aspirationBedside test; VFSS or FEES
Older adultsFood trouble blamed on teeth or ageScope if over 50 and new
ChildrenRefuses food, slow growth, pneumoniaEosinophilic esophagitis; foreign body, button battery
Opioid usersSpasm looks like motility diseaseStop before manometry

Reassurance that misleads

  • A normal EGDDoes not exclude motility disease or eosinophilic esophagitis, so take biopsies
  • A normal bariumCan miss a ring; ask for a tablet or marshmallow
  • Pointing to the throatThe lower end is often felt there
  • No coughSilent aspiration is common after stroke
  • ImprovingThey have changed to soft food
  • HeartburnBoth achalasia and cancer can have it
  • No weight lossEarly cancer, or ring

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The throat that was not

  1. A 61-year-old says food sticks in the throat, for four months

    What it changes

    The throat is where it is felt, not where it fails. Distal obstruction is often felt at the neck, because the upper and lower esophagus share nerves. Asking what happens in the first second is the next step.

  2. Swallowing starts normally; meat sticks, and soup goes down

    What it changes

    A normal start argues against the mouth and the pharynx, so this is esophageal. Solids alone means narrowing rather than weakness. The question is now what is narrowing it, and whether it is cancer.

  3. It was bread at first, then rice, and now mashed food

    What it changes

    The trouble is climbing down the scale, so the lumen is shrinking steadily. Rings and eosinophilic esophagitis come and go, and do not progress like this. Steady worsening over months at this age is cancer until shown otherwise.

  4. They had heartburn for 20 years but not for the last one

    What it changes

    Heartburn raises the thought of a peptic stricture, which also fits. But heartburn that stops can mean that Barrett mucosa has replaced the sensitive lining, or a tumor has narrowed the outlet. It is not a reassuring clue.

  5. EGD shows a tumor at the junction

    What it changes

    The throat was a poor guide, and the tempo was a good one. A drop in heartburn and a climb from bread to mashed food are worth asking for in everyone. holds the staging.

Case 2: The meal that gets harder

  1. A 34-year-old chokes on drinks, and it is worse by dessert

    What it changes

    Choking within a second of swallowing places the fault in the mouth or pharynx. Liquids worse than solids is the neuromuscular pattern, because thin fluid needs a fast, coordinated closure of the airway. A narrow lumen would have done the opposite.

  2. The voice becomes nasal as they speak for longer

    What it changes

    The palate is failing, so air escapes through the nose. It gets worse with use rather than being fixed, and that points to a fatigable junction rather than a lesion that stays the same. A stroke would not improve and worsen through a conversation.

  3. Eyelids droop by evening and recover after sleep

    What it changes

    Fatigable ptosis with bulbar weakness is myasthenia gravis until shown otherwise. The diagnosis came from asking about the eyes, which have nothing to do with the throat. The esophagus was never the problem, so an EGD would have been the wrong test.

  4. They cannot count to 20 in one breath

    What it changes

    This is now a breathing emergency, not a swallowing problem. Bulbar weakness with a failing breath count can become respiratory failure within hours, and saturation stays normal until late. Vital capacity, close watch, and no food by mouth come first.

  5. Antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor return positive

    What it changes

    The lesson is that timing within a meal, and signs elsewhere, place a fault that no endoscope can see. Myasthenia owns the treatment.

Case 3: Solids and liquids together

  1. A 72-year-old has had trouble with both water and food from the first week

    What it changes

    Both at once means no propulsion or no relaxation, rather than a narrow tube. A narrowing would have spared liquids at first. Achalasia, spasm, and scleroderma lead, and cancer is still possible if it infiltrates the nerves.

  2. They regurgitate undigested food at night and wake coughing

    What it changes

    Food is stored above a sphincter that does not open, which fits achalasia. It comes back unmixed with acid, unlike reflux. Nighttime cough is a warning of aspiration, so they should sleep propped up, and the chest should be examined.

  3. Barium shows a smooth, tapered, beak-like end

    What it changes

    The beak is the lower sphincter failing to relax, with a dilated esophagus above. The same picture can be made by a tumor at the junction, called pseudoachalasia. That is why a scope is done even when the film looks classic.

  4. They have lost 12 kg in five months

    What it changes

    Short history, marked weight loss, and older age are the triad for pseudoachalasia. A long history and slow weight loss would have pointed to the real one. The first clue was correct about the mechanism, but this clue changes the diagnosis.

  5. Endoscopy with ultrasound shows a submucosal mass

    What it changes

    The test that separates the two is a careful look at the cardia, sometimes with CT or ultrasound, before any myotomy. Dilating or cutting a tumor delays its treatment. owns achalasia, and the cancer page the rest.

Where it leads

Protect the airway, decide mouth or chest, and choose one test that splits the leading two.

  1. Airway safe?No food if choking
  2. Impacted?Endoscopy now
  3. Mouth or chest?VFSS or FEES, or EGD
  4. BiopsyEven if normal
  5. Then manometryIf EGD is clear

Which test first

If there isObtain
Trouble starting, cough, nasal regurgitationVFSS or FEES, after a neurological examination
Solids only, over 50 or with alarmEGD
Solids only, young, impactionEGD with biopsies from two levels
Both from the startEGD, then manometry
Old radiation, stricture, Zenker suspectedBarium first
Complete impactionEGD within hours; no barium

Localizing Jaundice

The question

Jaundice asks one question in three places: where has a bilirubin molecule been stopped? It is made in red-cell breakdown, joined in the liver, and carried out in bile, and the patient shows which step failed.

  1. Is it jaundice?Sclera, not just skin
  2. Where is it stopped?Prehepatic, hepatic, or posthepatic
  3. Urine and stoolRead the color
  4. Painful or painless?And how fast
  5. Then numbers and imagesSplit the leading two

Why follow the molecule

  • One pathEvery cause lies on it, so one question covers them all
  • The patient carries the evidenceUrine, stool, and itch tell before any test returns
  • The number is only a levelBilirubin is seen in the eye at about 40–50 µmol/L, so early jaundice is missed in skin

The mechanism

Bilirubin is made from heme, joined to sugar in the liver so that it dissolves, passed into bile, and colored by bacteria in the gut.

Four stops

  • 1Prehepatic: too much madeHemolysis, large hematoma, ineffective red-cell making: unconjugated, bound to albumin
  • 2Hepatic, conjugation: not joinedGilbert, Crigler-Najjar, drugs, newborns: unconjugated
  • 3Hepatic, excretion: joined but not passed outHepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, Dubin-Johnson, sepsis: conjugated, often both
  • 4Posthepatic: duct blockedStone, stricture, tumor: conjugated, with high ALP and itch

What colors the urine and stool

  • APrehepatic: too much bilirubin made (1)Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and cannot enter urine, so urine is normal; more pigment reaches the gut, so stool is dark
  • BHepatic: liver cells injured (3)Conjugated bilirubin leaks back into blood and then urine; some still reaches the gut, so stool is normal to pale
  • CPosthepatic: bile duct blocked (4)Bile backs up and none reaches the gut: dark urine, clay-colored stool, itch
If there isPoints toward
Normal urine and stoolPrehepatic, or failed conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome (2), which happens in the liver but leaves urine normal
Dark urine, normal or slightly pale stoolHepatic
Dark urine, clay stool, itchPosthepatic, or cholestasis within the liver
Bilirubin on urine dipstickConjugated rise, often before the eye is yellow
More urobilinogen in urineHemolysis, or a liver that cannot clear it
No urobilinogenComplete obstruction
Pale, greasy stool that floatsSteatorrhea: too few bile salts
Red urine, dipstick negative for bilirubinHemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis

How age changes the odds

  • DFirst dayAlways abnormal: hemolysis, infection
  • EFirst 2 weeksPhysiological or breast milk, if well and unconjugated
  • FOver 2 weeks with pale stoolBiliary atresia: conjugated at any age in infancy needs same-week review
  • GChildHepatitis A, hemolysis, Wilson disease
  • HYoung adultViral, drugs, Gilbert, alcohol
  • JMiddle ageStones, alcohol, autoimmune, PBC, hemochromatosis
  • KOlderCancer, stones, drugs, heart failure

Note: Conjugated bilirubin can bind to albumin for days, so the number may lag behind a duct that has already been opened.

Discriminators

These findings split groups before the blood tests return, and some split them better than the numbers.

What else it could be, and why it is missed: not jaundice, a patient who hides it, or a number that reassures.

Reassurance that misleads

  • A normal duct on ultrasoundEarly obstruction may not have dilated it, and a stiff liver cannot dilate
  • No stone on ultrasoundMisses many duct stones; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound
  • Normal ALTCirrhosis can be normal
  • GilbertCan be present with another disease; never assume after age 40
  • Improving enzymes with falling ALTMay mean a liver with no cells left, if INR rises
  • Normal hemoglobinDoes not exclude hemolysis; check haptoglobin, LDH, reticulocytes
  • A painless gallbladderCancer, not reassurance
  • Alcohol as the answerCancer and gallstones happen to drinkers too

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: Painless and itchy

  1. A 66-year-old has been itching for a month, and now notices yellow eyes

    What it changes

    Itch before jaundice points to bile salts building up, so the block is hepatic or posthepatic. Jaundice without pain in an older adult makes cancer the first thing to exclude. A stone usually hurts, so its absence matters.

  2. Urine is dark and stool is clay-colored

    What it changes

    Dark urine means the bilirubin is conjugated, and clay stool means none is reaching the gut. Together they make it posthepatic, in a duct that is close to completely blocked. That also makes a hepatitis very unlikely.

  3. A smooth, nontender mass is felt under the right ribs

    What it changes

    A palpable and painless gallbladder with jaundice suggests a block below the cystic duct that has been slow (Courvoisier). Stones scar the gallbladder so it does not distend. A tumor in the head of the pancreas, the ampulla, or the lower duct is now most likely.

  4. ALP is 620 U/L (30–120), bilirubin 240 µmol/L (2–17), ALT 88 U/L (4–36)

    What it changes

    The pattern is cholestatic, and the high bilirubin with only modest ALT fits. INR is also high in many with this, and it corrects with vitamin K because the liver is well but bile salts are missing. These numbers agree with the bedside and do not add to it.

  5. CT shows a mass in the head of the pancreas and a dilated duct

    What it changes

    The bedside placed the block before the scan did, and the scan chose the cause. Fever or pain would have turned the same story into a drainage emergency. and share the rest.

Case 2: Yellow with normal urine

  1. A 22-year-old is yellow in the eyes on the second day of a stomach upset

    What it changes

    Yellow eyes with a gut illness make hepatitis the first thought. But many things raise bilirubin in someone who has not eaten. The urine and stool decide before any blood test.

  2. Urine is pale and stool is brown

    What it changes

    Pale urine means there is no conjugated bilirubin in it, so the rise is unconjugated. Dark urine would have meant hepatitis or a duct. The stop is therefore at or before conjugation, which leaves hemolysis and Gilbert syndrome in someone this well.

  3. They feel fine between illnesses, and a brother had the same

    What it changes

    Recurrence with fasting and illness, in a well person with family, is Gilbert syndrome. The enzyme is slow, so the level rises when the liver has less fuel. It is harmless, but the pattern must be confirmed once.

  4. Hemoglobin 148 g/L (130–170), reticulocytes 1.2% (0.5–2), haptoglobin normal

    What it changes

    Hemolysis is excluded by normal reticulocytes and haptoglobin, so the red cells are not being lost. If it were hemolysis, reticulocytes would be up. The numbers make the bedside answer safe.

  5. LFTs are otherwise normal, and bilirubin is 52 µmol/L (2–17), mostly unconjugated

    What it changes

    No treatment is needed, but it is worth telling them that some drugs (irinotecan, atazanavir) raise it more. The trap was the illness, which suggested hepatitis. reads the numbers for other patterns.

Case 3: Yellow, hot, and confused

  1. An 81-year-old was found confused; the family say the eyes looked yellow

    What it changes

    Confusion in an older adult is the sign, and jaundice is the direction. Ask whether the brain is affected by infection, by ammonia, or by low pressure. All of them can come from the bile duct at this age.

  2. Temperature 36.1 °C, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg

    What it changes

    No fever does not exclude sepsis in an older adult, and a low temperature can be worse. Low pressure with jaundice means cholangitis until proven otherwise. It is the second half of Reynolds pentad, which asks for drainage rather than only antibiotics.

  3. WBC is 21 × 10⁹/L (4–11), bilirubin 110 µmol/L (2–17), ALP 480 U/L (30–120)

    What it changes

    Cholestatic with a high white count fits a blocked, infected duct. Lactate and cultures come before antibiotics but must not delay them. The pain was missing from the start, so Charcot triad was not complete and never should have been required.

  4. Ultrasound shows a dilated duct; no stone is seen

    What it changes

    Dilated without a visible stone is common, because ultrasound misses the lower duct. A stone or stricture is still the likely cause. Absence on ultrasound must not stop the drainage decision when the patient is septic.

  5. INR is 2.1 (0.9–1.1) and ERCP drains pus

    What it changes

    Pus under pressure explains both the confusion and the pressure, and drainage treats both. A high INR corrects with vitamin K and plasma so that it does not delay. owns the drainage steps.

Where it leads

Look for sepsis and liver failure first, then let the bedside place the stop, and let one image choose the cause.

  1. Septic or confused?Cultures, ABX, drain
  2. INR and mindLiver failure?
  3. Split the bilirubinAnd LFTs
  4. UltrasoundDuct size
  5. One next stepCT, MRCP, or serology

Localizing Nausea and Vomiting

The question

Nausea and vomiting ask which of four inputs is firing, what came up, and when, and only then whether the gut is at fault at all.

  1. Is it vomiting?Not regurgitation or rumination
  2. Which input?Gut, blood, ear, or brain
  3. What came up?Bile, food, feculent, blood
  4. When?With meals, morning, episodes
  5. What has it done?Fluid, acid, potassium

Why input comes first

  • One exit, four doorsThe act is the same, so the act does not place the cause
  • Each door has companyVestibular brings vertigo; the trigger zone brings a drug or a toxin
  • Treatment follows the doorThe antiemetic is chosen by input, not by diagnosis

The mechanism

The medulla gathers signals from four places and sends one program: breath held, glottis closed, abdomen squeezed, stomach emptied. Only the place differs.

Four inputs

  • AGut (vagus)Stretch, inflammation, poison: serotonin from enterochromaffin cells on 5-HT3
  • BChemoreceptor trigger zoneOutside the blood-brain barrier: drugs, uremia, DKA, opioids, hormones (dopamine, 5-HT3, NK1)
  • CVestibularMotion, inner ear: histamine and acetylcholine, M1-AChR
  • DCortexPain, fear, smell, increased ICP, meningitis

The center and its receptors are on Emetic Center.

What came up

  • EUndigested foodEsophagus, or Zenker; not from the stomach
  • FFood, no bile, sourGastric outlet: projectile in infants
  • GBileBelow the ampulla; in a newborn, volvulus until shown otherwise
  • HBrown, foulDistal small bowel or colon obstruction, rarely a gastrocolic fistula
  • JBlood or coffee groundsA bleed above the ligament of Treitz

When after eating

  • KMinutesRumination, eating disorder; food is recognized and not bitter
  • L1–6 hoursPreformed toxin; then virus
  • MOver 12 hoursGastroparesis, outlet; food eaten 6–12 hours or more before
  • NOn wakingPregnancy, uremia, alcohol, increased ICP

What it costs

  • Acid lostMetabolic alkalosis, low Cl−
  • Potassium lostFrom the kidney as aldosterone rises, more than in vomit
  • Volume lostThirst, tachycardia, AKI
  • Alkalosis replaced by acidosisSomething worse is adding acid: DKA, sepsis, ischemia
  • Vitamin B1Wernicke encephalopathy if prolonged
  • TearMallory-Weiss, Boerhaave

Note: Vomiting with headache and a slow pulse is increased ICP until shown otherwise, and it may come without any nausea.

Discriminators

Each row splits the inputs or the mimics of each other.

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The stomach bug

  1. A 19-year-old has vomited for two days; the flatmate had gastroenteritis

    What it changes

    A contact makes a virus likely, and most are. But the story of a contact is the story that everyone tells, and it should not stop the search. Ask what does not fit: the absence of diarrhea, or something that comes first.

  2. There is no diarrhea, and they are very thirsty

    What it changes

    Viral gastroenteritis nearly always brings loose stool. Thirst out of proportion to vomiting means water is being lost another way, such as by sugar in the urine. The missing diarrhea was the first clue.

  3. They are breathing deeply and fast, with a soft abdomen

    What it changes

    Deep and fast breathing is the body blowing off acid. In vomiting you would expect alkalosis, so this is not simple vomiting. A metabolic acid is being added, and ketones are the first suspect.

  4. Glucose 31 mmol/L (4–7.8), ketones 6.2 mmol/L (under 0.6), pH 7.12 (7.35–7.45)

    What it changes

    This is diabetic ketoacidosis, and the vomiting is the chemoreceptor trigger zone responding to it. The abdominal pain of DKA can look like appendicitis and settles with treatment. The virus was real, and may have started it.

  5. Na+ is 128 mmol/L (135–145) and K+ is 5.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)

    What it changes

    K+ is high in the blood but low in the body, because insulin lack moves it out of cells and urine loses it. Giving insulin alone would drop it dangerously, so it is watched from the start. The lesson is that vomiting with fast breathing is not the gut until acid is excluded.

Case 2: Relief in the shower

  1. A 28-year-old has come in for the fifth time this year with two days of vomiting

    What it changes

    The repeating, stereotyped story is itself a clue. Between attacks they are well, which argues against obstruction or cancer. Cyclic vomiting, migraine, cannabinoid hyperemesis, and porphyria all fit.

  2. They take several hot showers a day while it lasts

    What it changes

    Compulsive hot bathing is not specific, but it is the best-known sign of cannabinoid hyperemesis, and it is asked about too rarely. It may also be seen in cyclic vomiting. What settles it is what happens when cannabis stops.

  3. They have used cannabis daily for seven years, and say it settles the nausea

    What it changes

    Cannabis relieves nausea at low doses and drives it with long heavy use, so the belief is real and delays the truth. Explain this without blame. Opioids make it worse, and ordinary antiemetics often fail.

  4. K+ 2.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.0), HCO3− 34 mmol/L (22–28), pain 7 of 10

    What it changes

    Low K+ and alkalosis are the result of vomiting, not the cause. Severe pain alone should not be explained by cannabinoid, so pancreatitis, obstruction, and biliary disease are excluded first. The tests are for the cost, and to make sure.

  5. They stop cannabis, and have no attack over the next year

    What it changes

    Attacks come weeks or months apart, so a short gap proves little. Freedom over 6–12 months, or at least three of the usual cycles, confirms it, and a return with use confirms it again. Capsaicin cream or haloperidol may help the attack, and the plan is to stop. No other page covers it; covers the other episodic vomiting.

Case 3: Before breakfast

  1. A 37-year-old has vomited on waking for three weeks

    What it changes

    Morning vomiting has a short list: pregnancy, uremia, alcohol, and increased ICP. Pregnancy comes first because it is common, quick to test, and changes every drug. Ask also whether there is nausea with it.

  2. β-hCG is negative, and creatinine is normal

    What it changes

    Pregnancy and uremia fall away, and alcohol is unlikely from the story. That leaves the head. Vomiting from pressure is worst on waking because lying down raises pressure through the night.

  3. There is little nausea, and a dull headache that is worse on bending

    What it changes

    Vomiting without nausea is projectile and central, and a headache that changes with posture is pressure. Migraine would throb and not worsen lying. The combination moves the list to a mass, hydrocephalus, or venous clot.

  4. Papilledema is seen on both sides

    What it changes

    Swollen discs mean increased pressure for long enough to matter. Lumbar puncture before imaging could be dangerous, so the order is CT or MRI first. Vision must be checked, since it is the first thing lost.

  5. MRI shows a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus

    What it changes

    The gut was never involved, and an endoscopy would have wasted time. The order of questions, pregnancy then pressure, protected both patients this story could have been. Hydrocephalus and Adult brain tumors own the rest.

Where it leads

Replace what is lost, match the antiemetic to the input, and test only what splits the leading two.

  1. β-hCG, glucose, ECGIf either fits
  2. Fluid, K+And thiamine if prolonged
  3. Obstruction?Image, decompress
  4. Antiemetic by inputBelow
  5. Look againCause found?

Gut (A)Ondansetron or metoclopramideMetoclopramide in obstruction
Trigger zone (B)Ondansetron, droperidol, prochlorperazine; add dexamethasone or an NK1 blocker in chemotherapyLong QT
Vestibular (C)Antihistamine (cyclizine, promethazine) or hyoscine, brieflyLong use, which slows recovery
Cortex (D)Treat the pressure, pain, or fearSedation that hides change
PregnancyDoxylamine with pyridoxine; metoclopramideUnless needed, others
CannabinoidHaloperidol or droperidol, capsaicin cream; stop cannabisOpioids

In emergency departments, trials found little benefit over placebo for most single drugs, so fluids and the cause matter more; a newer network analysis puts prochlorperazine among the most effective and oral ondansetron among the least. Drug details are on Motility pharmacology.
