Reading Abdominal Imaging

The question

Reading an image asks four questions: is it the right patient, part, and phase; what should be here; what is in the wrong place; and what is missing? A sign is nearly always one ordinary substance somewhere it should not be.

  1. Right study?Name, date, contrast, phase
  2. One fixed orderEvery time, same path
  3. Wrong place?Gas, fluid, calcium
  4. Missing?Enhancement, fat plane, organ
  5. Does it fit?The patient and the story

A fixed order for CT

  • Lung bases and heart
  • Free gas
  • Liver, gallbladder, ducts
  • Spleen, pancreas, adrenals
  • Kidneys, ureters, bladder
  • Aorta, SMA, veins
  • Bowel from rectum to stomach
  • Appendix
  • Mesentery and nodes
  • Pelvis
  • Bones and wall

Why order beats looking

  • The eye stops at the first findingThe second finding is the one that is missed, so finish the list
  • The brain sees what was askedRead before reading the request, then again after
  • Old films are a testChange over time outranks any single look

The mechanism

CT measures density, x-ray adds it up along a line, ultrasound draws edges that reflect, and MRI shows water and fat. Each is blind where it has nothing to measure.

The CT grey scale

  • AGasAbout −1000 HU
  • BFatAbout −100 HU; grey streaks in it (stranding) mean inflammation
  • CWater0 HU: simple fluid, cyst, bile
  • DSoft tissue30–60 HU
  • EFresh blood50–80 HU; older blood falls toward water
  • FCalcium, contrast, metalOver 130 HU

When the contrast arrives

  • GNoneStones, calcium, fresh blood, air
  • HArterial (about 35 s)Aorta, active bleeding, liver cancer blush
  • JPortal venous (about 70 s)The usual abdominal study: liver, bowel wall, veins
  • KDelayed (minutes)Urinary leak, fibrous tumor, washout

What each test cannot see

TestGood atBlind to
X-rayFree gas, dilated bowel, some calciumFluid-filled bowel, early ischemia, most stones in the gallbladder
UltrasoundGallbladder, ducts, free fluid, aorta, young appendixAnything behind gas or fat; retroperitoneum; operator
CTAlmost everything acuteSmall duct stones, cholesterol gallstones, mucosa, early pancreatitis
MRI and MRCPDucts, liver lesions, pelvis, bowel in the youngTime, motion, metal, calcium
HIDAGallbladder that does not fillStructure

Note: Contrast belongs in the question: ask for CT angiography when the question is a vessel, because a portal venous study may miss an artery.

Discriminators

Each row of films compares a normal look with the same substance in the wrong place.

Gas

  • LNormalInside bowel only
  • MFree gasFront of the liver when lying; upright x-ray under the diaphragm. CT is more sensitive than x-ray
  • NIn the bile ductsCentral branches, follows bile outward: after sphincterotomy, surgery, or a fistula
  • OIn the portal veinReaches the edge, follows blood inward: ischemia until shown otherwise

The bowel wall

  • PNormalUnder 3 mm when distended
  • QWhite (enhances a lot)Inflammation or a vessel problem; check both
  • RTarget (water halo)Edema: IBD, infection, ischemia, radiation; fat in the middle layer is long-standing IBD
  • SGas in the wallLinear with sick patient → ischemia; cystic bubbles in a well one → often benign

Fluid

  • TWaterAscites, urine, bile
  • UBloodBrighter; brightest clot lies next to the source (sentinel clot)
  • VAbscessRim enhances, often gas inside, days after the illness
  • WFree fluid on ultrasoundBlack strip in the hepatorenal space; in blunt trauma a positive scan has LR 18.5 for injury and a negative one 0.27

Solid organs

  • XLiver cancerBright arterial, then washout, in a cirrhotic liver
  • YHemangiomaEdge nodules that fill toward the center
  • ZPancreatic necrosisPart does not enhance; best judged after 72 hours or more
  • AAStoneBright dot in a dilated duct, though many stones do not show

Pairs that are confused

PairThe finding that splits them
Pneumobilia or portal venous gasCentral → bile; edge of the liver → portal
Small or large bowelFull-width folds and central → small; partial folds and frame → large
Ileus or obstructionA transition point → obstruction
Ascites or bloodDensity, and a sentinel clot
Cyst or solidEnhancement after contrast: over 20 HU change → solid
Chilaiditi or free gasBowel folds between the liver and the diaphragm → Chilaiditi
Diverticulitis or cancerLong segment with stranding → diverticulitis; short with shoulders and nodes → cancer
Appendix or notFollow from the cecum to its blind end; over 6 mm with fat stranding

Differentials

One sign with several causes, normal variants that look bad, and scans that look normal and are not.

One sign, several causes

SignCausesWhat sorts them
Gas in the wallIschemia, chemotherapy, corticosteroids, after endoscopy, COPD, benign cystsPain, lactate, portal gas, wall enhancement
Fat strandingAppendix, diverticulum, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, ischemia, epiploic appendagitisWhere it is worst
Target signIBD, infection, ischemia, radiation, intussusceptionLength, vessel, history
Double-duct signCancer of the head or ampulla, stone, chronic pancreatitisMass, calcification
Portal venous gasIschemia; also after procedures, diverticulitis, gastric ileusThe patient
Wall of the gallbladder thickCholecystitis, heart failure, cirrhosis, low albuminTenderness, stone, fever
Free gasPerforation; after surgery for days; after peritoneal dialysis or endoscopyStory and tenderness
Free fluid, young womanOvulation, cyst rupture, ectopicβ-hCG

Looks bad, is normal

  • Colon between liver and diaphragmChilaiditi
  • Tongue of liver to the pelvisRiedel lobe
  • Fluid beside the hilum of a kidneyExtrarenal pelvis
  • Accessory spleenRound, near the hilum, enhances like the spleen
  • Unopacified bowelLooks like a mass; check the next slice
  • Retroperitoneal vein anomalyFollow it
  • Mesenteric lymph nodes in a childOften normal

A normal scan does not exclude

If there isConsiderObtain
Pain out of proportion, normal plain CTMesenteric ischemiaCT angiogram
Fever and jaundice, no duct stoneCholangitisMRCP, EUS, ERCP
Pain, normal CT on day 1Early appendicitis, early pancreatitisExamine again; repeat
Trauma, negative ultrasoundInjury (sensitivity 74%)CT if stable
Bleeding, normal CTBleeding slower than CT can showRepeat when bleeding; angiography
Weight loss, normal CTMucosal cancer

Who makes it hard

WhoWhySo
ObesityUltrasound is poorCT
Slim, little fatPlanes lie togetherContrast, MRI
After surgeryAnatomy moved; gas expectedRead the operation note
PregnancyOrgans pushed upUltrasound, then MRI
Metal or motionArtifactOther views

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The finding that was first

  1. A 67-year-old has left lower abdominal pain, and CT shows diverticulitis

    What it changes

    The first finding fits the story, so the eye wants to stop. This is satisfaction of search, the most common reason a second finding is missed. Finish the list before accepting the diagnosis.

  2. The lung bases are clear, the aorta is normal

    What it changes

    Working down the fixed order finds nothing here, which is expected, and is still a finding. The kidneys and the pancreas come next. Only after the whole list is the first finding safe.

  3. The sigmoid wall is thick for 4 cm with overhanging edges

    What it changes

    Diverticulitis usually involves a longer, smoother segment with fat stranding. A short, shouldered segment is a tumor’s shape. The first diagnosis has become a question.

  4. There are three enlarged mesenteric nodes and a 1 cm liver lesion

    What it changes

    Nodes may be reactive, but a liver lesion with a short thick segment is a pattern for metastatic cancer. The request said diverticulitis, and the reader who read only the request would have missed it.

  5. Colonoscopy after recovery shows a cancer

    What it changes

    The lesson is that the first finding changes nothing about the rest of the list. and share the two mimics.

Case 2: Gas in the wrong branch

  1. An 80-year-old has abdominal pain and gas in the liver on CT

    What it changes

    Gas in the liver is either in the bile ducts or the portal vein, and they mean opposite things. The first is often from an old sphincterotomy, and the second is ischemia until shown otherwise. Where it sits is the whole question.

  2. The branches reach to within a centimeter of the capsule

    What it changes

    Bile flows toward the hilum, so gas in ducts stays central. Portal blood flows toward the edge, so gas in the veins reaches the periphery. These branches are peripheral, so this is portal venous gas.

  3. The small bowel wall is thin and does not enhance in one segment

    What it changes

    Thin and unenhanced wall means blood is not arriving, unlike the thick bright wall of colitis. It supports infarction. Gas in the wall may also be present, and if so it is linear rather than cystic.

  4. Lactate is 6.4 mmol/L (under 2), and the pulse is irregular

    What it changes

    The picture now has a source, an unenhanced segment, and a lactate that suggests necrosis. This is mesenteric infarction, and waiting for another study would only delay. Surgery and vascular teams are called now.

  5. The past notes say ERCP four years ago

    What it changes

    An old sphincterotomy would have explained central gas, and it explains none of this. The history and the branch agreed only by chance, and the branch was the stronger evidence. owns the plan.

Case 3: The scan that looked normal

  1. A 73-year-old with fever, confusion, and jaundice has a normal CT

    What it changes

    Fever, confusion, and jaundice are cholangitis until shown otherwise, and CT is not the test that excludes it. Many duct stones do not show on CT, because they are close to bile in density. The scan has answered a question that was not asked.

  2. The bile duct measures 9 mm, and the gallbladder has been removed

    What it changes

    After cholecystectomy a duct of up to about 10 mm can be normal, so 9 mm neither proves nor excludes it. A stone may be there. Looking again at the same scan cannot add information, only another test can.

  3. Ultrasound shows no stone and the lower duct is hidden by gas

    What it changes

    Ultrasound misses most stones in the lower duct for this reason. Two studies that cannot see the place have not shown that the place is clear. The absence of evidence here is worth little.

  4. MRCP shows two stones and the patient is now hypotensive

    What it changes

    MRCP sees water, so a stone is a hole in it. It answered the question that CT could not. With low pressure, drainage matters more than another picture, and ERCP is arranged at once.

  5. ERCP drains pus, and the fever settles

    What it changes

    The lesson is to know what each test is blind to before using its silence as evidence. owns the plan.

Where it leads

Ask the question first, then pick the test that can see the answer and that this patient can have.

  1. Pregnant? Kidney? Allergy?Before the request
  2. One questionWritten on the request
  3. Right phaseArtery, vein, delayed
  4. Read it in orderThen compare
  5. Call the findingIf it changes the hour

Reading Endoscopy

The question

Reading a scope asks four questions: did it reach, what is the lesion's shape, how is it spread, and what must the biopsy answer? The eye names a pattern, and the biopsy names a disease.

  1. Did it reach?Cecum, ileum, second part
  2. Was it clean?Preparation, time, views
  3. Flat, protruding, or hollow?And the edge
  4. Where, and how spread?Continuous, patchy, one
  5. What must the biopsy say?Decide before taking it

Why the report matters more than the picture

  • A normal report has a depthHow far, how clean, how long, how many biopsies
  • A lesion has three wordsSite, shape, surface
  • A scope sees one layerAnything below the mucosa shows only as a bulge

The mechanism

A scope shows the surface and its vessels, by color, texture, and outline, and nothing below. What it can see depends on how far it goes and how clean the surface is.

How far each reaches

  • AEGDEsophagus to the second part of the duodenum
  • BEnteroscopyPush: first jejunum; balloon: much more, and can treat
  • CCapsuleAll the small bowel, but takes no biopsy, and can lodge in a stricture
  • DColonoscopyRectum to cecum, and the last ileum
  • ESigmoidoscopyRectum to the splenic flexure, little preparation
  • FERCP and EUSERCP treats ducts; EUS sees the wall, pancreas, and small stones, and takes needle samples

Why the mucosa changes color

  • Vessels visibleNormal: thin, clear lining
  • No vessels, redEdema hides them: inflammation
  • PaleThin mucosa with vessels in view: atrophy; or no flow
  • Purple or blackIschemia
  • Salmon in the esophagusColumnar lining: Barrett
  • White plaquesCandida, pseudomembrane, or eosinophils
  • BrownPigment: melanosis

What a scope does not see

Blind spotWhySo
Below the mucosaIntact lining covers a tumorEUS, CT
Behind folds and flexuresThe scope looks forwardSlow withdrawal, look back, cap
Small bowelToo farCapsule, MRE
Dirty wallStool hides flat lesionsWash or repeat
Microscopic diseaseLooks normalBiopsy normal mucosa
What movesMotilityManometry

Note: Adenomas were missed in about 26% at tandem colonoscopy, and upper cancers in about 11% in the 3 years before diagnosis, so a clean report has limits.

Discriminators

Each row compares a normal look with the same area in disease, and then the biopsy question that settles it.

Esophagus

  • GNormalPale and smooth
  • HRefluxBreaks at the lower end; grade by how far they join
  • JEosinophilicRings, furrows, white spots; can look normal: biopsy at two levels
  • KCandidaWhite, scrapes off to raw; brush or biopsy
  • LHSVMany small shallow; biopsy the edge
  • MCMVFew large deep; biopsy the base
  • NBarrettSalmon tongue; biopsy for intestinal metaplasia
  • OVaricesBlue columns; do not biopsy

Stomach and duodenum

  • PBenign ulcerSmooth, flat edge, folds reach it; still biopsy the edge
  • QMalignant ulcerIrregular heaped edge, folds stop or fuse
  • RWatermelon (GAVE)Red stripes; not portal gastropathy, which is mosaic
  • SCeliacFewer, scalloped folds, mosaic; or normal

Colon

  • TUlcerative colitisContinuous from the rectum
  • UCrohn diseasePatches, deep ulcers, ileum, rectum often spared
  • VPseudomembranesYellow plaques: C. difficile, or ischemia
  • WIschemicSharp edge, one segment, rectum spared
  • XAdenomaRemove whole; ridged surface
  • YSerratedFlat and pale with mucus: easy to miss
  • ZEarly cancerDip, irregular, does not lift: do not pull, refer
  • AAMelanosisLaxative pigment; harmless, and lesions stand out pale

Pairs that are confused

PairThe finding that splits them
Ulcerative colitis or Crohn diseaseRectum and continuous → ulcerative; skip, ileum, granuloma → Crohn
Ulcerative colitis or infectionChronic changes on biopsy → ulcerative
Ischemic or infectious colitisSegment with a sharp edge, rectum spared → ischemic
HSV or CMVSmall many, edge → HSV; large few, base → CMV
Benign or malignant ulcerEdge and folds, but six or more biopsies decide
Adenoma or hyperplasticColor, size, and place; left-sided under 5 mm → usually hyperplastic
GAVE or portal gastropathyStripes at the antrum → GAVE; mosaic in the upper stomach → portal
Varices or gastric foldsBlue, compressible, along the cardia → varices

Differentials

One look with several causes, artifacts that look like disease, and normal scopes that are not.

  • Suction marksRound red spots, fresh, with no history
  • Bowel preparationAphthous spots after sodium phosphate
  • NSAID or enema effectsFocal ulcers; treated rectum can look spared
  • Biopsy ulcersRound, at the place just sampled
  • MelanosisBrown after laxatives
  • Lymphoid nodulesNormal in the last ileum of the young

A normal scope does not exclude

If there isConsiderObtain

DysphagiaEosinophilic esophagitis, motilityAt least 6 biopsies; manometry

Who makes it hard

WhoWhySo
Incomplete to cecumRight cancers missedRepeat, CT colonography
Poor preparationFlat lesions hiddenSplit doses, repeat

Worked cases

These are illustrative. Say what each clue changes before you open it.

Case 1: The normal colon

  1. A 68-year-old has had watery diarrhea for five months; colonoscopy to the cecum is normal

    What it changes

    The colon looks normal, but many causes of chronic diarrhea do not change its surface. A report that says normal without biopsies answers only half the question. Ask whether any were taken.

  2. They take an NSAID and a PPI, and wake at night to pass stool

    What it changes

    Nighttime stool argues against IBS. NSAIDs and PPIs are linked with microscopic colitis, and older women are most often affected. The pattern of patient fits a disease that can only be found under the microscope.

  3. No biopsies were taken

    What it changes

    This is the missed step. ESGE advises two biopsies from the right colon and two from the left when microscopic colitis is suspected, in separate pots, because the right is often worse. Repeating the scope for samples is needed, and sigmoidoscopy can be enough if the left is affected.

  4. Biopsies show a thickened collagen band

    What it changes

    The mucosa looked normal because the surface was intact, and the change lies below it. Collagenous colitis is the answer. It also shows why a biopsy of normal tissue is never wasted in diarrhea.

  5. Celiac serology is positive as well

    What it changes

    Microscopic colitis and celiac disease travel together, so both are treated. The lesson is that an endoscopic diagnosis and a histological one are different tests. and share the rest.

Case 2: The benign ulcer

  1. A 59-year-old has a 1.5 cm gastric ulcer with smooth edges, and biopsy is benign

    What it changes

    Smooth edges and benign biopsies are reassuring and are not proof. A few ulcers that look benign prove malignant, so a gastric ulcer is not finished at the first scope. A duodenal ulcer would be different, because it is almost never cancer.

  2. H. pylori is found and treated; pain goes away

    What it changes

    Symptoms and healing are two different things. A cancer can be covered by a benign slough and even improve on a PPI. The plan for repeat endoscopy should be made the day the ulcer is found.

  3. Six biopsies were taken, all from the base

    What it changes

    Cancer lies at the edge, where the base can be dead slough. Six or more samples are needed, from the edge and including all four quarters. A negative set from the base is close to no test at all.

  4. At 8 weeks, the ulcer is smaller but not gone

    What it changes

    A benign ulcer should have healed by eight to twelve weeks with treatment, and a small remainder is a red flag. Take new samples from the rim. Delay beyond this is how early cancer becomes late.

  5. The new biopsies show adenocarcinoma

    What it changes

    The first scope told the truth about the base and nothing about the edge. The lesson is that where samples come from is part of the result. owns staging.

Case 3: The spared rectum

  1. A 24-year-old has bloody diarrhea; the colon is inflamed from sigmoid to hepatic flexure, but the rectum is normal

    What it changes

    Rectal sparing is the sign that separates Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis, so Crohn moves ahead. But sparing has other causes, and the sign depends on the rectum being untouched. Ask what has been put into it.

  2. They have used 5-ASA enemas for a month

    What it changes

    Enemas treat the rectum and can heal it completely, which makes it look spared. The sign has been made by treatment. It has no value until we know how the rectum looked before.

  3. The inflammation is continuous, with no skip areas

    What it changes

    Continuous inflammation from the sigmoid is the usual form of ulcerative colitis, in spite of the rectum. Crohn would leave normal patches. The distribution is stronger evidence than the rectum now.

  4. Biopsies show crypt abscesses and no granulomas; the ileum is normal

    What it changes

    No granuloma does not exclude Crohn, because only up to a third show them. A normal ileum argues against, but not fully. Taken together, they now favor ulcerative colitis.

  5. An old sigmoidoscopy shows an inflamed rectum two months ago

    What it changes

    The picture before treatment settled it. Distribution is only evidence when nothing has changed it, and the lesson is to ask what has been given before reading a pattern. owns the next step.

Where it leads

Choose the scope that reaches the question, and decide what the biopsy must prove before it begins.

  1. Is it safe?Perforation, toxic colon, airway
  2. Which scope?Reach and purpose
  3. PrepareSplit doses, drugs
  4. Biopsy planNumber and place
  5. Then read it againWith the pathologist

Autoimmune Hepatitis

Pathophysiology

In a person with the right genes, a trigger breaks tolerance to hepatocytes, so T cells and plasma cells attack the edge of the portal tract and, untreated, scar the liver.

  1. GenesHLA-DRB1; women 3 or 4 to 1
  2. TriggerVirus, drug, or unknown
  3. Tolerance lostT cells, weak regulatory cells
  4. Interface hepatitisHigh ALT, high IgG
  5. FibrosisCirrhosis in a third at diagnosis

What the biopsy shows

  • APortal infiltrateLymphocytes and plasma cells
  • BInterface hepatitisThe limiting plate is eroded
  • CEmperipolesisA lymphocyte within a hepatocyte
  • DRosettesRegenerating hepatocytes around a space
  • EBridging necrosisScar from tract to tract

Why it looks as it does

  • High IgGActivated B cells make antibodies to self
  • Other autoimmunityThyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis
  • Fatigue and joint painCytokines
  • Sudden liver failureMassive necrosis with little IgG

Etiology

  • Classic
  • 1Type 1ANA and ASMA; any age, most adults; anti-SLA marks a severe course
  • 2Type 2Anti-LKM1 or anti-LC1; children and young women; often more severe
  • Variants
  • 3Drug-inducedMinocycline, nitrofurantoin, infliximab, statins, checkpoint inhibitors
  • 4OverlapWith PBC (AMA, high ALP) or PSC (duct beading)

Triggers and associations

  • HAV or EBV infection
  • Nitrofurantoin
  • Anti-TNF
  • Herbal products
  • Pregnancy: flare after birth
  • Hashimoto thyroiditis
  • Type 1 diabetes
  • Celiac disease

Note: a quarter are found by chance, and a third already have cirrhosis.

Symptoms and complications

Natural history

  1. Silent or fatigueMonths to years
  2. Acute hepatitisJaundice, ALT over 500
  3. Remission on treatmentMost
  4. RelapseAfter stopping, in most
  5. CirrhosisIf untreated

Ways it presents

  • InsidiousFatigue, itch, arthralgia, amenorrhea, acne
  • AcuteLike viral hepatitis
  • Acute severeINR 1.5 or more, little IgG, antibodies can be negative
  • CirrhosisFound late; ascites or varices
  • Postpartum flareFirst 3–6 months

Associated disease

  • Thyroid disease
  • Type 1 diabetes
  • Celiac disease
  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Vitiligo
  • Sjögren syndrome

Signs of severity

  • INR 1.5 or more
  • Encephalopathy
  • Bilirubin rising on corticosteroid
  • Ascites
  • MELD over 20

Complications

  • Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
  • Acute liver failure
  • HCCWith cirrhosis
  • Corticosteroid harmDiabetes, bone, infection
  • Azathioprine harmMarrow, pancreatitis, skin cancer
  • RecurrenceAfter transplant, 20–30%

Diagnosis

Autoantibodies, high IgG, and a compatible biopsy together make the diagnosis once viral, drug, and other causes are excluded, because each alone also occurs in other liver diseases.

  1. ExcludeViruses, drugs, Wilson disease, alcohol
  2. IgG and antibodiesANA, ASMA, LKM1, SLA
  3. BiopsyNearly always, before treatment
  4. ScoreSimplified score: 6 probable, 7 definite
  5. TPMTBefore azathioprine

Simplified diagnostic score

The International Autoimmune Hepatitis Group's 2008 score has four items of up to 2 points each: 6 is probable and 7 or 8 definite.

FeaturePoints
ANA or ASMA 1:40 or more1
ANA or ASMA 1:80, or LKM1 1:40, or SLA positive2
IgG above normal1
IgG over 1.1 times normal2
Compatible histology1
Typical histology2
No viral hepatitis2

Count only the highest antibody and IgG result. It misses acute severe disease, where antibodies and IgG can be normal.

Other tests

  • ALT and AST200 to over 1000; ALP near normal
  • Antibody negativeRepeat, and test SLA, LC1, and atypical pANCA
  • Duct pictureMRCP in children, or with bowel disease or high ALP
  • FibrosisElastography, once inflammation settles
  • BaselineBone density, HBV, HBsAg, vaccines

Red flags

  • INR 1.5 or more
  • Confusion
  • Bilirubin over 300 µmol/L
  • Not better at 7–14 days

Mimics

ForFavored byObtain
Viral hepatitisExposureSerology, PCR
Drug-induced injuryNew drug; resolves off itHistory, time
PBCItch, high ALP, AMAAMA, IgM
PSCUlcerative colitis, beadingMRCP
Wilson diseaseYoung, hemolysisCeruloplasmin, 24-hour copper
MASLDLow-titer ANA, metabolic riskBiopsy if unsure
SLE hepatitisRash, low complementAnti-dsDNA

Find the cause

  • 1Type 1ANA, ASMA, anti-SLA, IgG
  • 2Type 2Anti-LKM1 and anti-LC1
  • 3Drug-inducedDrug list, then watch off it; relapse is rare if truly drug-induced
  • 4OverlapAMA and ALP; MRCP and colon history

Treatment

Corticosteroid brings it under control, azathioprine keeps it there for years, and normal ALT with normal IgG is the target.

  1. ConfirmBiopsy, TPMT, HBV
  2. InducePrednisolone or budesonide
  3. MaintainAzathioprine
  4. TargetNormal ALT and IgG by 6 months
  5. WatchRelapse, drug harm, HCC

Induction

If there isTreat with
MostPrednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg, then taper; add azathioprine after 2 weeks
No cirrhosis, mildBudesonide 9 mg a day, with azathioprine
Acute severeHigh-dose IV corticosteroid, at a transplant center; stop if not better at 7 days
Jaundice or cirrhosisNot budesonide
Mild, elderly, no fibrosisCan watch

Maintenance

  • Azathioprine1–2 mg/kg; TPMT first; FBC often
  • Not toleratedMycophenolate (never in pregnancy), or tacrolimus
  • No responseCheck diagnosis and adherence; tacrolimus, or rituximab
  • DurationAt least 2–3 years, with 2 years of remission; many need it for life
  • Before stoppingNormal ALT and IgG; biopsy in some
  • RelapseMost in the first year: restart and keep

Protect

  • Vaccines before
  • Bone density, calcium, vitamin D
  • HBV prophylaxis if anti-HBc
  • Skin checks
  • Eye and glucose checks
  • Pregnancy: continue azathioprine

Transplant

  • WhoAcute liver failure, or MELD over 15 with decompensation
  • ResultAbout 80% alive at 5 years
  • Returns20–30%: watch

Treat the cause

  • 1Type 1Corticosteroid and azathioprine
  • 2Type 2The same; children need more and longer
  • 3Drug-inducedStop the drug; corticosteroid if severe or not settling, then taper off
  • 4OverlapAdd ursodeoxycholic acid for PBC; treat the PSC as usual

Guidelines differ: EASL 2025 accepts budesonide first in early, non-cirrhotic disease, and others reserve it for corticosteroid harm.
